case_summary.text: TPO can’t ignore certificates issued by third-party vendors of AE confirming price charged from assessee: ITAT
Transfer pricing provisions couldn’t be applied if CA certificate of US co. verified that it wasn’t an AE of Indian Co.

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had imported raw materials from third party vendors under an agreed arrangement claiming that said transaction was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rate charged by assessee-company was lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors but TPO rejected said certificates as same were signed by vendors which were also AEs of assessee, since certificates issued by third party vendors whereby, they confirmed that price they had charged to assessee-company was lower than original price, could not be ignored by holding that these certificates were issued by AEs, matter required remission to Assessing Officer/TPO to examine benchmarking analysis furnished by assessee

TRANSFER PRACING : Even when assessee was eligible for tax exemption at rate of hundred percent under section 10A/10B, then also arm's length price on its international transactions deserved to be determined under section 92C
No TP adjustment of Import if proportion of certification of import value was high for transaction with AE
Auditor's certificate can't be a substitute for TP study to benchmark international transaction

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had imported raw materials from third party vendors under an agreed arrangement claiming that said transaction was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rate charged to assessee-company was lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors, TPO could not have rejected said certificates on basis that same were signed by vendors which were also AEs of assessee
Reference made by AO to seek info. from TPO wouldn’t fall under scope of Sec. 92CA(2B)/(2C): HC
AO can't test genuineness of transaction under Chapter X of transfer pricing : Ahmedabad ITAT

IT/ILT : Export of commodities to AE at the same price at which those were purchased from local market did not call for transfer pricing adjustment if transaction was made by assessee to retain the status of Star Export House
No TP adjustment if assessee provided certificates from third parties certifying discounts available on import: ITAT

IT/ILT: Export of commodities to AE at same price at which those were purchased from local market did not call for transfer pricing adjustment if transaction was made by assessee to retain status of Star Export House

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee claimed that transaction of import of raw materials from third parties was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rates charged to assessee-company were lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors, since by certificate issued by third party vendors, they confirmed that discount of 10 per cent to 20 per cent had been given to assessee on raw materials and price they had charged to assessee-company was lower than original price, said certificates could not be ignored and matter required remission to Assessing Officer/TPO to examine above benchmarking analysis furnished by assessee
ITAT deletes TP adjustment as average price of certain transactions with AEs matched with actual transaction price
TRANSFER PRICING : Order passed by TPO under section 92CA(3) even before issuance of notice under section 143(2) is without jurisdiction

TRANSFER PRICING : Where as per section 92CA read with section 153, due date to pass order under section 92CA for relevant A.Y. was 29-1-2014 and 29-1-2015 but order under section 92CA(5) had been passed on 30-1-2014 and 30-1-2015, it was beyond limitation period, and, therefore, had to be quashed

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had carried out its transfer pricing study in accordance with section 92C and no specific defect with such TP study had been pointed out by any of departmental authorities, it could not be said that such TP study was not prepared in good faith or due diligence and in terms of Explanation 7 to section 271(1)(c), no penalty would be leviable upon assessee
No penalty if assessee got TP study done by an outside expert
TP adjustment on IGS payments to AE deleted as charges accepted at arm's length under sec. 92C: ITAT
TRANSFER PRICING : Under section 92CA(3A) read with section 153, TPO is required to pass order within period of 60 days prior to date of completion of assessment as per section 153
TRANSFER PRICING : Internal TNMM cannot be rejected as MAM merely because segmental audit report refers to "information and explanation provided to us(auditor)"
IT/ILT: Transfer pricing computation is also to be made even for years in which assessee is entitled to section 10A exemption

IT/ILT : In relation to a specified domestic transaction, TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C . Sub-section (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with aid of any interpretive process, said provision cannot be applied to empower TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by Assessing Officer under sub-section (1).

TRANSFER PRICING : Statutory Form 3CEB is a report of Chartered Accountant furnished under section 92E relating to international transactions and specific domestic transactions based on documents prescribed and maintained by assessee in respect of international transactions and Chartered Accountant report is based on Audited books of account maintained by assessee were international transaction have been incorporated and are authenticated therefore, report of CA cannot be ruled out and also factual position has to be considered to correct any mistake in calculating of ALP for valuation
TRANSFER PRICING : Segmental results cannot be rejected on ground that same are not audited, TPO/DRP are required to examine same if same were maintained in ordinary course of business
TRANSFER PRICING : High Court issued notice to revenue in respect of penalty order under section 271AA in case of assessee
TRANSFER PRICING : Availability of unaudited accounts could not be any reason to reject a company which satisfies all filters

TRANSFER PRICING : Basic requirement of provision for filing documents under section 92D read with rule 10D is to enable department for determination of ALP and when Assessing Officer has referred matter to TPO ultimately, all documents would have to be examined by TPO and therefore, non-filing of such documents before Assessing Officer is a mere technical hitch which will not cause any prejudice to revenue

TRANSFER PRICING: In view of Explanation to sub-section (2) of section 92C, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in extending benefit of second proviso to section 92C(2) to assessee in respect of assessment year 2009-10

TRANSFER PRICING : Prior to amendment in section 92CA by Finance Act, 2022 with effect from 1-4-2022, order of TPO under section 92CA was not subject to revision under section 263 by PCIT and, therefore, order passed by PCIT under section 263 for assessment year 2013-14 was not sustainable in law and, hence, was to be quashed

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee has proved that price charged or paid in an international transaction was computed in accordance with provisions of section 92C and in manner prescribed under that section in good faith and with due diligence and also assessee-company furnished all required details called for from time to time, and had disclosed all material facts before TPO then, a deeming fiction under Explanation 7 to section 271(1)(c) cannot apply
TRANSFER PRICING : Period of 60 days stipulated for passing an order under section 92CA(3) is mandatory
ITAT set aside TP adjustment made on basis of unaudited financial statement of comparable

TRANSFER PRICING : As per provisions of section 92CA and as per CBDT instructions, reference to TPO under section 92CA is a must in case where such transaction as per Form 3CEB is more than Rs. 15 crores but there is no such provision in Act or in CBDT instruction that any such reference to TPO is bad in law in a case where international transaction as per Form 3CEB is less than Rs. 15 crores
No penalty u/s 271 if revenue unable to point out defects on TP study carried out in accordance with sec. 92C: ITAT
Transfer of title of goods to customers or multiple transfers within FTWZ will not be covered under Schedule III: AAR

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee a Singapore based company challenged impugned assessment order passed under section 143(3) contending to be an eligible assessee under section 144C and being denied benefit of exemption under India-Singapore DTAA, revenue is bound to pass a draft assessment order in case any variation is to be made which is prejudicial to interest of assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Where TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) for assessment year 2011-12 on 30-1-2015, since order under section 92CA(3) ought to have been passed on or before 28-1-2015, i.e. 60 days prior to expiry of limitation as per section 153(1), impugned order passed by TPO was barred by limitation

TRANSFER PRICING : Notice to be issued to assessee at instance of revenue against High Court ruling that provisions of section 144C would be applicable only prospectively and that right enured to parties in 2009 after insertion of section 144C into Act vide Finance (No.2) Act, 2009 could not be modified by a Clarificatory Circular issued by CBDT after three years which said that provisions of section 144C would be applicable to all proceedings pending as on 1-4-2009

TRANSFER PRICING : CBDT's Instruction No.3/2003 dated 20-5-2003 had mandated that wherever aggregate value of international transaction exceeds Rs. 5 crores, case should be pricked up for scrutiny and reference under section 92CA be made to TPO. If there are more than one transaction with an AE or there are transactions with more than one associated enterprises, aggregate value of which exceeds Rs. 5 crores, transactions should be referred to TPO
Transfer pricing adjustment deleted as revised segmental margins showed higher AE profits and difference within sec. 92C tolerance:ITAT
ITAT quashes TP order passed under sec. 92CA beyond period of limitation

TRANSFER PRICING : Where both assessee as well as TPO has not compared transactions with transactions of unrelated parties then transfer pricing study done by both assessee as well as TPO is against provisions of Act and issue requires fresh examination at end of AO/TPO and matter should be restore to file of AO/TPO for examining it afresh
TPO rightly rejected TP study as doc. maintained by assessee wasn’t in accordance with Sec. 92C & Rule 10B/10C: ITAT

TRANSFER PRICING : Notice issued in SLP against order of High Court that where at stage of passing draft order, ACIT had assessed tax, passed a final order and also issued a demand notice, procedure followed by ACIT was contrary to law and said mistake could not be cured under section 292B
IT/ILT: TPO cannot assume jurisdiction to determine arm's length price of a specified domestic transaction not reported to him
TRANSFER PRICING : Availability of unaudited accounts of a branch outside India of a company cannot be reason to reject comparablity of such company, which satisfied all filters
No TP adjustment without pointing out specific defects in TP documentation as required under section 92C(3): ITAT
TRANSFER PRICING : Word 'may' used in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and same would imply that TPO can pass order any day before expiry of 60 days
TRANSFER PRICING: Mere issuance of a show-cause notice cannot be equated and treated as a draft assessment order as same would make provisions of section 144C redundant

HEADNOTE: Section 65 (83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered accountant’s services - Assessee was a practising chartered accountant - Revenue levied service tax on certification service provided by assessee holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 - Whether since certification follows transfer pricing audit, certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ - Held, yes - Whether, since verification of books of account precedes issue of certificate and such verification would fall within scope of ‘Accounting and auditing’, it could not be said that assessee was not rendering auditing service liable to tax and, therefore, impugned order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 3] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998

FACT: The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

HELD: The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]

S. Ramachandran for the Appellant. Ms. Indira Sisupal for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Sections 3-D and 7 of the Uttar Pradesh Trade Tax Act, 1948  - Exemption against the Form 3-C(5) - 9-R were issued in respect of the purchases by the dealer and also furnished the details of the payment made through cheques - Held: Exemption was wrongly denied by the Assessing Authority

HELD: "High Court does not found any error in the order of Tribunal. Admittedly, M/s. Ganesh Trading Company, Kanpur was registered dealer and the alleged Form 3-C (5) were issued by the Assessing Authority of M/s. Ganesh Trading Company, Kanpur to it. Thus, the said Form 3-C (5) were genuine, issued by the department. In respect of the purchases, dealer had issued 9-R and had also furnished the details of the payment made through bank. If Assessing Authority failed to make enquiry as directed by the First Appellate Authority while remanding back the matter, present dealer cannot be held responsible. Assessing Authority has also not been able to make out any collusion between the dealer and M/s. Ganesh Trading Company, Kanpur. In the case o f M/s. Chunni Lal Parsadi Mall v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, reported in 1986 U.P.T.C. 747(SC), Apex Court held that the exemption against the declaration forms cannot be refused unless form is found to be forged and case of collusion between the parties is made out." (Para 4)

There is nothing on record to show that the Notification G.O. Ms. No. 75 stood amended or rescinded. In fact, this legal position was rightly construed and the Secretary to the Commercial Tax and Registration Department issued a Government Letter dated 29-12-2006, to the Commissioner stating that by virtue of section 88(3)(i), the notification granting exemption already issued under TNGST shall continue to be in force under TNVAT Act. [Para 11] In the light of the above discussion and taking into consideration of sections 87, 88(1), 88(3)(i), coupled with the Notification G.O. Ms. No. 75 read along with the Government Letter dated 29-12-2006, it has to be necessarily held that the interpretation given by the Assessing Authority to deny the benefit of exemption to the assessee is unsustainable. [Para 12]

Hence, the assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption by virtue of section 12(1) of the TNSEZ Act and not liable to pay purchase tax under the TNVAT Act on the purchases in question. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Sections 4B and 10B of the U.P. Trade Tax Act, 1948 - Notification No. 7037, dated 31st May, 1985 - Exemption - Corrugated boxes sold by dealer to institution certified by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission - Packing material being goods connected with manufacture of products eligible for exemption unless form is forged or there is any collusion between the parties - In case it is found that exemption is not available to the goods action can be taken against the purchaser.

HELD: "Tribunal held that packing material is goods connected with the manufacture of products and, therefore, eligible for exemption under the notification. Tribunal, further held that certificate which was issued by the Village Industries was not found non-genuine or and it has also not been found that there was any collusion between the parties and, therefore, once the certificate as required under the notification is submitted, the claim of exemption in the hand of the seller cannot be denied and in case, if department is of the view that the exemption is not eligible to the goods action can only be taken against the purchaser and not the seller Court not found any infirmity in the order of Tribunal. Unless certificate is found forged or obtained as a result of collusion, in the hand of the seller exemption cannot be denied." (Paras 5,6)

Thus, it is observed as per the CBDT's explanation, provisions of Transfer Pricing has been enacted to ensure that no income otherwise taxable in India is reduced and even a transaction resulting in exempt income is also subjected to provisions of Transfer Pricing. [Para 33]

In such circumstances, one is confronted with the issue as to how and why the provisions of Transfer Pricing should be applied in respect of an international transaction giving rise to exempt income in the hands of the assessee. [Para 34] In such circumstances, where the income derived from international transactions is exempt from tax in India, it cannot be alleged that the assessee had arranged its affairs in such a manner so as to show lesser taxable income in India but it can be alleged that the assessee has arranged its affairs in such a manner so as to reflect more exempt income in India. [Para 35]

Therefore, a harmonious reading can be construed in the provisions of section 92C(4) and the object and purport of insertion of the provisions of Transfer Pricing as explained by the CBDT. [Para 36]

In a case where the international transaction entered into by the assessee with the AEs is giving rise to exempt income in the hands of the assessee, it is to be benchmarked with the ALP determined in accordance with the provisions of Transfer Pricing to ensure that no excess exempt income is disclosed by the assessee and assessee is entitled for exemption of income under section 10A of the total income determined as per the Transfer Pricing Provisions only and where the assessee has claimed more exempt income, then exemption under section 10A shall be allowed in accordance with the profit compared as per ALP only. [Para 37]

Keeping in view the above in mind in the instant case, as per the decisions of the lower authorities the assessee had not reported any excess exempt income from its international transactions with AE. On the other hand, as per the opinion of the lower authorities when exempt income declared by the assessee was benchmarked with the ALP determined in accordance with the provisions of Transfer Pricing, it was found that assessee has declared lesser exempt income and thereby no taxable base in India was eroded. Therefore, no adjustment with the exempt income of the assessee was required to be made as per provisions contained in Chapter X of the Act. [Para 38]

In view of the above, the Assessing Officer was directed to treat the income declared from the business in question at the amount as shown by the assessee in its return of income. [Para 40]

give details of defects and rectificatory action under various heads, namely leakages, electricals, mechanicals, body paint, body fitments.

The rectification job of these defects certainly seems to be activities conducted by any vehicle repair shop. If the argument of revenue is accepted, every motor garage will become a 'technical inspection and certification' agency. This would lead to a ridiculous situation. The meaning of technical inspection and certification conveys the purpose of certification along with inspection to meet specified standards. The kind of certification covered under this definition refers to certification to ensure that characteristics of the goods meet specified standards. The standards may relate to functionality, utility, quality or safety. The definition of technical inspection cannot be read to mean that any checks on functionality, safety etc. would amount to technical inspection and certification. The word "technical inspection and certification" would appropriately refer to certain standards laid down in some statute or some Guidelines.

For example in the Motor Vehicles Act certain standards are required to be met. Other examples of technical inspection are the Food Safety Standards which require articles of food and drinks to meet certain standards of composition of ingredients etc. Similar is the case where pharmaceutical products are required to meet certain specified standards by law.

In the present case the job card or vehicle data sheets clearly indicate that AGPL are merely rectifying/replacing some damaged/defective parts etc. By no stretch of imagination can this activity be termed as technical inspection and certification. Hence, demand was set aside. [Para 7]

Storage and Warehousing :

AGPL has merely rented space out to TML. Although they arranged for security, the expenses on this account are met by TML. There is a clear finding of the Commissioner that handling, management and safekeeping of the vehicles is the responsibility of TML. Even the security is paid for by TML and so are the telephone expenses and diesel expenses.

None of the ingredients which are essential part of 'warehousing and storage service' are fulfilled so as to cover the activity of AGPL under this service. In fact this view is supported by Board Circular referred to above. Hence, demand was dropped. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India read with section 5 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Writ Petition - Alternative Remedy - Petitioner was engaged in development of software technology park and imported various capital goods claiming exemption under Foreign Trade Policy read with Notification No. 153/93-Cus. - Petitioner transferred entire property with rights and obligations to various companies - Department issued show-cause notice in April 2011 seeking denial of exemption, confiscation of goods and imposition of penalties - Petitioner challenged said notice in writ filed in August 2012 - HELD : Unless show cause notice is found to be without jurisdiction, court shall not interfere - In this case, show cause notice is not actually challenged on ground of want of jurisdiction - Since notice was issued not only to petitioner, but also to other transferees and petitioner had transferred entire properties to transferees, and since other transferees had not challenged notice, petitioner should also take part in adjudication - Since imports were made by petitioner and various obligations could have been complied with only by him, validity of transfer of obligation to transferees and consequent impact could be taken up in adjudication - Moreover, since impact of adjudication would primarily lie on transferees, except penalty that may be levied on petitioner, petitioner's writ was not maintainable - Petitioner's ground that notice could not be issued without approval of Director of Software Technology Park of India under Foreign Trade Policy, was rejected - Moreover, writ was filed after gap of 16 months of dillydallying, hence, writ petition was not bona fide - If liability is imposed by department on petitioner, petitioner can always take up matter with transferees [Paras 12 to 37] [In favour of revenue]Excise  Customs : Where petitioner took exemption and later transferred all properties, rights and obligations to transferees, he could not challenge mere show-cause notice issued to him, as obligation under exemption notification could not, prima facie, be transferred

FACT: Facts

The petitioner-company Citilights Properties Private Limited entered into an agreement with the owners of a vast extent of land for the development of an information technology park complex, in the year 2005.

As per the development agreement, the petitioner was entitled to 74% of the undivided share of the land and they were obliged to develop the park and hand over 26% of the constructed area to the land owners.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with a company by name Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited, for the development of the software technology park and the transfer of 74% of the share of the petitioner to the said company, on the understanding that the transferee company had to fund the development of the park.

Thereafter, the petitioner made an application in November 2005 to the Chairman of the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee through the office of the Director of Software Technology Park of India, Chennai, for setting up an information technology park under the STP Scheme.

The petitioner also entered into two agreements with Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited and another company by name E-lights Technopark Private Limited for the effective funding and implementation of the project.

On 17.10.2006, the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee granted in principle approval for the setting up of the infrastructure facility under the STP Scheme in 'Freedom IT Campus '. The Government of India, in turn, granted permission by a communication dated 22.10.2006 in terms of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2004-2009.

As per the letter of permission so granted, the petitioner was entitled to import capital goods worth Rs. 2500 lakhs, by availing the benefits of Notification No. 153/93 dated 13.8.1993. But, the goods and services were to be used for the purpose of export of software and IT services by the STP Units located within the infrastructure facility at the park. The permission for import of items was valid for a period of two years from the date of issue of the letter of permission.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with the Software Technology Park of India, binding itself to the obligations and conditions of the letter of permission and a green card was issued to the petitioner. In pursuance of the above, the premises were declared as a private bonded warehouse by the Department of Central Excise.

Therefore, the petitioner caused import of capital goods availing the benefit of the exemption Notification.

Thereafter, the petitioner handed over Block-1 of the IT Park to the two transferee companies such as E-lights Technopark Private Limited and Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited in March 2008.

Therefore, the petitioner caused import of capital goods availing the benefit of the exemption Notification.

Thereafter, the petitioner handed over Block-1 of the IT Park to the two transferee companies such as E-lights Technopark Private Limited and Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited in March 2008. After two years, the special purpose vehicle - one of the transferee companies namely E-lights Technopark Private Limited applied on 30.3.2010 to the Software Technology Parks of India for approval of name transfer and green card to itself.

But, the Preventive Unit of the Commissionerate of Central Excise initiated an investigation into the affairs of the petitioner.

The Commissioner of Central Excise issued a show cause notice alleging various irregularities and calling upon the petitioner as well as the special purpose vehicle and the other transferee company to show cause as to why the benefit of the exemption Notification should not be denied and why the capital goods imported and sold should not be confiscated, apart from levy of penalty.

Meanwhile, the Inter-Ministerial Committee approved the letter of permission for a further period of four years from its expiry i.e., 21.12.2008.

The assessee filed writ challenging notice of Department and also pleading for execution of extension of letter of permission.

Issue Involved

Whether impugned notice could be challenged ?

HELD: What is challenged is only a show cause notice issued by the Competent Authority for the withdrawal of benefit of two exemption Notifications and for the confiscation of the capital goods imported by the petitioner under section 111(O) of the Customs Act, 1962. [Para 12]

The jurisdiction of this Court to interfere at the stage of show cause notice is extremely limited and circumscribed. Unless the show cause notice is found to be without jurisdiction, this court shall not interfere with a show cause notice under Article 226. [Para 13]

It is clear that the show cause notice is not actually challenged on the ground of want of jurisdiction. The petitioner attempts to project the show cause notice as one that has been issued without jurisdiction, by contending that once the transfer of the letter of permission is permitted by the Software Technology Parks of India, the Commissioner of Central Excise would not have jurisdiction to proceed against the petitioner. [Para 14]

But, the above contention is fundamentally flawed. A look at the impugned show cause notice shows that the same had not been issued only as against the petitioner herein. The show cause notice has been issued also against both the transferees namely E-lights Technopark Private Limited and Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited. The show cause notice fixes responsibility not only upon the petitioner, but also seeks to levy penalty upon the transferees in terms of section 112(b) of the Customs Act, 1962. The transferees have no qualms about giving a reply to the show cause notice and facing an adjudication on merits and in accordance with law. Therefore, merely because a transfer of the letter of permission is permitted, the Commissioner of Central Excise forfeited his jurisdiction to initiate proceedings under sections 111 and 112 of the Customs Act, 1962. [Para 15]

Admittedly, the petitioner is only an infrastructure service provider. The very proposal presented by the petitioner was to develop, operate and maintain an information technology park. But, even before the submission of the said proposal, the petitioner entered into an agreement with Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited for the transfer of their 74% undivided interest in the land and building. Subsequently, the petitioner also entered into agreement with Pacific Infrastructure Company Private Limited and E-lights Technopark Private Limited. It is not known how, after entering into an agreement for the transfer of the property rights, the petitioner could have submitted a proposal ? [Para 16]

The first letter of approval of the Government for setting up of infrastructure facility for STP Units under the STP Scheme was conveyed by the Government only on 22.12.2006. It is under this approval that the petitioner was permitted to import goods valued at Rs. 2,500 lakhs as per the Customs Notification dated 13.8.1993. By this time, the petitioner had already transferred their rights in favour of two companies. There is nothing on record to show that the petitioner informed the Government of India about the transfer to the two companies. In fact, the letter of approval requires the petitioner to furnish progress reports for the implementation of the project on a quarterly basis. This condition could have never been complied with by the petitioner in view of the agreements that they had already entered into with the transferees. [Para 17]

As rightly pointed out by the department, what was granted to the petitioner was a licence to have a private bonded warehouse under section 58 of the Customs Act, 1962. That is why the general bond in Form B-17 was actually executed by the petitioner. This is a general bond required to be executed by 100% export oriented units. If the petitioner had already transferred their rights as well as obligations to third parties, the general bond executed by the petitioner on 29.12.2006 was actually meaningless. [Para 18]

HELD: From the perusal of the records filed during the course of assessment proceedings, it is seen that the Assessing Officer from time-to-time has raised several queries to examine the claim/deduction under section 80 IA, which is evident from the fact that the assessee had placed copy of audit report in Form No. 10 CCB in support of deduction under section 80-IA alongwith past assessment history and orders for the earlier assessment years, wherein this issue has been discussed and allowed by the respective Assessing Officers. All these documents were placed before the Assessing Officer in response to queries raised by him with regard to sale of undertaking to subsidiary of the assessee. The assessee has filed the 'business transfer agreement' entered for sale of undertaking alongwith the 'valuation report' of the Govt. Approved Valuer wherein the valuation of the property has been done as per the prevailing market rate and the value of the entire property was determined, and the said valuation report contains drawings, pictures, comparative sale instances and various schedules to arrive at the market rate. Not only that, before the Assessing Officer the assessee has also filed detailed report of the accountant regarding the 'related party transaction' undertaken by the assessee with its subsidiary in Form No. 3 CEB alongwith the transfer pricing document wherein the entire details of the specified domestic transaction and the manner in which arms length price has been determined has been provided. After calling for all these evidences and examining the entire facts brought on record, the Assessing Officer has examined the allowability of claim under section 80-IA and in fact has made part disallowance on such deduction. Hence, it cannot be held that the Assessing Officer has not conducted any enquiry or investigated the issue which he was required to do so before allowing the claim of deduction under section 80-IA or has allowed without examining the assessee's transaction with its subsidiary. One of the key allegations of the Commissioner is that the Assessing Officer should have made a reference to the TPO as per the CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003. First of all, it would be relevant to see, whether there was any such instruction issued by the CBDT to the Assessing Officer for making any reference to the TPO for specified domestic transaction. From the perusal of the said Instruction No. 3/2003, it is seen that guidelines for reference to the TPO has been made only in respect of determination of arm's length price in relation to the international transaction under section 92B. There is no whisper about specified domestic transaction for the reason that there was no concept of specified domestic transaction under the Act when said instruction was issued on 20-5-2003. The specified domestic transaction for the purpose of determination of ALP has been brought in the statute only by the Finance Act, 2012. Hence, holding the assessment order erroneous for the reason that, the Assessing Officer should have made a reference to the TPO in accordance with CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003 is wholly misconceived and misinterpreted. Once there was no CBDT instruction or guidelines for reference to the issue involving specified domestic instruction to the TPO at the time of passing the assessment order, then where is the question of any non-compliance of CBDT Instruction by the Assessing Officer.

The Tribunal has also considered the fact that the certificate does not specify the factual basis on which the Singapore Tax Authority has concluded that the income from shipping business have been derived by the assessee from "business carried on in Singapore". Thus, in effect, the Tribunal has overreached the findings arrived at by this Court in case of M.T. Maersk Mikage v. DIT (International Taxation) (supra) in absence of any material brought on record by the Revenue before the Tribunal to show that the certificate issued by the IRAS is not reliable or cannot be considered for the income of ST Shipping to be taxed in Singapore on accrual basis. It is also pertinent to note that from the documents placed in form of paper- book filed before the Tribunal, in fact, the ST Shipping has shown the income arising from the operations as per letter dated 09.10.2012 issued by the Deloitte and Touche LLP, Certified Public Accountants, Singapore stating that the ST Shipping has confirmed that the position adopted in the Year of Assessment 2010 to treat charter income derived by the overseas branches as Singapore sourced income and part of qualifying income under Approved International Shipping Enterprise Incentive remains unchanged in the Year of Assessment 2012. [Para 16]

■

The impugned order of the Tribunal is, therefore, contrary to the decision of this Court as the Tribunal could not have restored the matter back to the Assessing Officer only on mere suspicion and the doubts contrary to the findings arrived at by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by IRAS. The Tribunal ought not to have analysed the certificate in its order more particularly in Para 22 of the order in absence of any material on record. On perusal of Para 22 of the impugned order it is clear that the Tribunal has made the observation with regard to the language of the certificate more particularly, when this Court has accepted the part of the certificate which certified that the income earned by the ST Shipping from the operations carried out in ports at India was liable to be taxed at Singapore on accrual basis and as per Article 8 of DTAA, when the income accrues in Singapore and was taxed as such, the same would be exempt from tax in India. This Court has further clarified that reference to Article 24 of DTAA in the certificate is nothing but an opinion of the IRAS. [Para 17]

■

Hence, the Tribunal ought not to have further deliberated upon contents of the certificate which is already held to be applicable in the facts of the case in the absence of any other material on record to demonstrate that the veracity of the certificate issued by IRAS is doubtful and merely because the Tribunal is of the opinion that the language of the certificate is not conducive to the opinion of the Tribunal, the matter could not have been restored to the Assessing Officer in face of the observation made by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by the IRAS. Thus, the initial onus under section 9(1)(vii)( b) lay squarely on the assessee to prove that the exemption available thereunder was in fact available to it. The assessee had maintained throughout that the testing and certification services provided by 'C' were utilized only for its export activity and that the same were not utilized for its business activities of production in India. Thus, the assessee had discharged the onus, which lay on it under section 9(1)(vii)(b ). Therefore, the impugned payment made by the assessee to 'C' was not chargeable to tax in India. [Para 21]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had erred in confirming the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 30]

Manufacture of the vessel is a complex and costly affair and service provider gives certification as regards to the standard of the developed model. In view of the above, service is to be classified under the category of 'Technical inspection and certification service'. The consideration of this aspect is material before issuing notice under section 92D(3), if it is to serve its purpose. The abovesaid prescribed information is gathered from the assessee through various means and at different stages of the assessment proceedings. The initial or first information relating to international transactions is gathered from the assessee in the prescribed audit report in Form 3CEB. This report is required to be submitted along with the return of income as per section 92E. [Para 22.5]

It is clear from Form 3CEB that the name and addresses of the assessee, its associated concerns, nature of relationship with such concerns, brief description of business and details of international transactions carried on with the associated enterprises, besides the method used for determining ALP in respect of each international transaction is required to be given in the audit report. [Para 24]

The Assessing Officer must have the audit report in Form 3CEB with him to determine the question whether total value of the transactions is more or less than Rs. 5 crore (now enhanced to Rs. 15 crore) to consider the question whether determination of ALP is to be referred to the TPO or not. If the total value exceeds the prescribed limit, the Assessing Officer has to refer the matter to the TPO. [Para 24.1]

It is, therefore, reasonable to presume that in every transfer pricing case, relevant information, along with Form 3CEB is available on record and the Assessing Officer/TPO is supposed to proceed with the basic and initial information of international transactions carried by the assessee in the relevant period as disclosed in Form 3CEB. He is supposed to have specialized training and, therefore, understand what job he is to perform for achieving the purpose of the Regulations. [Para 24.2]

Therefore, it is clear that information prescribed under rule 10D in different column is voluminous, alternative and it would have to be seen as to what information and from which clause, is required on the facts of the given case. Secondly, information from certain clauses of rule 10D is obtained in audit report in Form 3CEB required to be filed along with the return. Thirdly, the TPO, before proceeding to determine ALP, has above basic and initial information of international transactions carried by the assessee. [Para 24.3]

Armed with the said initial information and when knowing details of international transactions carried by the assessee and the method employed to determine the ALPs of transactions, further proceedings are carried towards determination of ALP. [Para 24.4]

Provisions of section 92D(3) can be applied in the following circumstances :

(i)

in the course of the proceedings under the Act before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals).

(ii)

Any documents or information prescribed under sub-section (1) may be required.

(iii)

information is required to be furnished under sub-section (3) within 30 days (as extended by another 30 days) from the receipt of notice issued in this regard.

Thus, the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) may require (from any person) any information or document as may be prescribed. Word 'any' information or document cannot ordinarily mean 'all' the documents prescribed under rule 10D. The word 'required' is important as it rules out option with the assessee and makes it obligatory to furnish the requisite information.

It is clear from above that the power under section 92D(3) can be used in the course of the assessment proceedings, i.e., in proceedings for determination of ALP and only for requiring to furnish prescribed information or documents under rule 10D. It being a provision connected with procedure to help an assessment, must be purposefully construed. But, regulation does not provide any time or stage when power to issue notice is to be exercised. However, scheme of assessment do indicate the stage at which it is to be issued and the purpose which is required to be achieved through the issuance of such a notice. [Para 24.6]

From the annual audit report under the Companies Act as well as tax audit report under the Act, it was found that the auditor had taken a view that the short term capital gains arising on account of transfer of plant and machinery by assessee-company to its holding company was not to be considered as transfer within the meaning of section 45 inasmuch as the assessee’s case was covered by provision contained in section 47(v ). [Para 14] Now, the question arose as to whether view of the auditor could be considered to be a bona fide basis upon which the assessee had made a claim in the return of income that short term capital gain arising on transfer of plant and machinery to its holding company was not taxable. [Para 15]

On perusal of the provision of section 47(v ), it is clear that this section grants exemption in case of transfer of a capital asset as between holding company and wholly owned subsidiary, where the transferee is an Indian company. It provides that nothing contained in section 45 shall apply to any transfer of a capital asset by a subsidiary company to the holding company if the whole of the share capital of the subsidiary company is held by the holding company and the holding company, i.e., transferee is an Indian company. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the capital asset had been transferred by the assessee-company, being a subsidiary company, to its holding company. The share capital of the assessee-company to the extent of 99.66 per cent was held by the holding company to which the capital assets were transferred. The balance share capital to the extent of 0.36 per cent were held by the directors of holding company and their relatives. The auditor in the annual audit report had given an opinion that any loss or gain arising from the transaction of sale of fixed assets by the assessee company to its holding company would be covered by section 47(v) and as such any gain arising therefrom would not be chargeable to tax under section 45. The observation made in the annual audit report under Companies Act was at the stage at which the account were first audited under the Companies Act. The assessee had to file its return of income as per provisions contained in the Act. However, in the instant case, the tax consultant, who was also the tax auditor of the assessee-company, in its tax audit report under section 44AB, had also given an identical view that the transaction in question would be covered by section 47(v ) and, hence, short term capital gain arising on sale of plant and machinery would not be chargeable to tax under section 45. This view given by the tax consultant and the tax auditor in its report was on the basis that 99.64 per cent of the shares of assessee company were held by its holding company to which the assets were transferred and the remaining 0.36 per cent of share capital were held by directors of holding company and their relatives implying thereby that whole of the share capital of the assessee-company were being controlled or held by holding company. This opinion given by the tax auditor might not be acceptable in the light of the language used in section 47(v ) where one of the conditions provided is that whole of the share capital of the subsidiary company must be held by the holding company. In the instant case, 100 per cent share capital of the subsidiary company was not held by the holding company but the share capital was being by the holding company only to the extent of 99.64 per cent. There was not much difference between 100 per cent share capital and 99.64 per cent capital, which is held by the holding company particularly in view of the fact that the balance 0.36 per cent of share capital of assessee-company were held by the directors of holding company and their relatives. Therefore, the view taken by the tax consultant could be a plausible one taken to advance the benefit of transfer of assets by subsidiary company to holding company within the meaning of section 47(v ) read with section 45 after giving a liberal and wider meaning to section 47(v ). The assessee had acted upon the advise given by the auditor in both annual tax report prepared under Companies Act as well as tax audit prepared under Income-tax Act. It was not the case where an opinion was given only at the time of preparing the audit report under Companies Act but it was the case where the opinion was also given by the Tax consultant while preparing the return of income for the assessee. It was, thus, a case where the assessee had acted upon the advice given by the tax auditor. [Para 16]

Now, the question arose as to whether the deduction claimed by the assessee on the basis of advise of the tax consultant supported by tax audit report as well as annual audit report could said to be a false claim made by the assessee so as to attract penalty provisions contained in section 271(1)(c). [Para 17]

goods in terms of notification dated 4-9-1995 by urging that such exemption was in respect of sale of goods which were manufactured by any dealer in the State of Haryana who held a valid exemption certificate. The core controversy pertains to the interpretation of notification dated 4-9-1995 which has been issued by the competent authority in exercise of power under section 8(5) of the CST Act. [Para 13]

Notification dated 4-9-1995 The notification dated 4-9-1995 has been issued in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (5) to section 8 of the CST Act by the Governor of Haryana in public interest. As per the notification, no tax is payable under the aforesaid Act with effect from 1-4-1988 on sale of goods during the period of exemption that are manufactured in the State of Haryana by any dealer, who holds a valid exemption certificate under rule 28A. Proviso to the said notification stipulates that the dealers should have also not charged any tax under the CST Act on the sale of goods manufactured by him. [Para 14]

Sub-section (5) to section 8 begins with the non obstante clause and empowers the State Governments to issue a notification in the official gazette subject to the condition(s) as may be specified and under clause (a) direct that no tax shall be payable by any dealer having his place of business in the State in respect of sale in the course of inter-State trade or commerce, etc. and under clause (b) in respect of all sales of goods or classes of goods, etc. [Para 15]

Provisions of rule 28A of Haryana Rules

The rule 28A as per heading relates to class of industries, period and other conditions for exemption/deferment from payment of tax.

Sub-rule (1) of rule 28A makes it clear that industries are covered under this rule and the said industries would not be entitled to any deferment or exemption from payment of tax under any other provisions of these rules. The expression 'eligible industrial unit' is defined in clause (f) to sub-rule (2). Similarly 'eligibility certificate', 'exemption certificate', etc. are defined in clauses (j) and (k) to sub-rule (2). Clause (n) to sub-rule (2) defines the expression 'notional sales tax liability' and clause (ii) states that the amount of tax payable under the CST Act on sales of finished product of eligible industrial unit made in the course of inter-State trade or commerce shall be computed at the rate of tax applicable as if the sales were made against Form 'C'.

In other words, inter-State trade or commerce of finished products of eligible industrial units will be treated as notional sales tax liability. The reference in this clause is to the eligible industrial unit and sales of finished products made by the said units, which are sold in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. [Para 16]

The purport and impact of rule 28A is with reference to eligible industrial unit is not only clear from the definition clauses which define eligibility certificate, exemption certificate, etc. but also from sub-rule (4)(a) which stipulates that the benefit of tax exemption or deferment shall be given to an eligible industrial unit holding exemption or entitlement certificate for the period specified.

Clause (c) to sub-rule (4)(2) postulates that goods manufactured by an eligible industrial unit availing of exemption under this rule shall be exempt from levy of tax on all successive stage/stages of sale or purchase, subject to the dealer affecting the said purchase or sale furnishing a certificate in Form ST-14A obtained from the Assessing Authority. This clause has the effect of granting exemption from levy of tax at all successive stages of sale and purchase in intra-State trade or commerce, i.e., within the State of Haryana. To put it differently, it extends the benefit granted under clause (n)(ii) which relates to inter-State trade or commerce to intra-State sale or purchase. Such sales may be one or successive and tax at all stages is exempt. The exemption, therefore, is good specific, subject of course to other conditions being satisfied. [Para 17]

Consideration of case

It is not disputed that on all intra-State sales no tax has been charged as the said transactions were treated as exempt by the tax authorities. However, in respect of inter-State sales, it is submitted by the revenue that the exemption would be limited and available only if the manufacturer, i.e., the eligible industrial unit makes sale in inter-State trade or commerce. But if a third party, who had procured the goods from the eligible industrial unit makes inter-State sale, such trade or commerce would not be exempt.

refer to sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92CD. [Para 18]

■

The provisions of section 92CD(1) are unambiguous and even if a return has been filed prior to an assessee entering into an APA, he is entitled to furnish a modified return declaring his income in accordance with the terms of the APA. Subject to certain exceptions, the APA is binding both on the assessee and the revenue. [Para 19]

■ It is clear that the scheme of providing for an APA is to remove any uncertainty as to the determination of an income of an assessee engaged in international transactions with associated enterprises. The assessee is required to declare his income in accordance with the APA. Except in certain cases, where there is a change in law and facts or the agreement is occasioned by fraud or misrepresentation, the APA would be binding. Sub-sections (5), (6) and (7) of section 92CC provide for the same in unambiguous terms. [Para 20]

■

It is apparent from a plain reading of sub-section (4) of section 92C that the same is inapplicable. The said sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to compute the total income, having regard to the ALP determined by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (3) of section 92C. [Para 22]

■

Sub-section (3) of section 92C provides that the Assessing Officer can proceed to determine the ALP only in cases he is of the opinion on the basis of material that (a) the price charged or paid in international transaction, has not been determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92C; or (b) that information and documentation relating to the international transaction has not been maintained as mandatorily required; or (c) that the information or data for computing the ALP is unreliable; or there is failure on the part of the assessee to furnish any information or document required to be furnished along with the notice. [Para 23]

■

It is apparent that in a case where the assessee voluntarily computes the ALP pursuant to an APA entered into with CBDT, none of the conditions as set out in sub-section (3) of section 92C are attracted. It follows that sub-section (4) of section 92C is not attracted. [Para 24]

■

More importantly, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C also clearly states that no deduction under section 10A or 10AA or 10B or under Chapter VI-A would be allowed in respect of the amount of income by which the total income of the assessee is enhanced after computation under the said section. Thus in a case where the assessee voluntarily declares his income based on the ALP determined on the basis of an APA, there would be no occasion for the Assessing Officer to enhance the income of the assessee. [Para 25]

■

Absent any enhancement of income, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is clearly inapplicable. [Para 26]

■

It is also necessary to bear in mind that in terms of section 10AA(1), the profits and gains of an enterprise, as referred to in clause (j) of section 2 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, from an eligible unit, which is derived from export of articles or things are exempt. [Para 27]

■

The ALP is imputed to transactions to determine the profits and gains that are derived by the assessee from any international transactions (or specified domestic transactions) in order to assess the real income of the assessee after eliminating any bias or element of transfer of profits. [Para 28]

■

Thus, indisputably, the income computed on the basis of ALP would provide a measure of the profits or income derived by the activities carried on by an assessee. The proviso to section 92C(4) essentially limits exemption under section 10AA in cases where the income computed is enhanced by the Assessing Officer under section 92C. [Para 29]

■

It is also relevant to refer to the CBDT Circular No.14/2006. [Para 30]

■

The said circular also amply clarifies that the first proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is applicable where the total income of the assessee as computed by the Assessing Officer is "higher than the income declared by the assessee". [Para 31]

■

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer has not enhanced the income declared by the assessee. The assessee had voluntarily factored in the ALP pursuant to the APA entered into with the CBDT, for computing the income as declared in its returns. [Para 32]

■

In view of the above, there is no infirmity in the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal in rejecting the revenue's contention that exemption under section 10AA of Chapter VI-A, is not available in respect of declared income of the assessee insofar as it relates to the TP adjustments made pursuant to the APA. [Para 34]

[Para 5] Once it is concluded that in respect of those goods where brand name of other party is used on manufactured goods and that other party is not a SSI unit, exemption is not available, it would lead to inevitable result that the value of such goods cannot be added as well, while considering the value of the goods cleared by the assessee in the previous year. The following observations of Tribunal were incorrect :

letters such as 'HM' and 'PAL', no doubt, were initials of the buyers of the goods and they constitute the brand name as well, however, what was indicated was only initials with the sole purpose to identify the goods for particular automobile company ;

after the supply of these goods, the said automobile companies were affixing their proper trade mark/brand name thereupon ;

No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 - Whether an applicant can seek an Advance Ruling only in relation to supply of goods or services or both undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by it - Held, yes - Whether since applicant is recipient of services and not supplier of service, application in question is not liable for admission and, therefore, rejected without going into merits of case - Held, yes - Whether thus, application is not admitted under section 98(2), read with section 95(a) - Held, yes [Paras 4.2 and 5]GST : An applicant can seek an Advance Ruling only in relation to supply of goods or services or both undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by them and, therefore, advance ruling application filed by applicant, a government authority, who is recipient of service is not to be admitted in terms of section 98

FACT: Applicant is a governmental authority providing drinking water and off-take of sewerage in Chennai Metropolitan area.

Applicant is seeking advance ruling on question as to whether services provided to it can be termed as 'pure services' to avail exemption provided by Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017, dated 28-6-2017.

HELD: The applicant seeks ruling as to whether the services received by it are Pure Services to avail exemption under Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. The admissibility of the application was examined during the hearing extended to them. The applicant stated that they had sought ruling regarding the services received by them for which charges are paid by them, the activity in which they are recipient and not supplier of services. Thus, the question is on the eligibility of a notification in respect of the services received by them and not on the supply made by them. [Para 4.1]

It is evident that an applicant can seek an Advance Ruling only in relation to supply of goods or services or both undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by them. Further, as per section 103(1), the ruling is binding only on the applicant and the concerned officer or the jurisdictional officer of the applicant. In the instant case, the applicant is the recipient of the services and not supplier of such service. Accordingly, this question is not liable for admission and, therefore, rejected without going into the merits of the case. [Para 4.2]

Thus, application is not admitted, under section 98(2) read with section 95(a). [Para 5]

Section 2(f) of the TNSEZ Act envisages that the expressions used and not defined in TNSEZ Act but defined in the SEZ Act have the meanings respectively assigned to them in the said Act. Therefore, the expressions 'developer', entrepreneur' and 'domestic tariff area' defined in the SEZ Act would apply to TNSEZ Act. [Para 29] As per section 2(c) of the SEZ Act, authorized operations means the operations which were authorized by the Development Commissioner by granting a letter of approval to the developer to undertake in a special economic zone. In the instant case, the assessee was granted a letter of approval dated 7-3-2011 by the Special Economic Zone Authority for undertaking authorized operations, namely, trading and warehousing services for mobile phone handsets and mobile phone parts and accessories. [Para 30]

As per SEZ scheme, the SEZ area is deemed to be a foreign territory for the purposes of trade operations and levy of various taxes and duties. As per the provisions of section 53 of the SEZ Act, SEZ area is deemed to be foreign territory.

The domestic tariff area has been defined in section 2(j) of the SEZ Act, which means the whole of India but does not include the areas of the SEZ. The term 'export' has been defined in section 2(m) of the SEZ Act. The term import has been defined in section 2(o) of the SEZ Act, which reads as : Import means (i) bringing goods or receiving services, in a special economic zone, by a unit or developer from a place outside India by land, sea or air or by any other mode, whether physical or otherwise ; or (ii) receiving goods, or services by a unit or developer from another unit or developer of the same special economic zone or a different special economic zone.

The supply of goods by the dealer of domestic tariff area to SEZ unit is treated as export of the dealer and import of the SEZ unit. Vice versa the sale of goods by SEZ unit to a dealer of domestic tariff area will be import of the dealer and export of the SEZ unit. Thus all sales effected by SEZ unit to a dealer situated anywhere in India is export sales of SEZ unit because SEZ territory is deemed to be a foreign territory.

The assessee cleared the goods from SEZ unit to domestic tariff area and such removal of goods claimed as branch transfers. However, such domestic tariff area clearances consequently attract provisions of section 15 of TNSEZ Act. Therefore, section 12(1)(b) of the VAT Act stands attracted justifying levy of purchase tax.

Section 12 of the TNSEZ Act provides exemption from the levy of taxes on the sale or purchase of goods subject to the condition that such goods are meant to carry on the authorized operations by the developer or entrepreneur. The purchase tax was imposed on the inter-State stock transfer and the assessee cannot seek exemption thereof, since effecting inter-State stock transfer has not been authorized by the Development Commissioner, nor it would fall within the definition of authorized operations.

It is very deplorable to note that being a SEZ unit, having availed the hospitality and resources of the State of Tamil Nadu, the assessee had diverted significant part of the turnover to other States by effecting inter-State stock transfer which would not only defeat the very object of the SEZ Policy but also would have a considerable impact both on the revenue and economic growth of State of Tamil Nadu. In order to avoid these kind of repercussions, section 15 has been brought into TNSEZ Act, which specifically insists that any goods removed from SEZ to domestic tariff area, shall be chargeable to tax. Further section 30 of the SEZ Act also provides specifically that any goods removed from a SEZ area to domestic tariff area shall be liable for import duty as is leviable on import of such goods as per the provision of Custom Tariff Act.

It is admitted fact that the assessee had accepted the terms prescribed in the approval letter dated 7-3-2011 for setting up the unit in SEZ, of which, one of the conditions is that the assessee can supply/sell the goods or services in the domestic tariff area in terms of the provisions of the SEZ Act and rules and orders made thereunder. Therefore, levy of purchase tax on the inter-State stock transfer effected by the assessee from warehouse located in SEZ area was perfect in order. [Para 31]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 13 of DTAA between India and Singapore - Income - Deemed to accrue and arise in India (Capital gain - General) - Assessment year 2018-19 - Assessee, a tax resident of Singapore, was engaged in investment holding and general wholesale trade - It was subsidiary company of company resident in BVI - During year, assessee earned short-term capital gain on account of sale of shares of a company and claimed same to be exempt as per article 13 of DTAA - Assessing Officer noticed that assessee's holding company was situated in BVI with which India had no DTAA and in order to avail treaty benefits entire investment and sale transactions had been routed through Singapore entity and thus, he held assessee to be ineligible for treaty benefits due to lack of commercial substance in Singapore - DRP observed that Assessing Officer had not established that beneficial owner was BVI and directed him to verify whether affairs of assessee were controlled from outside Singapore - However, Assessing Officer had simply repeated what was said in draft assessment order - Assessing Officer had not made any efforts to make further verification but assessee had given enough evidences to prove that its entire affairs were not controlled from outside Singapore and it had duly reflected acquisition of shares in its balance sheet and its audited balance sheets were subjected to verification by Singapore tax authorities - Whether all these documents proved that affairs of assessee-company were not controlled from outside Singapore and, consequently, short-term capital gain was not taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was a subsidiary company situated in BVI and engaged in the investment holding and general wholesale trade. Shares owned by assessee were disposed of in the year under consideration by the assessee and it earned short-term capital gains and incurred long-term capital loss. Assessee claimed short-term capital gains to be exempt as per article 13 of India Singapore Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

The Assessing Officer observed that the scheme of arrangement employed by the assessee was one of tax avoidance through treaty shopping mechanism. There was a clear lack of beneficial ownership at the level of the assessee as the TRC was not sufficient to establish the tax residency and there was no commercial rationale of establishment of assessee company in Singapore.

The Assessing Officer held the assessee ineligible for treaty benefit due to lack of commercial substance in Singapore.

DRP appreciated the contention of the assessee and held that the observation made by the Assessing Officer that affairs and governance structure of the company were managed just to take benefit of treaty, as inconclusive. The assessee was regularly engaged in the business for last many years and the Assessing Officer had not brought any incidence showing that the management of affairs of the company were carried out from a place outside Singapore.

DRP, accordingly, observed that, the Assessing Officer had not established that the beneficial owner in this case was BVI company. Accordingly, the DRP directed the Assessing Officer to verify whether the affairs of the assessee were controlled from outside Singapore or whether the benefits arising out of the transactions are passed on to the parent company.

Assessing Officer reiterated the findings given by him in the draft assessment order.

On appeal:

HELD: Assessing Officer while passing the final assessment order had not followed the directions of the DRP. As per the provisions of section 144C(10), every direction issued by the DRP shall be binding on the Assessing Officer and that the Assessing Officer is not empowered to raise any new issue in the giving effect proceedings and continue the addition based on some other reasoning. [Para 19]

its letter dated 25-11-2009 the assessee had claimed exemption on the ground that the sale was effected by transfer of documents of title before the goods had crossed the customs frontiers. The assessee's intention was to sell the goods and there was a sale. It did not act as the agent of 'R'. It had filed the bill of entry for warehousing and home consumption. The customs duty was assessed on the assessee alone vide bill of entry for ex-bond. After assessment to customs duty was made on filing of the bill of entry, the goods get mingled with the general mass of goods and merchandise of the country attracting the character of local goods. As ascertainable from the bills of entry from warehousing and ex-bond, transfer of title had not taken place before filing of the bills of entry and assessment of customs duty. The sale took place after assessment of customs duty was made on the assessee and on its filing the bills of entry. The goods must be held to have crossed the customs frontiers of India after the bill of entry was made and the goods were assessed to customs duty. Therefore, the sale could not be said to be sale in the course of import or high seas sale. The transaction should be treated as inter-State sale falling under section 3(a).

On writ petition, the assessee contended that the assessment orders were without jurisdiction in the absence of any valid authorisation from the Deputy Commissioner, Visakhapatnam authorising the above Commercial Tax Officer to take up assessment under the Central Act. It also contended that denying exemption under section 5(2) on the sale in question was contrary to the documents on record.

HELD: Jurisdiction of Assessing Authority

In view of section 9(2) of the Central Act, the Assessing Authority under the A.P. VAT Act would ordinarily have been the Assessing Authority under the Central Act also. [Para 11]

Section 2(1)(b) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (1957 Act) defined Assessing Authority to mean any person authorised by the State Government or by any other authority empowered in this behalf, to make any assessment in such area or areas or the whole of the State of Andhra Pradesh under the Act. Section 14 thereof empowered the Assessing Authority to undertake assessment if a return submitted was found to be incorrect. In the exercise of the powers conferred by section 2(1)(b), the Governor of Andhra Pradesh issued G.O. Ms. No. 728, dated 14-7-1970 authorising (a) the Assistant Commercial Tax officers to exercise the powers of the Assessing Authority in the case of dealers whose assessments were transferred to them by the Deputy Commercial Tax officer concerned, (b) the Deputy Commercial Tax Officers to exercise the powers of an Assessing Authority in the case of dealers whose total turnover was less than Rs. 15 lakhs, (c) the Commercial Tax Officers to exercise the powers of an Assessing Authority in the case of dealers whose total turnover was Rs. 15 lakhs or more a year. Under the proviso thereto, any of the higher authorities, viz., the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer and the Commercial Tax Officer could, in his discretion, exercise the powers of a lower authority within his jurisdiction in respect of any dealer or class of dealers and the Deputy Commissioner of the division concerned could, by order, authorise any Deputy Commercial Tax Officer to exercise the powers of an Assessing Authority in the case of any dealer or class of dealers whose total turnover exceeded Rs. 15 lakhs a year. [Para 17]

The 1957 Act was repealed by section 80(1) of the A.P. VAT Act. However, in view of the proviso thereto, such repeal did not effect the previous operation of the 1957 Act or any right, title, obligation or liability already acquired, accrued or incurred thereunder and subject thereto anything done or any action taken including any appointment, notification, etc. in the exercise of any power conferred by or under the 1957 Act must be deemed to have been done or taken in the exercise of the powers conferred by or under the VAT Act, as if the VAT Act was in force on the date on which such thing was done or action was taken. While the Assessing Authority, as prescribed in G.O. Ms. No. 728, dated 14-7-1970, continues to be the Commercial Tax Officer of the circle even after the VAT Act came into force, the power of assessment under the VAT Act is conferred not on the Assessing Authority, but on the prescribed authority. It is only the authority prescribed under rule 59 of the A.P. VAT Rules, who can make assessment under the VAT Act and not the Assessing Authority under section 2(4) thereof or in G.O. Ms. No. 728, dated 14-7-1970.

(iii)

Under 'Method. of sampling from grape farms/plots', the laboratories authorized for Grape Net, dated 8-1-2018 is given. These authorized laboratories are to draw sample from the farm/plot and the samples of grapes, soil and water are to be drawn and the sampling to be done as per the procedure. The applicant is not one of the authorized laboratory so listed.

(iv) The procedure for issue of Certificate of Agmark Grading (CAG) and Phyto Sanitary Certificate (PSC) are provided at Sl.No.7 and under 'Procedure for obtaining Certificate of Agmark Grading (CAG) for export of grapes to EU Countries', the list of offices of Directorate of Marketing & Inspection (DMI) and list of Approved Laboratories approved by DMI for the grading and marking of fruits and vegetables for export are provided. It is seen that the applicant is a laboratory approved by DMI for the Grading and marking of fruits. Sampling Plan and the 'Inspection Report for Grapes' are given.

From the above, it is evident that when NRL has authorized certain laboratories to undertake testing of soil, water, from the plot/farm along with the grown grapes in such plot, DMI has authorized laboratories for the Grading and marking of fruits. APEDA ensures registration of all the stakeholders and traces the events in the 'Grape Net'. In the case at hand, the applicant Laboratory is an approved laboratory by the Directorate of Marketing & Inspection (DMI) and undertakes testing for Agmark Grading' and 'Final Inspection'. The applicant is not authorized to undertake testing of soil, water, farm/plot where the cultivation is undertaken but is authorized to sample and grade the cultivated grapes based on physical attributes for issuance of 'Certificate of Agmark Grading'. It is seen from the test reports submitted by the applicant, they conduct test to detect residue of various chemicals, pesticides etc. The recommended chemicals for which testing is to be done is specified in APEDA trade Notice. Thus the 'testing' undertaken by the applicant is to detect residue of various chemicals in the cultivated grapes and can also be to grade the cultivated grapes as per the 'Criteria for Grade designation' given in Schedule-II of 'Fruits and Vegetables Grading and Marking Rules, 2004'. Further, it is seen that 'Fruits and Vegetables Grading and Marketing Rules 2004', apply to commercial varieties of Fruits and Vegetables; Rule 7 of the said rule states that 'Fruits and Vegetables may be graded and marked as per buyer requirements for exports provided the minimum requirements specified in the relevant schedule are met'; and Rule 8 states that: 'For domestic trade, Fruits and Vegetables shall comply with the residue levels of heavy metals, pesticides, aflatoxin and other food safety parameters as specified in Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules 1955.'

In view of the foregoing, it is clear that, grading of fresh table grapes undertaken by the applicant is in accordance with the guidelines/provisions stipulated in the mentioned Trade notice of APEDA and the Fruits and Vegetables Grading and Marketing Rules and testing for residue of various chemicals/pesticides is as per 'Procedures for Export of Fresh Table Grapes to the European Union' of APEDA.[Para 7.2]

It is the contention of the applicant that they undertake testing of 'agricultural produce' and therefore would be covered under Entry 54 (a) of the Exemption Notification No. 12/2017-C.T.(Rate), dated 28-6-2017, the description of which is 'agricultural operations directly related to production of any agricultural produce including cultivation, harvesting, threshing, plant protection or testing' and chargeable to Nil rate of tax.[Para 7.3]
