Further the scheme of the Central SEZ Act, State SEZ Act and the Rules make the position clear that benefit is intended to the SEZ units for 'the authorised operations' which essentially is the export activity for which approval has been granted. [Para 21] The contention that the phrase 'goods exempted by notification' occurring in section 15 of VAT Act would not cover transaction under clause (b) of section 30(1) of VAT Act does not merit acceptance. Section 15 seeks to define what is exempted sale in the absence of any definition in section 2 of VAT Act, as section 2(20) only defines exempted goods. For the purpose of VAT, sale of goods specified in the Fourth Schedule and goods exempted by notification by the Government are exempted sale. Section 30 of the VAT Act is in pari materia with section 17 of Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act dealing power to notify exemption or reduction of tax. Clauses (a) or (b) or (c) under section 30(1) circumscribes the power of Government to notify exemption/reduction of tax in specified contingencies and would fall within the ambit of exempted sale as defined under section 15. Hence, no exception could be carved out as contended by the assessee. [Para 23]

In view of the aforesaid, the impugned circular No. 9 of 2013, dated 24-7-2013 sets out the statutory provision and the benefit of zero rating which accrues to the dealer under section 18 and the said circular is neither contrary nor ultra vires of the provisions of the VAT Act, not is it violative of article 14 of the Constitution or irrational. [Para 29]

facts.text:
The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

■

The AO had made a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) under section 92CA. Pursuant to this reference, the TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) accepting that the international transactions entered into by the assessee with its Associated Enterprises were at an Arms Length Price. In other words, the TPO made no variation.

■

The Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order under section 144C(1) and thereafter passed a final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(3) and section 144B.

■

On writ:

The assessee was a firm of chartered accountants. The original authority confirmed demand of service tax on the assessee for the period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 under the heads ‘Practising chartered accountant’, ‘Manpower recruitment service’, ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Business auxiliary service’. Modifying the findings of the original authority, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax under the head ‘Business auxiliary service’. He affirmed the demand on the assessee in respect of other categories of services. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had rendered services as management consultant and man-power recruitment agent which were exempt in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998. The assessee also contended that Commissioner (Appeals) had wrongly held that the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002 which inserted an Explanation to Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, had come into effect from 16-10-1998.

■

The assessee had claimed exemption under section 10(38) on LTCG arising out of trades carried out by him in the shares of company CCL. The Assessing Officer passed assessment order accepting claim of the assessee.

■

Subsequently, the Principal Commissioner noted that there was a very detailed report of the DGIT (Inv) based on the searches/survey conducted on a large number of hawala operators and entities controlled by them where they admitted to be providing entries through penny stock which also included name of CCL. He further noted that the Assessing Officer had evidence in hand in form of report from the investigation Wing, which alluded that the scrip of CCL was one of 84 scrips which was used by conniving operators and brokers to book unlawful LTCG and claim exemption under section 10(38). He thus invoked revisionary jurisdiction under section 263 on ground that the Assessing Officer had failed to take into account factual matrix and had not conducted any kind of independent verification or enquiries of his own and had merely allowed claim of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was engaged in providing taxable service under the category of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ and was also liable to pay service tax on goods transport service received by it. It availed benefit of abatement under Notification No. 32/2004-ST, dated 3-12-2004 with respect to goods transport service received. The revenue issued show-cause notice to the assessee denying benefit of said notification on ground that in view of relevant Boards’ circular in the consignment notes issued to the assessee by goods transport agencies, there was no declaration to the effect that no credit on input or capital goods used for providing services had been taken nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 was availed. However, the Commissioner taking into consideration the Chartered Accountant’s certificate to the effect that the transporters had neither availed CENVAT credit nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003, dropped the demand against the assessee.

On appeals :

The Appellants supplied Zinc Oxide to M/s. Premier Tyres for industrial purpose, namely, manufacture of rubber goods. They were denied the benefit of Notfn. No. 21/55-CE dt. 28.4.1975 on the ground that they did not follow the Chapter X Procedure prescribed in the Notfn. The Appellants produced CT2 certificate from the Departmental Officer at the user's end and also the connected L-6 Licence for using the exempted material.

■

The assessee–company operated CPPs qualifying under Section 80-IA. Inter-unit power transfers constituted Specified Domestic Transactions. After a search, the AO made a reference to the TPO under Section 92CA. The TPO called for details of cost allocation; the assessee’s TP study defended a 'Direct Nexus' methodology that excluded common HO costs from the CPPs. By order, the TPO accepted this methodology and reduced the transfer price to Rs. 2.48 per unit.

■

Relying on Section 92CA(4), the AO adopted the TPO’s findings while completing assessment, which eliminated eligible profits and reduced the Section 80-IA deduction to NIL.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reworked the grid rate and recomputed eligible profit at about Rs. 42.18 crores, directing allowance of deduction; the Revenue’s further appeal led to a limited remand to verify the recomputed figures.

■

Subsequently, the PCIT issued a SCN under Section 263 on the ground that the AO had not ensured proportionate allocation of common HO expenses to the eligible units and set aside the assessment on this limited issue for fresh examination.

■

The Tribunal affirmed the PCIT’s Section 263 action despite the TPO’s order, holding that the cost-allocation for computing eligible profits remained unexamined. On the assessee’s appeal to the High Court.

■

The assessee had established two captive electricity and steam generation units for the generation of electricity and steam. The assessee had sought exemption under section 80-IA(4)(iv) in respect of Co-generation Unit 1, specifically for the supply of electricity and steam to its non-specified unit, the Paper Unit.

■

The assessee had adopted the Transaction Net Margin Method (TNMM) for determining the arm''s length price for the transfer of power from the specified Co-generation Unit-1 to the non-specified Paper Unit and the sale value of the power had been determined by the assessee at Rs. 41.21 crores, based on a rate of Rs. 6.73 per KWH for a total of 61.24 crores units of power.

■

The Assessing Officer adopted a rate of Rs. 3.875 per unit (KVAH), instead of the assessee’s applied rate of Rs. 6.73 per unit (KWH). The Assessing Officer derived this rate by averaging the adjusted rate of Rs. 4.74 per unit (after making adjustments from Rs. 4.74 per unit) from PSPCL and the rate of Rs. 3.01 per unit from the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX). Consequently, the Assessing Officer computed a difference in the sale price of power and made an addition of Rs. 17.48 crores.

■

On appeal, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer''s approach was inconsistent with the provisions of section 92C(1), read with rule 10B, and section 80-IA(8), which govern the determination of arm''s length price and transfer pricing adjustments.The rate of 76.73 per KWH adopted by the assessee for the transfer of power was lower than the comparable rate for generating electricity from biomass fuel, as available in the public domain and the rate adopted by the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) of Rs. 5.98 per unit of PSPCL(Power Corporation) for deriving average was not justified, as the assessee was categorized as a power-intensive unit, and not under the general category.TPO wrongly deducted distribution loss, transmission loss, and cross-subsidy from the rate, leading to an incorrect revised adjusted sale rate of Rs. 4.74 per KVAH per unit for power supplied by PSPCL and the TPO failed to apply the appropriate division factor of 0.92 to convert KVAH into KWH. The price at which surplus power was supplied by producers to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) is determined by state regulations and contracts and, therefore, cannot be considered the market value for the purposes of Section 80-IA(8).

■

For AY 2021-22, the dispute pertained to a transfer pricing adjustment of about Rs. 33.60 crores on account of transfer of power, involving determination of arm’s length price/market value under Section 80IA read with Section 92F.

■

The assessee’s appeal before the Tribunal was partly allowed; on the specific issue of the transfer pricing adjustment on transfer of power, the Tribunal granted relief by relying on the Delhi High Court decision in Principal Commissioner of Income-tax v. DCM Shriram Ltd. [2025] 170 taxmann.com 631 (Delhi).

■

On appeal to the High Court.

■

The assessee was engaged in business of Gems and Jewellery, primarily manufacturing and export of diamond studded Jewellery. The assessee was having one of its units located in Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone-Special Economic Zone (SEEPZ- SEZ) Andheri (East), Mumbai. The assessee had another unit located outside of SEZ, which mainly supplied diamonds to manufacturing unit in SEZ. The assessee filed its return of income for assessment year 2021-22 declaring income of Rs.50.97 crores. Since, the assessee reported certain Specified Domestic Transaction (SDT) with its related party/associated enterprises, the Assessing Officer (AO) made reference under section 92CA (1) to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) for computation of Arm Length Price.

■

The Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) passed his order under section 92CA(3)and suggested addition/made downward adjustment of Rs.11.62 crore on account transaction of sale of jewelry.

■

The assessee before DRP submitted that Assessing Officer had erred in making reference to TPO by invoking provisions of section 80IA(10) without determining and establishing existence of an arrangement between the concerned parties which results in more than ordinary profit and therefore, whole proceedings initiated under transfer pricing provisions was bad in law.

■

. The DRP agreed with the stand of TPO.

■

On receipt of direction of DRP, the Assessing Officer passed final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C (13) read with section 144B and computed the final adjustment on account of sale transaction to its AE at Rs. 10.98 crore and straightway added the same to the income of assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee filed its return of income. Further, the assessee received notices under section 148 and under section 92CA from the Transfer Pricing Officer seeking details about the international transactions entered into by the assessee with the group companies on a reference made by the Assessing Authority. In reply to the notice issued, the assessee filed a letter requesting the Assessing Authority to treat the return filed as return in compliance with the notice under section 148. In fact, the Transfer Pricing Officer passed an order under section 92CA accepting the pricing of the Assessing Authority.

However, the Commissioner invoked section 263 and set aside the order of the Assessing Authority.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that when two views were possible and when the Transfer Pricing Authority accepted valuation by the Assessing Authority determining the arm's length price, the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to interfere with the said order under section 263. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the order of the Commissioner.

On revenue's appeal to the High Court :

Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It is cardinal rule of interpretation that where the language used by the legislature is clear and unambiguous then plain and natural meaning of those words should be applied to the language and resort to any rule of interpretation to unfold intentions is permissible where the language is ambiguous. [Para 9]

Now, the controversy in the instant case is disguised in the question as to whether the provisions of chapter X shall be invoked in a situation where the assessee is enjoying tax exemption under section 10A and/or where there is no motive to avoid tax. The purpose of enacting transfer pricing provisions was to put a stop to the avoidance of tax by shifting taxable income outside India. Similarly, extending the fundamental of intendment to section 10A it is comprehended that this particular section is purported to boost the business of those undertakings which are situated in free trade zones (FTZ) and engaged in export of article or things or computer software services etc. by exempting their income from levy of tax. Thus, here the question arises as to whether the transfer pricing provisions can be invoked concerning the international transaction carried out by the assessee with its AE where the former is enjoying exemption under section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the assessee might not have any motive to shift the income from India to a foreign country as the same has already been exempted under section 10A [Para 9.8]

In this connection, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. [Para 9.9]

Further, there is no express provision under the Act restricting the application of section 92C for determining the income at arm's length where such income is eligible for deduction under section 10A. On the contrary, there is a proviso to section 92C(4) which prohibits the deduction under section 10A on the income to the extent enhanced as an effect of a determination of ALP. [Para 9.10]

Thus, the proviso itself vividly reflects the intent of lawmakers that the provisions of chapter X shall prevail in all the cases of international transactions falling under the umbrella of section 92 including the income-qualified for exemption under section 10A. In other words, it can be said that the intention of the statute was very much lucid that section 92 should be invoked even when the assessee is entitled to deduction under section 10A. In the light of above perceivance, there is no need to refer to other means of interpretation if the words are clear and free from any ambiguity. However, if the words in the statute are vague and ambiguous, then external aid may be consulted for interpretation. This connotes that the statute should be read as a whole; therefore, the point which is not clear in one section may be explained in another section. [Para 9.11]

Accordingly, if the purpose or object of Chapter X and/or section 10A is being defeated, then it is up to the legislature, if they think so, to reconstruct the law as per the required object. [Para 9.12]

However, language used in section 92 is clear, unambiguous, and do not lead to any absurd meaning. Thus, there is no need to look into the intention or purpose of the statute or application of reasonable construction. Accordingly, it is meaningless to apply the principles of purposive or object-based rules of interpretation as contended by the assessee [Para 9.13]

Regarding the contentious of the assessee that budget speech & memorandum explaining the provisions, it is noted that it is also a settled legal position that headings or marginal notes do not govern a provision where the legislature has used plain and unambiguous language. It is when the language is equivocal only then, help can be taken from the circulars, marginal notes or the Finance Minister speech or memorandum explaining the provisions to interpret the provision of the Act. The Finance Minister speech and memorandum explaining the bill will not provide any aid to the assessee in the given facts & circumstances. [Para 9.15]

In the context of the CBDT Circulars bearing Nos. 12/2001 dated 23-08- 2001 and 14/2001 dated 9-11-2001, it is merely explaining the understanding of statutory provisions regarding the transfer pricing. Further, it is a well-settled principle that the departmental circulars are not binding on this court. These circulars cannot be used to usurp the power of a judicial body while exercising its jurisdiction, including interpreting the statutory provisions [Para 10]

It is well settled through series of judgments of the High Courts and Supreme Court that writ jurisdiction of the High Courts in exercise of powers under article 226 of Constitution of India is extremely wide. If a jurisdictional error is pointed out or it is shown that an authority has acted wholly without jurisdiction, the Court can, without relegating the petitioner/assessee to the departmental or even statutory remedies, strike down exercise of such powers. Therefore, if it is found that the action of the TPO or a part of it which can be severed from the rest is wholly without jurisdiction, such order or part thereof is to be struck down even though statute provides certain appeal remedies to the aggrieved assessee.[Para 4]

It is indisputable that by virtue of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, in case of an international transaction, the TPO would have an authority to examine any international transaction which comes to his notice during the proceedings, whether a reference in this respect was made by the Assessing Officer or not and whether the assessee had reported such transaction under section 92E or not. However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13]

In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

It is material to note that the TP adjustments are made pursuant to the APA entered into by the assessee with CBDT. Section 92CC empowers the CBDT to enter into an APA with any person for determining an ALP or specify the manner in which the ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person and income referred to in section 9(1)(i) or the manner in which said income is to be determined as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India. [Para 17]

■

It is relevant to refer to sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92CD. [Para 18]

■

The provisions of section 92CD(1) are unambiguous and even if a return has been filed prior to an assessee entering into an APA, he is entitled to furnish a modified return declaring his income in accordance with the terms of the APA. Subject to certain exceptions, the APA is binding both on the assessee and the revenue. [Para 19]

■

It is clear that the scheme of providing for an APA is to remove any uncertainty as to the determination of an income of an assessee engaged in international transactions with associated enterprises. The assessee is required to declare his income in accordance with the APA. Except in certain cases, where there is a change in law and facts or the agreement is occasioned by fraud or misrepresentation, the APA would be binding. Sub-sections (5), (6) and (7) of section 92CC provide for the same in unambiguous terms. [Para 20]

■

It is apparent from a plain reading of sub-section (4) of section 92C that the same is inapplicable. The said sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to compute the total income, having regard to the ALP determined by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (3) of section 92C. [Para 22]

■

Sub-section (3) of section 92C provides that the Assessing Officer can proceed to determine the ALP only in cases he is of the opinion on the basis of material that (a) the price charged or paid in international transaction, has not been determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92C; or (b) that information and documentation relating to the international transaction has not been maintained as mandatorily required; or (c) that the information or data for computing the ALP is unreliable; or there is failure on the part of the assessee to furnish any information or document required to be furnished along with the notice. [Para 23]

■

It is apparent that in a case where the assessee voluntarily computes the ALP pursuant to an APA entered into with CBDT, none of the conditions as set out in sub-section (3) of section 92C are attracted. It follows that sub-section (4) of section 92C is not attracted. [Para 24]

■

More importantly, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C also clearly states that no deduction under section 10A or 10AA or 10B or under Chapter VI-A would be allowed in respect of the amount of income by which the total income of the assessee is enhanced after computation under the said section. Thus in a case where the assessee voluntarily declares his income based on the ALP determined on the basis of an APA, there would be no occasion for the Assessing Officer to enhance the income of the assessee. [Para 25]

■

Absent any enhancement of income, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is clearly inapplicable. [Para 26]

■

It is also necessary to bear in mind that in terms of section 10AA(1), the profits and gains of an enterprise, as referred to in clause (j) of section 2 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, from an eligible unit, which is derived from export of articles or things are exempt. [Para 27]

■

The ALP is imputed to transactions to determine the profits and gains that are derived by the assessee from any international transactions (or specified domestic transactions) in order to assess the real income of the assessee after eliminating any bias or element of transfer of profits. [Para 28]

■

Thus, indisputably, the income computed on the basis of ALP would provide a measure of the profits or income derived by the activities carried on by an assessee. The proviso to section 92C(4) essentially limits exemption under section 10AA in cases where the income computed is enhanced by the Assessing Officer under section 92C. [Para 29]

Section 92CA(1) empowers the Assessing Officer to make reference to TPO for the computation of arm's length price of international transactions. Further, the TPO as defined in Explanation to section 92CA to be the person authorized by board to perform functions of Assessing Officer specified in section 92C. It is an undisputed fact that the Investigation Wing, during search and survey operations on N and his syndicate, unearthed a countrywide network engaged in providing accommodation entries of bogus long-term capital gains through manipulation of prices of penny-stock companies. Oasis, the scrip involved in the assessee's LTCG claim, is one of the companies identified by the Investigation Wing as being used for providing artificial gains. The Investigation Wing findings were specific, concrete and based on seized digital data, communications and statements. These findings were duly communicated to the jurisdictional Assessing Officer. The assessee was identified as a beneficiary who had derived exempt LTCG in the trading of penny scrip allegedly manipulated by the syndicate. Once such information was available, the Assessing Officer was under a statutory obligation to conduct a thorough, meaningful and logical inquiry into genuineness of the purchase of shares, source of funds and identity of transferor, manner of allotment and the subsequent bonus issue, dematerialisation process and trail, price movement of the scrip, role of the alleged operators and linkage, if any, between the assessee's transactions and the syndicate. [Para 9.1]

■

On perusal of the assessment record, it is evident that the Assessing Officer merely called for basic details such as contract notes, demat account, bank statements etc., which were furnished by the assessee. However, the Assessing Officer did not conduct even a single inquiry on the abnormal price rise of the scrip Oasis, the findings of the Investigation Wing and the material therein, the role of N and linkages to beneficiaries, cash trail behind the corresponding exit providers, verification of purchase entries prior to IPO and bonus issuance, genuineness of counterparty identity or the operators' role. The assessment order is a one-page acceptance of the returned income without any discussion, without any analysis of the material on record and without application of mind to the highly make believe LTCG claim flagged by the Investigation Wing. Mere production of documents by the assessee does not absolve the Assessing Officer of the responsibility to verify their genuineness. Hence, the order was erroneous and is duly covered by the Explanation 2 below sub-section (1) of section 263. [Para 9.2]

■

The Assessing Officer had before him credible, specific and detailed information from the Investigation Wing which concluded that Oasis was a penny stock used for providing artificial LTCG. The failure of the Assessing Officer to examine this crucial information or even discuss it in the assessment order makes the order per se erroneous. When the Assessing Officer is armed with such adverse material and still accepts the claim without inquiry, the assessment order becomes one passed in complete non-application of mind, a clear ground for revision under section 263. It is fully covered under the substantive part as well as the Explanation - 2 of section 263. [Para 9.3]

■

The assessee claimed exemption under section 10(38). Had the Assessing Officer conducted appropriate inquiry, he would have been in a position to verify whether the LTCG was genuine or the same was accommodation entry liable to addition under section 68 read with section 115BBE. Omission to examine a claim of this magnitude, especially when it arises from a scrip tainted by Investigation Wing reports, undeniably causes prejudice to the interests of the revenue. [Para 9.4]

■

The assessee argued that Oasis was listed after IPO, bonus shares were issued lawfully and the demat entries and STT payment demonstrate genuineness. However, it is well settled that payment of STT or existence of demat entries does not ipso facto establish genuineness, if the underlying transaction is part of a manipulative chain and the fact that shares were listed on BSE does not negate the possibility of price rigging, which is precisely what the Investigation Wing unearthed. Most importantly, the assessee's submissions do not cure the fundamental defect that the Assessing Officer failed to investigate these very aspects. [Para 9.5]

■

The Principal Commissioner has examined the assessment record, identified lack of inquiry and non-application of mind and gave adequate opportunity to the assessee. He also recorded clear reasons why the Assessing Officer's order was erroneous and prejudicial. The Principal Commissioner has not set aside the assessment for a fishing inquiry; rather, for conducting specific, meaningful verification of the suspicious LTCG claim, which the Assessing Officer ought to have undertaken. Thus, the jurisdiction under section 263 was correctly and lawfully invoked. [Para 9.6]

The following issues need to be adjudicated in the case of the assessee, which emanates from the issues raised:

(i)

What is role of the Assessing Officer before/while making reference to the TPO. Is any hearing to be allowed to the assessee under section 92CA(1)/92C(3)?

(ii)

Whether while benchmarking a reported transaction (in Form No.3CEB) can the TPO enlarge his scope and look at other connected international transactions, not referred to him?

(iii)

Whether in above scenario, can TPO also decide the issue of control and management of other AEs in the hands of the assessee and extent of world profits to be attributed to the assessee?

(iv)

Whether jurisdiction of the TPO was to determine ALP of international transactions and not compute the income arising out of such international transactions and related income of world profits i.e. out of group concerns?

(v)

Whether the said transaction of control and management was international transaction as envisaged under section 92B?

(vi)

Whether the exercise carried on by the TPO was beyond his jurisdiction of determination of ALP of international transaction in view of provisions of section 6(3)? [Para 58]

Reference to TPO - Precondition

The first step is for the Assessing Officer to give show cause notice to the assessee as to why transfer pricing proceedings should not be initiated in his case and thereafter, the Assessing Officer is to proceed to determine ALP of international transaction and pass consequent order thereto. In other words, a safeguard is provided under the Act itself where the Assessing Officer exercises the power to determine ALP of international transactions in the given circumstances. The revenue has time and again announced value of international transactions, wherein if the value of international transactions is less than threshold limits, then such power is exercised by the Assessing Officer and in case it is above the threshold limit then power vests with the TPO to determine ALP of international transactions undertaken by the assessee. [Para 63]

Where the assessee had entered into an international transaction, in any previous year and if the Assessing Officer considers it necessary or expedient to do so, he may with the previous approval of Commissioner refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to international transaction under section 92CA to the TPO. As referred in the paras above, under section 92, what has to be determined is 'the income arising from an international transaction', which needs to be computed in the hands of the assessee, having regard to arm's length price of international transaction undertaken by the assessee. In other words, the Assessing Officer before making reference to the TPO has to come to a finding that it is either necessary or expedient to make reference to the TPO for computation of ALP of international transactions undertaken by him. So, the first step in this regard is that the Assessing Officer should come to a finding that some income arises from the international transaction undertaken by the assessee, which needs to be benchmarked and its ALP needs to be determined. [Para 65]

The question which arises is how the Assessing Officer comes to know that there is an international transaction undertaken by the assessee. The first and foremost is the audit report submitted by the assessee in Form No.3CEB, which is self declaration made by the assessee that it has entered into international transactions with its AE/s. Once such declaration is made, then the Assessing Officer has to come to a finding that the income arising from such an international transaction needs to be computed to find out whether it is at ALP by applying any one of the prescribed methods under section 92C(1). This is the preliminary satisfaction of the Assessing Officer. [Para 66]

The Courts have held that this satisfaction needs to be recorded by the Assessing Officer before making reference to the TPO, who shall carry out detailed analysis of international transactions undertaken by the assessee applying the most appropriate method and determine ALP of international transactions. It may be pointed out that role played by the Assessing Officer while making reference to the TPO is at variance to the role of the TPO, who has to finally determine ALP of international transactions undertaken by the assessee. [Para 67]

The Assessing Officer is not required to demonstrate the existence of the circumstances set out in clauses (a) to (d) of section 92C(3) before referring the case of the assessee to the TPO for determining the ALP under section 92CA(1) for the reasons given hereafter. [Para 26]

A close reading of sections 92C and 92CA reveals that proceedings in both the sections are quite independent of and distinct from each other and the proceedings under section 92CA(1) are not dependent on the proceedings under section 92C(3). This is due to historical reasons as two provisions were introduced at different times. The provisions of section 92C(3) confer powers on the Assessing Officer to determine the ALP himself where the circumstances mentioned in clauses (a ) to (d) of the sub section exist. This is apparent from a bare reading of the provision. In such cases, the Assessing Officer is not bound to refer the case of the assessee to the TPO. On the other hand, the Assessing Officer may refer the case of the assessee to the TPO if he considers it necessary or expedient to do so. The expression ‘necessary’ or ‘expedient’ is quite distinct from and independent of the circumstances mentioned in section 92C(3). The Assessing Officer may consider it necessary or expedient to refer the case of the assessee to the TPO even without considering existence of circumstances mentioned in section 92C. The Assessing Officer has only to be satisfied that it is necessary or expedient to make a reference to the TPO. No other condition is prescribed in the provision. Now under what circumstances, the Assessing Officer would consider it ‘necessary’ or ‘expedient’ would depend upon facts of each case. No doubt, even in cases covered by section 92C(3), the Assessing Officer may in appropriate cases consider it necessary or expedient to refer the case of the assessee to the TPO for determining the ALP but that does not mean that powers of the Assessing Officer to refer the case to the TPO are restricted to those cases which are covered by section 92C(3). Had the L egislature contemplated to refer the case of the assessee to the TPO only in the circumstances mentioned in section 92C(3), then the L egislature would have to provide such conditions in place of words ‘necessary’ or ‘expedient’ in section 92CA(1). The requirements under both the sections are quite distinct as procedure to be followed in the sections is different. In section 92CA(1), there is no reference to section 92C(3). Moreover, it is mandatory for the TPO to determine ALP in accordance with section 92C(3). If above section is to be applied by the TPO under section 92CA(3) at the prescribed stage, there is no question of applying the same provision at the stage of making reference. It would be sufficient for invoking provisions of section 92CA(1) if it is shown that there existed circumstances which prompted the Assessing Officer to consider it necessary or expedient to refer the computation of ALP to the TPO. Once it is shown that there existed circumstances on the basis of which the Assessing Officer could consider it necessary or expedient, the matter ends. [Para 27]

From the explanation of the CBDT vide circular No. 14 of 2001 dated 9-11-2001 and judicial precedents, it is clear that the provisions of the Transfer Pricing were introduced in the statute to ensure that due to any arrangement made by the assessee with its AE in the course of an international transaction, income taxable in India is not reduced for any reason. Further in a case where the income derived from an international transaction is exempt from tax in India because of provisions of section 10A, then it cannot be held that because of an arrangement between the assessee and its AE any income taxable in India had been under-reported. [Para 31]

At the same time, there is no provision in the statute to show that in case of an assessee whose income is exempt under section 10A, international transaction made with an AE should not be benchmarked with ALP determined on the basis of the provisions of Transfer Pricing. [Para 32]

TPO has not accepted the contention of the assessee on the ground that the provisions of section 92C (4) envisaged a situation wherein it has been provided that no deduction under section 10A etc. will be allowed to the assessee in respect of total income which is enhanced because of provisions of Transfer Pricing. Thus, it is observed as per the CBDT's explanation, provisions of Transfer Pricing has been enacted to ensure that no income otherwise taxable in India is reduced and even a transaction resulting in exempt income is also subjected to provisions of Transfer Pricing. [Para 33]

In such circumstances, one is confronted with the issue as to how and why the provisions of Transfer Pricing should be applied in respect of an international transaction giving rise to exempt income in the hands of the assessee. [Para 34]

In such circumstances, where the income derived from international transactions is exempt from tax in India, it cannot be alleged that the assessee had arranged its affairs in such a manner so as to show lesser taxable income in India but it can be alleged that the assessee has arranged its affairs in such a manner so as to reflect more exempt income in India. [Para 35]

Therefore, a harmonious reading can be construed in the provisions of section 92C(4) and the object and purport of insertion of the provisions of Transfer Pricing as explained by the CBDT. [Para 36]

In a case where the international transaction entered into by the assessee with the AEs is giving rise to exempt income in the hands of the assessee, it is to be benchmarked with the ALP determined in accordance with the provisions of Transfer Pricing to ensure that no excess exempt income is disclosed by the assessee and assessee is entitled for exemption of income under section 10A of the total income determined as per the Transfer Pricing Provisions only and where the assessee has claimed more exempt income, then exemption under section 10A shall be allowed in accordance with the profit compared as per ALP only. [Para 37]

Keeping in view the above in mind in the instant case, as per the decisions of the lower authorities the assessee had not reported any excess exempt income from its international transactions with AE. On the other hand, as per the opinion of the lower authorities when exempt income declared by the assessee was benchmarked with the ALP determined in accordance with the provisions of Transfer Pricing, it was found that assessee has declared lesser exempt income and thereby no taxable base in India was eroded. Therefore, no adjustment with the exempt income of the assessee was required to be made as per provisions contained in Chapter X of the Act. [Para 38]

In view of the above, the Assessing Officer was directed to treat the income declared from the business in question at the amount as shown by the assessee in its return of income. [Para 40]

There was registration certificate dated 30-6-2000 with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991. The object of the exemption notification was neither to protect the owners of the trade mark nor the consumers from being misled. These were considerations which were relevant in disputes arising under the Trade Marks Act. The object of the exemption Notification No. 1/93-CE was to grant benefits to those industries, which did not have the advantage of a brand name. [Para 16] It is correct to say that the Registrar of Trade Marks can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect. Making the registration certificate applicable from retrospective date is based on principle of deemed equivalence to public user of such mark. This deeming fiction cannot be extended to Excise Law. It is confined to the provisions of the Trade Marks Act. In a given case like the instant one, where there was evidence with the department of the trade mark being owned by company ‘K’ and there was evidence of the appellants trading on the reputation of ‘K’ which was not rebutted by them, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect could not confer the benefit of exemption notification upon them. In the instant case, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991 would not tantamount to conferment of exemption benefit under the Excise Law, once it was found that the appellants had wrongly used the trade mark of company ‘K’. [Paras 17 & 18]

If the SSI unit wrongly affixes a trade mark of another person, be it registered or not, or if it uses the trade mark of an ineligible person, such default would not be eliminated by the principle of deemed equivalence embodied in section 28; as that principle is based on a deeming fiction, which fiction is confined only to the provisions of that Act. [Para 20]

Consequently, the appeals were to be dismissed.

PER COURT

"The Trade Marks Act has been enacted to amend and consolidate the law relating to trade marks, to provide for registration and better protection of trade marks and for prevention of the use of fraudulent marks. Under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act, registration gives to the registered proprietor of the trade mark the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods in respect of which the trade mark is registered and to obtain relief in respect of infringement of the trade mark in the manner provided by the Trade Marks Act. It is correct to say that the Registrar, Trade Marks, can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect". [Para 17]

The statute has primarily conferred certain functions of Assessing Officer on TPO but that does not imply that jurisdiction of Assessing Officer to determine ALP gets excluded on reference being made by him to TPO for determining ALP. The substantive power of determining ALP vests in Assessing Officer as per section 92C. The reference to TPO as per section 92CA is only to facilitate proper determination of ALP. TPO has to simply pass an order determining the ALP and send the same to Assessing Officer who is ultimately authorized to pass the assessment order though in conformity with ALP determined by TPO. Thus, primarily section 92CA has been incorporated in order to ensure proper determination of ALP. The TPO primarily performs the functions which are to be performed by the Assessing Officer only. As per CBDT Instruction No. 3 of 2003, the Assessing Officer can make a valid reference to the TPO only if the correct value of international transaction exceeds Rs. 5 crores. Thus, the services of office of TPO can be utilized by Assessing Officer in such cases where revenue effect is likely to be considerable. This is primarily a legislative in-built check on the quasi judicial functions to be performed by Assessing Officer. For the purposes of performance of all or any of the functions of an Assessing Officer, the TPO is considered at par with an Assessing Officer. But essentially it is the function of Assessing Officer only to determine the ALP. Therefore, there is no infirmity in the ALP being determined by the Assessing Officer as per section 92C(3) even after making a reference to TPO under section 92CA which was returned by TPO without determining the ALP. [Para 15]

Thus, the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) may require (from any person) any information or document as may be prescribed. Word 'any' information or document cannot ordinarily mean 'all' the documents prescribed under rule 10D. The word 'required' is important as it rules out option with the assessee and makes it obligatory to furnish the requisite information.

It is clear from above that the power under section 92D(3) can be used in the course of the assessment proceedings, i.e., in proceedings for determination of ALP and only for requiring to furnish prescribed information or documents under rule 10D. It being a provision connected with procedure to help an assessment, must be purposefully construed. But, regulation does not provide any time or stage when power to issue notice is to be exercised. However, scheme of assessment do indicate the stage at which it is to be issued and the purpose which is required to be achieved through the issuance of such a notice. [Para 24.6]

The TPO is thereafter required to serve notice under sub-section (2) of section 92CA. The statutory scheme envisages that the TPO shall serve a notice requiring the assessee to produce evidence in support of his computation of ALP. Therefore, an opportunity to prove that its ALP is correct has to be allowed to the assessee. It is mandatory requirement of the regulations. Thereafter, notices under section 92D(3) may be issued requiring the assessee to furnish information on 'specified points', depending upon the facts of the case. It is not that issuance of notice under section 92D(3) along with notice under section 92CA(2) is illegal, but where heavy penalty is attracted for non-compliance, it has to be shown that the notice under section 92D(3) is complied, both in letter and in the spirit of the statute. This conclusion is based on the scheme and the clear language used in the regulations. Steps as per regulations are to be followed in sequence. Report in Form No. 3CEB in the first instance, is obtained from the assessee. Next step is to issue notice under section 92CA(2) to the assessee to produce evidence in support of ALP. [Para 24.7]

Under sub-section (2) of section 92CA, evidence in support of ALP would ordinarily include information and documents referred to in sub-section (3) of section 92D which are prescribed in various clauses of rule 10D(1). Documents and information prescribed are required to be maintained to help to determine ALP and are to be filed to support ALP by the assessee in response to the notice under section 92CA(2). If on consideration of evidence produced by the assessee, the TPO is satisfied that ALP has been properly and correctly determined by the assessee, it is the end of the matter. There is no question of issuing further notice under any provision to the assessee. However, if complete information is not furnished, or otherwise, the TPO is of the view that more information on specified points is required from the assessee, he can issue notice under sub-section (3) of section 92D. The TPO can also issue notice under section 92CA(3), depending upon the facts of the case and the information needed. Only in case of failure of the assessee to support its ALP by filing necessary evidence, question of requiring the assessee to furnish prescribed information would arise. There is no rationality in requiring information, documents from the assessee first under section 92D(3) and thereafter provide opportunity to the assessee to support its ALP. Further, having regard to purpose of the regulations, the notice under section 92D(3) must require specific information (or document) which the assessee failed to furnish under section 92CA(2), but which, according to the TPO, is necessary for determination of ALP of international transactions.

9.7 The above judgment makes it vivid and beyond any reasonable doubt that courts are not required to look into the object or intention of the Legislature by resorting to the aids of interpretation where the language used in the statute is clear and free from any ambiguity. To strengthen our findings, we also find support and guidance from the Apex court in case of Rishabh agro industries Ltd v. P.N.B. Capital services Ltd. [2000] 5 SCC 515 wherein it was held as under:

"While interpreting, this Court only interprets the law and cannot legislate it. If a provision of law is misused and subjected to the abuse of process of law, it is for the Legislature to amend modify or repeal it by having recourse to appropriate procedure, if deemed necessary."

9.8 Now, the controversy in the instant case is disguised in the question as to whether the provisions of chapter X shall be invoked in a situation where the assessee is enjoying tax exemption under section 10A of the Act and/or where there is no motive to avoid tax. We find that the purpose of enacting transfer pricing provisions was to put a stop to the avoidance of tax by shifting taxable income outside India. Similarly, extending the fundamental of intendment to section 10A of the Act, we comprehend that this particular section is purported to boost the business of those undertakings which are situated in free trade zones (FTZ) and engaged in export of article or things or computer software services etc. by exempting their income from levy of tax. Thus, here the question arises as to whether the transfer pricing provisions can be invoked concerning the international transaction carried out by the assessee with its AE where the former is enjoying exemption under section 10A of the Act. It is because, in such a situation, the assessee might not have any motive to shift the income from India to a foreign country as the same has already been exempted under section 10A of the Act.

9.9 In this connection, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. It reads as under:

92C. (1) The arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction shall be determined by any of the following methods, being the most appropriate method, having regard to the nature of transaction or class of transaction or class of associated persons or functions performed by such persons or such other relevant factors as the Board may prescribe36, namely :—

(a)

comparable uncontrolled price method;

(b)

resale price method;

(c)

cost plus method;

(d)

profit split method;

(e)

transactional net margin method;

(f)

such other method as may be prescribed36 by the Board.

(2) The most appropriate method referred to in sub-section (1) shall be applied, for determination of arm's length price, in the manner as may be prescribed 36:

Provided that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the arithmetical mean of such prices:

Provided further that if the variation between the arm's length price so determined and price at which the international transaction or specified domestic transaction has actually been undertaken does not exceed such percentage not exceeding three per cent of the latter, as may be notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette in this behalf, the price at which the international transaction or specified domestic transaction has actually been undertaken shall be deemed to be the arm's length price :

Provided also that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction undertaken on or after the 1st day of April, 2014, shall be computed in such manner as may be prescribed and accordingly the first and second proviso shall not apply.

34 [Reference to Transfer Pricing Officer.

92CA. (1) Where any person, being the assessee, has entered into an international transaction in any previous year, and the Assessing Officer considers it necessary or expedient so to do, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner, refer the computation of the arm’s length price in relation to the said international transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer.

(2) Where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the Transfer Pricing Officer shall serve a notice on the assessee requiring him to produce or cause to be produced on a date to be specified therein, any evidence on which the assessee may rely in support of the computation made by him of the arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction referred to in sub-section (1).

(3) On the date specified in the notice under sub-section (2), or as soon thereafter as may be, after hearing such evidence as the assessee may produce, including any information or documents referred to in sub-section (3) of section 92D and after considering such evidence as the Transfer Pricing Officer may require on any specified points and after taking into account all relevant materials which he has gathered, the Transfer Pricing Officer shall, by order in writing, determine the arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction in accordance with sub-section (3) of section 92C and send a copy of his order to the Assessing Officer and to the assessee.

(4) On receipt of the order under sub-section (3), the Assessing Officer shall proceed to compute the total income of the assessee under sub-section (4) of section 92C having regard to the arm’s length price determined under sub-section (3) by the Transfer Pricing Officer.

(5) With a view to rectifying any mistake apparent from the record, the Transfer Pricing Officer may amend any order passed by him under sub-section (3), and the provisions of section 154 shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly.

(6) Where any amendment is made by the Transfer Pricing Officer under sub-section (5), he shall send a copy of his order to the Assessing Officer who shall thereafter proceed to amend the order of assessment in conformity with such order of the Transfer Pricing Officer.

(7) The Transfer Pricing Officer may, for the purposes of determining the arm’s length price under this section, exercise all or any of the powers specified in clauses (a ) to (d) of sub-section (1) of section 131 or sub-section (6) of section 133.

5.1 Exempted services - The services which were made exempt due to this notification are all the services except the services mentioned in the notification. The main service which had been made exempt through this exemption notification was tax consultancy or taxation work of the chartered accountants and now withdrawal of the same is the main cause of concern to the practising chartered accountants because at present for vast majority of chartered accountants, the main professional work is tax practice and specially in the small cities the work related to taxation matters and tax consultancy is proportionately much higher than the audit work. The same thing cannot be said for the cost accountants and company secretaries because practically the number of cost accountants and company secretaries engaged in doing tax consultancy is very minimum compared to the chartered accountants but if any cost accountant or company secretary is also providing the taxation and other consultancy service, then the effect of withdrawal of this notification on them will be the same.

Withdrawal of exemption is discriminatory

6. The affected and concerned chartered accountants have termed this withdrawal of exemption as totally discriminatory and unwarranted. In their opinion this exemption was given after due and prolonged deliberation and after considering the whole situation and circumstances in 1998 and it is based on the fact that the field other than the audit work and statutory certification work is not exclusively reserved for the chartered accountants or company secretaries or cost accountants, as the case may be. For the same type of service the other professionals including the legal and tax practitioners are not liable to pay service tax. Then how the chartered accountants or cost accountants or company secretaries, as the case may be, can alone be taxed in this respect. The affected chartered accountants have rightly pointed out that the taxation practice related to VAT, income tax and service tax is major part of their professional receipts and these fields are open for the other professionals also. Then why the chartered accountants are chosen for this tax and why they have been denied the level playing field.

FAQ 90. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

FAQ 91. Whether Treaty Shopping is ipso facto an IAA and reportable in Clause 30C?

Treaty shopping is not, per se, an IAA. Treaty Shopping is to be reported only if it is abusive, i.e. it satisfies the definition of IAA. In Her Majesty The Queen v. Alta Energy Luxembourg S.A.R.L [2022] 144 taxmann.com 23 (SCC), the Supreme Court of Canada held that GAAR could be invoked against treaty shopping only if it perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states. Treaty Shopping per se is not abusive tax avoidance [Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement in Indian GAAR] so as to attract GAAR. Treaty shopping is abusive tax avoidance and attracts GAAR, but only when treaty shopping perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states.

tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable. Before going into the impact of the rescission of the exemption notification, one should first understand the statutory charge of service tax on the practising chartered accountants, as given in Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994,—

(a) Meaning of practising chartered accountant [Section 65(83)] : Practising chartered accountant means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

(b) Taxable service [Section 65(105 )(s)] : Taxable service means any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity, in any manner.

Position before withdrawal of exemption notification

2. Before rescission of the service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, i.e., upto February 28, 2006, all services, except those mentioned below, provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA were exempt from service tax—

(a)accounting and auditing; or

(b)cost accounting and cost auditing; or

(c)secretarial auditing; or

(d)verification of declarations in prescribed forms of compliances for obtaining a certificate of commencement of business or commencement of other business under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(e)signing of the annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(f)certification that requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, 1956 have been complied with as regards statutory guidelines for appointment of managerial personnel and payment of managerial remuneration to them without the approval of the Central Government under section 269 and Schedule XIII, of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(g)certification of documents to be filed by companies with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956; or

(h)certification in Form No. 1 that the whole of the amount remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a period of three years from the date of transfer to the special account under section 205(1)/(2) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been transferred to the General Revenue Account of the Central Government under the Companies Unpaid Dividend (Transfer to General Revenue Account of the Central Government) Rules, 1978; or

(i)certification of documents under the Exports and Imports Policy of the Government of India; or

(j)certification for exchange control purposes which a practising chartered accountant can issue as documentary evidence in support of certain applications under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973; or

(k)certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957.

Thus, in case any practising CA/CS/ICWA was rendering any service other than (a) to (k ) enumerated above, like legal or taxation consultancy service, etc., he wasn’t liable for service tax.

However, any service provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, which fell under the ambit of any other taxable service, was liable to service tax under the category of that other taxable service. For example, if a chartered accountant also provided manpower recruitment services to his clients, then he was liable to service tax on such services under the category of manpower recruitment service.

Reasons behind issuance of earlier exemption notification

3. The said exemption notification was issued on the principles of equity. The then Government had recognized the fact that the—

(i)practising CA/CS/ICWAs were providing services like legal consultancy, etc., which were equally being provided by other professionals like advocates and legal practitioners and, therefore,

(ii)levy of service tax on such services provided by practising CA/CS/ICWAs and non-levy of service tax on the same services provided by advocates and legal practitioners would be inequitable levy.

Having recognized the abovesaid facts the aforesaid exemption notification was issued to prevent the levy of service tax from being unjust and inequitable.

Position after withdrawal of exemption notification

4. After the withdrawal of the aforesaid exemption notification by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, i.e., with effect from March 1, 2006 all the services provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, in his professional capacity, are chargeable to service tax.

Section 65(105)(zzi) - Technical inspection and certification service - Jewellery

Prima facie, it appears, ‘technical inspection’ must involve some technique. In the case of jewellery, this technique should be capable of revealing the chemical composition of the goods in terms of the percentage of gold and copper.

Where it was apparent from the records that the appellant received remuneration on a monthly basis from the bank for the service of examining jewellery and certifying its quality but the revenue had not established that the appellant’s touchstone was capable of yielding such result, the Tribunal held that it was difficult to sustain the decision of the lower authorities.

[S. Murugan v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 34 (Chennai - CESTAT)]

Section 65(105)(zzzq) - Business support services - Verification of details given by loan seekers

The assessee was appointed by bank to verify correctness, fairness and authenticity of informations furnished by those seeking bank loans. The Tribunal held that the verification of details given by loan seekers could not be treated as promoting bank’s business and, hence, could not be treated as ‘Business auxiliary service’. Services rendered by the assessee would be covered under category of ‘Business support service’ which was taxable with effect from 1-5-2006; however, since service was rendered prior to 1-5-2006, the assessee was held not liable to pay service tax.

[S.R. Kalyanakrishnan v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 454 (Bang. - CESTAT)]

Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - GTA services

The assessees were recipients of GTA services which was an input for final products produced by them. They paid service tax by utilization of Cenvat credit on aforesaid services. The Department objected to such payment by utilization of Cenvat credit. The Tribunal held that since GTA service is very much an output service by definition, the appellants were entitled to utilize credit available to them in respect of input service towards payment of service tax on GTA services.

[Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd. v. CCE, C&ST [2008] 12 STT 155 (Kol. - CESTAT)]

Rule 4, read with rule 3, of the Export of Services Rules, 2005 - Export without payment of service tax

The assessee was providing taxable service under category of ‘Courier agency service’. The revenue proceeded against the assessee on the ground that it had not paid service tax for the period from 15-3-2005 to 15-6-2005 on international consignments. The assessee contended that the international consignments during the relevant period were exempted under rule 4. However, the Commissioner held that in the instant case, the service provider, viz., the assessee was in India and the service receiver who handed over the consignment, was also in India and, in such circumstances, there was no question of any export of service. Accordingly, he confirmed the demand along with interest and also imposed penalties.

FAQ 72. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

FAQ 74. How to calculate the interest on excess money that needs to be repatriated after a primary adjustment?

Rule 10CB provides the rate of interest at which interest has to be calculated on excess money or part thereof that is not repatriated within the time limit. Where the international transaction is denominated in Indian rupees, the rate of interest will be the one-year marginal cost of fund lending rate of the State Bank of India as of 1st April of the relevant previous year, plus 325 basis points (plus 3.25%). Where the international transaction is denominated in foreign currency, the rate of interest shall be the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) as of 30th September of the relevant previous year plus 300 basis points (plus 3%).

It is possible that the amount of imputed interest income on the excess money not repatriated to India may relate to more than one year. Having regard to Rule 10CB, the interest liability extends till the date of repatriation. Accordingly, for the relevant year under audit, such liability in respect of imputed interest may extend not only to the primary adjustment but may also relate to the primary adjustment made in the earlier years.

1. A Firm of chartered accountants has the gross billing for the year ending on 31-3-2006 as under:— Since the service provided by the firm with respect to audit was only 2.30 Lakh hence the firm is not collecting and paying service tax in the year 2006-07 on the assumption that it is eligible for the benefit of exemption available to the small service providers as per Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) up to the value of 4 Lakh of collection. Please advise properly.

The total taxable service rendered by this firm of Rs.4.30 Lakhs in the previous year ended on 31-3-2006 hence the firm is not eligible for the exemption scheme available to this firm.

For this purpose there is clear provision in the Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) in the form of conditions mentioned in clause 2 of the scheme. The exact wording of clause 2(viii) is as under:—

"(viii)The aggregate value of taxable services rendered by a provider of taxable service from one or more premises, does not exceed rupees four lakhs in the preceding financial year."

Here, to be eligible for exemption scheme available to small service providers, the aggregate value of taxable service should not be more than Rupees 4 Lakh in the preceding financial year and both the Audit services and taxation services were part of taxable service though the tax was exempt on the taxation services. Let us see the exact wordings of the Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 in this respect:—

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994(32 of 1994); and in suppression of the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) No. 57/98 Service tax, dated 7-10-1998, the Central Government, being satisfied that it is necessary in the Public interest so to do, hereby exempts the taxable service provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity to a client, other than the taxable service related to—

(i)Accounting and auditing; or

(ii)to (xi) Various services Like certification etc. mentioned,

from whole of the service tax leviable thereon.

Here that the service is taxable but this taxable service is exempt from paying the whole of tax. The point here is that the taxable service is exempt from paying the tax and in that case its structure of taxable service remained intact but the tax payable on it is exempt.

Hence the value of taxable service provided by the firm of Chartered Accountant is Rs. 4.30 Lakhs and as per provisions of clause 2(viii) of the exemption notification, the service provider having turnover of taxable service over Rs.4 Lakhs is not eligible for exemption scheme provided to the small service provider.

Though while claiming exemption under this notification "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" means excluding the taxable service on which no service tax is payable and this has been provided in Explanation (B) the said notification and the "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" is applicable for the claiming the exemption but to ascertain the status "Small service provider" and the eligibility of the assessee to claim the exemption which is based on "the aggregate value of taxable service rendered" of the previous year, no such explanation is issued and in absence of any clarification from the Government in this respect,the opinion mentioned above is given.
