Who is primarily responsible to furnish information in Form No. 3CEB - Taxpayer or the auditor?

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill,2012 clarifies that "If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under section 92E then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction so as to make a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer." Thus, from the Explanatory Memorandum, it is clear that it is the primary responsibility of an asssessee to furnish correct and complete details of all international transactions/SDTs undertaken by him during the year.

Who can be appointed for conduct the audit envisaged under section 92E

Who is eligible to be the auditor u/s 92E?

According to section 92E, the report should be an 'accountant'. Section 92F(i) defines 'accountant' has having the same meaning as in Explanation below section 288(2). According to the above mentioned explanation, it covers a CA and Restricted State auditor.

According to ICAI's 'Guidance Note on Report on International Transactions under section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Transfer Pricing)' hereinafter referred to as "Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing" :

♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

♦ Ascertaining and reporting whether the assessee has maintained proper information and documentations prescribed in respect of international transactions entered into by him.

(a)Income-tax Officers, Central Excise Officers and Sales-tax Officers when they are adjudicating an issue or hearing an appeal.

(b)Registrar of Companies, Regional Director in Ministry of Company Affairs, Registrar of [Cooperative Societies etc. only when they are adjudicating an issue.

(c)Other statutory authorities like Municipal Corporations etc. when some adjudication or appeal is there.

(d)Adjudication by SEBI Authorities under SEBI Act.

(e)Tribunals like ITAT, CESTAT, CLB, CAT, SAT etc.

2.1 No relief in case of other non-statutory services - Admittedly, Government has realised that there was discrimination and some relief has been given. However, the relief is partial.

There is no relief in case of other non-statutory services like tax consultation, preparation and filing of tax returns, accounts writing work and issuing non-statutory certificates.

There is also no relief in case of other services like appearing before various authorities for permissions, clearances, licenses etc. where there is no legal proceeding is pending.

All these services (except probably non-statutory certificates) can be issued even by professionals other than practising CA/CWA/CS. Hence, these services should also be exempt, to ensure level playing field.

2.2 Hope for complete and retrospective relief - It is hoped that full relief will be given and status quo ante shall be fully restored.

It is also hoped that relief will be granted at least for the period 1-4-2006 to 12-7-2006. It is true that an exemption notification cannot be issued with retros-pective effect but retrospective exemption can be given by Parliament which has plenary powers.

If retrospective amendments can be made to nullify effects of judgments of Supreme Court and High Courts, there is no reason why retrospective amendment cannot be made for granting relief to practising CA/CS/CWA who were and are facing discriminatory treatment.

Similarly, detailed provisions relating to APAs are also contained in the US Code. Given the uncertainties associated with the current Indian transfer pricing legislation, India would do well to institute an advance pricing mechanism immediately.1

Relationship with customs laws 8. The concept of transfer pricing was already present in the Customs Act in the form of Customs Valuation Rules. Under these rules, unless an exception applies, the ‘Assessable Value’ is the invoice value (i.e., ‘Transaction Value’). For customs duty, either the transaction value is accepted as the assessable value or the case is referred to the Special Valuation Branch (SVB), which then determines the assessable value. The issue is whether the assessable value determined under the Customs Act would be accepted by the IT Department as an ‘Arm’s Length Price’? There is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect. The invoice value of imported goods shall be the transaction value, only if the Customs Officer has no reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of the value declared. However, the IT Department may contend that customs authorities merely ensure that the import price is at least equal to the assessable value and in particular, customs authorities may not investigate whether the goods are overpriced. However, it appears that the customs authorities’ acceptance of a transaction value could serve as documentation support for proving that it is an arm’s length prie. In the event, the IT Department arrives at an arm’s length price, which is different from the assessable value, can the customs authorities reopen their assessment and revalue the imports? As per the Customs Act, the authorities can reopen assessment within a period of 5 years provided there is concealment. Practically, the chances of reopening the case are remote because the objective of customs authorities and IT authorities are contrary.2

Relationship with FEMA

9. Under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), an issue could arise in case of imports, wherein the IT Department determines an arm’s length price, which is lower than actual import price. In such a case, it will be interesting to see whether the RBI would take a stand that the Indian entity has overpaid and hence the excess amount paid by Indian entity should be brought back into India. As per section 8 of the FEMA, an Indian resident has to bring into India all foreign exchange amounts, which are due or accrued to him. The issue is whether an Indian resident has to bring into India, additional foreign exchange on account of an adjustment made by the IT authorities under TP regulations? Broadly, the literal interpretation of the word ‘due’ would mean the amount ‘due’ as per contractual agreement and not the amount assessed by IT authorities which is determined long after the transaction is completed. Currently, consultancy fees up to US $ 100,000 can be remitted abroad under automatic approval and for fees exceeding US $ 100,000, one has to apply to RBI, which may accept or reject the same. The issue is whether the RBI approval is sufficient confirmation that the transaction is at arm’s length? Though there is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect, the RBI approval could serve as supporting document. Secondly, can the IT authorities determine an arm’s length price, which is specially rejected by the RBI? Example: Indian company makes an application for payment of consultancy fees exceeding US $ 100,000 to its foreign parent company, which is rejected by the RBI. Can IT authorities assess the foreign parent company for "arm’s length price" exceeding US $ 100,000 ?1

Conclusion

10. Hence, it is felt that though India has made a very good start in amending section 92 of the Act and making transfer pricing illegal and punishable with huge amount of fines, it is felt that a lot more can still be done. As already stated above, the said changes are still to come on lines with the international standards in this field. The analysis done in this paper was only an illustration of the flaws in the present law of transfer pricing in India and the possible changes that can be introduced in it. A lot more needs to done in areas like that of documentation where a large number of documents needs to be submitted, irrespective of the size of the enterprise. This would obviously result in a huge administrative and financial burden on the smaller enterprises. Similarly, it is felt that the penalties imposed in case of violations are excessive as compared to similar laws in other jurisdictions etc.

Keeping in mind the fact that tax legislations ought to be guided by certain canons such as that of neutrality, effectiveness, certainty, simplicity and flexibility, it is clear that the existing section 92 does not in anyway achieve this goal. The ambiguity that is present in the existing provisions becomes all the more worrisome given the economic context of India, which is a developing country and which clearly requires assistance of the FDIs brought in by the MNCs into the country for its economic development. The inflow of this FDI is bound to be affected unless the issue of vagueness in section 92 is immediately addressed to and suitable amendments be made thereto.

However, the Government has brought insurance auxiliary service in relation to life insurance business also within the ambit of service tax by the Finance Act, 2002 with effect from 16-8-2002 as per Notification No. 8/2002, dated 1-8-2002. 7.3 Services of third party inspection and certification are not covered - Some doubts have been raised before the Government as to whether "third party inspections and certification" carried out by certifying agencies in respect of marine as well as non-marine equipments, can be considered as service provided by a consulting engineer or not. The main point raised by some service providers is that where they are carrying out any certification as required by any statute can it come under the purview of consultancy, advice or technical assistance. The Government clarified the same through the Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX. 4, dated 26-2-2002. It was clarified that the certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job. It is then to be examined whether this activity can come under the purview of advice or technical assistance. An advice is generally understood to be optional in nature and has no statutory force. It is up to the client to accept the advice or not. The activity of certification will, therefore, not fall under the category of advice. As regards ‘technical assistance’, it is observed that an assistance is normally for the purpose of achieving a particular aim or result. A certificate given by, say, the Boiler Inspector under the Factories Act, 1948, about the safety of a boiler, cannot be considered to be ‘assistance’ to the person using the said boiler in his factory. To issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purposes of issuing certificates by the same agency under an authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency, before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. It will, therefore, be essential to examine each activity of a service provider on the basis of facts, the terms of agreement between the assessee and the clients and the corresponding provision of Indian or International statute/convention/protocol, or code, to determine whether the certificate being given is under the authority of any such statute, convention protocol or code. If it is so, the payment received for that service will not be taxable under the head "Consulting engineer". Any other inspection, survey, assessment, technical assistance, consultancy, recommendation, advice, undertaken/provided directly or indirectly, by the assessee would be liable to service tax under the head ‘Consulting engineer’. But the Madras High Court in V. Shanmughavel (Dr.) v. CCE 12, held that "registered valuers" of plant and machinery would fall within the definition of "consulting engineer" and their services of valuation of plant and machinery would be covered as "taxable service" offered by an "consulting engineer" within the meaning of section 65(48)(g) of the Finance Act, 1994. A re-consideration of the ruling of Madras High Court according to the circular is, hence, necessitated. In the case of Central Power Research Institute v. CCE13, the assessee was carrying on research activities in power generation. The assessee contended, inter alia, that it was not consulting engineer and activity carried on by it did not fall within the definition of ‘consulting engineer’, and that it was carrying on research and testing of electrical equipments, namely, voltage equipments, motor transformer insulation, tower transmitters, circuit breakers, transformers, etc., which were sent by various clients. It was held that the Tribunal in a similar matter in the case of Turbotech Precision Engg. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Stay Order No. 1169 of 2004, dated 22-11-2004] had granted full waiver of pre-deposit of service tax and penalty. Therefore, the stay application was allowed granting full waiver of pre-deposit of the disputed amount and staying its recovery till the disposal of the appeal. It is to be noted that the tax on technical testing and analysis services/technical inspection and certification services was introduced with effect from 1-7-2003.

SAFE HARBOUR RULES-INTRODUCTION

1.0.-"Safe Harbour" means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by assessee. Section 92CB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) was inserted by the Finance (No.2) Act, 2009 with retrospective effect from 1-4-2009. The said section empowered CBDT to notify safe harbour rules. CBDT's Circular No. 5/2010 dated 3-6-2010 explains the object behind section 92CB. The Circular explains that since the introduction of transfer pricing rules in 2002, "the number of transfer pricing adjustments locked up in disputes have increased". Therefore, "in order to reduce the number of transfer pricing audits and prolonged disputes", section 92CB has been inserted. Safe harbour rules can be notified under section 92CB only in respect of international transactions and not in respect of "specified domestic transactions".

Pursuant to the powers conferred on it by section 92CB of the Act, the CBDT has put out section 44AD-like draft safe harbour rules Rule 10TA to Rule 10TG in the public domain.

SALIENT FEATURES OF THE DRAFT SAFE HARBOUR RULES

2.0. The following are the features of draft safe harbour rules:

(i)

These safe harbour rules ('SHR') apply for assessment years 2013-14 and 2014-15

(ii)

"Eligible assessee" can opt for the safe harbour rules in respect of "eligible international transactions".

(ii)

Safe Harbour Rules are in the nature of safe harbour % of operating margins/ interest rates/corporate guarantee fees specified in Rule 10TD in respect of eligible international transactions.

(iii)

Safe Harbour ('SFH') in respect of international transactions of "intra-group loans" and "corporate guarantees" are applicable to all assessees entering into them irrespective of the nature of business activity in which they are engaged. (Non-Sector-specific SHR)

(iv)

SFH in respect of eligible international transactions being provision of software development services, ITES, knowledge Process outsourcing services, contract R&D services for software development/generic pharma drugs and manufacture only apply to eligible assessees engaged in these activities. In all these cases services are rendered with insignificant risk to eligible assessee to foreign AE(foreign principal). SFH in respect of eligible international transactions being manufacture and export of core/non-core auto components apply to persons engaged in such manufacture and export where 90% or more of total turnover during relevant previous year is in the nature of OEM sales. (SECTORAL/Sector-specific SHR)

(v)

These safe harbour rules shall not apply to eligible international transactions entered into with AE located in any country or territory notified under section 94A or in a no tax country or low tax country or territory.

(vi)

If eligible assessee declares transfer price in eligible international transactions in which % of operating margins/ interest rates/corporate guarantee fees is not less than the safe harbour % specified in Rule 10TD, the transfer price will be accepted by Department without "transfer pricing audit" by Department. In this respect, safe harbour rules resemble section 44AD of the Act.

(vii)

Where SHR differs from section 44AD is that section 44AD exempts assessees who opt for presumptive tax under it from maintaining books of account and tax audit. However, eligible assessees opting for SHR will have to comply with sections 92D (Documentation) and 92E (Audit by CA) of the Act. Further, there is no need foe assessee to apply to AO to opt for section 44AD. For exercising this option, an application is to be made to AO in Form No.3CEG. AO will determine whether assessee is eligible assessee and transaction in question is eligible international transaction ('EIT'). If satisfied, AO will proceed to determine that the transfer price declared by assessee for EIT is acceptable or not having regard to safe harbour operating margins/interest rates/corporate guarantee fees specified in Rule 10TD

(viii)

Where no option for safe harbour is exercised by an eligible assessee in respect of an eligible international transaction entered into by the assessee, the arm's length price in relation to the international transaction shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92C and 92CA without having regard to the profit margin or the price as specified in of rule 10TD

TRANSFER PRICING : AN INDIAN OVERVIEW

CHITRANGADA SHUKLA ASHHAR MUSTAFA

Rajiv Bhutani

Partner, Transfer Pricing, Tax & Regulatory Services

Transfer Pricing (TP) continues to be one of the most significant international tax issues for multinational enterprises globally. India, recognising its importance in curbing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)introduced TP provisions in 2001. Since its inception, the Indian TP regime has evolved, keeping pace with both market dynamics and continued global tax developments.

As the Indian tax landscape continues to evolve, there are several critical areas that require attention in the upcoming Union Budget 2025. The following outlines key areas where we believe regulatory intervention and reform are necessary, along with our specific expectations for the forthcoming budget.

Compliance

Maintenance of TP Documentation: Since the introduction of TP provisions in 2001, the threshold for maintaining TP documentation for taxpayers has been set at INR 1 crore in aggregate value of international transactions. However, as businesses expand and related-party transactions increase, this threshold appears outdated. The expectation is to raise the threshold for mandatory TP documentation at INR 10 crores, in line with the growing scale of multinational enterprises in India.

Exemption of Non-Residents from TP Certification: Currently, non-resident taxpayers earning income from interest, dividends, royalties, or technical fees, do not need to file their income tax return in India, provided taxes have been appropriately deducted on said income by the taxpayer. However, these taxpayers are still required to mandatorily furnish a TP Certificate if such taxable income is earned from parties in India. Given that these non-resident taxpayers are exempted from furnishing their income tax return subject to meeting the above stated conditions, it is recommended that such taxpayers should also be exempted from furnishing the TP certificate, aligning with the broader tax compliance simplification.

Recalibration of the Arm's Length Range: Under the existing TP regulations, India uses an arm's length range between the 35th and 65th percentiles while determining arm's length pricing. However, this range diverges from internationally accepted standards.

To align India's regulations with global norms, the expectation is to revise the range to an interquartile range, spanning from 25th percentile to the 75th percentile, which better reflects the true variability in arm's length pricing.

Dispute Management and Resolution

Expedited Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) Process: The APA regime has been a powerful tool for Indian taxpayers looking to mitigate related-party transaction disputes and achieve certainty on their arm's length pricing. While the APA program has been successful as compared to traditional dispute resolution routesdelays in processing APA applications have resulted in a significant backlog. To enhance efficiency, we recommend streamlining the APA process by categorising applications based on their complexity. Complex cases could be allocated to more experienced teams, while simpler cases should be subject to shorter timelines for resolution. This bifurcation would enable faster conclusions, benefitting both the tax authorities and taxpayers.

Expansion and Re-evaluation of Safe Harbour Provisions: Plenty of small taxpayers have opted for the Safe Harbour regime in order to conclude their arm's length pricing in a streamlined manner. However, the applicable benchmarks are typically higher in this regime as compared to available alternatives. While the small taxpayers do get to enjoy this benefit of convenience, the threshold restrictions in the Safe Harbour regime makes it inaccessible to the taxpayers with comparatively higher value of transactions, forcing them into complex dispute resolution processes. To make this regime more accessible, the Government may re-evaluate the Safe Harbour provisions by (a) increasing the transaction thresholds to cover a larger number of companies, and (b) adjusting the rates to be closer to actual comparable benchmarks, thereby encouraging broader adoption and reducing litigation risks.

Statutory authorities would mean to include both the quasi-judicial authorities performing various functions under a statute and the appellate authorities who are created by virtue of provisions of the statute.

Notification No. 25/2006, dated July 13, 2006 - Issue of notice a pre-condition 3. In view of the specific wordings employed in Notification No. 25/2006 ST, dated July 7, 2006, the services rendered by the professionals under reference are not taxable, provided they represent their clients before such authorities in a proceeding initiated by issue of notice. This particular pre-condition appears to be unwarranted as it may usher in some practical difficulties. Field formations may try to interpret in such a way that exemption would apply only if it precedes with the so-called Show-Cause Notice (SCN) which is normal practice in such statutory proceedings. On the other hand, those who avail of the exemption would argue that even a letter/correspondence to a client or even a notice of personal hearing to the authorized representative/client would fall within the ambit of the term ‘notice’ and, therefore, virtually all such appearance before authorities concerned is exempt.

The circumstances which necessitated CBEC to impose a pre-condition in the exemption notification, that the taxable service rendered shall be sequel to a ‘notice’ issued, are not known. In the normal circumstances, there may be instances of so-called ‘show-cause notice’ issued by the authorities concerned under the Central Excise Act, 1944 and the Customs Act, 1962 and the Finance Act, 1944 (relating to service tax) which culminate into statutory proceedings. But the Board lost sight of the fact that in a number of cases the professionals and also the legal practitioners represent their client under various Central and State enactments even without receipt of a formal ‘notice’, but in spite of that the proceedings are still statutory in nature. Under different enactments, proceedings may culminate even without issue of notice and they require representation before authorities concerned.

Various instances where representation before authorities is made without issue of notice

4. To cite a few instances, section 11A(2B) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 provides for waiver of a notice (corresponding section 73(3) of the Finance Act, 1994). Similarly, proviso to section 124 of the Customs Act states that the ‘notice’ in terms of section 124(a) may at the request of person concerned be oral (statute provides for waiver of notice).

The Authority of Advance Rulings (AAR) is available under the direct and indirect-tax enactments. Under section 23C of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 28H of the Customs Act, an applicant can approach the AAR for advance ruling in respect of classification, valuation, etc. Again section 96C of the Finance Act, 1994 provides for advance ruling in respect of service tax matters. The CA/CWA/CS are authorized to represent before the AAR under a power of Attorney/Authorisation. The proceeding before AAR is a one wherein the applicant himself voluntarily chooses the forum without receipt of notice. In other words, issue or receipt of notice does not arise in such proceedings.

Similarly, there may be occasions for such professionals to represent a client in proceedings arising out of the Income-tax Act, 1961, or the Companies Act, 1956 even without receipt of a notice. A company secretary may have to represent his client before the Registrar of Companies on various matters arising out of the Companies Act, and also before other forums like Consumer Forum, Arbitration, etc., wherein such representation would still be without the so-called ‘notice’.

A chartered accountant may have to represent his client at the assessment level before the income-tax authorities, sales tax (VAT) authorities, etc. They have to represent before the Registrar of Companies in various matters including incorporation, winding up, etc., even without ‘notice’ in the stricter sense.

Similarly, the professionals may have to appear before, other authorities like Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) for adjudication of any dispute relating to his client with or without receipt of notice.

There may be several cases where the quasi-judicial authorities may pass speaking orders, demand orders, even without issue of notice and such proceedings have to be contested before appellate authorities.

If the exemption is applied in its strict sense, all such proceedings may not qualify for exemption. Therefore, the very object of restoring the exemption to allow a level playing field stands defeated, in view of condition precedent that the proceedings shall be with reference to a ‘notice’. Further, to restrict the exemption only to cases where notices is issued would tantamount to restricting the professional activities and a disparity is created.

TRANSFER PRICING IS SERIOUS BUSINESS 14. Adoption of a transfer price different from declared price may have serious consequences. No deduction under section 10A, 10AA, 10B or Chapter VI-A is admissible in respect of addition consequent to adoption of the arm’s length price. There is no immunity from penalty leviable against deemed concealment on the difference between reported and assessed income, unless justified by reasonable cause under section 273B. Failure to keep accounts and documents as required under section 92D will merit penalty under section 271AA. Failure to get audit certificate will attract penalty under section 271BA.

It has been held that the burden to prove that declared rate is the transfer price under the rules is placed on the assessee as decided by the Tribunal in Aztec Software Technology Services Ltd.’s case (supra). In fact, that is also the view taken in the countries, where transfer pricing rules are in vogue. To take an example, Australian rulings would not discredit findings of the tax authorities unless bad faith could be shown as decided in San Remo Macaroni Co. v. Commissioner of Taxation [1999] FCA 1468. Deficiency of information is a fault, which could not be attributed to revenue, so that burden of proving arm’s length price lay on the taxpayer. New Business Tax System (Thin Capitalisation and Other Measures) Bill, 2000 would seek to place even greater responsibility on foreign investors with significant interest in Australian ventures.

The seriousness of transfer pricing is highlighted by a recent Instruction indicating the effect of transfer pricing exercise undertaken by tax administration in India. The resort can now be made to Mutual Agreement Procedure under Indo-U.S. Double Tax Avoidance Agreement in respect of taxes, inter alia, imposed by application of Transfer Pricing Rule vide Instruction No. 10 of 2007, dated October 23, 2007. It provides for stay on demand subject to pendency of reference for availing MAP on confirmation from Foreign Tax and Tax Research Division of the CBDT and bank guarantee for the amount due and interest thereon.

BACKGROUND AND GLOBAL HISTORY OF SAFE HARBOUR

Introduction

The UN TP manual defines Safe Harbour as-

"A provision in the tax laws, regulations or guidelines stating that transactions falling within a certain range will be accepted by the tax authorities without further investigation."

Safe Harbour Rules ("SH Rules"), in the Transfer Pricing ("TP") regime, are a set of rules or conditions, which relieve taxpayers from certain obligations, which are generally imposed on the taxpayers by provisions of Chapter X i.e. Transfer Pricing Regulations.

Determination of Arm's Length Price ("ALP") is often time-consuming, burdensome and costly, considering an Associated Enterprise ("AE") has a variety of intra-group transactions. Further, there have been many litigations on TP issues.

Hence, SH Rules provide certainty to taxpayers by ensuring that tax authorities will accept the price charged or paid by taxpayers with a limited scope of verification.

Need of SH Rules

Difficulties faced by taxpayers in finding comparable for low-value-adding services.

Significant increase in litigation w.r.t. TP issues.

Increased amount of confusion w.r.t. determination of ALP in sectors such as KPO Services, R&D Services and certain low value-adding services.

Burdon of TP compliances on smaller taxpayers or for low-value transactions.

Objectives behind SH Rules

Provide simplified methods for determining ALP for international transactions by AEs.

Reduce the number of litigations and compliance cost for eligible taxpayers.

'Administrative Simplicity' i.e. helps tax authorities to focus on more complex and higher risk areas.

Providing Certainty that the taxpayer's transaction value will be accepted by tax authorities.

OECD Guidelines on SH Regulation

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ("OECD") issued guidelines in relation to SH Regulations.

However, it was believed that such regulations will have negative impact on the tax revenues of the country.

Accordingly, the SH was not acceptable at that point of time.

Still, many countries implemented SH Rules and used them for limited type of transactions which were having less complications.

After realizing how SH Rules affected the nations who adopted them, OECD concluded that, when implemented properly, the advantages of SH Rules would exceed the drawbacks.

Thereafter, on 16 May 2013, OECD issued revised Section E on SH in Chapter IV of its TP Guidelines.

DRAWBACKS ASSOCIATED WITH SH RULES

Resulted into providing scope for Tax Planning and Tax Avoidance.

Resulted into risks which inter-alia includes double taxation, double non-taxation and mutual agreement concerns.

Introduction

In terms of recent development in the Indian Transfer pricing scenario, it would be worth-while to mention the following. The Indian government, in the previous month, notified the Safe Harbour Rules (SHR) for government owned electricity companies by releasing a new set of simplified Transfer Pricing (TP) Documentation Rules for such companies. Further, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) issued guidance on implementation of Transfer Pricing Documentation and Country-by-country (CbC) reporting and the framework for government-to-government mechanisms to exchange CbC Reports and implementation package.

In addition to the above, in a recent ruling in the case of Dy. CIT v. RAK Ceramics India Pvt. Ltd.1, the Hyderabad Tribunal deleted the royalty adjustment stating that the benefit test approach adopted by the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) was flawed.

Safe harbour rules for transfer pricing documentation: Notified for specified domestic transactions of government owned electricity companies

The CBDT has notified the Safe Harbour Rules (SHR) for eligible specified domestic transactions (SDT) of the electricity companies owned by the government under which a set of simplified Transfer Pricing (TP) documentation rules will have to be followed by Government companies engaged in the business of generation, transmission or distribution of electricity (eligible assessee), instead of the mandatory documentation prescribed currently under Rule 10D(1) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962.

These SHR provide that where an eligible assessee has entered into an eligible specified domestic transaction (SDT) in any previous year, it would be required to maintain specified documentation if it exercises the option to adopt these SHR. Under these SHR, the transfer price declared by the eligible assessee in respect of an eligible SDT shall be accepted by the income-tax authorities, if it is in accordance with the specifications of the rule i.e.

'The tariff in respect of supply of electricity, transmission of electricity, wheeling of electricity, as the case may be, is determined by the Appropriate Commission in accordance with the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003 (36 of 2003).'

These are the first set of SHRs prescribed for Domestic Transfer Pricing, though only for Government electricity companies as of now. These relaxed documentation requirements will help in saving the efforts that would have been spent by these companies in analysing and documenting arm's length compliance for their inter-company transactions, and divert their efforts to more developmental avenues leading to economic growth. In light of the fact that, the documentation for SDTs shall be tested from next year onwards by the Indian Revenue Authorities, the CBDT may consider issuing such relaxation rules for TP documentation for certain other industry sectors where pricing is regulated e.g. mutual funds where the expenditure charged to the mutual funds scheme including the management fee paid to the asset management companies is any ways regulated by SEBI.

BEPS Action Plan 13 - Guidance on implementation of Transfer Pricing Documentation and country-by-country reporting

In continuation of the September 2014 guidance, the OECD has issued a Guidance on 6 February 2015, relating to implementation of CbC Report (the Guidance). It has been recommended that the master file and local file documentation standards will be implemented by all countries in their local country legislations. Master file and local file will be required to be filed directly with the tax-authorities by group entities of each countries' jurisdiction.

The Guidance issued by OECD also covered the following important aspects:

1

Timing of preparation and filing of the CbC Report;

2

Threshold limit of Euro 750 million consolidated revenues has been prescribed for mandatory filing of CbC report by MNE;

3

Necessary conditions underlying the obtaining and use of CbC Report by Revenue Authorities; and

4

Framework for exchange of CbC Reports between governments and the work plan for developing an Implementation package.

The necessary conditions applicable to Revenue Authorities for obtaining and use of the CbC Report include Confidentiality of the reported information, consistency in implementation of the recommendations and appropriate use i.e. use the CbC Report for the limited purpose of assessing high level transfer pricing risk and other BEPS related risk.

The Guidance on Framework for government-to-government mechanisms to exchange CbC Reports suggests a secondary mechanism, in the event that a country fails to provide information to another country on the CbC Reporting. Countries participating in the OECD/G20 BEPS Project have agreed to develop a work-plan for exchange mechanisms of CbC Reports between governments by April 2015.

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Nor is the tax auditor required to examine or report whether the assessee has maintained proper records as required by Rule 10D regarding international transactions. Nor is he required to examine whether the Arm's Length Price has been determined for international transactions in accordance with any of the recognised methods specified in Section 92F. That is the subject of the audit to be carried out under Section 92E, and the report is to be furnished in Form No. 3CEB.

The tax auditor must report in this clause only if a primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1). If no primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1), the tax auditor has no duty to report. The tax auditor is not even required to report if the primary TP adjustment has not been made as per the APA entered into by the assessee. If primary TP adjustment has been made according to the APA, then the reporting obligation under this Clause is triggered.

This clause also does not deal with Thin Cap adjustments under Section 94B. That is the subject matter of Clause 30B.

This Clause also does not deal with the issue of shares at a premium to non-resident investors by a closely held company that attracts Section 56(2)(vii). That is the subject matter of Clause 29A.

Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. Nevertheless, the tax auditor may find it useful to examine if any of the non-price terms and conditions of international transactions are not at arm's length from the angle of Clause 30C.

9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

(a)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 69 taxmann.com 209 (Delhi - Trib.)

(b)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 651 (Delhi - Trib.)

(c)

Westfalia Separator India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 381 (Delhi - Trib.)

(d)

Rampgreen Solutions (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 64 taxmann.com 451 (Delhi - Trib.)

However, in Dy. CIT v. Minda Acoustic Ltd. [2019] 107 taxmann.com 475 (Delhi - Trib.), it was held that the Safe Harbour Rules can always be adopted as guidance in respect of the assessment years prior to their insertion.

9.2 Advance pricing agreement [Section 92CC]

Section 92CC relates to advance pricing agreement (APA).

Hitherto, section 92CC(1) provided that the CBDT, with the approval of the Central Government, may enter into an APA with any person, determining the ALP or specifying the manner in which ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person.

The scope of section 92CC(1) has been widened with effect from 1-4-2020 to provide that the CBDT may also enter into an APA with any person determining income referred to in section 9(1)(i), or specifying the manner in which said income is to be determined, as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India by or on behalf of that person, being a non-resident.

The Finance Minister, in her speech stated as follows:

"In order to provide tax certainty to taxpayers in the matter of attribution of profit to permanent establishment (PE), it is proposed to widen the scope of Advanced Pricing Agreement (APA) and Safe Harbour Regime (SHR), by providing that determination of attribution of profit to PE shall also be in the scope of SHR and APA." (para 2.1 of Annex to Part B of Budget Speech)

The rationale for the amendment is explained in Explanatory Memorandum as follows:

Primary Transfer Pricing Adjustments are what are known in popular parlance as "transfer pricing adjustments" or TP Adjustments."Primary adjustment" to a transfer price means the determination of transfer price in accordance with the arm's length principle resulting in an increase in the total income or reduction in the loss, as the case may be, of the assessee.

The e-tax Guide-Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2016 edition) of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore defines "transfer pricing adjustment" or what is referred to as "primary transfer pricing adjustment" in section 92CE(1) as under:

"3.34 Transfer pricing adjustment

In the event the related parties do not transact with each other at arm's length prices, tax authorities may for tax purposes, substitute the price of the transaction with one that could have been charged if the parties were unrelated. The adjustment to arrive at that price is known as a transfer pricing adjustment."

A primary TP adjustment covers the following TP adjustments,—

(i)

a TP adjustment to transfer price made suo motu by the assessee in his return of income;

(ii)

a TP adjustment to the transfer price made by the Assessing Officer has been accepted by the assessee;

(iii)

a TP adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement (APA) entered into by the assessee under section 92CC;

(iv)

a TP adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules framed under section 92CB; or

(v)

a TP adjustment arising from the resolution of an assessment by way of the mutual agreement procedure (MAP under an agreement (DTAA) entered into under section 90 or section 90A to avoid double taxa-tion.

In the context of Section 92CE and Clause 30A, it is clear that the primary TP adjustments contemplated in Clause 30A are those made regarding international transactions. Domestic TP adjustments are not contemplated

CC 2005 (189) ELT 135 (CESTAT 3 member LB), it has been held that once endorsement is made by DGFT about discharge of export obligation, transferee of license is eligible for exemption, even if it is found that transferability was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. As per Para 2.57(a) of FTP 2015-2020, decision of Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) is final in respect of interpretation of policy or classification under ITC. Special Audit of Cenvat Credit by Cost/Chartered Accountant

Section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 (as inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012) make provision for special audit by practicing Chartered/Cost Accountant [earlier, section 14AA of Central Excise Act was made applicable to service tax. This section provided only for special audit of Cenvat credit availed].

Special audit can be ordered by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Central Excise [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Such audit can be ordered if the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of CE has reason to believe that any person liable to pay service tax—

(i)

has failed to declare or determine the value of a taxable service correctly; or

(ii)

has availed and utilised credit of duty or tax paid - (a) which is not within the normal limits having regard to the nature of taxable service provided, the extent of capital goods used or the type of inputs or input services used, or any other relevant factors as he may deem appropriate; or (b) by means of fraud, collusion, or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts; or

(iii)

has operations spread out in multiple locations and it is not possible or practicable to obtain a true and complete picture of his accounts from the registered premises falling under the jurisdiction of the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(1) of Finance Act, 1994].

In such cases, the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner may direct such person to get his accounts audited by a chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by him, to the extent and for the period as may be specified by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(2) of Finance Act, 1994, inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012] [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

The provisions of special audit apply even if audit was conducted under some other law [section 72A(3) of Finance Act, 1994]

The auditee (person liable to pay service tax) shall be given opportunity of hearing in respect of any material gathered on the basis of such special audit and proposed to be utilised in any proceedings against him [section 72A(4) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012]

Section 14AA of Central Excise Act provides that the audit fees will be paid by Central Government (i.e. service tax department). However, section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 makes no provision of fees of the Chartered/Cost Accountant for such audit.

As per rule 5A(2) of Service Tax Rules (as amended w.e.f. 5-12-2014), assessee is required to produce records maintained by him to cost/chartered accountant nominated under section 72A of Finance Act, 1994.

9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

(a)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 69 taxmann.com 209 (Delhi - Trib.)

(b)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 651 (Delhi - Trib.)

(c)

Westfalia Separator India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 381 (Delhi - Trib.)

(d)

Rampgreen Solutions (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 64 taxmann.com 451 (Delhi - Trib.)

However, in Dy. CIT v. Minda Acoustic Ltd. [2019] 107 taxmann.com 475 (Delhi - Trib.), it was held that the Safe Harbour Rules can always be adopted as guidance in respect of the assessment years prior to their insertion.

basically self assessment. There will be no compulsory assessment at end of the year. If notice is not issued within prescribed time, dealer will be deemed to have been self assessed [para 2.12 of White Paper on State-Level VAT].

Returns will be filed monthly/quarterly, as prescribed, along with challans. Returns will be scrutinised and if there is technical mistake, it will have to be rectified by dealer [para 2.11 of White Paper on State-Level VAT] As per West Bengal VAT Act, if dealer does not receive any intimation within two years from end of the accounting year, it is deemed that his return has been accepted by sales tax authority. In case of Andhra Pradesh, the time limit is four years from date of filing of return. Each State has different but similar provisions.

Since there is no regular assessment, checks will be by way of audit of accounts of dealers.

Internal audit - There will be audit wing in department and certain percentage of dealers will be taken up for audit every year on scientific basis. The audit wing will be independent of tax collection wing, to remove bias. There will be cross verification with Central Excise and Income Tax also. [para 2.13 of White Paper on State-Level VAT]

Audit by outside Agencies - VAT laws of some States provide for audit by outside agencies.

This is practically outsourcing of work of State tax department. Once the figures are checked by an independent auditor, work of tax authorities is considerably reduced and scrutiny of returns by departmental officers becomes easy.

In some States, audit can be done only by Chartered Accountants. In some eight States (Assam, Kerala, Orissa, Uttaranchal, Maharashtra etc.), audit can be done either by Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountants.

In AP, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Karnataka, audit can be done by CA, cost Auditor or Sales Tax Practitioner (STP).

In Karnataka, audit report is required if turnover exceeds Rs 25 lakhs.

In Delhi, the dealer is required to submit copy of audit report u/s 44AB of Income Tax Act (This report is required when turnover exceeds Rs 40 lakhs per annum) No separate audit is prescribed, unless special audit is ordered by department.

In Sales Tax Practitioners' Association of Maharashtra v. State of Maharashtra (2008) 170 Taxman 371 = 14 STT 348 = 14 VST 69 (Bom HC DB), it has been held that audit can be conducted only by Chartered Accountants and Cost Accountants. Audit cannot be conducted by Sales Tax Practitioners or Advocates - followed in Kar Salahakar Sangh v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2013) 60 VST 126 (MP HC DB), where rule providing certification only by Chartered Accountant was held valid.

Cross checking of Vat credit - In order to ensure that there is no fraud or bogus invoices, it has to be ensured that the invoice is genuine and the tax as shown in the invoice has been actually paid to State Government. For this, cross checking is done. The details of invoices on which the dealer has claimed credit are cross checked with the supplier who has issued that invoice. Since the invoices are numerous, such cross checking is done on sampling basis.

Cross checking will also include verifying Vat returns with Central Excise and Income Tax returns and records. This will ensure proper tax compliance.

Refund of input tax - Entire input tax will be refundable within three months, when final product is exported. In respect of sale to EOU/SEZ, there will be either exemption of input tax or tax paid will be refunded within three months [para 2.5 of White Paper on State-Level VAT].

If tax credit exceeds tax payable on sales, the excess credit will be carried to end of next financial year. Excess unadjusted credit at end of second year will be eligible for refund [para 2.4 of White Paper on State-Level VAT]

In Cenvat under Central Excise, there is provision to carry forward balance credit, while under State Vat, refund is to be claimed. This procedure is clumsy and prone to corruption.

Check posts and transit passes - Government can set up check posts. The invoice will have to be produced at the check posts. System, of transit pass may be introduced. This is bound to increase harassment of transporters and is bound to increase corruption to unprecedented level.

12.4 Change in the time limit to pass the order by the Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 166 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 92CA of ITA 1961)]

12.4-1 Position under the ITA 1961

Section 92CA of the ITA 1961 deals with the case where the assessee has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction in any previous year, and the AO may refer the computation of the Arm's Length Price (ALP) in relation to the said international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO).

Sub-section (3A) to section 92CA states that TPO is required to pass an order before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation under section 153, or as the case may be, in section 153B for making the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation or fresh assessment, as the case may be, expires.

12.4-1a Exclusion of the last day of assessment limitation - The interpretation of the phrase 'before sixty days prior to the date' has been a consistent point of contention between taxpayers and the revenue, leading to significant litigation.

The Madras High Court, in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), which affirmed the Single Judge's decision in Jt. CIT v. Pfizer Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 536 (Madras), held that the word 'date' in section 92CA(3A) refers to the last date for the AO to pass the assessment order under section 153 (e.g., December 31st). The crucial words 'prior to' indicate that, for the purpose of calculating the 60 days, this last date must be excluded. Therefore, if the assessment limitation expires on December 31st, the TPO order ought to have been passed on or before October 31st.

This interpretation was consistently followed across numerous ITAT benches, including in the following cases:

Teleperformance Global Services (P.) Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 658 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. [2024] 163 taxmann.com 349 (Ahmedabad-Trib.)

Frost & Sullivan (India) (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 739 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Shell India Markets (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 366 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Siemens Technology and Services (P.) Ltd. [2024] 162 taxmann.com 357 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Huhtamaki India Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 194 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Atos India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 217 (Mumbai-Trib.)

CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore-Trib.)

Pioneer India Electronics (P.) Ltd. [2025] 178 taxmann.com 553 (Delhi-Trib.)

Sigma Aldrich Chemicals (P.) Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 431 (Bangalore-Trib.)

12.4-1b Mandatory nature of the time limit - Another critical aspect clarified by the judiciary is whether the time limit prescribed in section 92CA(3A) is mandatory or merely directory. The revenue often argued that the use of the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) implies a directory nature.

However, the Madras High Court in Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), after a detailed analysis of the scheme of the Act and the consequences of non-compliance, unequivocally held that the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and the time period fixed therein has to be scrupulously followed.'

The court reasoned that the overall scheme of transfer pricing assessments, with various interlinked time limits (including extensions under the proviso to section 92CA(3A) and section 153), indicates a legislative intent to ensure timely completion. If the TPO's time limit were merely directory, it would undermine the entire assessment process. This principle has been reiterated in the case of Asstt. CIT v. CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore - Trib.).

5.10 Proceedings before TPO for determination of Arm's Length Price in respect of specified domestic transactions [Section 92CA]

5.10-1 Pre-amended provisions

Section 92CA of the Act provides that the Assessing Officer, if he considers it necessary or expedient to do so, may, with the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner, refer the mat-ter of determination of Arm's Length Price (ALP) in respect of an international transaction or Specified Domestic Transaction (SDT) to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). Once a reference is made to the TPO, the TPO is competent to exercise all powers that are available to the Assessing Officer under Section 92C(3) for the determination of ALP and consequent adjustment.

Further, under Section 92E of the Act, there is a reporting requirement on the taxpayer to file an audit report in the prescribed form before the Assessing Officer (AO) containing details of all international transactions or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer during the year. This audit report is the primary document with the AO, which contains the details of international transactions and/or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer. If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under Section 92E, then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction/SDT so as to make a reference to the TPO.

Section 92CA provides that if, during the course of proceeding before him, an international transaction comes to the notice of the TPO, which has not been referred to him by the AO, the TPO can proceed to determine the ALP in its respect as well. It also provides for the computation of ALP by the TPO of those international transactions, details of which have not been furnished in the audit report referred to above. These provisions are in place in sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of the section 92CA. However, at present, the above-noted provisions of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA do not extend to SDTs.

5.10-2 Amendment by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 has amended sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of Section 92CA to enable the TPO to deal with SDTs which have not been referred to him by the AO and/or in whose respect audit report under section 92CE has not been filed.

These amendments will take effect from 01-04-2025 and will, accord-ingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2025-26 and subsequent assessment years.

CST (2014) 43 GST 1 = 38 taxmann.com 183 (CESTAT SMB). Doctrine of unjust enrichment is not applicable if certified by Chartered Accountant that duty not recovered and shown in balance sheet as loans and advances - Deepak International v. CCST (2014) 304 ELT 438 (CESTAT SMB) * India Steel International v. CC (2015) 318 ELT 646 (CESTAT).

In CCE v. Paradeep Phosphates (2009) 238 ELT 690 (CESTAT), selling price was below cost price excluding excise duty as certified by Cost Accountant and the amount was shown as 'receivable' in balance sheet. It was held that doctrine of unjust enrichment is not applicable - similar view in South India Paper Mills v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 651 (CESTAT SMB).

Certificate of CA is only a piece of evidence and in itself not sufficient to show that burden has not been passed to other person - CC v. BPL Ltd. (2010) 259 ELT 526 (Mad HC DB) * CC v. SNS Overseas (2012) 275 ELT 621 (CESTAT).

In Tarapur Coatings v. CC (2009) 234 ELT 466 (CESTAT SMB), Chartered Accountant prepared cost sheet as per CAS-4 and certified that burden of excess duty was absorbed by appellant and that there was no price rise during relevant period. Duty was shown as receivable. It was held that refund is admissible.

In Quality Offset Printers v. CC (2008) 230 ELT 671 (CESTAT SMB), CA issued a general certificate based on balance sheets of previous year, current year and subsequent year that the incidence of duty has not been passed on. It was held that refund is admissible.

In Memirex & Co. v. CCE 2004(174) ELT 216 (CESTAT), it was held that certificate from Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence.

In A K Enterprise v. CC 2006 (199) ELT 67 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that mere certificate from Chartered Accountant is not sufficient to rebut presumption that duty has been passed on to buyer - same view in CC v. BPL Ltd. (2010) 259 ELT 526 (Mad HC DB).

In India Agencies v. CC (2007) 212 ELT 507 (CESTAT), it was observed that Chartered Accountants are professional interested in their clients and issue such statements. In absence of conclusive evidence that duty has not been passed on, doctrine of unjust enrichment applies.

In Chambal Fertilisers v. CC 2006 (200) ELT 231 (CESTAT), it was held that though certificate of Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence of not passing duty burden, department can ask for records to check whether statement of Chartered Accountant is correct. Refund cannot be rejected simply on the ground that certificate of Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence. - followed in Flair Impex v. CC (2009) 238 ELT 794 (CESTAT SMB).

However, mere certificate of CA that service tax has not been recovered separately in invoice is not sufficient to establish that the burden of tax has not been passed on to the buyer - Multi Mantech International v. CST (2009) 18 STT 229 (CESTAT SMB).

When Amount treated as 'claim receivable' or 'refund receivable' in accounts or shown as expenditure

42.6-1 In Jaipur Syntex Ltd. v. CCE 2002(143) ELT 605 (CEGAT), assessee had paid higher duty and the differential amount was treated in accounts as 'claims receivable'. This was treated as part of Balance Sheet and not charged to P&L account. It was held that it is evident that incidence of duty has not been passed on to customers. [In this case, duty was not shown separately in invoice].

In CC v. Virudhunagar Textile Mills (2008) 230 ELT 411 (Mad HC DB), differential duty on capital goods was shown as duty receivable from customs department and balance sheet with CA certificate was produced. It was held that refund is admissible.

HEADNOTE: Section 65 (83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered accountant’s services - Assessee was a practising chartered accountant - Revenue levied service tax on certification service provided by assessee holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 - Whether since certification follows transfer pricing audit, certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ - Held, yes - Whether, since verification of books of account precedes issue of certificate and such verification would fall within scope of ‘Accounting and auditing’, it could not be said that assessee was not rendering auditing service liable to tax and, therefore, impugned order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 3] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998

FACT: The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

HELD: The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]
