HEADNOTE: Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule  10B  and rule  10D  of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Comparables - Factors to determine - Segmental Result) - Assessment year  2021-22  - Assessee provided software/IT enabled support services to support offshore functions of its AE which was benchmarked using TNMM - Assessee reported two operational segments: a Kochi unit catering exclusively to export/AE services and a Trivandrum unit serving both domestic and AE customers, and explained that COVID-19 significantly impacted domestic operations - TPO rejected TP documentation under section 92C(3), citing inappropriate/ambiguous filters and lack of audited segmental data and substantiation for allocation (including time-based allocation of employee costs) and computed PLI at entity level and made upward TP adjustment - Whether in absence of any defect/infirmity being pointed out in segmental accounts furnished by assessee, same could not be rejected by TPO as unreliable merely because such segmental accounts were not audited - Held, yes - Whether TPO was not justified in rejecting TP documentation and computing PLI at entity level without appreciating correct facts and material on record, particularly explanation for difference in PLI of domestic and export segments and impact of COVID-19 pandemic, and without considering segmental details and basis of allocation furnished by assessee - Held, yes - Whether, thus, TPO was directed to consider transfer pricing documentation and segmental details furnished by assessee afresh and carry out exercise of determining ALP of international transactions - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Matter remanded]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of providing consulting services in SAP solutions and products. Assessee provided software/IT enabled support services to support offshore functions of its AE whose services included business consulting services, SAP solutions and products to customers across multiple verticals. During relevant previous year, assessee undertook international transaction of provision of IT services which was benchmarked using TNMM. Assessee reported two operational segments: a Kochi unit catering exclusively to export/AE services and a Trivandrum unit serving both domestic and AE customers, and explained that COVID-19 significantly impacted domestic operations.

■

The TPO rejected TP documentation under section 92C(3), citing inappropriate/ambiguous filters and lack of audited segmental data and substantiation for allocation (including time-based allocation of employee costs) and computed PLI at entity level and made upward TP adjustment for ITeS/services segment

■

The Assessing Officer passed Draft Assessment Order under section 144C(1) proposing aforesaid transfer pricing adjustment. The assessee filed objections before the DRP which were disposed of vide order.

■

Based on the directions issued by the DRP, the Assessing Officer passed the final assessment order, making transfer pricing addition.

■

Assessee submitted that the authorities below did not consider the contentions raised by the Assessee and without appreciating the transfer pricing documentations and the response submitted by the Assessee during the course of assessment proceedings, rejected the transfer pricing documentation of the assessee.

HELD: ■

The above observations made by TPO neither referred to the explanation provided by the Assessee relating to impact of COVID 19 Pandemic nor factored its impact on the profit margins. On the other hand, the TPO returned a finding that in the absence of audited segmental data, and disproportionate allocation of expenses between two segments by Assessee, PLI should be computed at entity level. [Para 8.2]

■

In this regard, it is noted that before the DRP Assessee had submitted that details of expenses as requested by TPO were furnished in Response, dated 20/09/2023, filed before the TPO. Further, the Assessee had given detailed explanation regarding segment-wise PLI calculation which included ( a ) entity level PLI computed by TPO, ( b ) the basis of allocation of expenses ( c ) Assessee's segment-wise computation of PLI ( d ) computation of allocation of expenses alongwith the basis. Before the DRP it was specifically contended by the Assessee that during the assessment proceedings the Assessee has asserted that the Profit Level Indicator (PLI) for the export segment, constituting the international transaction, was 12.02%. However, the TPO did not consider the segment-wise bifurcation of revenue and expenses. Instead, the TPO calculated the PLI at the entity level, resulting in a value of 3.9%. [Para 8.3]

■

Asstt. CIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278 / [2023] 291 Taxman 11 / [2022] 449 ITR 1 (SC) clarifies that institutions such as the respondent, which claim GPU status, need to be scrutinised more closely and such activities are in the nature of service "in relation to" trade, commerce or business. [Para 7]

■ The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Asstt. CIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278 /[2023] 291 Taxman 11 /[2022] 449 ITR 1 (SC), under the Chapter 'Summation of Conclusion,' has held as below: "D. Trade promotion bodies Bodies involved in trade promotion (such as AEPC), or set up with the objects of purely advocating for, coordinating and assisting trading organisations, can be said to be involved in advancement of objects of general public utility. However, if such organisations provide additional services such as courses meant to skill personnel, providing private rental spaces in fairs or trade shows, consulting services, etc. then income or receipts from such activities, would be business or commercial in nature. In that event, the claim for tax exemption would have to be again subjected to the rigours of the proviso to Section 2(15) of the IT Act. H. Application of interpretation At the cost of repetition, it may be noted that the conclusions arrived at by way of this judgment, neither precludes any of the assessees (whether statutory, or non-statutory) advancing objects of general public utility, from claiming exemption, nor the Taxing Authorities from denying exemption, in the future, if the receipts of the relevant year exceed the quantitative limit. The assessing authorities must on a yearly basis, scrutinise the record to discern whether the nature of the assessee's activities amount to "trade, commerce or business" based on its receipts and income (i.e. whether the amounts charged are on cost-basis, or significantly higher). If it is found that they are in the nature of "trade, commerce or business", then it must be examined whether the quantified limit (as amended from time to time) in the proviso to Section 2(15), has been breached, thus disentitling them to exemption." [Para 8]

■

On cumulative reading of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, which now governs the field, Court is of the view that the case of the respondent has to be examined in the light of Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority (supra). [Para 9]

■

Hence, Directorate of Income Tax (Exemption), Chennai, is directed to re-examine the case of the respondent afresh and pass orders within a period of three months, following the dictum laid by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority (supra). [Para 10]

■

Accordingly, the Tax Case Appeal is disposed of. There shall be no order as to costs. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 92C,  read with section 92CA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustment - General) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether where in transfer pricing proceedings, Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to TP report filed by assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished, impugned addition made to assessee's ALP merely on basis of proposal made by TPO was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 54][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Where in transfer pricing proceedings, Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to TP report filed by assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished, impugned addition made to assessee's ALP merely on basis of proposal made by TPO was not sustainable  IT/ILT : Overseas taxes paid by assessee abroad were not eligible for relief under section 90

FACT: During relevant year, the Assessing Officer made certain addition on account of transfer pricing adjustments in relation to international transactions entered into by assessee with its AE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted said addition.

In appellate proceedings, invoking the provisions of rule 27 of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 the assessee sought to support the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) by raising a plea that under section 92C or 92CA, it was the statutory duty of the Assessing Officer to decide independently, whether the determination of arm's length price by the assessee should be accepted, or whether or not after applying the provisions of section 92CA, the transfer pricing adjustment should be made.

It was further submitted that in the present case, in compliance of the CBDT Instruction No. 3 of 2003, dated 20-5-2003 the Assessing Officer did not himself examine the issue of transfer pricing and with the approval of the Commissioner (Appeals), made a reference to the TPO under section 92CA(1). The Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply their minds to the transfer pricing report, or to any other material or information or document. The TPO made an adjustment which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order. On their part, the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) did not discharge necessary judicial functions conferred upon them under section 92C or 92CA.

HELD: The assessee's support to the impugned order on both counts is found to be correct. The Assessing Officer erred in not himself examining the issue of transfer pricing and with the approval of the Commissioner, made a reference to the TPO under section 92CA(1); that the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to the TP report filed by the assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished. The TPO made an adjustment which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order. Thereby, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) did not discharge necessary respective judicial functions conferred on them under sections 92C and 92CA.

Further, the assessee is also correct in contending that no TP adjustment can be made in a case like the present one, where the assessee enjoys benefit under section 10A or 80HHE, or where the tax rate in the country of the associated enterprises is higher than the rate of tax in India and where the establishment of tax avoidance or manipulation of prices or establishment of shifting of profits is not possible. [Para 54]

On the basis of the above reasons, accepting the pleas raised by the assessee to support the order of Commissioner (Appeals) order, without going into the merits of this ground, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 55]

purchase & order handling services and sales services under the CCA and hence, the DRP confirmed the action of the TPO in determining the arm's length price of the said services at NIL value. It is pertinent to note that the aforesaid actions of the DRP and the TPO go against the basic tenet of the Indian Transfer Pricing Laws and violate the provision of sub-section (3) of section 92CA read with sub-section (3) of section 92C. In the assessee's case under consideration, the TPO/Assessing Officer has not selected any method (out of six methods), therefore, the arm's length price (ALP) computed by the Assessing Officer/TPO is not in accordance with the provisions of section 92C (1), hence the TPO/Assessing Officer should delete the addition. [Para 32]

Now, addressing the issue relating to 'benefit test'. The revenue alleged that the assessee had failed to satisfy the 'benefit test' in respect of payments made by the assessee under the CCA (Agreement) for receiving purchase services, order handling services and sales services. The assessee has submitted before the TPO, the detailed nature of the aforesaid services and copies of documentary evidences of receipt of services on sample basis. The assessee submitted, a brief chart to prove the benefit test. This chart explains the nature of services, main functions, and documentary evidences for receipt of services along with paper book reference. This chart also explains the relevant para of the Cost Contribution Agreement (CCA). The assessee received the purchase & order handling services and sales services and documented them properly. The assessee also submitted the certificate issued by PWC Austria, about the costs allocated to AT&S India Pvt. Ltd. The copies of 78 chains of e-mail, job description sheets of 10 individual employees of the CCA team, evaluation reports of 6 global customers and flow chart of quotation processing services prove that assessee has received benefit from these services. The revenue has not disputed that these services have not been received by the assessee, he disputed only the 'benefit test', that assessee did not get the benefit out of these services. Assessee has proved that he had received the benefit from these services, by way of submitting a brief chart containing the services obtained. Therefore, the assessee has satisfied the 'benefit test', and for that rendering of intra group services by AE and payment made thereon were in the nature of third party, which would willing to pay. [Para 33]

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1), has not made any adverse comment under section 37 in respect of the services received under the CCA, for purchase services, order handling services and sales services. During the course of scrutiny assessment proceedings, the assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer the same evidences of receipt of purchase services, order handling services and sales services as those submitted to the TPO, as per the direction of the Assessing Officer. It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer, after examining the aforesaid details, did not make any adverse comment under section 37. As per the provision of sub-section (1) of section 37, the Assessing Officer is authorized to examine whether an expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) is incurred by an assessee wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business in the matter of computation of the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

In the assessee's case under consideration, the Assessing Officer has not disallowed the benefit of services received by the assessee under the Cost Contribution Agreement. The authority of the TPO would be to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price ('ALP') and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which the assessee benefits. That exercise of actual verification would be left to the Assessing Officer under section 37. The Assessing Officer could, therefore, determine under section 37 that the expenditure claimed was not for the benefit of the business, and thus, disallow that amount, this does not restrict or in any way bypass the functions of the TPO. The jurisdiction of the TPO is specific and limited i.e. to determine the arm's length price of an international transaction in terms of Chapter X read with rules 10A to 10E of the Income-tax Rules. Therefore, the assessee has derived benefits from these services as per CCA agreement and hence the arguments advanced by the revenue is not acceptable. [Para 34]

facts.text:
The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

One 'B' was engaged in the manufacture of radio pagers in the State of Haryana and held a valid exemption certificate under rule 28A of the Haryana General Sales Tax Rules, 1975 [Haryana Rules].

The assessee purchased radio pagers from 'B' and sold the same in the course of inter-State sale. It did not charge any sales tax from the purchaser on the basis of Notification No. SO 89/CA.74/56/S.8/95, dated 4-9-1995 issued under section 8(5) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 (CST Act) read with rule 28A(4)(c) of the Haryana Rules.

It claimed exemption from payment of tax on the sale in question placing reliance on the aforesaid notification.

The lower authorities including the High Court did not accept the claim of exemption.

The High Court held that successive sales of goods manufactured by dealer holding valid exemption certificate were exempt from payment of sales tax so long as they were inter-State sales but in respect of sale of goods by a dealer not holding exemption certificate under rule 28A in the course of inter-State trade, the benefit of exemption envisaged under notification dated 4-9-1995 was not available to such dealer. It proceeded to clarify that in respect of stages of sale which were exempt from payment of tax under the CST Act were covered by rule 28A(4)(c) but notification dated 4-9-1995 was applicable only to sale of goods manufactured by the exempted unit.

On appeal to Supreme Court:

Facts

The petitioner-company Citilights Properties Private Limited entered into an agreement with the owners of a vast extent of land for the development of an information technology park complex, in the year 2005.

As per the development agreement, the petitioner was entitled to 74% of the undivided share of the land and they were obliged to develop the park and hand over 26% of the constructed area to the land owners.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with a company by name Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited, for the development of the software technology park and the transfer of 74% of the share of the petitioner to the said company, on the understanding that the transferee company had to fund the development of the park.

Thereafter, the petitioner made an application in November 2005 to the Chairman of the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee through the office of the Director of Software Technology Park of India, Chennai, for setting up an information technology park under the STP Scheme.

The petitioner also entered into two agreements with Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited and another company by name E-lights Technopark Private Limited for the effective funding and implementation of the project.

On 17.10.2006, the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee granted in principle approval for the setting up of the infrastructure facility under the STP Scheme in 'Freedom IT Campus '. The Government of India, in turn, granted permission by a communication dated 22.10.2006 in terms of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2004-2009.

As per the letter of permission so granted, the petitioner was entitled to import capital goods worth Rs. 2500 lakhs, by availing the benefits of Notification No. 153/93 dated 13.8.1993. But, the goods and services were to be used for the purpose of export of software and IT services by the STP Units located within the infrastructure facility at the park. The permission for import of items was valid for a period of two years from the date of issue of the letter of permission.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with the Software Technology Park of India, binding itself to the obligations and conditions of the letter of permission and a green card was issued to the petitioner. In pursuance of the above, the premises were declared as a private bonded warehouse by the Department of Central Excise.

Therefore, the petitioner caused import of capital goods availing the benefit of the exemption Notification.

Thereafter, the petitioner handed over Block-1 of the IT Park to the two transferee companies such as E-lights Technopark Private Limited and Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited in March 2008.

After two years, the special purpose vehicle - one of the transferee companies namely E-lights Technopark Private Limited applied on 30.3.2010 to the Software Technology Parks of India for approval of name transfer and green card to itself.

But, the Preventive Unit of the Commissionerate of Central Excise initiated an investigation into the affairs of the petitioner.

The Commissioner of Central Excise issued a show cause notice alleging various irregularities and calling upon the petitioner as well as the special purpose vehicle and the other transferee company to show cause as to why the benefit of the exemption Notification should not be denied and why the capital goods imported and sold should not be confiscated, apart from levy of penalty.

Meanwhile, the Inter-Ministerial Committee approved the letter of permission for a further period of four years from its expiry i.e., 21.12.2008.

The assessee filed writ challenging notice of Department and also pleading for execution of extension of letter of permission.

Issue Involved

Whether impugned notice could be challenged ?

The assessee was a firm of chartered accountants. The original authority confirmed demand of service tax on the assessee for the period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 under the heads ‘Practising chartered accountant’, ‘Manpower recruitment service’, ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Business auxiliary service’. Modifying the findings of the original authority, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax under the head ‘Business auxiliary service’. He affirmed the demand on the assessee in respect of other categories of services. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had rendered services as management consultant and man-power recruitment agent which were exempt in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998. The assessee also contended that Commissioner (Appeals) had wrongly held that the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002 which inserted an Explanation to Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, had come into effect from 16-10-1998.

■

The AO had made a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) under section 92CA. Pursuant to this reference, the TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) accepting that the international transactions entered into by the assessee with its Associated Enterprises were at an Arms Length Price. In other words, the TPO made no variation.

■

The Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order under section 144C(1) and thereafter passed a final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(3) and section 144B.

■

On writ:

The assessee was engaged in providing taxable service under the category of ‘Technical inspection and certification service’ and was also liable to pay service tax on goods transport service received by it. It availed benefit of abatement under Notification No. 32/2004-ST, dated 3-12-2004 with respect to goods transport service received. The revenue issued show-cause notice to the assessee denying benefit of said notification on ground that in view of relevant Boards’ circular in the consignment notes issued to the assessee by goods transport agencies, there was no declaration to the effect that no credit on input or capital goods used for providing services had been taken nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 was availed. However, the Commissioner taking into consideration the Chartered Accountant’s certificate to the effect that the transporters had neither availed CENVAT credit nor the benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003, dropped the demand against the assessee.

On appeals :

■

The assessee–company operated CPPs qualifying under Section 80-IA. Inter-unit power transfers constituted Specified Domestic Transactions. After a search, the AO made a reference to the TPO under Section 92CA. The TPO called for details of cost allocation; the assessee’s TP study defended a 'Direct Nexus' methodology that excluded common HO costs from the CPPs. By order, the TPO accepted this methodology and reduced the transfer price to Rs. 2.48 per unit.

■

Relying on Section 92CA(4), the AO adopted the TPO’s findings while completing assessment, which eliminated eligible profits and reduced the Section 80-IA deduction to NIL.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reworked the grid rate and recomputed eligible profit at about Rs. 42.18 crores, directing allowance of deduction; the Revenue’s further appeal led to a limited remand to verify the recomputed figures.

■

Subsequently, the PCIT issued a SCN under Section 263 on the ground that the AO had not ensured proportionate allocation of common HO expenses to the eligible units and set aside the assessment on this limited issue for fresh examination.

■

The Tribunal affirmed the PCIT’s Section 263 action despite the TPO’s order, holding that the cost-allocation for computing eligible profits remained unexamined. On the assessee’s appeal to the High Court.

The assessee claimed to be a SSI Unit in terms of certificate dated 24-4-1998 issued by the Directorate of Industries where there was a clear endorsement that said certificate would come into effect from 10-12-1997, i.e., from the date of Government of India Notification. On basis of above certificate, the assessee claimed exemption from service tax on Goods transport service availed by it. The Deputy Commissioner allowed the claim of the assessee. However, the Commissioner, in the review proceedings, took a different view and held that the certificate had to be taken only from the date of registration, i.e., 24-4-1998 and rejected the claim of the assessee.

On appeal :

■

The assessee was engaged in business of Gems and Jewellery, primarily manufacturing and export of diamond studded Jewellery. The assessee was having one of its units located in Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone-Special Economic Zone (SEEPZ- SEZ) Andheri (East), Mumbai. The assessee had another unit located outside of SEZ, which mainly supplied diamonds to manufacturing unit in SEZ. The assessee filed its return of income for assessment year 2021-22 declaring income of Rs.50.97 crores. Since, the assessee reported certain Specified Domestic Transaction (SDT) with its related party/associated enterprises, the Assessing Officer (AO) made reference under section 92CA (1) to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) for computation of Arm Length Price.

■

The Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) passed his order under section 92CA(3)and suggested addition/made downward adjustment of Rs.11.62 crore on account transaction of sale of jewelry.

■

The assessee before DRP submitted that Assessing Officer had erred in making reference to TPO by invoking provisions of section 80IA(10) without determining and establishing existence of an arrangement between the concerned parties which results in more than ordinary profit and therefore, whole proceedings initiated under transfer pricing provisions was bad in law.

■

. The DRP agreed with the stand of TPO.

■

On receipt of direction of DRP, the Assessing Officer passed final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C (13) read with section 144B and computed the final adjustment on account of sale transaction to its AE at Rs. 10.98 crore and straightway added the same to the income of assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee had claimed exemption under section 10(38) on LTCG arising out of trades carried out by him in the shares of company CCL. The Assessing Officer passed assessment order accepting claim of the assessee.

■

Subsequently, the Principal Commissioner noted that there was a very detailed report of the DGIT (Inv) based on the searches/survey conducted on a large number of hawala operators and entities controlled by them where they admitted to be providing entries through penny stock which also included name of CCL. He further noted that the Assessing Officer had evidence in hand in form of report from the investigation Wing, which alluded that the scrip of CCL was one of 84 scrips which was used by conniving operators and brokers to book unlawful LTCG and claim exemption under section 10(38). He thus invoked revisionary jurisdiction under section 263 on ground that the Assessing Officer had failed to take into account factual matrix and had not conducted any kind of independent verification or enquiries of his own and had merely allowed claim of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

■

For AY 2021-22, the dispute pertained to a transfer pricing adjustment of about Rs. 33.60 crores on account of transfer of power, involving determination of arm’s length price/market value under Section 80IA read with Section 92F.

■

The assessee’s appeal before the Tribunal was partly allowed; on the specific issue of the transfer pricing adjustment on transfer of power, the Tribunal granted relief by relying on the Delhi High Court decision in Principal Commissioner of Income-tax v. DCM Shriram Ltd. [2025] 170 taxmann.com 631 (Delhi).

■

On appeal to the High Court.

The appellant - assessee is a manufacturer of toughened safety glass including wind screen, door screen, side screen and back screen. It applied for the grant of "recognition certificate" u/s 4B of the U.P. Trade Tax Act, but the certificate was granted only in relation to automobile safety toughened glass and not to other items. By Notification No.ST-II-7551×-91-76 dated 31st December 1976 issued under U.P. Trade Tax Act, 1948 purchase of raw materials and packing materials in relation to the items specified in the Notification was exempted from sales tax. Item No.2 of the Notification read, "Glass and glasswares, including optical glass in all forms". In the subsequent Notification No. ST-II 4519 /×-7 (19)/87 dated 29th August, 1987 the corresponding entry read as "Glass and glassware, including optical glass in all its forms, but excluding ornamented or cut glass "bangles". Since the assessee was granted recognition certificate only in relation to Automobile safety toughened glass and not to other items, the assessee preferred an appeal to the Asst. Commissioner, who directed to amend the recognition certificate including purchase of raw materials and packing materials in relation to all items manufactured by it. The Tribunal affirmed the decision of the First Appellate Authority. High Court, on the other hand, held that the appellant assessee was not entitled to exemption in relation to those articles. On further appeal to Supreme Court.

The Appellants supplied Zinc Oxide to M/s. Premier Tyres for industrial purpose, namely, manufacture of rubber goods. They were denied the benefit of Notfn. No. 21/55-CE dt. 28.4.1975 on the ground that they did not follow the Chapter X Procedure prescribed in the Notfn. The Appellants produced CT2 certificate from the Departmental Officer at the user's end and also the connected L-6 Licence for using the exempted material.

■

The assessee had established two captive electricity and steam generation units for the generation of electricity and steam. The assessee had sought exemption under section 80-IA(4)(iv) in respect of Co-generation Unit 1, specifically for the supply of electricity and steam to its non-specified unit, the Paper Unit.

■

The assessee had adopted the Transaction Net Margin Method (TNMM) for determining the arm''s length price for the transfer of power from the specified Co-generation Unit-1 to the non-specified Paper Unit and the sale value of the power had been determined by the assessee at Rs. 41.21 crores, based on a rate of Rs. 6.73 per KWH for a total of 61.24 crores units of power.

■

The Assessing Officer adopted a rate of Rs. 3.875 per unit (KVAH), instead of the assessee’s applied rate of Rs. 6.73 per unit (KWH). The Assessing Officer derived this rate by averaging the adjusted rate of Rs. 4.74 per unit (after making adjustments from Rs. 4.74 per unit) from PSPCL and the rate of Rs. 3.01 per unit from the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX). Consequently, the Assessing Officer computed a difference in the sale price of power and made an addition of Rs. 17.48 crores.

■

On appeal, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer''s approach was inconsistent with the provisions of section 92C(1), read with rule 10B, and section 80-IA(8), which govern the determination of arm''s length price and transfer pricing adjustments.The rate of 76.73 per KWH adopted by the assessee for the transfer of power was lower than the comparable rate for generating electricity from biomass fuel, as available in the public domain and the rate adopted by the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) of Rs. 5.98 per unit of PSPCL(Power Corporation) for deriving average was not justified, as the assessee was categorized as a power-intensive unit, and not under the general category.TPO wrongly deducted distribution loss, transmission loss, and cross-subsidy from the rate, leading to an incorrect revised adjusted sale rate of Rs. 4.74 per KVAH per unit for power supplied by PSPCL and the TPO failed to apply the appropriate division factor of 0.92 to convert KVAH into KWH. The price at which surplus power was supplied by producers to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) is determined by state regulations and contracts and, therefore, cannot be considered the market value for the purposes of Section 80-IA(8).

The assessee filed its return of income. Further, the assessee received notices under section 148 and under section 92CA from the Transfer Pricing Officer seeking details about the international transactions entered into by the assessee with the group companies on a reference made by the Assessing Authority. In reply to the notice issued, the assessee filed a letter requesting the Assessing Authority to treat the return filed as return in compliance with the notice under section 148. In fact, the Transfer Pricing Officer passed an order under section 92CA accepting the pricing of the Assessing Authority.

However, the Commissioner invoked section 263 and set aside the order of the Assessing Authority.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that when two views were possible and when the Transfer Pricing Authority accepted valuation by the Assessing Authority determining the arm's length price, the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to interfere with the said order under section 263. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the order of the Commissioner.

On revenue's appeal to the High Court :

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of blended packet tea at its two units located at Dharwad and outside Dharwad. Dharwad unit was exempt from payment of sales tax under Notification dated 19-6-1991.

The Assessing Authority inspected the business premises of the assessee and having noticed that the maximum retail price (MRP) mentioned on the tea packets sold from the Dharwad unit and outside Dharwad unit was similar opined that the assessee had added the tax component to the sale price of Dharwad tea though not under the nomenclature of tax or cess. Hence, the assessee had violated clause (e) of Explanation III to the Notification dated 19-6-1991 and was not entitled to the benefit of exemption. He, therefore, rejected the claim of exemption on the turnover of Dharwad tea based on notification dated 19-6-1991.

The First Appellate Authority upheld the view of the Assessing Authority.

The Tribunal held that though the assessee had considered the local tax element in the price fixed, but it could not be stated that it had collected the local taxes as such from the consumers in view of the fact that in the invoice against Karnataka Sales Tax and Central Sales Tax it was specifically left blank in respect of Dharwad tea. Mere mentioning of MRP on the Dharwad tea did not by itself a proof of any collection of tax in terms of sales tax laws. It accordingly allowed the appeal of the assessee.

The High Court affirmed the order passed by the Tribunal. It held that on the Dharwad tea there was a clear mention of exemption of tax in terms of the note at the end of the invoice itself. Therefore, the buyer was told in unmistakable terms that what was being paid as sale price and not as sales tax.

On appeal to Supreme Court:

The appellants manufacture P & P medicines falling under TI 14E and claimed exemption under Notification 85/85-CE for the year 1985-86. However, later, the Assistant Collector confirmed a demand for Rs. 2,33,859.47 on the ground that they were not eligible for exemption under Notification 85/85-CE since the total clearance during 1985-86 from their factory and as a loan licensee of M/s. Natco Fine Pharmaceuticals had exceeded Rs. 75 lakhs. This order was upheld by Collector (Appeals).

■

The petitioner, an assessee–SEZ unit, was incorporated on 10.02.2009, granted approval by the Development Commissioner on 16.10.2014 to establish its unit at Madurai, with approval renewed on 13.04.2020 and extended up to 26.04.2025. It claimed that under the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, supplies to and by an SEZ enjoyed exemptions for authorised operations. Post introduction of GST on 01.07.2017, it asserted that supplies to/by an SEZ are treated as inter-State under Section 7(5)(b) of the IGST Act and constitute zero-rated supplies under Section 16, and that the services received, including professional and consultancy services, were for authorised operations as per Government communication dated 02.01.2018. The writ petitions challenged assessment orders passed under Section 73 of the TNGST Act.

■

The adjudicating authority passed the impugned assessment orders under Section 73. As recorded from the respondent’s submissions and the counter affidavit referred to before the Court, the orders were issued primarily on account of the petitioner’s failure to produce the Letter of Undertaking (LUT) and the SEZ Certificate for verification.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

■

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading of chemical, PVC Resins, PVC compounds, UPVC Windows & Door Systems, Cement, Sugar, Fertilizers, seeds, textile yarn, power generation etc. It owned various captive power plants for production of power and supply of power generated among its other units. The power production units were eligible for deduction under section 80-IA and, therefore, power transferred from the eligible unit to non-eligible unit had been treated as specified domestic transaction and the assessee had taken transfer price at cost. The assessee had benchmarked transfer of electricity at rate of INR 8.35 per KWH i.e. rate at which electricity was actually purchased from JVVNL in Rajasthan region. The TPO accepted all transactions be as per ALP other than transactions between eligible and non-eligible units of Kota. The TPO had obtained rates from IEX and asked the assessee as to why External CUP method should not be applied, and sale rate of the power should not be taken at average price at which power was purchased by the assessee from JVVNL and average price of IEX. Accordingly, the TPO had worked out average rate at Rs. 66.117255 per KWH and made adjustment. The Assessing Officer had made adjustment as proposed by the TPO.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) had deleted the adjustment made by the TPO.

■

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee-firm was engaged in manufacture and export of studded jewellery from its SEEPZ-SEZ unit and claimed deduction under section 10AA for assessment year 2021-22. Though it claimed that it had neither entered into any international transaction with an associated enterprise nor any specified domestic transaction, it reported certain transactions in Form 3CEB as a matter of abundant caution and benchmarked them under TNMM.

■

The Assessing Officer referred the matter to the TPO under section 92CA. Invoking section 80IA(10) read with section 10AA, the TPO proposed a downward adjustment to sales and the Assessing Officer incorporated the same in the draft assessment order.

■

The DRP rejected the objections and upheld the adjustment.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee had two CPPs or eligible units generating electricity which were consumed captively by other non-eligible units for carrying out the manufacturing. It determined the arm's length price (ALP) of the specified domestic transactions at rate ranging from Rs. 7.66 per unit to Rs. 7.87 per unit which was the Average Annual Landed Cost (AALC) at which the non-eligible unit procured power from State Electricity Board (SEB) and followed internal CUP for benchmarking the specified domestic transactions of transfer of power from the SEB by taking non-eligible units as the tested party in the TP study report. The assessee had also reported these transactions in the audited report in Form 3CEB.

For the purposes of section 80-IA(8) and in order to determine the stand-alone profits of the eligible unit, the transfer value of power to non-eligible unit was adopted at Rs. 7.66 - 7.87/unit having reference to average landed cost (ALC) at which the non-eligible unit procured power from the (SEB).

The TPO, however, opined that the average tariff orders issued by the SEB in respect of other independent power producers was the most relevant indicator of the ALP for power supplied by CPPs to non-eligible unit as opposed to the assessee's internal CUP i.e. the rate at which the non-eligible units procured from unrelated entity i.e. SEB apart from the CPP.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) being of view that eligible CPP supplied power only to the Associated Enterprise (AE) i.e, the non-eligible unit and it did not have any transaction with any unrelated enterprises. On contrary, the non-eligible unit was sourcing power both from the AE i.e. the eligible undertaking as well as unrelated enterprises i.e. the SEB. Accordingly, held that the methodology and benchmarking adopted by the assessee was justified and, accordingly, directed the TPO to delete the adjustment and further directed the TPO to grant the deduction under section 80-IA.

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacture & sale of paper. It had set-up a captive power plant (CPP) to meet the power requirements of the paper manufacturing unit (non-eligible unit) which had been qualified as an eligible unit under section 80-IA(4)(iv).

As power generated by the assessee was actively consumed by the paper manufacturing unit, such transfer of power qualified as a reportable specified domestic transaction in terms of section 80-IA(8) read with section 92BA. On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee was engaged in the business of execution of construction contracts. It entered into a contract with one 'A' for construction of power project in the Special Economic Zone (SEZ).

It filed an application under section 80 for determination on the question as to whether any tax was payable by it on the sale of goods in the course of execution of works contract to 'A' in the SEZ.

The Determining Authority held that in view of provisions of section 5A, the assessee was not liable to pay tax on the sale of goods in the SEZ to 'A'. But there should be an endorsement of the Customs Authority to prove that the sale was made to the developer or co-developer of SEZ.

The assessee obtained endorsement of the Customs Authority on the purchase bills before the entry of the goods into SEZ for use in execution of the works contract. It raised running bills to 'A' on achievement of milestone as stipulated in the works contract.

In the return filed for the assessment year 2008-09, it claimed exemption under section 5A from payment of tax on the sale of goods to 'A' in the SEZ.

The Assessing Authority denied exemption under section 5A on sale of goods to 'A'.

The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on the ground that the running bills which were issued by the assessee to 'A' did not bear the endorsement of the Customs Authority. For this purpose, he placed reliance upon rule 42(2A).

The Tribunal held that while rule 42(2A) prescribed a procedure to the effect that if the tax invoice was endorsed by the Customs Authority, then the sale will be treated as a zero rated sale under section 5A, it was simply a procedural rule and did not lay down any condition precedent that only on fulfilment of such condition, the sale had to be treated as zero rated sale. It was directory in nature, non compliance of which would not deprive the assessee of the right to claim zero rated sale under section 5A. Section 21(1) of the Gujarat Special Economic Zone Act, 2004 granted exemption from payment of tax on sale or purchase of goods in the SEZ. Hence, tax was not leviable on the sales in question.

The assessee was in the business of diamond and jewellery. The assessee was having transaction with its Associated Enterprises (AE). The assessee while filing return of income furnished transfer pricing study report, reporting transaction with its AEs.

■

The Assessing Officer made reference to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) for determination of Arm’s Length Price in respect of transactions reported by assessee in its transfer pricing report. During the proceedings before the TPO, the assessee furnished required information along with its Transfer Pricing Study Report.

■

The TPO was of the view that price charged by the assessee from its AE was not at Arm’s Length and made recommendation of adjustment on account of sale and purchase of jewellery and diamonds with its AE. The TPO also recommended adjustment on account of delay in receivable from AE.

■

The Assessing Officer on the basis of report/order of TPO made addition in draft Assessment Order.

■

The DRP upheld the order TPO. On receipt of direction of DRP, the Assessing Officer passed final Assessment Order.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee was engaged in the trading of cut and polished diamonds and the manufacturing of diamond jewellery and had a jewellery manufacturing unit situated in a Special Economic Zone (SEZ), which claimed deduction under section 10AA.

■

During the year, the SEZ unit purchased cut and polished diamonds from the assessee’s Diamond Division (Domestic Tariff Area unit) as well as from third parties. Since deduction under section 10AA was claimed, the inter-unit purchases qualified as specified domestic transactions and were subjected to transfer pricing provisions.

■

The assessee benchmarked the specified domestic transactions under the Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM). In the transfer pricing study, the Jewellery SEZ unit was initially selected as the tested party. During transfer pricing proceedings, however, the assessee submitted that the Diamond Division was the least complex entity and should be treated as the tested party, furnishing workings to show that transactions were at arm’s length.

■

The TPO rejected the assessee’s request and treated the Jewellery SEZ unit as the tested party, benchmarking its margins with jewellery manufacturing comparables, resulting in an upward transfer pricing adjustment of about Rs. 10.88 crores.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the Diamond Division as the appropriate tested party and granted relief, noting inter alia that in a subsequent assessment year the TPO had accepted the same tested party in the assessee’s own case.

It is material to note that the TP adjustments are made pursuant to the APA entered into by the assessee with CBDT. Section 92CC empowers the CBDT to enter into an APA with any person for determining an ALP or specify the manner in which the ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person and income referred to in section 9(1)(i) or the manner in which said income is to be determined as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India. [Para 17]

■

It is relevant to refer to sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92CD. [Para 18]

■

The provisions of section 92CD(1) are unambiguous and even if a return has been filed prior to an assessee entering into an APA, he is entitled to furnish a modified return declaring his income in accordance with the terms of the APA. Subject to certain exceptions, the APA is binding both on the assessee and the revenue. [Para 19]

■

It is clear that the scheme of providing for an APA is to remove any uncertainty as to the determination of an income of an assessee engaged in international transactions with associated enterprises. The assessee is required to declare his income in accordance with the APA. Except in certain cases, where there is a change in law and facts or the agreement is occasioned by fraud or misrepresentation, the APA would be binding. Sub-sections (5), (6) and (7) of section 92CC provide for the same in unambiguous terms. [Para 20]

■

It is apparent from a plain reading of sub-section (4) of section 92C that the same is inapplicable. The said sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to compute the total income, having regard to the ALP determined by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (3) of section 92C. [Para 22]

■

Sub-section (3) of section 92C provides that the Assessing Officer can proceed to determine the ALP only in cases he is of the opinion on the basis of material that (a) the price charged or paid in international transaction, has not been determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92C; or (b) that information and documentation relating to the international transaction has not been maintained as mandatorily required; or (c) that the information or data for computing the ALP is unreliable; or there is failure on the part of the assessee to furnish any information or document required to be furnished along with the notice. [Para 23]

■

It is apparent that in a case where the assessee voluntarily computes the ALP pursuant to an APA entered into with CBDT, none of the conditions as set out in sub-section (3) of section 92C are attracted. It follows that sub-section (4) of section 92C is not attracted. [Para 24]

■

More importantly, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C also clearly states that no deduction under section 10A or 10AA or 10B or under Chapter VI-A would be allowed in respect of the amount of income by which the total income of the assessee is enhanced after computation under the said section. Thus in a case where the assessee voluntarily declares his income based on the ALP determined on the basis of an APA, there would be no occasion for the Assessing Officer to enhance the income of the assessee. [Para 25]

■

Absent any enhancement of income, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is clearly inapplicable. [Para 26]

■

It is also necessary to bear in mind that in terms of section 10AA(1), the profits and gains of an enterprise, as referred to in clause (j) of section 2 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, from an eligible unit, which is derived from export of articles or things are exempt. [Para 27]

■

The ALP is imputed to transactions to determine the profits and gains that are derived by the assessee from any international transactions (or specified domestic transactions) in order to assess the real income of the assessee after eliminating any bias or element of transfer of profits. [Para 28]

■

Thus, indisputably, the income computed on the basis of ALP would provide a measure of the profits or income derived by the activities carried on by an assessee. The proviso to section 92C(4) essentially limits exemption under section 10AA in cases where the income computed is enhanced by the Assessing Officer under section 92C. [Para 29]

Technical Inspection service :

The work order requires AGPL to carry out jobs such as the following : Washing; Preparing Vehicle for display; PDI w/o. O/C/; PDI with O/C, PT as per Schedule, Waxing as per Schedule; Rewaxing; PDI & PT with O/C; Removing & Redoing PT Refurnishing etc.

On receiving this work order AGPL undertakes the jobs as indicated in the vehicle data sheet. The data sheets give details of defects and rectificatory action under various heads, namely leakages, electricals, mechanicals, body paint, body fitments.

The rectification job of these defects certainly seems to be activities conducted by any vehicle repair shop. If the argument of revenue is accepted, every motor garage will become a 'technical inspection and certification' agency. This would lead to a ridiculous situation. The meaning of technical inspection and certification conveys the purpose of certification along with inspection to meet specified standards.

The kind of certification covered under this definition refers to certification to ensure that characteristics of the goods meet specified standards. The standards may relate to functionality, utility, quality or safety. The definition of technical inspection cannot be read to mean that any checks on functionality, safety etc. would amount to technical inspection and certification. The word "technical inspection and certification" would appropriately refer to certain standards laid down in some statute or some Guidelines.

For example in the Motor Vehicles Act certain standards are required to be met. Other examples of technical inspection are the Food Safety Standards which require articles of food and drinks to meet certain standards of composition of ingredients etc. Similar is the case where pharmaceutical products are required to meet certain specified standards by law.

In the present case the job card or vehicle data sheets clearly indicate that AGPL are merely rectifying/replacing some damaged/defective parts etc. By no stretch of imagination can this activity be termed as technical inspection and certification. Hence, demand was set aside. [Para 7]

There was registration certificate dated 30-6-2000 with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991. The object of the exemption notification was neither to protect the owners of the trade mark nor the consumers from being misled. These were considerations which were relevant in disputes arising under the Trade Marks Act. The object of the exemption Notification No. 1/93-CE was to grant benefits to those industries, which did not have the advantage of a brand name. [Para 16] It is correct to say that the Registrar of Trade Marks can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect. Making the registration certificate applicable from retrospective date is based on principle of deemed equivalence to public user of such mark. This deeming fiction cannot be extended to Excise Law. It is confined to the provisions of the Trade Marks Act. In a given case like the instant one, where there was evidence with the department of the trade mark being owned by company ‘K’ and there was evidence of the appellants trading on the reputation of ‘K’ which was not rebutted by them, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect could not confer the benefit of exemption notification upon them. In the instant case, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991 would not tantamount to conferment of exemption benefit under the Excise Law, once it was found that the appellants had wrongly used the trade mark of company ‘K’. [Paras 17 & 18]

If the SSI unit wrongly affixes a trade mark of another person, be it registered or not, or if it uses the trade mark of an ineligible person, such default would not be eliminated by the principle of deemed equivalence embodied in section 28; as that principle is based on a deeming fiction, which fiction is confined only to the provisions of that Act. [Para 20]

Consequently, the appeals were to be dismissed.

PER COURT

"The Trade Marks Act has been enacted to amend and consolidate the law relating to trade marks, to provide for registration and better protection of trade marks and for prevention of the use of fraudulent marks. Under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act, registration gives to the registered proprietor of the trade mark the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods in respect of which the trade mark is registered and to obtain relief in respect of infringement of the trade mark in the manner provided by the Trade Marks Act. It is correct to say that the Registrar, Trade Marks, can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect". [Para 17]

■

When this Court has already considered the certificate dated 09.01.2013 and during the pendency of the appeal before the Tribunal for the year under consideration, the Revenue has not been able to bring any material on record or has challenged or doubted the certificate issued by the Singapore Tax Authority, as observed by the Tribunal in Para 20 of the impugned order, it has noted that the Departmental Representative has challenged the veracity of the certificate issued by the IRAS during the course of the appellate proceedings before the CIT (A) and thereafter, the Tribunal has referred to the territorial tax system of the Singapore Income Tax Act to hold that the certificate has not given any basis whatsoever as to how the assessee is deriving income from "business carried on in Singapore", when admittedly, the appellants-assessee have been operating in international waters. The Tribunal has also considered the fact that the certificate does not specify the factual basis on which the Singapore Tax Authority has concluded that the income from shipping business have been derived by the assessee from "business carried on in Singapore". Thus, in effect, the Tribunal has overreached the findings arrived at by this Court in case of M.T. Maersk Mikage v. DIT (International Taxation) (supra) in absence of any material brought on record by the Revenue before the Tribunal to show that the certificate issued by the IRAS is not reliable or cannot be considered for the income of ST Shipping to be taxed in Singapore on accrual basis. [Para 15]

■

It is also pertinent to note that from the documents placed in form of paper- book filed before the Tribunal, in fact, the ST Shipping has shown the income arising from the operations as per letter dated 09.10.2012 issued by the Deloitte and Touche LLP, Certified Public Accountants, Singapore stating that the ST Shipping has confirmed that the position adopted in the Year of Assessment 2010 to treat charter income derived by the overseas branches as Singapore sourced income and part of qualifying income under Approved International Shipping Enterprise Incentive remains unchanged in the Year of Assessment 2012. [Para 16]

■

The impugned order of the Tribunal is, therefore, contrary to the decision of this Court as the Tribunal could not have restored the matter back to the Assessing Officer only on mere suspicion and the doubts contrary to the findings arrived at by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by IRAS. The Tribunal ought not to have analysed the certificate in its order more particularly in Para 22 of the order in absence of any material on record. On perusal of Para 22 of the impugned order it is clear that the Tribunal has made the observation with regard to the language of the certificate more particularly, when this Court has accepted the part of the certificate which certified that the income earned by the ST Shipping from the operations carried out in ports at India was liable to be taxed at Singapore on accrual basis and as per Article 8 of DTAA, when the income accrues in Singapore and was taxed as such, the same would be exempt from tax in India. This Court has further clarified that reference to Article 24 of DTAA in the certificate is nothing but an opinion of the IRAS. [Para 17]

■

Hence, the Tribunal ought not to have further deliberated upon contents of the certificate which is already held to be applicable in the facts of the case in the absence of any other material on record to demonstrate that the veracity of the certificate issued by IRAS is doubtful and merely because the Tribunal is of the opinion that the language of the certificate is not conducive to the opinion of the Tribunal, the matter could not have been restored to the Assessing Officer in face of the observation made by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by the IRAS. The Advance Ruling is sought on the applicability of exemption under Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 to the Third Party Inspection Services rendered by the applicant to CMWSSB and TWAD under the two contracts. The facts of the case as stated by the applicant are that it has entered into agreements with CMWSSB and TWAD for rendering the services of Third Party Inspection on being empanelled. The applicant has stated that CMWSSB and TWAD are of the view that Third Party Inspection Services are within the ambit of 'Pure Services', as it is an activity in relation to any function entrusted to a Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution and will not reimbursed the GST component of the invoice. The issue to be decided is whether the applicant is rendering 'Pure Services' and whether CMWSSB and TWAD are 'Governmental Authority' as defined in the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 5]

From a reading of Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 and definition of 'Government Authority' given under 2(zf) of the said Notification, it is evident that if any 'pure services' are provided to a Governmental Authority by way of any activity in relation to any function entrusted to a Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution or a Panchayat under article 243G (from 13-10-2017) of the Constitution and that 'Governmental Authority' is an Authority or a Board set up by an Act of Parliament or a State legislature or established by the Government with 90 per cent or more participation by way of equity or control to carry out any function entrusted to a Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution, then the same is exempted vide Sl. No. 3 of the Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 6.1]

In the case at hand, CMWSSB is created vide The Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Act, 1978 with 100 per cent contribution by way of Government [i.e., by way of takeover of assets and liabilities from Chennai Municipal Corporation and Tamil Nadu Water Supply and Drainage Board] and controlled by the Government by way of appointing Directors of the CMWSSB to carry out the functions of supplying water for Domestic, Industrial and Commercial purposes as well as Sanitation Conservancy by way of disposal of Sewerage. TWAD is a Board constituted by an Act of Tamil Nadu State Legislature called Tamil Nadu Water Supply and Drainage Board Act, 1970 with 100 per cent contribution by way of Government and controlled by Government by way of appointing Directors of the TWAD entrusted with the development of Water Supply and Sewerage facilities in Municipalities and Panchayats in the State of Tamil Nadu, except Chennai Metropolitan Development. The Twelfth Schedule or article 243W of the Constitution list the functions of the Municipality at Sl. No. 5 as 'Water Supply for Domestic, Industrial and Commercial purposes' and at Sl. No. 6 as 'Public Health, Sanitation Conservancy and Solid Waste Management'. The Eleventh Schedule or article 243G of the Constitution list the functions of the Municipality at Sl. No. 5 as 'Water Supply for Domestic, Industrial and Commercial purposes' and at Sl. No. 6 as 'Public Health, Sanitation Conservancy and Solid Waste Management'. Thus it is clear that the Constitution list the functions of the Panchayat at Sl. No. 11 as 'Drinking Water' and at Sl. No. 23 as 'Health and Sanitation'. Thus it is clear that in respect of services received in relation to functions pertaining to Municipality, CMWSSB is a 'Governmental Authority' as defined under 2(zf) of the Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended. However, in respect of services received in relation to functions pertaining to Panchayat, TWAD is a 'Governmental Authority' only from 13-10-2017 as defined under 2(zf) of the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended. [Para 6.2]

One of the key allegations of the Commissioner is that the Assessing Officer should have made a reference to the TPO as per the CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003. First of all, it would be relevant to see, whether there was any such instruction issued by the CBDT to the Assessing Officer for making any reference to the TPO for specified domestic transaction. From the perusal of the said Instruction No. 3/2003, it is seen that guidelines for reference to the TPO has been made only in respect of determination of arm's length price in relation to the international transaction under section 92B. There is no whisper about specified domestic transaction for the reason that there was no concept of specified domestic transaction under the Act when said instruction was issued on 20-5-2003. The specified domestic transaction for the purpose of determination of ALP has been brought in the statute only by the Finance Act, 2012. Hence, holding the assessment order erroneous for the reason that, the Assessing Officer should have made a reference to the TPO in accordance with CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003 is wholly misconceived and misinterpreted. Once there was no CBDT instruction or guidelines for reference to the issue involving specified domestic instruction to the TPO at the time of passing the assessment order, then where is the question of any non-compliance of CBDT Instruction by the Assessing Officer.

At the year-end the sales tax portion, which formed the part of dealers’ price had been bifurcated and had been claimed as a capital subsidy. The State Government through the Notification No. 1179, dated 31-3-1995 had provided sales tax exemption with an objective to promote the development of certain industries which had been set-up or undertaken modernisation, diversification, backward integration by way of fixed capital investment of Rs. 50 crores or more. The exemption from sales tax or benefit of reduced rate of tax was available to those units which had started production or had carried out expansion or modernisation or backward integration, etc., between 1-12-1994 and 31-3-2000. Para 2 of the Notification specifies that the exemption or reduction in the rate of sales tax including the additional tax would not be more than 5 per cent of the sale of goods. In case where tax rate was more than 5 per cent including additional tax, the balance was to be paid by the unit. Para 7(2) of the Notification provides for the exemption of sales tax to the extent of exemption or reduction in tax. Item (2) of the Schedule includes Greater Noida Industrial Development Area wherein exemption from sales tax to the extent of 200 per cent of capital investment had been provided. None of the clauses of the notification authorised the assessee to collect the sales tax and retain the same with it. The exemption of sales tax was available from the date of first sale or the date within the period of six months from the date of production, whichever was earlier. The said notification also provided that the eligibility certificate to the assessee would be issued by the Joint/Additional Director of concerned development authority and the same would be produced before the concerned Assessing Officer. The Additional Director Industries, Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority, issued eligibility certificate to the assessee. As per this certificate fixed capital investment was of Rs. 51,57,95,446. The date of commencement of production was 9-3-1998 and the first sale was affected on 27-3-1998. The assessee applied for exemption from trade tax [sales tax]. The exemption from trade tax [sales tax] was provided from 27-3-1998 to 26-3-2013 for a period of 15 years or till the time the exemption of sales tax was availed of to the extent of 200 per cent of the fixed capital investment, i.e., Rs. 1,02,75,90,892, whichever was earlier. This certificate also provided the items, i.e., colour TVs, washing machines and air-conditioners on which exemption from sales tax was provided. Another certificate was issued on 27-9-2000 in respect of printed circuit voice for CTV number 8,12,000 and microwave oven 1,00,000. In this certificate, the sales tax exemption in the first three years had been provided to the extent of 100 per cent; for next three years at 75 per cent; for next two years at 50 per cent; and for next two years at 25 per cent. In all exemption from sales tax was provided for 10 years. [Para 9]

Neither the certificates issued by the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority nor the notification issued by the State Government authorised the assessee to collect sales tax from its customers. The assessee had been exempted from collecting the sales tax from customers on the sales made with effect from 27-3-1998. In fact, during the course of hearing, neither the notification had authorized the assessee to collect sales tax nor the assessee had collected the sales tax as such. The assessee had included the element of sales tax in the dealers’ price as a sale price of the product. In the States other than Uttar Pradesh, the sales tax so collected as a part of dealer’s price had been paid to the respective State Governments, whereas in the case of the assessee the assessee was not liable to pay sales tax, as exemption had been provided to the extent of 200 per cent of fixed capital investment, the sales tax element which was embedded in the sale price had been retained by the assessee as excess sales consideration. At the year-end the assessee had allocated the sales tax element from dealer’s price and had claimed the same as capital subsidy. Therefore, the collection of dealer’s price had been made in the ordinary course of trading activities. When the assessee was not permitted to collect the sales tax under the notification issued by the State Government the collection of sales tax as a part of dealer’s price was nothing but constituted a trading receipt. [Para 10]

2. The issue of the eligibility certificate is not within the control of the dealers and is depending on the manner in which the conserned authorities choose to deal with it. Provisions of section 8 of CST Act

The provisions of sub-sections (2A) and (5) of section 8 of the CST Act clearly enable the State Government to exempt the tax payable under the CST Act in public interest by issuing appropriate notification. For the said purpose, the State Government has to be satisfied and is also entitled to impose conditions which have to be specified in the notification. [Para 12]

Sequence of facts on record

It is not in dispute that the assessee had sold the goods in question which were manufactured by 'B' that was holding a valid exemption certificate under rule 28A. The assessee had claimed central sales tax exemption of such goods in terms of notification dated 4-9-1995 by urging that such exemption was in respect of sale of goods which were manufactured by any dealer in the State of Haryana who held a valid exemption certificate. The core controversy pertains to the interpretation of notification dated 4-9-1995 which has been issued by the competent authority in exercise of power under section 8(5) of the CST Act. [Para 13]

Notification dated 4-9-1995

The notification dated 4-9-1995 has been issued in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (5) to section 8 of the CST Act by the Governor of Haryana in public interest. As per the notification, no tax is payable under the aforesaid Act with effect from 1-4-1988 on sale of goods during the period of exemption that are manufactured in the State of Haryana by any dealer, who holds a valid exemption certificate under rule 28A. Proviso to the said notification stipulates that the dealers should have also not charged any tax under the CST Act on the sale of goods manufactured by him. [Para 14]

Sub-section (5) to section 8 begins with the non obstante clause and empowers the State Governments to issue a notification in the official gazette subject to the condition(s) as may be specified and under clause (a) direct that no tax shall be payable by any dealer having his place of business in the State in respect of sale in the course of inter-State trade or commerce, etc. and under clause (b) in respect of all sales of goods or classes of goods, etc. [Para 15]

Provisions of rule 28A of Haryana Rules

The rule 28A as per heading relates to class of industries, period and other conditions for exemption/deferment from payment of tax.

Sub-rule (1) of rule 28A makes it clear that industries are covered under this rule and the said industries would not be entitled to any deferment or exemption from payment of tax under any other provisions of these rules. The expression 'eligible industrial unit' is defined in clause (f) to sub-rule (2). Similarly 'eligibility certificate', 'exemption certificate', etc. are defined in clauses (j) and (k) to sub-rule (2). Clause (n) to sub-rule (2) defines the expression 'notional sales tax liability' and clause (ii) states that the amount of tax payable under the CST Act on sales of finished product of eligible industrial unit made in the course of inter-State trade or commerce shall be computed at the rate of tax applicable as if the sales were made against Form 'C'.

In other words, inter-State trade or commerce of finished products of eligible industrial units will be treated as notional sales tax liability. The reference in this clause is to the eligible industrial unit and sales of finished products made by the said units, which are sold in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. [Para 16]

The purport and impact of rule 28A is with reference to eligible industrial unit is not only clear from the definition clauses which define eligibility certificate, exemption certificate, etc. but also from sub-rule (4)(a) which stipulates that the benefit of tax exemption or deferment shall be given to an eligible industrial unit holding exemption or entitlement certificate for the period specified.

5. Yes, the applicant is liable to be registered under section 22 of the CGST Act, 2017. [Para 22]
