66. It was also stated that the prices charged from PGA were loaded with octroi, CST, freight and other taxes, and delivery charges.

67. The comparison for arriving at the differential duty has been made of the prices as shown in the GP-1s under the column "total assessable value", and as shown in the invoices under column "rate per Kg/litre". Central Excise duty has been calculated on these values which are obviously ex-duty assessable values. There is no reference to any other charge like octroi, CST, freight or any other taxes or delivery charges. Thus, the comparison was between the ex-duty assessable values, and the version in the statement of Shri T.L. Chudiwala is beyond the point.

68. It has also been staled that the products in liquid form were not sold from the depots/branches in the same Slate as these were received from the manufacturing unit; rather some blending process was carried as per specifications of the particular customers. It was at the same time added that the product in solid state viz., rosin, synthetic resin etc. were sold as such, that is, as they were cleared from the factory.

69. In this connection, it is seen that the two prices, one charged from the PGA and the other charged from the customers, other than PGA, were compared, in respect of the goods as cleared from the factory. Processing at subsequent stage, does not account for the large difference in prices of the same goods, in the same form when cleared for PGA, and for other customers, other than PGA.

70. The facts and circumstances of the case clearly establish that the invoices raised by the PTS against PGA were not the genuine invoices as are usually raised in a free market, the prices shown in the invoices were not the correct invoice prices, prices were not genuine and correct prices, and that the relationship between PGA and PTS was not only of the buyer and seller, and the invoice price was influenced by other considerations, other than the relationship of buyer and seller. The price was not the sole consideration for the sale. Thus the party was not eligible for availing of the benefit under Notification No. 120/75-CE for invoice value assessments.

71. While availing of the exemption under Notification No. 120/75-CE, the party has filed an affidavit that they satisfied the various conditions subject to which the exemption under Notification No. 120/75-CE was available. As is obvious from the statement of Shri Chudiwala himself, this affidavit did not correctly disclose the special relationship between PGA and PTS and, suppressed the facts of their mutual relationship. The price charged from PGA were not at 'arm's length and PTS were not eligible for exemption under Notification No. 120/75-CE.

(a)

From the above, it is evident that an applicant can seek an Advance Ruling only in relation to supply of goods or services or both undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by them. However, the Customs Department cannot go into the correctness or otherwise and sit in judgment of the certification or satisfaction arrived at by the DGFT when the certificate or endorsement creates an irrebuttable presumption that the exporter has not availed input credit. This principle was once again reiterated by the Supreme Court in a recent decision of Ashok Leyland Ltd. vs. State of Tamil Nadu - 2004 (3) SCC 1, in paras 59 and 61, the Supreme Court held as under:

This order is conclusive for all purposes, as the above two stated elements clearly go out to show. No appeal has been provided for depicting the will of the legislature to make the order of such authority final".

"61. In State of Madras v. Radio and Electricals, it has been held that satisfaction once reached in absence of any provision, review of such an order is not permissible".

24. If the DGFT finds that the satisfaction or endorsement has been obtained by the exporter by mis-representation, then DGFT may, perhaps, take appropriate action against the exporter for the mis-representation, under the FTDR Act or the Rules framed thereunder.

The Central Board of Direct Taxes, therefore, have decided that wherever the aggregate value of international transaction exceeds Rs. 5 crores, the case should be picked up for scrutiny and reference under section 92CA be made to the TPO. If there are more than one transaction with an associated enterprise or there are transactions with more than one associated enterprises the aggregate value of which exceeds Rs. 5 crores, the transactions should be referred to the TPO." It is well-settled principle that instructions/circulars issued by the CBDT have a binding effect on the Assessing Officer. More specifically, the binding nature of the above-mentioned instruction issued by the CBDT has been confirmed by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in case of Sony India (P.) Ltd. v. CBDT [2007] 288 ITR 52. At para 37 of the said order, the Delhi High Court has concluded as below:

"For these reasons, we hold that the impugned Instruction No. 3, dated 20-5-2003 issued by the CBDT is consistent with the statutory objective underlying section 92CA(1) and acts as a guidance to the Assessing Officer in the exercise of discretion in referring an international transaction to the TPO for determination of its ALP. It is neither arbitrary nor unreasonable, and is not ultra vires the Act."

This view has also been taken by the ITAT, Bangalore Bench in the case of Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. (supra). At paras 44 and 45 of the order, the Tribunal has observed as below:

"44 . . . . Therefore, when provisions of section 92CA(1) are read with Circular of CBDT (Instruction No. 3), dated 20-5-2003, it becomes 'necessary' for the Assessing Officer to refer the question of determination of transfer pricing of international transactions to the TPO. He has no discretion in the matter in the light of limit fixed by the board. The Assessing Officer has only to look at the aggregate value of international transactions disclosed by the assessee in the audit report and then follow directions of CBDT. The Assessing Officer, therefore, is left with a very limited role under section 92CA(1). Likewise while granting approval to the action of the Assessing Officer the CIT has only to see whether aggregate value of international transaction is more than Rs. 5 crores or not. If it is more, he has also to grant approval in the light of directions of CBDT. These directions are mandatory and binding on the Assessing Officer and the CIT(A). The fact that directions are not binding on the assessee or courts is immaterial. The relevant question to be answered is whether circulars are binding on the departmental authorities. The question has an obvious answer.

The issue of legality and validity of above directions was raised before Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Sony India (P.) Ltd. (supra). Their Lordships have also upheld validity of directions of CBDT.

45. In the light of above discussions, we do not find any illegality in the directions issued by the Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)."

Since the circulars issued by the CBDT have a binding affect on the tax authorities, Circular No. 14/2001 issued by the CBDT would also have a binding effect on the Assessing Officer/TPO who is duty bound to demonstrate that the assessee has manipulated its prices to shift profits outside India, before any transfer pricing adjustment is made. Section 92C(3) provides that the Assessing Officer may proceed to determine the ALP if he is of the opinion that certain conditions have been satisfied. Relevant extracts of the said sub-section are reproduced as under:

"(3) Where during the course of any proceeding for the assessment of income, the Assessing Officer is, on the basis of material or information or document in his possession, of the opinion that -

(g )the price charged or paid in an international transaction has not been determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2); or

(h)any information and document relating to an international transaction have not been kept and maintained by the assessee in accordance with the provisions contained in sub-section (1) of section 92D and the rules made in this behalf; or

(i )the information or data used in computation of the arm's length price is not reliable or correct; or

(j )the assessee has failed to furnish, within the specified time, any information or document which he was required to furnish by a notice issued under sub-section (3) of section 92D.

The Assessing Officer may proceed to determine the ALP in relation to the said international transaction in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2), on the basis of such material or information or document available with him. . . ."

(a)

The applicant, in this case, referred a particular transaction when the Board of SMPK is managing and exercising the administrative and financial power, so the Central Government had no control over the management in that period and the Central Government only plays a supervisory role. It is also to be mentioned here that the Central Government is liable to place a full report to be laid before the Parliament for taking control of the management of the Board, as prescribed u/s 49 of the Act.

When the board of SMPK takes administrative and financial decisions, raises loans, pays salaries and other financial benefits to its employees and retired employees, decides the rate for assets and services available at the port, creates master plan for infrastructural projects, without any intervention from the Central Government, it should not considered that the Central Government has an ownership, by way of control, in SMPK. Hence, SMPK is controlled by the Board which is an autonomous body.

3.19 SMPK is audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Art 149 of the Constitution of India mentions

"The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States and of any other authority or body as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States as were conferred on or exercisable by the Auditor-General of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution in relation to the accounts of the Dominion of India and of the Provinces respectively." (emphasis added)

As the audit of SMPK is done by the CA&G, it does not prove that Central Government holds the ownership of SMPK.

3.20 It is a settled principle that the exemption notification should be interpreted strictly and the person who prays for exemption from tax is liable to prove that such exemption notification is applicable for him. So, in this case, the burden of proof lies on the appellant who fails to determine the percentage of ownership of the Central Government in SMPK. In this matter, I would like to rely on the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case of Commissioner of Customs (Import) v. Dilip Kumar & Company (Civil Appeal No. 3327 of 2007)/[2018] 95 taxmann.com 327/69 GST 239/361 ELT 577 (SC) where the apex court pronounced:

"To sum up, we answer the reference holding as under

(1) Exemption notification should be interpreted strictly; the burden of proving applicability would be on the assessee to show that his case comes within the parameters of the exemption clause or exemption notification.

(2) When there is ambiguity in exemption notification which is subject to strict interpretation, the benefit of such ambiguity cannot be claimed by the subject/assessee and it must be interpreted in favour of the revenue."

3.21 Therefore, in paucity of supporting evidences, the undersigned prayed before the authority that the exemption should not be allowed as it does not cover all conditions laid down in the notification mentioned above.

92CA. (1) Where any person, being the assessee, has entered into an international transaction in any previous year, and the Assessing Officer considers it necessary or expedient so to do, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner, refer the computation of the arm’s length price in relation to the said international transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer.

(2) Where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the Transfer Pricing Officer shall serve a notice on the assessee requiring him to produce or cause to be produced on a date to be specified therein, any evidence on which the assessee may rely in support of the computation made by him of the arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction referred to in sub-section (1).

(3) On the date specified in the notice under sub-section (2), or as soon thereafter as may be, after hearing such evidence as the assessee may produce, including any information or documents referred to in sub-section (3) of section 92D and after considering such evidence as the Transfer Pricing Officer may require on any specified points and after taking into account all relevant materials which he has gathered, the Transfer Pricing Officer shall, by order in writing, determine the arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction in accordance with sub-section (3) of section 92C and send a copy of his order to the Assessing Officer and to the assessee.

(4) On receipt of the order under sub-section (3), the Assessing Officer shall proceed to compute the total income of the assessee under sub-section (4) of section 92C having regard to the arm’s length price determined under sub-section (3) by the Transfer Pricing Officer.

(5) With a view to rectifying any mistake apparent from the record, the Transfer Pricing Officer may amend any order passed by him under sub-section (3), and the provisions of section 154 shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly.

5.1 Exempted services - The services which were made exempt due to this notification are all the services except the services mentioned in the notification. The main service which had been made exempt through this exemption notification was tax consultancy or taxation work of the chartered accountants and now withdrawal of the same is the main cause of concern to the practising chartered accountants because at present for vast majority of chartered accountants, the main professional work is tax practice and specially in the small cities the work related to taxation matters and tax consultancy is proportionately much higher than the audit work. The same thing cannot be said for the cost accountants and company secretaries because practically the number of cost accountants and company secretaries engaged in doing tax consultancy is very minimum compared to the chartered accountants but if any cost accountant or company secretary is also providing the taxation and other consultancy service, then the effect of withdrawal of this notification on them will be the same.

Withdrawal of exemption is discriminatory

6. The affected and concerned chartered accountants have termed this withdrawal of exemption as totally discriminatory and unwarranted. In their opinion this exemption was given after due and prolonged deliberation and after considering the whole situation and circumstances in 1998 and it is based on the fact that the field other than the audit work and statutory certification work is not exclusively reserved for the chartered accountants or company secretaries or cost accountants, as the case may be. For the same type of service the other professionals including the legal and tax practitioners are not liable to pay service tax. Then how the chartered accountants or cost accountants or company secretaries, as the case may be, can alone be taxed in this respect. The affected chartered accountants have rightly pointed out that the taxation practice related to VAT, income tax and service tax is major part of their professional receipts and these fields are open for the other professionals also. Then why the chartered accountants are chosen for this tax and why they have been denied the level playing field.

Since the circumstances and the reasons for which this exemption was issued and persist, the withdrawal of the exemption is unwarranted and discriminatory.

Before going into the impact of the rescission of the exemption notification, one should first understand the statutory charge of service tax on the practising chartered accountants, as given in Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994,—

(a) Meaning of practising chartered accountant [Section 65(83)] : Practising chartered accountant means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

Position before withdrawal of exemption notification

2. Before rescission of the service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, i.e., upto February 28, 2006, all services, except those mentioned below, provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA were exempt from service tax—

(a)accounting and auditing; or

(c)secretarial auditing; or

(g)certification of documents to be filed by companies with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956; or

(h)certification in Form No. 1 that the whole of the amount remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a period of three years from the date of transfer to the special account under section 205(1)/(2) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been transferred to the General Revenue Account of the Central Government under the Companies Unpaid Dividend (Transfer to General Revenue Account of the Central Government) Rules, 1978; or

(i)certification of documents under the Exports and Imports Policy of the Government of India; or

(j)certification for exchange control purposes which a practising chartered accountant can issue as documentary evidence in support of certain applications under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973; or

(k)certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957.

Thus, in case any practising CA/CS/ICWA was rendering any service other than (a) to (k ) enumerated above, like legal or taxation consultancy service, etc., he wasn’t liable for service tax.

However, any service provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, which fell under the ambit of any other taxable service, was liable to service tax under the category of that other taxable service. For example, if a chartered accountant also provided manpower recruitment services to his clients, then he was liable to service tax on such services under the category of manpower recruitment service.

Reasons behind issuance of earlier exemption notification

3. The said exemption notification was issued on the principles of equity. The then Government had recognized the fact that the—

(i)practising CA/CS/ICWAs were providing services like legal consultancy, etc., which were equally being provided by other professionals like advocates and legal practitioners and, therefore,

(ii)levy of service tax on such services provided by practising CA/CS/ICWAs and non-levy of service tax on the same services provided by advocates and legal practitioners would be inequitable levy.

Having recognized the abovesaid facts the aforesaid exemption notification was issued to prevent the levy of service tax from being unjust and inequitable.

Position after withdrawal of exemption notification

4. After the withdrawal of the aforesaid exemption notification by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, i.e., with effect from March 1, 2006 all the services provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, in his professional capacity, are chargeable to service tax.

FAQ 90. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

FAQ 91. Whether Treaty Shopping is ipso facto an IAA and reportable in Clause 30C?

Treaty shopping is not, per se, an IAA. Treaty Shopping is to be reported only if it is abusive, i.e. it satisfies the definition of IAA. In Her Majesty The Queen v. Alta Energy Luxembourg S.A.R.L [2022] 144 taxmann.com 23 (SCC), the Supreme Court of Canada held that GAAR could be invoked against treaty shopping only if it perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states. Treaty Shopping per se is not abusive tax avoidance [Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement in Indian GAAR] so as to attract GAAR. Treaty shopping is abusive tax avoidance and attracts GAAR, but only when treaty shopping perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states.

FAQ 72. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

FAQ 74. How to calculate the interest on excess money that needs to be repatriated after a primary adjustment?

Rule 10CB provides the rate of interest at which interest has to be calculated on excess money or part thereof that is not repatriated within the time limit. Where the international transaction is denominated in Indian rupees, the rate of interest will be the one-year marginal cost of fund lending rate of the State Bank of India as of 1st April of the relevant previous year, plus 325 basis points (plus 3.25%). Where the international transaction is denominated in foreign currency, the rate of interest shall be the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) as of 30th September of the relevant previous year plus 300 basis points (plus 3%).

It is possible that the amount of imputed interest income on the excess money not repatriated to India may relate to more than one year. Having regard to Rule 10CB, the interest liability extends till the date of repatriation. Accordingly, for the relevant year under audit, such liability in respect of imputed interest may extend not only to the primary adjustment but may also relate to the primary adjustment made in the earlier years.

Relationship with customs laws 8. The concept of transfer pricing was already present in the Customs Act in the form of Customs Valuation Rules. Under these rules, unless an exception applies, the ‘Assessable Value’ is the invoice value (i.e., ‘Transaction Value’). For customs duty, either the transaction value is accepted as the assessable value or the case is referred to the Special Valuation Branch (SVB), which then determines the assessable value. The issue is whether the assessable value determined under the Customs Act would be accepted by the IT Department as an ‘Arm’s Length Price’? There is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect. The invoice value of imported goods shall be the transaction value, only if the Customs Officer has no reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of the value declared. However, the IT Department may contend that customs authorities merely ensure that the import price is at least equal to the assessable value and in particular, customs authorities may not investigate whether the goods are overpriced. However, it appears that the customs authorities’ acceptance of a transaction value could serve as documentation support for proving that it is an arm’s length prie. In the event, the IT Department arrives at an arm’s length price, which is different from the assessable value, can the customs authorities reopen their assessment and revalue the imports? As per the Customs Act, the authorities can reopen assessment within a period of 5 years provided there is concealment. Practically, the chances of reopening the case are remote because the objective of customs authorities and IT authorities are contrary.2

Relationship with FEMA

9. Under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), an issue could arise in case of imports, wherein the IT Department determines an arm’s length price, which is lower than actual import price. In such a case, it will be interesting to see whether the RBI would take a stand that the Indian entity has overpaid and hence the excess amount paid by Indian entity should be brought back into India. As per section 8 of the FEMA, an Indian resident has to bring into India all foreign exchange amounts, which are due or accrued to him. The issue is whether an Indian resident has to bring into India, additional foreign exchange on account of an adjustment made by the IT authorities under TP regulations? Broadly, the literal interpretation of the word ‘due’ would mean the amount ‘due’ as per contractual agreement and not the amount assessed by IT authorities which is determined long after the transaction is completed. Currently, consultancy fees up to US $ 100,000 can be remitted abroad under automatic approval and for fees exceeding US $ 100,000, one has to apply to RBI, which may accept or reject the same. The issue is whether the RBI approval is sufficient confirmation that the transaction is at arm’s length? Though there is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect, the RBI approval could serve as supporting document. Secondly, can the IT authorities determine an arm’s length price, which is specially rejected by the RBI? Example: Indian company makes an application for payment of consultancy fees exceeding US $ 100,000 to its foreign parent company, which is rejected by the RBI. Can IT authorities assess the foreign parent company for "arm’s length price" exceeding US $ 100,000 ?1

Conclusion

10. Hence, it is felt that though India has made a very good start in amending section 92 of the Act and making transfer pricing illegal and punishable with huge amount of fines, it is felt that a lot more can still be done. As already stated above, the said changes are still to come on lines with the international standards in this field. The analysis done in this paper was only an illustration of the flaws in the present law of transfer pricing in India and the possible changes that can be introduced in it. A lot more needs to done in areas like that of documentation where a large number of documents needs to be submitted, irrespective of the size of the enterprise. This would obviously result in a huge administrative and financial burden on the smaller enterprises. Similarly, it is felt that the penalties imposed in case of violations are excessive as compared to similar laws in other jurisdictions etc.

Keeping in mind the fact that tax legislations ought to be guided by certain canons such as that of neutrality, effectiveness, certainty, simplicity and flexibility, it is clear that the existing section 92 does not in anyway achieve this goal. The ambiguity that is present in the existing provisions becomes all the more worrisome given the economic context of India, which is a developing country and which clearly requires assistance of the FDIs brought in by the MNCs into the country for its economic development. The inflow of this FDI is bound to be affected unless the issue of vagueness in section 92 is immediately addressed to and suitable amendments be made thereto.

The main point raised by some service providers is that where they are carrying out any certification as required by any statute can it come under the purview of consultancy, advice or technical assistance. The Government clarified the same through the Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX. 4, dated 26-2-2002. It was clarified that the certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job. It is then to be examined whether this activity can come under the purview of advice or technical assistance. An advice is generally understood to be optional in nature and has no statutory force. It is up to the client to accept the advice or not. The activity of certification will, therefore, not fall under the category of advice. As regards ‘technical assistance’, it is observed that an assistance is normally for the purpose of achieving a particular aim or result. A certificate given by, say, the Boiler Inspector under the Factories Act, 1948, about the safety of a boiler, cannot be considered to be ‘assistance’ to the person using the said boiler in his factory. To issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purposes of issuing certificates by the same agency under an authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency, before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. It will, therefore, be essential to examine each activity of a service provider on the basis of facts, the terms of agreement between the assessee and the clients and the corresponding provision of Indian or International statute/convention/protocol, or code, to determine whether the certificate being given is under the authority of any such statute, convention protocol or code. Transfer Pricing (TP) continues to be one of the most significant international tax issues for multinational enterprises globally. India, recognising its importance in curbing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)introduced TP provisions in 2001. Since its inception, the Indian TP regime has evolved, keeping pace with both market dynamics and continued global tax developments.

As the Indian tax landscape continues to evolve, there are several critical areas that require attention in the upcoming Union Budget 2025. The following outlines key areas where we believe regulatory intervention and reform are necessary, along with our specific expectations for the forthcoming budget.

Compliance

Maintenance of TP Documentation: Since the introduction of TP provisions in 2001, the threshold for maintaining TP documentation for taxpayers has been set at INR 1 crore in aggregate value of international transactions. However, as businesses expand and related-party transactions increase, this threshold appears outdated. The expectation is to raise the threshold for mandatory TP documentation at INR 10 crores, in line with the growing scale of multinational enterprises in India.

Exemption of Non-Residents from TP Certification: Currently, non-resident taxpayers earning income from interest, dividends, royalties, or technical fees, do not need to file their income tax return in India, provided taxes have been appropriately deducted on said income by the taxpayer. However, these taxpayers are still required to mandatorily furnish a TP Certificate if such taxable income is earned from parties in India. Given that these non-resident taxpayers are exempted from furnishing their income tax return subject to meeting the above stated conditions, it is recommended that such taxpayers should also be exempted from furnishing the TP certificate, aligning with the broader tax compliance simplification.

Recalibration of the Arm's Length Range: Under the existing TP regulations, India uses an arm's length range between the 35th and 65th percentiles while determining arm's length pricing. However, this range diverges from internationally accepted standards.

To align India's regulations with global norms, the expectation is to revise the range to an interquartile range, spanning from 25th percentile to the 75th percentile, which better reflects the true variability in arm's length pricing.

Dispute Management and Resolution

Expedited Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) Process: The APA regime has been a powerful tool for Indian taxpayers looking to mitigate related-party transaction disputes and achieve certainty on their arm's length pricing. While the APA program has been successful as compared to traditional dispute resolution routesdelays in processing APA applications have resulted in a significant backlog. To enhance efficiency, we recommend streamlining the APA process by categorising applications based on their complexity. Complex cases could be allocated to more experienced teams, while simpler cases should be subject to shorter timelines for resolution. This bifurcation would enable faster conclusions, benefitting both the tax authorities and taxpayers.

Expansion and Re-evaluation of Safe Harbour Provisions: Plenty of small taxpayers have opted for the Safe Harbour regime in order to conclude their arm's length pricing in a streamlined manner. However, the applicable benchmarks are typically higher in this regime as compared to available alternatives. While the small taxpayers do get to enjoy this benefit of convenience, the threshold restrictions in the Safe Harbour regime makes it inaccessible to the taxpayers with comparatively higher value of transactions, forcing them into complex dispute resolution processes. To make this regime more accessible, the Government may re-evaluate the Safe Harbour provisions by (a) increasing the transaction thresholds to cover a larger number of companies, and (b) adjusting the rates to be closer to actual comparable benchmarks, thereby encouraging broader adoption and reducing litigation risks.

Exemption granted to certain services provided by CAs, CSs and ICWAs, by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 stands withdrawn by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006. Is this withdrawal unjust and unjustifiable? Is it discriminatory? How damaging is it to the practice of CAs, etc.? The author here examines the issues from legal as well as moral angle. The abrupt move on the part of the Government is going to create a feeling of insecurity among the professional affected and cause harm to the healthy growth of their profession. Applying the logic of the Kerala High Court decision in Malappuram District Parallel College Association v. Union of India [2006] 150 Taxman 624, wherein levy of service tax on parallel colleges was held to be discriminatory, the author feels that the withdrawal of exemption to CAs/CSs/ICWAs may not pass the test of constitutionality.

Introduction

1. Chartered accountants, being professionally qualified and proficiently trained, are providing most valuable services to the people of this nation and abroad in the matters pertaining to accountancy, audit, management and technical consultancy and consultancy in the matters pertaining to various State as well Central laws. Their professional attitude and devotion are earning name and fame for the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and also for other fellow chartered accountants. Now, the chartered accountants are equally competing with the legal practitioners in the field of State and Central legislations as well as with the advocates and owing to varied experience and vast potential of the chartered accountants, the people are preferring to avail the services of the chartered accountants in place of other practitioners engaged in the similar fields. The facts aforesaid are widely accepted ones, which need no evidence.

Is it wrong for a person providing valuable services to the society and the Government to expect equitable treatment from the Government? But if the readers answer this question as ‘No’, then, one should read the succeeding paras of this article to know how the move of the Government in issuance of Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants has turned out to be unjust and devastating for the practising chartered accountants.

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. This clause will apply only to assessees who carry on international transactions and to whom transfer pricing provisions of Chapter X apply. Primary Transfer Pricing Adjustments are what are known in popular parlance as "transfer pricing adjustments" or TP Adjustments."Primary adjustment" to a transfer price means the determination of transfer price in accordance with the arm's length principle resulting in an increase in the total income or reduction in the loss, as the case may be, of the assessee.

The e-tax Guide-Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2016 edition) of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore defines "transfer pricing adjustment" or what is referred to as "primary transfer pricing adjustment" in section 92CE(1) as under:

"3.34 Transfer pricing adjustment

In the event the related parties do not transact with each other at arm's length prices, tax authorities may for tax purposes, substitute the price of the transaction with one that could have been charged if the parties were unrelated. The adjustment to arrive at that price is known as a transfer pricing adjustment."

A primary TP adjustment covers the following TP adjustments,—

(i)

a TP adjustment to transfer price made suo motu by the assessee in his return of income;

(ii)

a TP adjustment to the transfer price made by the Assessing Officer has been accepted by the assessee;

(iii)

a TP adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement (APA) entered into by the assessee under section 92CC;

(iv)

a TP adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules framed under section 92CB; or

(v)

a TP adjustment arising from the resolution of an assessment by way of the mutual agreement procedure (MAP under an agreement (DTAA) entered into under section 90 or section 90A to avoid double taxa-tion.

In the context of Section 92CE and Clause 30A, it is clear that the primary TP adjustments contemplated in Clause 30A are those made regarding international transactions. Domestic TP adjustments are not contemplated

9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

(a)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 69 taxmann.com 209 (Delhi - Trib.)

(b)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 651 (Delhi - Trib.)

(c)

Westfalia Separator India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 381 (Delhi - Trib.)

(d)

Rampgreen Solutions (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 64 taxmann.com 451 (Delhi - Trib.)

However, in Dy. CIT v. Minda Acoustic Ltd. [2019] 107 taxmann.com 475 (Delhi - Trib.), it was held that the Safe Harbour Rules can always be adopted as guidance in respect of the assessment years prior to their insertion.

9.2 Advance pricing agreement [Section 92CC]

Section 92CC relates to advance pricing agreement (APA).

Hitherto, section 92CC(1) provided that the CBDT, with the approval of the Central Government, may enter into an APA with any person, determining the ALP or specifying the manner in which ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person.

The scope of section 92CC(1) has been widened with effect from 1-4-2020 to provide that the CBDT may also enter into an APA with any person determining income referred to in section 9(1)(i), or specifying the manner in which said income is to be determined, as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India by or on behalf of that person, being a non-resident.

The Finance Minister, in her speech stated as follows:

"In order to provide tax certainty to taxpayers in the matter of attribution of profit to permanent establishment (PE), it is proposed to widen the scope of Advanced Pricing Agreement (APA) and Safe Harbour Regime (SHR), by providing that determination of attribution of profit to PE shall also be in the scope of SHR and APA." (para 2.1 of Annex to Part B of Budget Speech)

The rationale for the amendment is explained in Explanatory Memorandum as follows:

"It has been represented that the attribution of profits to the PE of a non-resident under clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 9 of the Act in accordance with rule 10 of the Rules also results in avoidable disputes in a number of cases. In order to provide certainty, the attribution of income in case of a non-resident person to the PE is also required to be clearly covered under the provisions of the SHR and the APA.

In view of the above, it is proposed to amend section 92CB and section 92CC of the Act to cover determination of attribution to PE within the scope of SHR and APA."

5.10 Proceedings before TPO for determination of Arm's Length Price in respect of specified domestic transactions [Section 92CA]

5.10-1 Pre-amended provisions

Section 92CA of the Act provides that the Assessing Officer, if he considers it necessary or expedient to do so, may, with the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner, refer the mat-ter of determination of Arm's Length Price (ALP) in respect of an international transaction or Specified Domestic Transaction (SDT) to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). Once a reference is made to the TPO, the TPO is competent to exercise all powers that are available to the Assessing Officer under Section 92C(3) for the determination of ALP and consequent adjustment.

Further, under Section 92E of the Act, there is a reporting requirement on the taxpayer to file an audit report in the prescribed form before the Assessing Officer (AO) containing details of all international transactions or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer during the year. This audit report is the primary document with the AO, which contains the details of international transactions and/or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer. If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under Section 92E, then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction/SDT so as to make a reference to the TPO.

Section 92CA provides that if, during the course of proceeding before him, an international transaction comes to the notice of the TPO, which has not been referred to him by the AO, the TPO can proceed to determine the ALP in its respect as well. It also provides for the computation of ALP by the TPO of those international transactions, details of which have not been furnished in the audit report referred to above. These provisions are in place in sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of the section 92CA. However, at present, the above-noted provisions of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA do not extend to SDTs.

5.10-2 Amendment by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 has amended sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of Section 92CA to enable the TPO to deal with SDTs which have not been referred to him by the AO and/or in whose respect audit report under section 92CE has not been filed.

These amendments will take effect from 01-04-2025 and will, accord-ingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2025-26 and subsequent assessment years.

Inform discrepancies to registered person - The proper officer may inform the registered person of the discrepancies, if any, noticed as observations of the audit and the said person may file his reply and the proper officer shall finalise the findings of the audit after due consideration of the reply furnished - Rule 101(4) of CGST and SGST Rules, 2017.

Inform audit findings to registered person on conclusion of audit - On conclusion of the audit, the proper officer shall inform the findings of audit to the registered person in accordance with the provisions of section 65(6) in form GST ADT-02 - Rule 101(5) of CGST and SGST Rules, 2017.

CC (2009) 234 ELT 466 (CESTAT SMB), Chartered Accountant prepared cost sheet as per CAS-4 and certified that burden of excess duty was absorbed by appellant and that there was no price rise during relevant period. 9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

12.4 Change in the time limit to pass the order by the Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 166 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 92CA of ITA 1961)]

12.4-1 Position under the ITA 1961

Section 92CA of the ITA 1961 deals with the case where the assessee has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction in any previous year, and the AO may refer the computation of the Arm's Length Price (ALP) in relation to the said international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO).

Sub-section (3A) to section 92CA states that TPO is required to pass an order before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation under section 153, or as the case may be, in section 153B for making the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation or fresh assessment, as the case may be, expires.

12.4-1a Exclusion of the last day of assessment limitation - The interpretation of the phrase 'before sixty days prior to the date' has been a consistent point of contention between taxpayers and the revenue, leading to significant litigation.

The Madras High Court, in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), which affirmed the Single Judge's decision in Jt. CIT v. Pfizer Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 536 (Madras), held that the word 'date' in section 92CA(3A) refers to the last date for the AO to pass the assessment order under section 153 (e.g., December 31st). The crucial words 'prior to' indicate that, for the purpose of calculating the 60 days, this last date must be excluded. Therefore, if the assessment limitation expires on December 31st, the TPO order ought to have been passed on or before October 31st.

This interpretation was consistently followed across numerous ITAT benches, including in the following cases:

Teleperformance Global Services (P.) Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 658 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. [2024] 163 taxmann.com 349 (Ahmedabad-Trib.)

Frost & Sullivan (India) (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 739 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Shell India Markets (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 366 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Siemens Technology and Services (P.) Ltd. [2024] 162 taxmann.com 357 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Huhtamaki India Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 194 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Atos India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 217 (Mumbai-Trib.)

CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore-Trib.)

Pioneer India Electronics (P.) Ltd. [2025] 178 taxmann.com 553 (Delhi-Trib.)

Sigma Aldrich Chemicals (P.) Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 431 (Bangalore-Trib.)

12.4-1b Mandatory nature of the time limit - Another critical aspect clarified by the judiciary is whether the time limit prescribed in section 92CA(3A) is mandatory or merely directory. The revenue often argued that the use of the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) implies a directory nature.

However, the Madras High Court in Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), after a detailed analysis of the scheme of the Act and the consequences of non-compliance, unequivocally held that the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and the time period fixed therein has to be scrupulously followed.'

The court reasoned that the overall scheme of transfer pricing assessments, with various interlinked time limits (including extensions under the proviso to section 92CA(3A) and section 153), indicates a legislative intent to ensure timely completion. If the TPO's time limit were merely directory, it would undermine the entire assessment process. This principle has been reiterated in the case of Asstt. CIT v. CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore - Trib.).

Large Tax Payers Units

16.1-6 In many countries, special systems have been developed to administer large tax payers. The international trend is to establish full fledged LTU (Large Tax Payers Units) that are responsible for most of tax administration functions relating to taxpayer, including collection, enforcement of tax arrears and audit. Many Asian countries have established such LTU.

LTU (Large Tax Payers Units) have been established at various places in India so that they can get all facilities of tax payments, filing of returns and documents, assessments, rebates/refunds, audit, recovery and refunds at one place, irrespective of geographical location of their units. This is to ensure uniformity in matters of tax/duty determination and quick actions [Information from Ministry of Finance - 194 ELT T3 and 3 STT 85 (Stat) - see also CBE&C circular Nos. 833/10/2006-CX dated 5-10-2006 and 834/11/2006-CX dated 5-10-2006].

It will be a 'single window clearance' for all matters relating to central excise, income tax, corporation tax and service tax. LTU will provide single point interface with tax administration to large tax payers.

LTU will be self-contained tax administration office of Department of Revenue acting as single window clearance point for all matters relating to central excise, income tax, corporation tax and service tax.

LTU will be headed by Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioner (either from CBDT or CBEC). Each large taxpayer will be assisted by Client Executive (Additional/Joint/Asstt Commissioner) from income tax or excise department [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

It is voluntary for a tax payer to join LTU. He has to make application for that purpose and give consent to join LTU in form prescribed vide notification No. 21/2006-CE(NT) dated 30-9-2006.

LTU can opt out of the scheme by giving 30 days notice, from the first day of following financial year [rule 12BB(6)]

The scheme is not open to manufacturers of tobacco products and pan masala.

Bangalore LTU has become functional w.e.f. 1-10-2006. Chennai LTU has become operational w.e.f. 1-12-2007. Mumbai LTU has started functioning from 27-3-2008. Delhi LTU has started functioning from 2-6-2008.

Registration as LTU - Application for registration as LTU should be made to Assistant/Deputy Commissioner under Central Excise and to Superintendent under service tax (amendment to Notification No. 20/2006-CE(NT) made on 18-7-2011).

Administrative Control in case of LTP-EOU - Even in case of large taxpayer-EOU, administrative control will be under control of LTUs. Where specific function requires physical presence of officers for warehousing, sealing etc., it will be dealt with by jurisdictional Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs (in case of port cities) or Central Excise (in case of other than port cities), who will have concurrent jurisdiction over these LTP-EOUs - MF(DR) circular No. 15/2007-Cus dated 20-3-2007 [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Reference to Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 92CA]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act provides that the Assessing Officer may refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction to a Transfer Pricing Officer. Such a reference can be made where:—

(a)

The Assessing Officer considers it is necessary or expedient to do so, and

(b)

The Assessing Officer has taken previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner to refer the computation to Transfer Pricing Officer.

This section specifies the entire process through which the arm's length price is determined by the Transfer Pricing Officer.

With effect from 1-11-2020, the Amendment Act, 2020 has inserted a new sub-section (8) in section 92CA to empower the Central Government to frame a scheme for the purpose of determination of arm's length price to impart greater efficiency, transparency and accountability by:—

(a)

Eliminating the interface between the Transfer Pricing Officer and the assessee or any other person to the extent technologically feasible;

(b)

Optimising utilisation of the resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation; and

(c)

Introducing a team-based determination of arm's length price (ALP) with dynamic jurisdiction.

HEADNOTE: Section 65 (83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered accountant’s services - Assessee was a practising chartered accountant - Revenue levied service tax on certification service provided by assessee holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 - Whether since certification follows transfer pricing audit, certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ - Held, yes - Whether, since verification of books of account precedes issue of certificate and such verification would fall within scope of ‘Accounting and auditing’, it could not be said that assessee was not rendering auditing service liable to tax and, therefore, impugned order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 3] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998

FACT: The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

HELD: The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]

5.1 Exempted services - The services which were made exempt due to this notification are all the services except the services mentioned in the notification. The main service which had been made exempt through this exemption notification was tax consultancy or taxation work of the chartered accountants and now withdrawal of the same is the main cause of concern to the practising chartered accountants because at present for vast majority of chartered accountants, the main professional work is tax practice and specially in the small cities the work related to taxation matters and tax consultancy is proportionately much higher than the audit work. The same thing cannot be said for the cost accountants and company secretaries because practically the number of cost accountants and company secretaries engaged in doing tax consultancy is very minimum compared to the chartered accountants but if any cost accountant or company secretary is also providing the taxation and other consultancy service, then the effect of withdrawal of this notification on them will be the same.

Withdrawal of exemption is discriminatory

6. The affected and concerned chartered accountants have termed this withdrawal of exemption as totally discriminatory and unwarranted. In their opinion this exemption was given after due and prolonged deliberation and after considering the whole situation and circumstances in 1998 and it is based on the fact that the field other than the audit work and statutory certification work is not exclusively reserved for the chartered accountants or company secretaries or cost accountants, as the case may be. For the same type of service the other professionals including the legal and tax practitioners are not liable to pay service tax. Then how the chartered accountants or cost accountants or company secretaries, as the case may be, can alone be taxed in this respect. The affected chartered accountants have rightly pointed out that the taxation practice related to VAT, income tax and service tax is major part of their professional receipts and these fields are open for the other professionals also. Then why the chartered accountants are chosen for this tax and why they have been denied the level playing field.

Since the circumstances and the reasons for which this exemption was issued and persist, the withdrawal of the exemption is unwarranted and discriminatory.

tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable. Before going into the impact of the rescission of the exemption notification, one should first understand the statutory charge of service tax on the practising chartered accountants, as given in Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994,—

(a) Meaning of practising chartered accountant [Section 65(83)] : Practising chartered accountant means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

(b) Taxable service [Section 65(105 )(s)] : Taxable service means any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity, in any manner.

Position before withdrawal of exemption notification

2. Before rescission of the service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, i.e., upto February 28, 2006, all services, except those mentioned below, provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA were exempt from service tax—

(a)accounting and auditing; or

(b)cost accounting and cost auditing; or

(c)secretarial auditing; or

(d)verification of declarations in prescribed forms of compliances for obtaining a certificate of commencement of business or commencement of other business under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(e)signing of the annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(f)certification that requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, 1956 have been complied with as regards statutory guidelines for appointment of managerial personnel and payment of managerial remuneration to them without the approval of the Central Government under section 269 and Schedule XIII, of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(g)certification of documents to be filed by companies with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956; or

(h)certification in Form No. 1 that the whole of the amount remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a period of three years from the date of transfer to the special account under section 205(1)/(2) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been transferred to the General Revenue Account of the Central Government under the Companies Unpaid Dividend (Transfer to General Revenue Account of the Central Government) Rules, 1978; or

(i)certification of documents under the Exports and Imports Policy of the Government of India; or

(j)certification for exchange control purposes which a practising chartered accountant can issue as documentary evidence in support of certain applications under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973; or

(k)certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957.

Thus, in case any practising CA/CS/ICWA was rendering any service other than (a) to (k ) enumerated above, like legal or taxation consultancy service, etc., he wasn’t liable for service tax.

However, any service provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, which fell under the ambit of any other taxable service, was liable to service tax under the category of that other taxable service. For example, if a chartered accountant also provided manpower recruitment services to his clients, then he was liable to service tax on such services under the category of manpower recruitment service.

Reasons behind issuance of earlier exemption notification

3. The said exemption notification was issued on the principles of equity. The then Government had recognized the fact that the—

(i)practising CA/CS/ICWAs were providing services like legal consultancy, etc., which were equally being provided by other professionals like advocates and legal practitioners and, therefore,

(ii)levy of service tax on such services provided by practising CA/CS/ICWAs and non-levy of service tax on the same services provided by advocates and legal practitioners would be inequitable levy.

Having recognized the abovesaid facts the aforesaid exemption notification was issued to prevent the levy of service tax from being unjust and inequitable.

Position after withdrawal of exemption notification

4. After the withdrawal of the aforesaid exemption notification by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, i.e., with effect from March 1, 2006 all the services provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, in his professional capacity, are chargeable to service tax.

FAQ 90. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

FAQ 91. Whether Treaty Shopping is ipso facto an IAA and reportable in Clause 30C?

Treaty shopping is not, per se, an IAA. Treaty Shopping is to be reported only if it is abusive, i.e. it satisfies the definition of IAA. In Her Majesty The Queen v. Alta Energy Luxembourg S.A.R.L [2022] 144 taxmann.com 23 (SCC), the Supreme Court of Canada held that GAAR could be invoked against treaty shopping only if it perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states. Treaty Shopping per se is not abusive tax avoidance [Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement in Indian GAAR] so as to attract GAAR. Treaty shopping is abusive tax avoidance and attracts GAAR, but only when treaty shopping perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states.

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Nor is the tax auditor required to examine or report whether the assessee has maintained proper records as required by Rule 10D regarding international transactions. Nor is he required to examine whether the Arm's Length Price has been determined for international transactions in accordance with any of the recognised methods specified in Section 92F. That is the subject of the audit to be carried out under Section 92E, and the report is to be furnished in Form No. 3CEB.

The tax auditor must report in this clause only if a primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1). If no primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1), the tax auditor has no duty to report. The tax auditor is not even required to report if the primary TP adjustment has not been made as per the APA entered into by the assessee. If primary TP adjustment has been made according to the APA, then the reporting obligation under this Clause is triggered.

This clause also does not deal with Thin Cap adjustments under Section 94B. That is the subject matter of Clause 30B.

This Clause also does not deal with the issue of shares at a premium to non-resident investors by a closely held company that attracts Section 56(2)(vii). That is the subject matter of Clause 29A.

Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. Nevertheless, the tax auditor may find it useful to examine if any of the non-price terms and conditions of international transactions are not at arm's length from the angle of Clause 30C.

FAQs on Transfer Pricing Audit

SRINIVASAN ANAND G.

CA

Who is primarily responsible to furnish information in Form No. 3CEB - Taxpayer or the auditor?

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill,2012 clarifies that "If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under section 92E then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction so as to make a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer." Thus, from the Explanatory Memorandum, it is clear that it is the primary responsibility of an asssessee to furnish correct and complete details of all international transactions/SDTs undertaken by him during the year.

Who can be appointed for conduct the audit envisaged under section 92E

Who is eligible to be the auditor u/s 92E?

According to section 92E, the report should be an 'accountant'. Section 92F(i) defines 'accountant' has having the same meaning as in Explanation below section 288(2). According to the above mentioned explanation, it covers a CA and Restricted State auditor.

According to ICAI's 'Guidance Note on Report on International Transactions under section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Transfer Pricing)' hereinafter referred to as "Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing" :

♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

♦ Ascertaining and reporting whether the assessee has maintained proper information and documentations prescribed in respect of international transactions entered into by him.
