FAQ 74. Mr. A, a sole proprietor, agreed to transfer his personal property to Mr. X and received some non-refundable advance against such a deal. The sale could not materialise as Mr. X could not pay the whole amount, and the advance money was forfeited by Mr. A. What are the disclosure requirements? Section 56(2)(ix) of the Income-tax Act provides for taxability of any sum received as an advance in the course of negotiations for the transfer of a capital asset, and such sum was forfeited due to non-transfer of such capital asset. A new Clause 29A to Form 3CD has been inserted to report any advance received from the buyer but forfeited due to the non-materialisation of a deal to the sale of the capital asset.

The auditor is not required to report any such forfeited amount in respect of a personal capital asset or stock-in-trade. Any advances received and forfeited towards the sale of stock-in-trade would be taxable under section 28(i), and would not be required to be reported since the amount would be credited to the profit & loss account.

The requirement of reporting arises only on forfeiture of advance. If an advance has been received and has been outstanding for a considerable time, there is no requirement to report such amount unless and until it is forfeited by an act of the assessee.

FAQ 75. Should any consideration for the issue of shares that exceed the fair market value of the shares received by a start-up be reported in clause 29?

Reporting obligation under Clause 29 is triggered if a closely held company issues unquoted shares at a premium. In such case, the excess of the premium over the fair market value of the shares shall be taxable as income from other sources in the hands of the company.

The DPIIT's recognised start-ups are exempted from the applicability of Section 56(2)(viib) subject to the satisfaction of various conditions prescribed under the notification issued by the DPIIT13. Therefore, Clause 29 shall apply only to closely held companies except DPIIT-recognised start-ups that satisfy the condition for exemption. If the private limited company in question is a DPIIT-recognised start-up eligible for exemption under section 56(2)(viib), the e-mail received from CBDT regarding eligibility for exemption must be verified by the tax auditor, and suitable remarks should be made regarding the applicability of the exemption and the non-applicability of Clause 29.

Section 56(2)(viib) and Notification issued by the DPIIT16 prescribe various conditions for a start-up to claim exemption from payment of tax under this provision. In case of failure to comply with these conditions, the consideration received from the issue of shares, as exceeding the fair market value of such shares, shall be deemed to be the income of the company chargeable to tax for the previous year in which such failure takes place. When the exemption is withdrawn, it shall be deemed that the company has underreported the income in consequence of the misreporting, and consequently, a penalty of an amount equal to 200% of tax payable on the underreported income shall be levied as per Section 270A14.

FAQ 76. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

Eligibility of small service provider

1. A Firm of chartered accountants has the gross billing for the year ending on 31-3-2006 as under:— Since the service provided by the firm with respect to audit was only 2.30 Lakh hence the firm is not collecting and paying service tax in the year 2006-07 on the assumption that it is eligible for the benefit of exemption available to the small service providers as per Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) up to the value of 4 Lakh of collection. Please advise properly.

The total taxable service rendered by this firm of Rs.4.30 Lakhs in the previous year ended on 31-3-2006 hence the firm is not eligible for the exemption scheme available to this firm.

For this purpose there is clear provision in the Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) in the form of conditions mentioned in clause 2 of the scheme. The exact wording of clause 2(viii) is as under:—

"(viii)The aggregate value of taxable services rendered by a provider of taxable service from one or more premises, does not exceed rupees four lakhs in the preceding financial year."

Here, to be eligible for exemption scheme available to small service providers, the aggregate value of taxable service should not be more than Rupees 4 Lakh in the preceding financial year and both the Audit services and taxation services were part of taxable service though the tax was exempt on the taxation services. Let us see the exact wordings of the Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 in this respect:—

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994(32 of 1994); and in suppression of the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) No. 57/98 Service tax, dated 7-10-1998, the Central Government, being satisfied that it is necessary in the Public interest so to do, hereby exempts the taxable service provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity to a client, other than the taxable service related to—

(i)Accounting and auditing; or

(ii)to (xi) Various services Like certification etc. mentioned,

from whole of the service tax leviable thereon.

Here that the service is taxable but this taxable service is exempt from paying the whole of tax. The point here is that the taxable service is exempt from paying the tax and in that case its structure of taxable service remained intact but the tax payable on it is exempt.

Hence the value of taxable service provided by the firm of Chartered Accountant is Rs. 4.30 Lakhs and as per provisions of clause 2(viii) of the exemption notification, the service provider having turnover of taxable service over Rs.4 Lakhs is not eligible for exemption scheme provided to the small service provider.

Though while claiming exemption under this notification "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" means excluding the taxable service on which no service tax is payable and this has been provided in Explanation (B) the said notification and the "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" is applicable for the claiming the exemption but to ascertain the status "Small service provider" and the eligibility of the assessee to claim the exemption which is based on "the aggregate value of taxable service rendered" of the previous year, no such explanation is issued and in absence of any clarification from the Government in this respect,the opinion mentioned above is given.

FAQ 74. How to calculate the interest on excess money that needs to be repatriated after a primary adjustment?

Rule 10CB provides the rate of interest at which interest has to be calculated on excess money or part thereof that is not repatriated within the time limit. Where the international transaction is denominated in Indian rupees, the rate of interest will be the one-year marginal cost of fund lending rate of the State Bank of India as of 1st April of the relevant previous year, plus 325 basis points (plus 3.25%). Where the international transaction is denominated in foreign currency, the rate of interest shall be the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) as of 30th September of the relevant previous year plus 300 basis points (plus 3%).

It is possible that the amount of imputed interest income on the excess money not repatriated to India may relate to more than one year. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998. But this is not all. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated August 1, 2002 with effect from August 16, 2002 by inserting an Explanation under this notification. This Explanation provides that, ‘Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act’. Also, the same was clarified by the following illustration :

"The service provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant."

It was clarified that w.e.f. 16-8-2002 only those services are taxable under service tax which are either covered under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 or covered under any of the other category of services. Not all services, which are not covered under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, are exempt in case of these three professionals, as was the thinking of these professionals. This clarification seems to be heartening for these professionals so far. But, this clarification also seems to be against section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994, which was inserted by the Finance Act, 2003, with effect from May 14, 2003 and provides the mode of classification of taxable services. But this was not the end. By Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated October 16, 1998 [G.S.R. 624(E), dated October 16, 1998] has been withdrawn. Now all the services provided by these professionals are liable for service tax. Simply, there is no specific exemption notification available for these professions [except general exemptions which are available in case of all services]

Scope of services taxable

2. The question now for consideration is that, what is the scope of services taxable under these services and also whether the services provided by these professionals can be covered under any other category? According to section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, ‘taxable service’ in this context means any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a practising chartered accountant/practising cost accountant/practising company secretary in his professional capacity, in any manner. The words professional capacity are very confusing and may be very controversial. If these words were not there in this definition, then all the services provided by these practising professionals would have been taxable. But due to presence of these words there is going to be a dispute.

There can be two aspects of this situation :

u First, whatever can be provided only by these practising professionals can be called as provided in professional capacity and all other services are not covered under these services. For example, certain statutory audit can be done only by these professionals, so the same is covered under these services. But accounting work can be done even by the non-practising professionals, so the same is not covered under these services. This interpretation also seems to be in accordance with this definition, otherwise the words ‘professional capacity’ had not been used.

1. UAE Govt. releases norms for maintenance of TP documents for Corporate Tax Law

The Finance Ministry of UAE issued Ministerial Decision No. 97 of 2023, specifying the requirements for the maintenance of Transfer Pricing (TP) documentation for the purposes of taxation of corporations and businesses. The decision also listed down the requirement of maintaining the Master file and Local file.

(a) Maintenance of both Master File and Local File

A person that meets either of the following conditions shall maintain both a master file and a local file:

Taxable persons that are part of a Multinational Enterprises Group having a total consolidated group revenue of AED 3.15 billion or above in the relevant tax period.

Taxable persons whose revenues are AED 200 million or abovein the relevant tax period.

(b) Transactions to be included in Local File

The Taxable Person shall include transactions or arrangements with all of the following Related Parties and Connected Persons in the local file:

A Non-Resident Person;

An Exempt Person;

Resident Person that has been elected for Small Business Relief; and

Resident Person whose income is subject to a different corporate tax rate.

(c) Transactions not to be included in Local File

The Taxable Person shall not include transactions or arrangements with the following Related Parties and Connected Persons in the local file:

Resident Person other than those specified above.

A Natural Person, as long as the parties to the transaction or arrangement are acting independently of each other

A Judicial Person, who is a related party or a connected person because of being a partner in an unincorporated partnership as long as the parties to the transaction or arrangement are acting independently of each other.

A Non-resident person having a Permanent Establishment in the UAE and whose income is subjected to the same corporate tax rate.

Similarly, detailed provisions relating to APAs are also contained in the US Code. Relationship with customs laws 8. The concept of transfer pricing was already present in the Customs Act in the form of Customs Valuation Rules. Under these rules, unless an exception applies, the ‘Assessable Value’ is the invoice value (i.e., ‘Transaction Value’). For customs duty, either the transaction value is accepted as the assessable value or the case is referred to the Special Valuation Branch (SVB), which then determines the assessable value. The issue is whether the assessable value determined under the Customs Act would be accepted by the IT Department as an ‘Arm’s Length Price’? There is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect. The invoice value of imported goods shall be the transaction value, only if the Customs Officer has no reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of the value declared. However, the IT Department may contend that customs authorities merely ensure that the import price is at least equal to the assessable value and in particular, customs authorities may not investigate whether the goods are overpriced. However, it appears that the customs authorities’ acceptance of a transaction value could serve as documentation support for proving that it is an arm’s length prie. In the event, the IT Department arrives at an arm’s length price, which is different from the assessable value, can the customs authorities reopen their assessment and revalue the imports? As per the Customs Act, the authorities can reopen assessment within a period of 5 years provided there is concealment. Practically, the chances of reopening the case are remote because the objective of customs authorities and IT authorities are contrary.2

Relationship with FEMA

9. Under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), an issue could arise in case of imports, wherein the IT Department determines an arm’s length price, which is lower than actual import price. In such a case, it will be interesting to see whether the RBI would take a stand that the Indian entity has overpaid and hence the excess amount paid by Indian entity should be brought back into India. As per section 8 of the FEMA, an Indian resident has to bring into India all foreign exchange amounts, which are due or accrued to him. The issue is whether an Indian resident has to bring into India, additional foreign exchange on account of an adjustment made by the IT authorities under TP regulations? Broadly, the literal interpretation of the word ‘due’ would mean the amount ‘due’ as per contractual agreement and not the amount assessed by IT authorities which is determined long after the transaction is completed. Currently, consultancy fees up to US $ 100,000 can be remitted abroad under automatic approval and for fees exceeding US $ 100,000, one has to apply to RBI, which may accept or reject the same. The issue is whether the RBI approval is sufficient confirmation that the transaction is at arm’s length? Though there is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect, the RBI approval could serve as supporting document. Secondly, can the IT authorities determine an arm’s length price, which is specially rejected by the RBI? Example: Indian company makes an application for payment of consultancy fees exceeding US $ 100,000 to its foreign parent company, which is rejected by the RBI. Can IT authorities assess the foreign parent company for "arm’s length price" exceeding US $ 100,000 ?1

Conclusion

10. Hence, it is felt that though India has made a very good start in amending section 92 of the Act and making transfer pricing illegal and punishable with huge amount of fines, it is felt that a lot more can still be done. As already stated above, the said changes are still to come on lines with the international standards in this field. The analysis done in this paper was only an illustration of the flaws in the present law of transfer pricing in India and the possible changes that can be introduced in it. A lot more needs to done in areas like that of documentation where a large number of documents needs to be submitted, irrespective of the size of the enterprise. This would obviously result in a huge administrative and financial burden on the smaller enterprises. Similarly, it is felt that the penalties imposed in case of violations are excessive as compared to similar laws in other jurisdictions etc.

Keeping in mind the fact that tax legislations ought to be guided by certain canons such as that of neutrality, effectiveness, certainty, simplicity and flexibility, it is clear that the existing section 92 does not in anyway achieve this goal. The ambiguity that is present in the existing provisions becomes all the more worrisome given the economic context of India, which is a developing country and which clearly requires assistance of the FDIs brought in by the MNCs into the country for its economic development. The inflow of this FDI is bound to be affected unless the issue of vagueness in section 92 is immediately addressed to and suitable amendments be made thereto.

TRANSFER PRICING IS SERIOUS BUSINESS 14. Adoption of a transfer price different from declared price may have serious consequences. No deduction under section 10A, 10AA, 10B or Chapter VI-A is admissible in respect of addition consequent to adoption of the arm’s length price. There is no immunity from penalty leviable against deemed concealment on the difference between reported and assessed income, unless justified by reasonable cause under section 273B. Failure to keep accounts and documents as required under section 92D will merit penalty under section 271AA. Failure to get audit certificate will attract penalty under section 271BA.

It has been held that the burden to prove that declared rate is the transfer price under the rules is placed on the assessee as decided by the Tribunal in Aztec Software Technology Services Ltd.’s case (supra). In fact, that is also the view taken in the countries, where transfer pricing rules are in vogue. To take an example, Australian rulings would not discredit findings of the tax authorities unless bad faith could be shown as decided in San Remo Macaroni Co. v. Commissioner of Taxation [1999] FCA 1468. Deficiency of information is a fault, which could not be attributed to revenue, so that burden of proving arm’s length price lay on the taxpayer. New Business Tax System (Thin Capitalisation and Other Measures) Bill, 2000 would seek to place even greater responsibility on foreign investors with significant interest in Australian ventures.

The seriousness of transfer pricing is highlighted by a recent Instruction indicating the effect of transfer pricing exercise undertaken by tax administration in India. The resort can now be made to Mutual Agreement Procedure under Indo-U.S. Double Tax Avoidance Agreement in respect of taxes, inter alia, imposed by application of Transfer Pricing Rule vide Instruction No. 10 of 2007, dated October 23, 2007. It provides for stay on demand subject to pendency of reference for availing MAP on confirmation from Foreign Tax and Tax Research Division of the CBDT and bank guarantee for the amount due and interest thereon.

LEVEL PLAYING FIELD FOR C.As IN SERVICE TAX AFFECTED - ICAI

1. The practising chartered accountants will be adversely affected due to the withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98-Service tax, dated 16th October, 1998. The withdrawal of this notification is not unintentional and it is very clear from the initial Government reaction issued through a letter written by the Joint Secretary, TRU, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue to all Commissioners, Chief Commissioners immediately after release of the notification withdrawing the exemption. Let us see the relevant portion related to the notification under consideration in this article which we can term as first Departmental clarification in this respect :—

2. Exemption for services, other than accounting, auditing, and statutory certification services, provided by a practising chartered accountant, company secretary or cost accountant in his professional capacity. No. 334/4/2006- TRU, dated 28-02-2006 to all Commissioners, Chief Commissioner and DG.

Service tax is a tax on services and not on a tax on the service provider or on the professionals providing the services. This fact was also pronounced by various Courts while deciding the constitutional validity of the service tax on various services.

The exemption notification was also issued on the same consideration because the field of providing this service is open for various other professionals and if getting same type of services from a particular professional, say chartered accountants, attracts service tax then this has two side effects. One is that the other professional will have the upper hand compared to the chartered accountants only because they need not to pay service tax. Secondly, it will snatch the level playing field from a professional. Hence, in this particular case this is a tax on a professional or on a particular profession and not on a particular service because the others providing the same service need not to pay the tax.

On both these grounds the withdrawal of this exemption notification is totally discriminatory, unwarranted and unjustified and as a remedial action the exemption notification should be restored in the same spirit in which it was initially provided.

Paras 54.1 to 54.14 of the Tax Audit Guidance Note of ICAI require the tax auditors to adopt the following approach with regard to Clause 30A:

Verify and report whether a primary adjustment to the transfer price, as referred to in section 92CE(1), has been made during the previous year under audit, irrespective of the previous year to which the primary adjustment relates. Suppose the assessee makes a voluntary adjustment in his return of income filed in November 2023 (pertaining to FY 2022-23/AY 2023-24). Such primary adjustment is to be reported in the FY 2023-24 (AY 2024-25) tax audit report filed on or before November 2024 because the primary adjustment occurred in November 2023 (i.e., during FY 2023-24). If, in this case, the excess money or part thereof with the AE is not repatriated to India within 90 days from the due date of filing of ROI, i.e. by 28th February 2024, interest on such excess money computed as per Rule 10CB will need to be reported in the tax audit report filed in October 2024.

If any primary adjustment to transfer price, as referred to in section 92CE(1), has been made during the previous year, state "Yes" even if the adjustment pertains to any earlier previous year.

Reporting in clause 30A(b)(i) is required of each and every primary adjustment made in the previous year under audit, irrespective of the previous year to which the adjustment pertains. For example, an assessment order making a primary adjustment relating to FY 2022-23 is passed in FY 2023-24, and the assessee accepts it. This must be reported in the FY 2023-24 tax audit report in Clause 30A(b)(i).

An APA may have been signed in FY 2023-24, which may provide for a primary adjustment for four rollback years from FY 2019-20 to FY 2022-23. The adjustment made pursuant to the APA must be reported in the FY 2023-24 tax audit report IN Clause 30A.

Obtain a certificate from the assessee as to (i) TP ad-justments made voluntarily in ITRs filed during the previous year under audit, (ii) APAs entered into during the previous year under audit and TP adjustment made in the year under audit whether pertaining to the year under audit or preceding previous years (iii) whether any TP adjustment was made/confirmed by any appellate order and has been accepted by the assessee in the previous year under audit; and (iv) whether MAP entered into during the previous year under audit and whether any TP adjustment made pursuant to MAP.

Check tax records for occurrence of events in (i) to (iv) above during the previous year.

If there is any such occurrence relating to AY 2017-18 or later years and the primary adjustment exceeds ` 1 crore, report the fact that adjustment has been made against clause 30A(b)(i).

Also Report in clause 30A(b)(i) the Primary adjust-ments for earlier years before AY 2017-18 and the primary adjustments totalling less than ` 1 crore for a previous year, which do not warrant secondary adjustment.

If the answer to the question in clause 30A(b)(i) is "yes", report in clause 30A(b)(ii) the rele-vant clause of section 92CE(1) under which adjustment falls and the amount of adjustment also. Obtain a certificate from management re-garding this. The primary onus for correctness would be on manage-ment.

Clause 30A(b)(iii) requires reporting whether the excess money available with the associated enterprise is required to be repatriated to India as per the provisions of section 92CE(2). This question should be answered as "Yes" only if the adjustment relates to the assessment year 2017-18 or later assessment years and if the adjustment exceeds ` 1 crore. This question should be answered as "No" if the adjustment relates to an assessment year before the assessment year 2017-18, or if the primary adjustment is of less than ` 1 crore.

If any such primary adjustment has taken place, which requires repatriation of the excess money, verify and report whether the excess money has been received and whether it has been received within the prescribed time.

The main point raised by some service providers is that where they are carrying out any certification as required by any statute can it come under the purview of consultancy, advice or technical assistance. The Government clarified the same through the Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX. 4, dated 26-2-2002. It was clarified that the certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job. It is then to be examined whether this activity can come under the purview of advice or technical assistance. An advice is generally understood to be optional in nature and has no statutory force. It is up to the client to accept the advice or not. The activity of certification will, therefore, not fall under the category of advice. As regards ‘technical assistance’, it is observed that an assistance is normally for the purpose of achieving a particular aim or result. A certificate given by, say, the Boiler Inspector under the Factories Act, 1948, about the safety of a boiler, cannot be considered to be ‘assistance’ to the person using the said boiler in his factory. To issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purposes of issuing certificates by the same agency under an authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency, before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. It will, therefore, be essential to examine each activity of a service provider on the basis of facts, the terms of agreement between the assessee and the clients and the corresponding provision of Indian or International statute/convention/protocol, or code, to determine whether the certificate being given is under the authority of any such statute, convention protocol or code. If it is so, the payment received for that service will not be taxable under the head "Consulting engineer". Any other inspection, survey, assessment, technical assistance, consultancy, recommendation, advice, undertaken/provided directly or indirectly, by the assessee would be liable to service tax under the head ‘Consulting engineer’. But the Madras High Court in V. Shanmughavel (Dr.) v. CCE 12, held that "registered valuers" of plant and machinery would fall within the definition of "consulting engineer" and their services of valuation of plant and machinery would be covered as "taxable service" offered by an "consulting engineer" within the meaning of section 65(48)(g) of the Finance Act, 1994. A re-consideration of the ruling of Madras High Court according to the circular is, hence, necessitated. In the case of Central Power Research Institute v. CCE13, the assessee was carrying on research activities in power generation. The assessee contended, inter alia, that it was not consulting engineer and activity carried on by it did not fall within the definition of ‘consulting engineer’, and that it was carrying on research and testing of electrical equipments, namely, voltage equipments, motor transformer insulation, tower transmitters, circuit breakers, transformers, etc., which were sent by various clients. It was held that the Tribunal in a similar matter in the case of Turbotech Precision Engg. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Stay Order No. 1169 of 2004, dated 22-11-2004] had granted full waiver of pre-deposit of service tax and penalty. Therefore, the stay application was allowed granting full waiver of pre-deposit of the disputed amount and staying its recovery till the disposal of the appeal. It is to be noted that the tax on technical testing and analysis services/technical inspection and certification services was introduced with effect from 1-7-2003.

A Person engaged in an Extractive Business that meets the conditions of Article 7 of the Corporate Tax Law;

Transfer Pricing (TP) continues to be one of the most significant international tax issues for multinational enterprises globally. India, recognising its importance in curbing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)introduced TP provisions in 2001. Since its inception, the Indian TP regime has evolved, keeping pace with both market dynamics and continued global tax developments.

As the Indian tax landscape continues to evolve, there are several critical areas that require attention in the upcoming Union Budget 2025. The following outlines key areas where we believe regulatory intervention and reform are necessary, along with our specific expectations for the forthcoming budget.

Compliance

Maintenance of TP Documentation: Since the introduction of TP provisions in 2001, the threshold for maintaining TP documentation for taxpayers has been set at INR 1 crore in aggregate value of international transactions. However, as businesses expand and related-party transactions increase, this threshold appears outdated. The expectation is to raise the threshold for mandatory TP documentation at INR 10 crores, in line with the growing scale of multinational enterprises in India.

Exemption of Non-Residents from TP Certification: Currently, non-resident taxpayers earning income from interest, dividends, royalties, or technical fees, do not need to file their income tax return in India, provided taxes have been appropriately deducted on said income by the taxpayer. However, these taxpayers are still required to mandatorily furnish a TP Certificate if such taxable income is earned from parties in India. Given that these non-resident taxpayers are exempted from furnishing their income tax return subject to meeting the above stated conditions, it is recommended that such taxpayers should also be exempted from furnishing the TP certificate, aligning with the broader tax compliance simplification.

Recalibration of the Arm's Length Range: Under the existing TP regulations, India uses an arm's length range between the 35th and 65th percentiles while determining arm's length pricing. However, this range diverges from internationally accepted standards.

To align India's regulations with global norms, the expectation is to revise the range to an interquartile range, spanning from 25th percentile to the 75th percentile, which better reflects the true variability in arm's length pricing.

Dispute Management and Resolution

Expedited Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) Process: The APA regime has been a powerful tool for Indian taxpayers looking to mitigate related-party transaction disputes and achieve certainty on their arm's length pricing. While the APA program has been successful as compared to traditional dispute resolution routesdelays in processing APA applications have resulted in a significant backlog. To enhance efficiency, we recommend streamlining the APA process by categorising applications based on their complexity. Complex cases could be allocated to more experienced teams, while simpler cases should be subject to shorter timelines for resolution. This bifurcation would enable faster conclusions, benefitting both the tax authorities and taxpayers.

Expansion and Re-evaluation of Safe Harbour Provisions: Plenty of small taxpayers have opted for the Safe Harbour regime in order to conclude their arm's length pricing in a streamlined manner. However, the applicable benchmarks are typically higher in this regime as compared to available alternatives. While the small taxpayers do get to enjoy this benefit of convenience, the threshold restrictions in the Safe Harbour regime makes it inaccessible to the taxpayers with comparatively higher value of transactions, forcing them into complex dispute resolution processes. To make this regime more accessible, the Government may re-evaluate the Safe Harbour provisions by (a) increasing the transaction thresholds to cover a larger number of companies, and (b) adjusting the rates to be closer to actual comparable benchmarks, thereby encouraging broader adoption and reducing litigation risks.

However, a plain reading of the section provides for the business or goods or services or transaction referred in the relevant sections and does not suggest the applicability of SDT provisions only in case of claim of tax holiday. Keeping in perspective the stringent penal provisions, taxpayers are recommended to maintain robust transfer pricing documentation and make appropriate disclosures in the Form irrespective of whether tax holiday is being claimed. Another interesting case could be when a transaction gets covered by two clauses of the Form. An example may be that of an expenditure incurred by the taxpayer, payment of which has been made to a person referred to under section 40A(2)(b) of the Act. The same expenditure may also get covered under the clause that provides to cover any business transacted between the assessee and other person as referred to in section 80-IA(10) (where the taxpayer is required to determine the arm's length price of the expenses and income of the eligible undertaking and demonstrate that the same has not resulted in more than ordinary profits). The question in such case is whether such item should be included under one clause or both the clauses. In the event, the same is included under both the clauses, it will automatically increase the aggregate value of transactions, which appears to be not intended by law. However, it may also be noted that justification of arm's length price under two clauses may require use of different methodology (depending on the facts of the case). Prima-facie, since double inclusion leading to increased value of transactions may not represent the facts correctly, the taxpayers may choose to disclose the same under one clause while justifying the same to meet with arm's length standard under both the clauses in the TP documentation.

Apart from the above, another important milestone is the online filing of the Form from AY 2013-14. The e-utility for uploading Form No. 3CEB is supported by a java application unlike the excel utility which is commonly used for filing of the income tax returns online by individuals as well as corporate taxpayers. Though this is a welcome step, however being a transition phase, there would be a lot of challenges both for the taxpayers as well as the Chartered Accountants (CAs) to overcome, for successful implementation of the same.

The online filing process is also complex. It requires the CA to register himself/ herself and his/her digital signature certificate (DSC) on the income tax website. Thereafter, the taxpayer is also required to register his/her CA who would be signing off his Form No. 3CEB. Post uploading of the Form by the CA, the taxpayer is required to approve the same with his/her DSC on the income tax website. Thus, once this two way process is completed, the Form would be considered as filed in all respects The date of filing the Form No. 3CEB would be the date on which the CA has uploaded the Form.

In view of the various practical issues (in disclosures and filing/uploading) in the Form, it is expected that the CBDT would clarify certain areas in the Form shortly. Though the amendments in the Form are to include various recent amendments, the CBDT has also tried to cover certain cases with a view to reduce controversy on account of exclusion/inclusion of certain items from the ambit of transfer pricing, which is a welcome step. The amendments would clearly achieve more disclosures in a structured way.

What are the matters not covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

As per ICAI's views, scope of audit u/s 92E does not cover matters as under: Form No. 3CEB

What are the matters required to be stated by the auditor in Form No. 3CEB?

Form No. 3CEB requires the auditor to state:

(a) that he has examined all accounts and records relating to international transactions entered into by the assessee during the relevant previous year. [Para 1 of Form No. 3CEB]

(b) that proper information and documents as are prescribed have been kept by the assessee in respect of international transactions entered into. [Para 2 of Form No. 3CEB]

(c) that the particulars required to be furnished under section 92E are given in the Annexure to the form and these particulars are true and correct. [Para 3 of Form No. 3CEB]

The words "true and correct" emphasize factual accuracy of the information given in the Annexure to Form No. 3CEB (Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing)

What are the matters required to be given in Annexure to Form No. 3CEB?

The Annexure to Form No. 3CEB are divided into 2 parts - Part A containing clauses 1 to 6 which are dealing with routine information about the assessee. Part B containing clauses 7 to 13 require list of associated enterprises and details about various international transactions.

According to the Guidance Note on Transfer pricing, the following points should be kept in mind :

♦ Obtain an authenticated statement of particulars to be given in Form No. 3CEB from the assessee.

♦ If any item is covered by more than one of the clauses in the Annexure, the auditor should make a suitable cross references to such items at appropriate places.

♦ If there is difference of opinion between the auditor and the assessee, both points of view should be stated with the relevant information. This will enable the tax authority to take a decision in the matter.

♦ If a particular clause in the Annexure is not applicable, the auditor should state 'N.A.' or 'Not Applicable' against the relevant item.

♦ Particulars should be examined and furnished in accordance with the law in force during the relevant previous year even though form of report may not have been amended to bring it in conformity with amended Income-tax Act.

♦ The Annexure should be signed by the auditor after completing his procedures on the information contained in it.

What are the points to be kept in mind by auditor regarding Para 1 of Form No. 3CEB?

Para 1 requires that auditor to affirm that he has examined the accounts and records of assessee relating to the international transactions entered into by the assessee during the previous year ending on 31st March. The auditor is required to examine only records relating to international transactions. The auditor should:

♦ Obtain from the assessee a complete list of both financial and non-financial accounts and records maintained. From this list, identify and call for the records required for his examination.

♦ Obtain a management representation as to the completeness of 'accounts and records'.

♦ If the auditor under section 92E is not the statutory auditor, he should:

1. Clearly state in his report that figures from general purpose audited financial statements have been used and relied upon.

2. Give in report a reconciliation between the figures given in his report and the figures shown in the general purpose financial statements.

3. State that he has relied upon the work done by the statutory auditors.

4. Keep in mind SA 600(Revised)Using the Work of Another Auditor.

♦ Use his professional skill and expertise and apply such tests as required in the circumstances.

♦ Apply appropriate sampling techniques if internal controls are strong.

♦ Keep in view the concept of 'materiality' is relevant in audit under section 92E.

♦ Conduct audit as per Standards on Auditing(SAs) as well as guidance notes issued by ICAI.

♦ Ensuring completeness of the list of international transactions is assessee's and not auditor's responsibility.

♦ Use his professional skill and expertise and apply such tests as required by circumstances to ensure whether the register/list of international transactions meets the requirements of law.

Withdrawal of Service Tax Exemption to Practising Chartered Accountants - An unjust move by Government!

Exemption granted to certain services provided by CAs, CSs and ICWAs, by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 stands withdrawn by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006. Is this withdrawal unjust and unjustifiable? Is it discriminatory? How damaging is it to the practice of CAs, etc.? The author here examines the issues from legal as well as moral angle. The abrupt move on the part of the Government is going to create a feeling of insecurity among the professional affected and cause harm to the healthy growth of their profession. Applying the logic of the Kerala High Court decision in Malappuram District Parallel College Association v. Union of India [2006] 150 Taxman 624, wherein levy of service tax on parallel colleges was held to be discriminatory, the author feels that the withdrawal of exemption to CAs/CSs/ICWAs may not pass the test of constitutionality.

Introduction

1. Chartered accountants, being professionally qualified and proficiently trained, are providing most valuable services to the people of this nation and abroad in the matters pertaining to accountancy, audit, management and technical consultancy and consultancy in the matters pertaining to various State as well Central laws. Their professional attitude and devotion are earning name and fame for the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and also for other fellow chartered accountants. Now, the chartered accountants are equally competing with the legal practitioners in the field of State and Central legislations as well as with the advocates and owing to varied experience and vast potential of the chartered accountants, the people are preferring to avail the services of the chartered accountants in place of other practitioners engaged in the similar fields. The facts aforesaid are widely accepted ones, which need no evidence.

Is it wrong for a person providing valuable services to the society and the Government to expect equitable treatment from the Government? If the answer to this question is ‘Yes’, then, what the Government has done by issuing Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants is just and all right. But if the readers answer this question as ‘No’, then, one should read the succeeding paras of this article to know how the move of the Government in issuance of Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants has turned out to be unjust and devastating for the practising chartered accountants.

The same is the case with the professionals engaged in practice in the field of company secretaryship and cost accountancy. The exemption from service tax provided to practicing company secretaries and practising cost accountants has also been withdrawn by the aforesaid notification.

The service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable.

Commenting on the current assessment, appeal, and litigation process is redundant as these points have been mentioned many times in many forums. Keeping the points brief, the important factors to be considered for improving the audit process are the following: Incentives of the TPOs should be set to encourage fair dealing rather than maximizing adjustments at all costs;

Taxpayers should be picked for transfer pricing audits on the basis of risk assessment rather than simply meeting the Rs. 15 crore criterion. This is likely to reduce the burden on TPOs and will allow them to delve more deeply in more complicated situations;

The transfer pricing regulations should be modified to introduce the concept of interquartile range (which is an internationally accepted practice) to replace the current concept of using average for determining the arm's length price. Training of the TPOs in the concepts of transfer pricing to enable them to appreciate business and economic facts while determining the arm's length price.

4.1 We have carefully examined the submissions of the applicant in their application. It is seen that the applicant seeks ruling as to whether the services received by them are Pure Services to avail exemption under Sl. No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017-C.T. (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. The admissibility of the application was examined during the hearing extended to them. The applicant stated that they had sought ruling regarding the services received by them for which charges are paid by them, the activity in which they are recipient and not supplier of services. Thus, the question is on the eligibility of a notification in respect of the services received by them and not on the supply made by them.

4.2 Section 95(a) of CGST and TNGST Act defines 'advance ruling' as

(a)

"advance ruling" means a decision provided by the Authority or the Appellate Authority to an applicant on matters or on questions specified in sub-section (2) of section 97 or sub-section (1) of section 100, in relation to the supply of goods or services or both being undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by the applicant;

From the above, it is evident that an applicant can seek an Advance Ruling only in relation to supply of goods or services or both undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by them. Further, as per Section 103(1) of the GST Act, the ruling is binding only on the applicant and the concerned officer or the jurisdictional officer of the applicant. In the case at hand, the applicant is the recipient of the services and not supplier of such service. Accordingly, this question is not liable for admission and therefore rejected without going into the merits of the case.

Primary Transfer Pricing Adjustments are what are known in popular parlance as "transfer pricing adjustments" or TP Adjustments."Primary adjustment" to a transfer price means the determination of transfer price in accordance with the arm's length principle resulting in an increase in the total income or reduction in the loss, as the case may be, of the assessee.

The e-tax Guide-Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2016 edition) of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore defines "transfer pricing adjustment" or what is referred to as "primary transfer pricing adjustment" in section 92CE(1) as under:

"3.34 Transfer pricing adjustment

In the event the related parties do not transact with each other at arm's length prices, tax authorities may for tax purposes, substitute the price of the transaction with one that could have been charged if the parties were unrelated. The adjustment to arrive at that price is known as a transfer pricing adjustment."

A primary TP adjustment covers the following TP adjustments,—

(i)

a TP adjustment to transfer price made suo motu by the assessee in his return of income;

(ii)

a TP adjustment to the transfer price made by the Assessing Officer has been accepted by the assessee;

(iii)

a TP adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement (APA) entered into by the assessee under section 92CC;

(iv)

a TP adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules framed under section 92CB; or

(v)

a TP adjustment arising from the resolution of an assessment by way of the mutual agreement procedure (MAP under an agreement (DTAA) entered into under section 90 or section 90A to avoid double taxa-tion.

9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

(a)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 69 taxmann.com 209 (Delhi - Trib.)

(b)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 651 (Delhi - Trib.)

(c)

Westfalia Separator India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 381 (Delhi - Trib.)

(d)

Rampgreen Solutions (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 64 taxmann.com 451 (Delhi - Trib.)

However, in Dy. CIT v. Minda Acoustic Ltd. [2019] 107 taxmann.com 475 (Delhi - Trib.), it was held that the Safe Harbour Rules can always be adopted as guidance in respect of the assessment years prior to their insertion.

9.2 Advance pricing agreement [Section 92CC]

Section 92CC relates to advance pricing agreement (APA).

Hitherto, section 92CC(1) provided that the CBDT, with the approval of the Central Government, may enter into an APA with any person, determining the ALP or specifying the manner in which ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person.

The scope of section 92CC(1) has been widened with effect from 1-4-2020 to provide that the CBDT may also enter into an APA with any person determining income referred to in section 9(1)(i), or specifying the manner in which said income is to be determined, as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India by or on behalf of that person, being a non-resident.

The Finance Minister, in her speech stated as follows:

"In order to provide tax certainty to taxpayers in the matter of attribution of profit to permanent establishment (PE), it is proposed to widen the scope of Advanced Pricing Agreement (APA) and Safe Harbour Regime (SHR), by providing that determination of attribution of profit to PE shall also be in the scope of SHR and APA." (para 2.1 of Annex to Part B of Budget Speech)

The rationale for the amendment is explained in Explanatory Memorandum as follows:

"It has been represented that the attribution of profits to the PE of a non-resident under clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 9 of the Act in accordance with rule 10 of the Rules also results in avoidable disputes in a number of cases. In order to provide certainty, the attribution of income in case of a non-resident person to the PE is also required to be clearly covered under the provisions of the SHR and the APA.

In view of the above, it is proposed to amend section 92CB and section 92CC of the Act to cover determination of attribution to PE within the scope of SHR and APA."

The petitioner-company Citilights Properties Private Limited entered into an agreement with the owners of a vast extent of land for the development of an information technology park complex, in the year 2005.

As per the development agreement, the petitioner was entitled to 74% of the undivided share of the land and they were obliged to develop the park and hand over 26% of the constructed area to the land owners.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with a company by name Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited, for the development of the software technology park and the transfer of 74% of the share of the petitioner to the said company, on the understanding that the transferee company had to fund the development of the park.

Thereafter, the petitioner made an application in November 2005 to the Chairman of the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee through the office of the Director of Software Technology Park of India, Chennai, for setting up an information technology park under the STP Scheme.

The petitioner also entered into two agreements with Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited and another company by name E-lights Technopark Private Limited for the effective funding and implementation of the project.

On 17.10.2006, the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee granted in principle approval for the setting up of the infrastructure facility under the STP Scheme in 'Freedom IT Campus '. The Government of India, in turn, granted permission by a communication dated 22.10.2006 in terms of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2004-2009.

As per the letter of permission so granted, the petitioner was entitled to import capital goods worth Rs. 2500 lakhs, by availing the benefits of Notification No. 153/93 dated 13.8.1993. But, the goods and services were to be used for the purpose of export of software and IT services by the STP Units located within the infrastructure facility at the park. The permission for import of items was valid for a period of two years from the date of issue of the letter of permission.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with the Software Technology Park of India, binding itself to the obligations and conditions of the letter of permission and a green card was issued to the petitioner. In pursuance of the above, the premises were declared as a private bonded warehouse by the Department of Central Excise.

Therefore, the petitioner caused import of capital goods availing the benefit of the exemption Notification.

Thereafter, the petitioner handed over Block-1 of the IT Park to the two transferee companies such as E-lights Technopark Private Limited and Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited in March 2008.

After two years, the special purpose vehicle - one of the transferee companies namely E-lights Technopark Private Limited applied on 30.3.2010 to the Software Technology Parks of India for approval of name transfer and green card to itself.

But, the Preventive Unit of the Commissionerate of Central Excise initiated an investigation into the affairs of the petitioner.

The Commissioner of Central Excise issued a show cause notice alleging various irregularities and calling upon the petitioner as well as the special purpose vehicle and the other transferee company to show cause as to why the benefit of the exemption Notification should not be denied and why the capital goods imported and sold should not be confiscated, apart from levy of penalty.

Meanwhile, the Inter-Ministerial Committee approved the letter of permission for a further period of four years from its expiry i.e., 21.12.2008.

Section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 (as inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012) make provision for special audit by practicing Chartered/Cost Accountant [earlier, section 14AA of Central Excise Act was made applicable to service tax. This section provided only for special audit of Cenvat credit availed].

Special audit can be ordered by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Central Excise [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Such audit can be ordered if the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of CE has reason to believe that any person liable to pay service tax—

(i)

has failed to declare or determine the value of a taxable service correctly; or

(ii)

has availed and utilised credit of duty or tax paid - (a) which is not within the normal limits having regard to the nature of taxable service provided, the extent of capital goods used or the type of inputs or input services used, or any other relevant factors as he may deem appropriate; or (b) by means of fraud, collusion, or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts; or

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the activity of business process outsourcing (BPO) services in the field related to accounting & taxation such as book-keeping, VAT returns, payroll, management accounting, and audit. The assessee was providing these services to the firm, namely DC, which was an AE of the assessee. The assessee provided these services from the unit which was an STPI unit eligible for deduction/exemption under section 10A. The assessee benchmarked its transaction with AE by applying internal CUP method prescribed under section 92C and claimed that its transactions with the AE were at arm length price. However, the TPO opined that TNMM was the most appropriate method.

The assessee carried the matter to DRP and vehemently objected the rejection of CUP method and selection of TNM method as most appropriate method, comparable selected by the TPO and comparable rejected by the TPO as suggested by the assessee. The assessee also propositioned that it was enjoying the benefit of deduction under section 10A. Therefore, there was no reason to charge a lower price from the AE. Moreover, given the circumstances of the case, the effective tax rate in the UK would be higher than the effective tax rate in India, which as a result of section 10A was 0 per cent. As such, there was no motive and incentive in shifting the profits from India to the UK, where the rate of tax was comparatively higher. However, DRP rejected the contention of the assessee.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is cardinal rule of interpretation that where the language used by the legislature is clear and unambiguous then plain and natural meaning of those words should be applied to the language and resort to any rule of interpretation to unfold intentions is permissible where the language is ambiguous. [Para 9]

Now, the controversy in the instant case is disguised in the question as to whether the provisions of chapter X shall be invoked in a situation where the assessee is enjoying tax exemption under section 10A and/or where there is no motive to avoid tax. The purpose of enacting transfer pricing provisions was to put a stop to the avoidance of tax by shifting taxable income outside India. Similarly, extending the fundamental of intendment to section 10A it is comprehended that this particular section is purported to boost the business of those undertakings which are situated in free trade zones (FTZ) and engaged in export of article or things or computer software services etc. by exempting their income from levy of tax. Thus, here the question arises as to whether the transfer pricing provisions can be invoked concerning the international transaction carried out by the assessee with its AE where the former is enjoying exemption under section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the assessee might not have any motive to shift the income from India to a foreign country as the same has already been exempted under section 10A [Para 9.8]

In this connection, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. [Para 9.9]

Transfer of credit Rule 12A(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 provides an option to a large taxpayer to transfer CENVAT credit (of central excise duty or service tax) accumulated in one manufacturing unit or service providing unit to any of its other manufacturing or service providing units. Such transfer can be made by way of issue of a transfer challan containing the details as provided in the said sub-rule. The said transfer challan can be sent by fax or electronically by way of e-mail attaching the scanned copy of the challan to other unit for taking credit which should be followed by the original copy of the challan. Moreover, the credit cannot be transferred by units availing area based exemption notifications specified in the said rules.

V. Self-adjustment of excess duty paid

Rule 12BB of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 provides a facility that if a large taxpayer manufacturing excisable goods has paid at any time excess excise duty on account of arithmetical error, he would be permitted to adjust the said excess duty paid by him in the subsequent period. However, such adjustment is subject to the provisions of unjust enrichment and other applicable provisions of law.

VI. Duty payment

As the e-payment facility has been provided for payment of central excise duty and service tax, large taxpayer may be requested to opt for e-payment as far as possible as it will reduce the compliance cost, and it will be beneficial for the department also for revenue reconciliation. However, in case of difficulties in e-payment, a large taxpayer is permitted to pay the duty (except in such cases of Service Tax where e-payment is mandatory) in the respective jurisdiction where the factories or service providing premises are situated or even in the jurisdiction of LTU, Bangalore. However, in order to ensure proper accounting of taxes paid by them, the large taxpayer should be directed to write the following details in their TR-6 challan in addition to the details presently being filled up:

VIII. Export Procedures

In the Approach Paper issued by the Department, it has been clarified that facility of self-sealing of export consignment is available to all the large taxpayers. Therefore, all the taxpayers are expected to avail this facility. However, in exceptional cases, where the taxpayer intends to avail the facility of sealing by the Central Excise Officers or the Customs Officers, they should apply for the same to the LTU who in turn will request the jurisdictional Commissionerate to depute the staff for supervising the sealing of export cargo. However, the processing of accepting the proof of export shall be carried out only in the office of the LTU. The Chief Commissioner, LTU is requested to prescribe a modified procedure to ensure smooth processing of export documents that in case of any difficulty in following the present export procedure and the said procedure will be sent to the Board for post facto approval. However, in no case, export consignment should be held up for want of any procedural formalities.

Audit by outside Agencies - VAT laws of some States provide for audit by outside agencies.

This is practically outsourcing of work of State tax department. Once the figures are checked by an independent auditor, work of tax authorities is considerably reduced and scrutiny of returns by departmental officers becomes easy.

In some States, audit can be done only by Chartered Accountants. In some eight States (Assam, Kerala, Orissa, Uttaranchal, Maharashtra etc.), audit can be done either by Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountants.

In AP, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Karnataka, audit can be done by CA, cost Auditor or Sales Tax Practitioner (STP).

In Karnataka, audit report is required if turnover exceeds Rs 25 lakhs.

In Delhi, the dealer is required to submit copy of audit report u/s 44AB of Income Tax Act (This report is required when turnover exceeds Rs 40 lakhs per annum) No separate audit is prescribed, unless special audit is ordered by department.

5.10 Proceedings before TPO for determination of Arm's Length Price in respect of specified domestic transactions [Section 92CA]

5.10-1 Pre-amended provisions

Section 92CA of the Act provides that the Assessing Officer, if he considers it necessary or expedient to do so, may, with the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner, refer the mat-ter of determination of Arm's Length Price (ALP) in respect of an international transaction or Specified Domestic Transaction (SDT) to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). Once a reference is made to the TPO, the TPO is competent to exercise all powers that are available to the Assessing Officer under Section 92C(3) for the determination of ALP and consequent adjustment.

Further, under Section 92E of the Act, there is a reporting requirement on the taxpayer to file an audit report in the prescribed form before the Assessing Officer (AO) containing details of all international transactions or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer during the year. This audit report is the primary document with the AO, which contains the details of international transactions and/or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer. If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under Section 92E, then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction/SDT so as to make a reference to the TPO.

Section 92CA provides that if, during the course of proceeding before him, an international transaction comes to the notice of the TPO, which has not been referred to him by the AO, the TPO can proceed to determine the ALP in its respect as well. It also provides for the computation of ALP by the TPO of those international transactions, details of which have not been furnished in the audit report referred to above. These provisions are in place in sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of the section 92CA. However, at present, the above-noted provisions of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA do not extend to SDTs.

5.10-2 Amendment by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 has amended sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of Section 92CA to enable the TPO to deal with SDTs which have not been referred to him by the AO and/or in whose respect audit report under section 92CE has not been filed.

These amendments will take effect from 01-04-2025 and will, accord-ingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2025-26 and subsequent assessment years.

Procedure for departmental audit is as follows.

Notice of audit to registered person - Where it is decided to undertake the audit of a registered person in accordance with the provisions of section 65, the proper officer shall issue a notice in form GST ADT-01 within the time specified in section 65(3) of CGST Act.

Verification of records by audit team and audit notes - The proper officer authorised to conduct audit of the records and books of account of the registered person shall, with the assistance of the team of officers and officials accompanying him, verify the documents on the basis of which the books of account are maintained and the returns and statements furnished under the Act and the rules made thereunder, to check the correctness of following - (a) the turnover (b) exemptions and deductions claimed (c) the rate of tax applied in respect of supply of goods or services or both (d) the input tax credit availed and utilized (e) refund claimed. Inform discrepancies to registered person - The proper officer may inform the registered person of the discrepancies, if any, noticed as observations of the audit and the said person may file his reply and the proper officer shall finalise the findings of the audit after due consideration of the reply furnished - Rule 101(4) of CGST and SGST Rules, 2017.

Inform audit findings to registered person on conclusion of audit - On conclusion of the audit, the proper officer shall inform the findings of audit to the registered person in accordance with the provisions of section 65(6) in form GST ADT-02 - Rule 101(5) of CGST and SGST Rules, 2017.

Doctrine of unjust enrichment is not applicable if certified by Chartered Accountant that duty not recovered and shown in balance sheet as loans and advances - Deepak International v. CCST (2014) 304 ELT 438 (CESTAT SMB) * India Steel International v. CC (2015) 318 ELT 646 (CESTAT).

In CCE v. Paradeep Phosphates (2009) 238 ELT 690 (CESTAT), selling price was below cost price excluding excise duty as certified by Cost Accountant and the amount was shown as 'receivable' in balance sheet. It was held that doctrine of unjust enrichment is not applicable - similar view in South India Paper Mills v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 651 (CESTAT SMB).

Certificate of CA is only a piece of evidence and in itself not sufficient to show that burden has not been passed to other person - CC v. BPL Ltd. (2010) 259 ELT 526 (Mad HC DB) * CC v. SNS Overseas (2012) 275 ELT 621 (CESTAT).

In Tarapur Coatings v. CC (2009) 234 ELT 466 (CESTAT SMB), Chartered Accountant prepared cost sheet as per CAS-4 and certified that burden of excess duty was absorbed by appellant and that there was no price rise during relevant period. Duty was shown as receivable. It was held that refund is admissible.

In Quality Offset Printers v. CC (2008) 230 ELT 671 (CESTAT SMB), CA issued a general certificate based on balance sheets of previous year, current year and subsequent year that the incidence of duty has not been passed on. It was held that refund is admissible.

In Memirex & Co. v. CCE 2004(174) ELT 216 (CESTAT), it was held that certificate from Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence.

In A K Enterprise v. CC 2006 (199) ELT 67 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that mere certificate from Chartered Accountant is not sufficient to rebut presumption that duty has been passed on to buyer - same view in CC v. BPL Ltd. (2010) 259 ELT 526 (Mad HC DB).

In India Agencies v. CC (2007) 212 ELT 507 (CESTAT), it was observed that Chartered Accountants are professional interested in their clients and issue such statements. In absence of conclusive evidence that duty has not been passed on, doctrine of unjust enrichment applies.

In Chambal Fertilisers v. CC 2006 (200) ELT 231 (CESTAT), it was held that though certificate of Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence of not passing duty burden, department can ask for records to check whether statement of Chartered Accountant is correct. Refund cannot be rejected simply on the ground that certificate of Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence. - followed in Flair Impex v. CC (2009) 238 ELT 794 (CESTAT SMB).

However, mere certificate of CA that service tax has not been recovered separately in invoice is not sufficient to establish that the burden of tax has not been passed on to the buyer - Multi Mantech International v. CST (2009) 18 STT 229 (CESTAT SMB).

When Amount treated as 'claim receivable' or 'refund receivable' in accounts or shown as expenditure

42.6-1 In Jaipur Syntex Ltd. v. CCE 2002(143) ELT 605 (CEGAT), assessee had paid higher duty and the differential amount was treated in accounts as 'claims receivable'. This was treated as part of Balance Sheet and not charged to P&L account. It was held that it is evident that incidence of duty has not been passed on to customers. [In this case, duty was not shown separately in invoice].

In CC v. Virudhunagar Textile Mills (2008) 230 ELT 411 (Mad HC DB), differential duty on capital goods was shown as duty receivable from customs department and balance sheet with CA certificate was produced. It was held that refund is admissible.

Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

Once advance license is granted by licensing authority the customs authorities cannot refuse exemption on an allegation that there was misrepresentation. - Titan Medical Systems v. CC 2003(151) ELT 254 (SC) - followed in Autolite (India) Ltd. v. UOI 2003 (157) ELT 13 (Bom HC DB), where it was held that even assuming that licensing authorities have wrongly accepted the statement of petitioner and granted him advance license, so long as license is valid and subsisting, import against advance license cannot be denied. Customs authorities cannot sit in appeal over decision of licensing authority.

DEPB license issued by DGFT cannot be challenged or questioned by customs - Pradip Polyfils v. UOI 2004 (173) ELT 3 (Bom HC DB). Customs authorities are not competent to sit over decision of DGFT authorities regarding DEPB credit -Suresh Enterprises v. CC 2005 (179) ELT 466 (CESTAT).

CC 2005 (189) ELT 135 (CESTAT 3 member LB), it has been held that once endorsement is made by DGFT about discharge of export obligation, transferee of license is eligible for exemption, even if it is found that transferability was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. As per Para 2.57(a) of FTP 2015-2020, decision of Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) is final in respect of interpretation of policy or classification under ITC. Hence, the decision of DGFT in this regard is binding on customs authorities - R N Rajan Co. v. CC 1995 (77) ELT 600 (CEGAT).
