9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

12.4 Change in the time limit to pass the order by the Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 166 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 92CA of ITA 1961)]

12.4-1 Position under the ITA 1961

Section 92CA of the ITA 1961 deals with the case where the assessee has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction in any previous year, and the AO may refer the computation of the Arm's Length Price (ALP) in relation to the said international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO).

Sub-section (3A) to section 92CA states that TPO is required to pass an order before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation under section 153, or as the case may be, in section 153B for making the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation or fresh assessment, as the case may be, expires.

12.4-1a Exclusion of the last day of assessment limitation - The interpretation of the phrase 'before sixty days prior to the date' has been a consistent point of contention between taxpayers and the revenue, leading to significant litigation.

The Madras High Court, in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), which affirmed the Single Judge's decision in Jt. CIT v. Pfizer Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 536 (Madras), held that the word 'date' in section 92CA(3A) refers to the last date for the AO to pass the assessment order under section 153 (e.g., December 31st). The crucial words 'prior to' indicate that, for the purpose of calculating the 60 days, this last date must be excluded. Therefore, if the assessment limitation expires on December 31st, the TPO order ought to have been passed on or before October 31st.

This interpretation was consistently followed across numerous ITAT benches, including in the following cases:

Teleperformance Global Services (P.) Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 658 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. [2024] 163 taxmann.com 349 (Ahmedabad-Trib.)

Frost & Sullivan (India) (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 739 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Shell India Markets (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 366 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Siemens Technology and Services (P.) Ltd. [2024] 162 taxmann.com 357 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Huhtamaki India Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 194 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Atos India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 217 (Mumbai-Trib.)

CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore-Trib.)

Pioneer India Electronics (P.) Ltd. [2025] 178 taxmann.com 553 (Delhi-Trib.)

Sigma Aldrich Chemicals (P.) Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 431 (Bangalore-Trib.)

12.4-1b Mandatory nature of the time limit - Another critical aspect clarified by the judiciary is whether the time limit prescribed in section 92CA(3A) is mandatory or merely directory. The revenue often argued that the use of the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) implies a directory nature.

However, the Madras High Court in Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), after a detailed analysis of the scheme of the Act and the consequences of non-compliance, unequivocally held that the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and the time period fixed therein has to be scrupulously followed.'

The court reasoned that the overall scheme of transfer pricing assessments, with various interlinked time limits (including extensions under the proviso to section 92CA(3A) and section 153), indicates a legislative intent to ensure timely completion. If the TPO's time limit were merely directory, it would undermine the entire assessment process. This principle has been reiterated in the case of Asstt. CIT v. CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore - Trib.).

The assessee had established two captive electricity and steam generation units for the generation of electricity and steam. The assessee had sought exemption under section 80-IA(4)(iv) in respect of Co-generation Unit 1, specifically for the supply of electricity and steam to its non-specified unit, the Paper Unit.

■

The assessee had adopted the Transaction Net Margin Method (TNMM) for determining the arm''s length price for the transfer of power from the specified Co-generation Unit-1 to the non-specified Paper Unit and the sale value of the power had been determined by the assessee at Rs. 41.21 crores, based on a rate of Rs. 6.73 per KWH for a total of 61.24 crores units of power.

■

The Assessing Officer adopted a rate of Rs. 3.875 per unit (KVAH), instead of the assessee’s applied rate of Rs. 6.73 per unit (KWH). The Assessing Officer derived this rate by averaging the adjusted rate of Rs. 4.74 per unit (after making adjustments from Rs. 4.74 per unit) from PSPCL and the rate of Rs. 3.01 per unit from the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX). Consequently, the Assessing Officer computed a difference in the sale price of power and made an addition of Rs. 17.48 crores.

■

On appeal, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer''s approach was inconsistent with the provisions of section 92C(1), read with rule 10B, and section 80-IA(8), which govern the determination of arm''s length price and transfer pricing adjustments.The rate of 76.73 per KWH adopted by the assessee for the transfer of power was lower than the comparable rate for generating electricity from biomass fuel, as available in the public domain and the rate adopted by the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) of Rs. 5.98 per unit of PSPCL(Power Corporation) for deriving average was not justified, as the assessee was categorized as a power-intensive unit, and not under the general category.TPO wrongly deducted distribution loss, transmission loss, and cross-subsidy from the rate, leading to an incorrect revised adjusted sale rate of Rs. 4.74 per KVAH per unit for power supplied by PSPCL and the TPO failed to apply the appropriate division factor of 0.92 to convert KVAH into KWH. The price at which surplus power was supplied by producers to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) is determined by state regulations and contracts and, therefore, cannot be considered the market value for the purposes of Section 80-IA(8).

Large Tax Payers Units

16.1-6 In many countries, special systems have been developed to administer large tax payers. The international trend is to establish full fledged LTU (Large Tax Payers Units) that are responsible for most of tax administration functions relating to taxpayer, including collection, enforcement of tax arrears and audit. Many Asian countries have established such LTU.

LTU (Large Tax Payers Units) have been established at various places in India so that they can get all facilities of tax payments, filing of returns and documents, assessments, rebates/refunds, audit, recovery and refunds at one place, irrespective of geographical location of their units. This is to ensure uniformity in matters of tax/duty determination and quick actions [Information from Ministry of Finance - 194 ELT T3 and 3 STT 85 (Stat) - see also CBE&C circular Nos. 833/10/2006-CX dated 5-10-2006 and 834/11/2006-CX dated 5-10-2006].

It will be a 'single window clearance' for all matters relating to central excise, income tax, corporation tax and service tax. LTU will provide single point interface with tax administration to large tax payers.

LTU will be self-contained tax administration office of Department of Revenue acting as single window clearance point for all matters relating to central excise, income tax, corporation tax and service tax.

LTU will be headed by Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioner (either from CBDT or CBEC). Each large taxpayer will be assisted by Client Executive (Additional/Joint/Asstt Commissioner) from income tax or excise department [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

It is voluntary for a tax payer to join LTU. He has to make application for that purpose and give consent to join LTU in form prescribed vide notification No. 21/2006-CE(NT) dated 30-9-2006.

LTU can opt out of the scheme by giving 30 days notice, from the first day of following financial year [rule 12BB(6)]

The scheme is not open to manufacturers of tobacco products and pan masala.

Bangalore LTU has become functional w.e.f. 1-10-2006. Chennai LTU has become operational w.e.f. 1-12-2007. Mumbai LTU has started functioning from 27-3-2008. Delhi LTU has started functioning from 2-6-2008.

Registration as LTU - Application for registration as LTU should be made to Assistant/Deputy Commissioner under Central Excise and to Superintendent under service tax (amendment to Notification No. 20/2006-CE(NT) made on 18-7-2011).

Administrative Control in case of LTP-EOU - Even in case of large taxpayer-EOU, administrative control will be under control of LTUs. Where specific function requires physical presence of officers for warehousing, sealing etc., it will be dealt with by jurisdictional Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs (in case of port cities) or Central Excise (in case of other than port cities), who will have concurrent jurisdiction over these LTP-EOUs - MF(DR) circular No. 15/2007-Cus dated 20-3-2007 [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

of an international transaction, the TPO would have an authority to examine any international transaction which comes to his notice during the proceedings, whether a reference in this respect was made by the Assessing Officer or not and whether the assessee had reported such transaction under section 92E or not. However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13] In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

Even in such a situation, the statute does not permit the TPO to assume the jurisdiction to determine the arm's length price of a specified domestic transaction not reported to him. There may be number of cases where the assessee may bona fide hold a belief that certain transaction is not a specified domestic transaction and therefore, would not report the same under section 92E. Whether bona fide or not, not making a report by the assessee of a specified domestic transaction would not leave the revenue without remedy. As clarified by CBDT in the instructions dated 20-5-2013, it is always open for the TPO who notices such transaction during the course of the proceedings before him to call for a reference by the Assessing Officer. If the Assessing Officer does make a report, only then TPO can undertake further steps as envisaged under sub-section (2) and other sub-sections of section 92CA. As noted, the statute is sufficiently clear. The legislature while expanding the scope of the transfer pricing study by the TPO to a transaction not referred him or not reported by the Assessing Officer, under sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, has confined the applicability thereof only to international transactions. The TPO exercising such powers suo motu in relation to a specified domestic transaction would be transgressing his jurisdiction and in the process would render the requirement of sub-section (1) of section 92CA redundant. As noted, the reference that the Assessing Officer can make to the TPO would have the approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner.[Para 19]

Under these circumstances, in relation to the transaction of payment to creditors in demerger process, the TPO had no jurisdiction to make any adjustments. Under these circumstances and even otherwise, the adjustment on merits cannot be examined, though it was argued by the assessee.[Para 20]

Section 92CA(1) empowers the Assessing Officer to make reference to TPO for the computation of arm's length price of international transactions. Further, the TPO as defined in Explanation to section 92CA to be the person authorized by board to perform functions of Assessing Officer specified in section 92C. In sub-section (3) of section 144B, roles of Technical unit is clearly spelt out according to which, functions of technical unit includes assistance or advice on transfer pricing issues. During the course of performing such function, the technical unit can obtain advice from the TPO on the issue of determination of arm's length price of international transaction as they are expert in this field. Thus, the reference by technical unit to TPO is in accordance with the provisions of the Act and therefore, consequent orders passed are not barred by limitations. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section  92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing -  Computation of Arm’s length price (Adjustments - Deletion of) - Assessment year  2021-22 - Assessee-company was engaged in trading of spices, oil seeds, seeds, coffee, tea, dry fruits etc. - It had entered into international transaction with its Associated Enterprises (AEs) - TPO made certain adjustments to assessee's income - Assessee contended that solitary ground on basis of which TPO had discarded TP study of assessee was that segments filed by assessee were not audited - It was noted that TPO had discarded certificate of auditor in a summary manner - Whether even if, conclusion of TPO in arriving at PLI was taken into consideration, same was within tolerance limit of +/- 1 per cent - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no adjustment was called for in this case and adjustments made by TPO were to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of trading of spices, oil seeds, seeds, coffee, tea, dry fruits etc. It entered into international transaction with its associated enterprises (AEs) and third parties.

■

The Assessing Officer made reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) for computing the arm's length price (ALP) of the international transaction entered into by the assessee with its AE. The TPO made certain adjustments.

■

The assessee filed objections before the Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) and assailed the draft assessment order of the Assessing Officer. The DRP gave certain directions and then the TPO passed the fresh TP order.

■

It was pertinent to note here that in the fresh TP order, the adjustments were revised to the tune of Rs. 1.64 crores, after the directions of the DRP. Then, the Assessing Officer passed the final assessment order and framed the assessment.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

In this case, the solitary ground on the basis of which the TPO has discarded the TP study of the assessee is that the segments filed by the assessee were not audited. The TPO has discarded the certificate of the auditor in a summary manner. Further, even if the conclusion of the TPO in arriving the PLI is to be accepted, then also the same is within the +/-1 per cent tolerance limit. Therefore, no adjustment is called for in this case and the adjustments made by the TPO are hereby deleted. [Para 9]

■

Further, the assessee has rightly relied upon the order of the Co-ordinate Bench of the Madras Tribunal in the case of Honeywell Electrical Devices & Systems India Ltd., wherein, it has been held that filing of audited segments is not necessary, if the accounts are audited and the figures mentioned therein are not disturbed by the TPO. Respectfully, following the decision of the Co-ordinate Bench, the opinion of TPO with respect to filing of audited segments results is not correct. [Para 10]

■

In the result, the appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 11]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act provides that the Assessing Officer may refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction to a Transfer Pricing Officer. Such a reference can be made where:—

(a)

The Assessing Officer considers it is necessary or expedient to do so, and

(b)

The Assessing Officer has taken previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner to refer the computation to Transfer Pricing Officer.

Eliminating the interface between the Transfer Pricing Officer and the assessee or any other person to the extent technologically feasible;

(b)

Optimising utilisation of the resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation; and

(c)

Introducing a team-based determination of arm's length price (ALP) with dynamic jurisdiction.

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of blended packet tea at its two units located at Dharwad and outside Dharwad. Dharwad unit was exempt from payment of sales tax under Notification dated 19-6-1991.

The Assessing Authority inspected the business premises of the assessee and having noticed that the maximum retail price (MRP) mentioned on the tea packets sold from the Dharwad unit and outside Dharwad unit was similar opined that the assessee had added the tax component to the sale price of Dharwad tea though not under the nomenclature of tax or cess. Hence, the assessee had violated clause (e) of Explanation III to the Notification dated 19-6-1991 and was not entitled to the benefit of exemption. He, therefore, rejected the claim of exemption on the turnover of Dharwad tea based on notification dated 19-6-1991.

The First Appellate Authority upheld the view of the Assessing Authority.

The Tribunal held that though the assessee had considered the local tax element in the price fixed, but it could not be stated that it had collected the local taxes as such from the consumers in view of the fact that in the invoice against Karnataka Sales Tax and Central Sales Tax it was specifically left blank in respect of Dharwad tea. Mere mentioning of MRP on the Dharwad tea did not by itself a proof of any collection of tax in terms of sales tax laws. It accordingly allowed the appeal of the assessee.

The High Court affirmed the order passed by the Tribunal. It held that on the Dharwad tea there was a clear mention of exemption of tax in terms of the note at the end of the invoice itself. Therefore, the buyer was told in unmistakable terms that what was being paid as sale price and not as sales tax.

FACT: Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

Since CT-3 certificates were filed before department, each clearance could not have taken place without the knowledge of the officer as to the ultimate destination of the goods and the fact that they were cleared without payment of duty in terms of the exemption notification which was specified in the application.

Hence, charge of suppression was invalid and, consequently, extended period of limitation could not have been invoked. [Paras 5 and 6]

It is material to note that the TP adjustments are made pursuant to the APA entered into by the assessee with CBDT. Section 92CC empowers the CBDT to enter into an APA with any person for determining an ALP or specify the manner in which the ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person and income referred to in section 9(1)(i) or the manner in which said income is to be determined as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India. [Para 17]

■

It is relevant to refer to sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92CD. [Para 18]

■

The provisions of section 92CD(1) are unambiguous and even if a return has been filed prior to an assessee entering into an APA, he is entitled to furnish a modified return declaring his income in accordance with the terms of the APA. Subject to certain exceptions, the APA is binding both on the assessee and the revenue. [Para 19]

■

It is clear that the scheme of providing for an APA is to remove any uncertainty as to the determination of an income of an assessee engaged in international transactions with associated enterprises. The assessee is required to declare his income in accordance with the APA. Except in certain cases, where there is a change in law and facts or the agreement is occasioned by fraud or misrepresentation, the APA would be binding. Sub-sections (5), (6) and (7) of section 92CC provide for the same in unambiguous terms. [Para 20]

■

It is apparent from a plain reading of sub-section (4) of section 92C that the same is inapplicable. The said sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to compute the total income, having regard to the ALP determined by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (3) of section 92C. [Para 22]

■

Sub-section (3) of section 92C provides that the Assessing Officer can proceed to determine the ALP only in cases he is of the opinion on the basis of material that (a) the price charged or paid in international transaction, has not been determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92C; or (b) that information and documentation relating to the international transaction has not been maintained as mandatorily required; or (c) that the information or data for computing the ALP is unreliable; or there is failure on the part of the assessee to furnish any information or document required to be furnished along with the notice. [Para 23]

■

It is apparent that in a case where the assessee voluntarily computes the ALP pursuant to an APA entered into with CBDT, none of the conditions as set out in sub-section (3) of section 92C are attracted. It follows that sub-section (4) of section 92C is not attracted. [Para 24]

■

More importantly, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C also clearly states that no deduction under section 10A or 10AA or 10B or under Chapter VI-A would be allowed in respect of the amount of income by which the total income of the assessee is enhanced after computation under the said section. Thus in a case where the assessee voluntarily declares his income based on the ALP determined on the basis of an APA, there would be no occasion for the Assessing Officer to enhance the income of the assessee. [Para 25]

■

Absent any enhancement of income, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is clearly inapplicable. [Para 26]

■

It is also necessary to bear in mind that in terms of section 10AA(1), the profits and gains of an enterprise, as referred to in clause (j) of section 2 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, from an eligible unit, which is derived from export of articles or things are exempt. [Para 27]

■

The ALP is imputed to transactions to determine the profits and gains that are derived by the assessee from any international transactions (or specified domestic transactions) in order to assess the real income of the assessee after eliminating any bias or element of transfer of profits. [Para 28]

■

Thus, indisputably, the income computed on the basis of ALP would provide a measure of the profits or income derived by the activities carried on by an assessee. The proviso to section 92C(4) essentially limits exemption under section 10AA in cases where the income computed is enhanced by the Assessing Officer under section 92C. [Para 29]

It is settled principle of law that the claim of exemption against the form cannot be denied unless the form is found to be forged and obtained as a result of collusion between the parties." (Para 4)

Thus, it is observed as per the CBDT's explanation, provisions of Transfer Pricing has been enacted to ensure that no income otherwise taxable in India is reduced and even a transaction resulting in exempt income is also subjected to provisions of Transfer Pricing. [Para 33]

In such circumstances, one is confronted with the issue as to how and why the provisions of Transfer Pricing should be applied in respect of an international transaction giving rise to exempt income in the hands of the assessee. [Para 34] In such circumstances, where the income derived from international transactions is exempt from tax in India, it cannot be alleged that the assessee had arranged its affairs in such a manner so as to show lesser taxable income in India but it can be alleged that the assessee has arranged its affairs in such a manner so as to reflect more exempt income in India. [Para 35]

Therefore, a harmonious reading can be construed in the provisions of section 92C(4) and the object and purport of insertion of the provisions of Transfer Pricing as explained by the CBDT. [Para 36]

In a case where the international transaction entered into by the assessee with the AEs is giving rise to exempt income in the hands of the assessee, it is to be benchmarked with the ALP determined in accordance with the provisions of Transfer Pricing to ensure that no excess exempt income is disclosed by the assessee and assessee is entitled for exemption of income under section 10A of the total income determined as per the Transfer Pricing Provisions only and where the assessee has claimed more exempt income, then exemption under section 10A shall be allowed in accordance with the profit compared as per ALP only. [Para 37]

Keeping in view the above in mind in the instant case, as per the decisions of the lower authorities the assessee had not reported any excess exempt income from its international transactions with AE. On the other hand, as per the opinion of the lower authorities when exempt income declared by the assessee was benchmarked with the ALP determined in accordance with the provisions of Transfer Pricing, it was found that assessee has declared lesser exempt income and thereby no taxable base in India was eroded. Therefore, no adjustment with the exempt income of the assessee was required to be made as per provisions contained in Chapter X of the Act. [Para 38]

In view of the above, the Assessing Officer was directed to treat the income declared from the business in question at the amount as shown by the assessee in its return of income. [Para 40]

Technical Inspection service :

The work order requires AGPL to carry out jobs such as the following : Washing; Preparing Vehicle for display; PDI w/o. O/C/; PDI with O/C, PT as per Schedule, Waxing as per Schedule; Rewaxing; PDI & PT with O/C; Removing & Redoing PT Refurnishing etc.

If the argument of revenue is accepted, every motor garage will become a 'technical inspection and certification' agency. This would lead to a ridiculous situation. The meaning of technical inspection and certification conveys the purpose of certification along with inspection to meet specified standards.

The kind of certification covered under this definition refers to certification to ensure that characteristics of the goods meet specified standards. The standards may relate to functionality, utility, quality or safety. The definition of technical inspection cannot be read to mean that any checks on functionality, safety etc. would amount to technical inspection and certification. The word "technical inspection and certification" would appropriately refer to certain standards laid down in some statute or some Guidelines.

For example in the Motor Vehicles Act certain standards are required to be met. Other examples of technical inspection are the Food Safety Standards which require articles of food and drinks to meet certain standards of composition of ingredients etc. Similar is the case where pharmaceutical products are required to meet certain specified standards by law.

In the present case the job card or vehicle data sheets clearly indicate that AGPL are merely rectifying/replacing some damaged/defective parts etc. By no stretch of imagination can this activity be termed as technical inspection and certification. Hence, demand was set aside. [Para 7]

There was registration certificate dated 30-6-2000 with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991. The object of the exemption notification was neither to protect the owners of the trade mark nor the consumers from being misled. These were considerations which were relevant in disputes arising under the Trade Marks Act. The object of the exemption Notification No. 1/93-CE was to grant benefits to those industries, which did not have the advantage of a brand name. [Para 16] It is correct to say that the Registrar of Trade Marks can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect. Making the registration certificate applicable from retrospective date is based on principle of deemed equivalence to public user of such mark. This deeming fiction cannot be extended to Excise Law. It is confined to the provisions of the Trade Marks Act. In a given case like the instant one, where there was evidence with the department of the trade mark being owned by company ‘K’ and there was evidence of the appellants trading on the reputation of ‘K’ which was not rebutted by them, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect could not confer the benefit of exemption notification upon them. In the instant case, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991 would not tantamount to conferment of exemption benefit under the Excise Law, once it was found that the appellants had wrongly used the trade mark of company ‘K’. [Paras 17 & 18]

If the SSI unit wrongly affixes a trade mark of another person, be it registered or not, or if it uses the trade mark of an ineligible person, such default would not be eliminated by the principle of deemed equivalence embodied in section 28; as that principle is based on a deeming fiction, which fiction is confined only to the provisions of that Act. [Para 20]

Consequently, the appeals were to be dismissed.

HELD: ■

A conjoint reading of the relevant provisions of sections 92CA(3A) and 153(1) shows that the TPO is required to pass order under section 92CA(3A) at any time before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation referred to in section 153 for making assessment order expires. The Division Bench of the Madras High Court in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215/444 ITR 636 (Madras) has upheld the decision of Single Judge holding that [Para 15]

■

The period of limitation for passing the assessment order in the instant case expires on 31-3-2013. The time limit for passing the order under section 92CA(3A) is sixty days prior to the date on which the limitation referred in section 153 expires. Thus, the limitation in the present case for passing the order under section 92CA(3A) expires on 29-1-2013. The TPO passed the order under section 92CA(3A) expires on 29-1-2013. A perusal of clause 43 of Circular No. 3/2008, dated 12-3-2008 shows that the word 'month' has been used therein instead of 'days' used in the Act. Undoubtedly, two months may not necessarily be equal to sixty days always as specified in the Act. 'Two months' as mentioned in Circular can be more or even less than sixty days. Therefore, expression issued to evaluate limitation period as specified in the Act has to be strictly followed. [Para 16]

Such notice ought to have been issued at the very threshold of the proceedings initiated by the TPO. In any case, the bare minimum, that was expected from TPO for compliance of the statutory requirement of giving notice envisaged in sub-section (2) of section 92CA, and to comply with the principles of natural justice which are necessarily required to be observed before passing an order entailing civil consequences, was to record the grounds on which the adjustment was proposed to be made by him in the income of the assessee-company, in a precise, clear and unambiguous language in the proceedings recorded by him, get it signed from the authorized representative of the assessee, give it an opportunity to file a reply to those grounds and to produce such evidence as it might have in its possession to show that no such adjustment was called for in its case. If the procedure adopted by the TPO does not meet even this minimum requirement, it cannot be said to be a fair and reasonable procedure required to be followed by an authority exercising quasi-judicial and/or administrative powers, entailing serious consequences for the assessee in the form of not only additional tax liability on account of addition to the income but also on account of the penalty that may be imposed upon it under section 271, the Explanation 7 to which specifically provides that in the case of the assessee who has entered into an international transaction, in the event of any amount being allowed or disallowed in the process of computation of its income under sub-section (4) of section 92C, will be deemed to represent the income, in respect of which particulars have been concealed, or inaccurate particulars have been furnished, unless the assessee proves that the price charged or paid in such transaction was computed in accordance with the provision contained in section 92C and the manner prescribed under that section, in good faith and with due diligence. The arm's length principle of transfer pricing is based on the premise that the amount charged by one related party to another for a product must be the same as if the parties were not related. An arm's length price in respect of a foreign transaction, therefore, is the price which that transaction would obtain in the open market. Determination of arm's length price, when dealing with proprietary goods and services or intangibles, can be a much more complicated matter, as compared to determining such price in case of products such as commodities. A controlled transaction normally would meet the arm's length standard, if the results of the transaction are consistent with the results that would have been obtained if an uncontrolled entity was engaged in the same transaction, under the same circumstances. It may not always be possible to come across identical transactions and, therefore, the TPO, in such cases, would need to refer to comparable transactions made under comparable circumstances. In the return filed for the assessment year 2008-09, it claimed exemption under section 5A from payment of tax on the sale of goods to 'A' in the SEZ.

The Assessing Authority denied exemption under section 5A on sale of goods to 'A'.

The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on the ground that the running bills which were issued by the assessee to 'A' did not bear the endorsement of the Customs Authority. For this purpose, he placed reliance upon rule 42(2A).

The Tribunal held that while rule 42(2A) prescribed a procedure to the effect that if the tax invoice was endorsed by the Customs Authority, then the sale will be treated as a zero rated sale under section 5A, it was simply a procedural rule and did not lay down any condition precedent that only on fulfilment of such condition, the sale had to be treated as zero rated sale. It was directory in nature, non compliance of which would not deprive the assessee of the right to claim zero rated sale under section 5A. Section 21(1) of the Gujarat Special Economic Zone Act, 2004 granted exemption from payment of tax on sale or purchase of goods in the SEZ. Hence, tax was not leviable on the sales in question.

The consideration of this aspect is material before issuing notice under section 92D(3), if it is to serve its purpose. The abovesaid prescribed information is gathered from the assessee through various means and at different stages of the assessment proceedings. The initial or first information relating to international transactions is gathered from the assessee in the prescribed audit report in Form 3CEB. This report is required to be submitted along with the return of income as per section 92E. [Para 22.5]

It is clear from Form 3CEB that the name and addresses of the assessee, its associated concerns, nature of relationship with such concerns, brief description of business and details of international transactions carried on with the associated enterprises, besides the method used for determining ALP in respect of each international transaction is required to be given in the audit report. [Para 24]

The Assessing Officer must have the audit report in Form 3CEB with him to determine the question whether total value of the transactions is more or less than Rs. 5 crore (now enhanced to Rs. 15 crore) to consider the question whether determination of ALP is to be referred to the TPO or not. If the total value exceeds the prescribed limit, the Assessing Officer has to refer the matter to the TPO. [Para 24.1]

It is, therefore, reasonable to presume that in every transfer pricing case, relevant information, along with Form 3CEB is available on record and the Assessing Officer/TPO is supposed to proceed with the basic and initial information of international transactions carried by the assessee in the relevant period as disclosed in Form 3CEB. He is supposed to have specialized training and, therefore, understand what job he is to perform for achieving the purpose of the Regulations. [Para 24.2]

Therefore, it is clear that information prescribed under rule 10D in different column is voluminous, alternative and it would have to be seen as to what information and from which clause, is required on the facts of the given case. Secondly, information from certain clauses of rule 10D is obtained in audit report in Form 3CEB required to be filed along with the return. Thirdly, the TPO, before proceeding to determine ALP, has above basic and initial information of international transactions carried by the assessee. [Para 24.3]

Armed with the said initial information and when knowing details of international transactions carried by the assessee and the method employed to determine the ALPs of transactions, further proceedings are carried towards determination of ALP. [Para 24.4]

Provisions of section 92D(3) can be applied in the following circumstances :

(i)

in the course of the proceedings under the Act before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals).

(ii)

Any documents or information prescribed under sub-section (1) may be required.

(iii)

information is required to be furnished under sub-section (3) within 30 days (as extended by another 30 days) from the receipt of notice issued in this regard.

Thus, the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) may require (from any person) any information or document as may be prescribed. Word 'any' information or document cannot ordinarily mean 'all' the documents prescribed under rule 10D. The word 'required' is important as it rules out option with the assessee and makes it obligatory to furnish the requisite information.

It is clear from above that the power under section 92D(3) can be used in the course of the assessment proceedings, i.e., in proceedings for determination of ALP and only for requiring to furnish prescribed information or documents under rule 10D. It being a provision connected with procedure to help an assessment, must be purposefully construed. But, regulation does not provide any time or stage when power to issue notice is to be exercised. However, scheme of assessment do indicate the stage at which it is to be issued and the purpose which is required to be achieved through the issuance of such a notice. [Para 24.6]

[Para 14]

■

When this Court has already considered the certificate dated 09.01.2013 and during the pendency of the appeal before the Tribunal for the year under consideration, the Revenue has not been able to bring any material on record or has challenged or doubted the certificate issued by the Singapore Tax Authority, as observed by the Tribunal in Para 20 of the impugned order, it has noted that the Departmental Representative has challenged the veracity of the certificate issued by the IRAS during the course of the appellate proceedings before the CIT (A) and thereafter, the Tribunal has referred to the territorial tax system of the Singapore Income Tax Act to hold that the certificate has not given any basis whatsoever as to how the assessee is deriving income from "business carried on in Singapore", when admittedly, the appellants-assessee have been operating in international waters. The Tribunal has also considered the fact that the certificate does not specify the factual basis on which the Singapore Tax Authority has concluded that the income from shipping business have been derived by the assessee from "business carried on in Singapore". Thus, in effect, the Tribunal has overreached the findings arrived at by this Court in case of M.T. Maersk Mikage v. DIT (International Taxation) (supra) in absence of any material brought on record by the Revenue before the Tribunal to show that the certificate issued by the IRAS is not reliable or cannot be considered for the income of ST Shipping to be taxed in Singapore on accrual basis. [Para 15]

■

It is also pertinent to note that from the documents placed in form of paper- book filed before the Tribunal, in fact, the ST Shipping has shown the income arising from the operations as per letter dated 09.10.2012 issued by the Deloitte and Touche LLP, Certified Public Accountants, Singapore stating that the ST Shipping has confirmed that the position adopted in the Year of Assessment 2010 to treat charter income derived by the overseas branches as Singapore sourced income and part of qualifying income under Approved International Shipping Enterprise Incentive remains unchanged in the Year of Assessment 2012. [Para 16]

■

The impugned order of the Tribunal is, therefore, contrary to the decision of this Court as the Tribunal could not have restored the matter back to the Assessing Officer only on mere suspicion and the doubts contrary to the findings arrived at by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by IRAS. The Tribunal ought not to have analysed the certificate in its order more particularly in Para 22 of the order in absence of any material on record. On perusal of Para 22 of the impugned order it is clear that the Tribunal has made the observation with regard to the language of the certificate more particularly, when this Court has accepted the part of the certificate which certified that the income earned by the ST Shipping from the operations carried out in ports at India was liable to be taxed at Singapore on accrual basis and as per Article 8 of DTAA, when the income accrues in Singapore and was taxed as such, the same would be exempt from tax in India. This Court has further clarified that reference to Article 24 of DTAA in the certificate is nothing but an opinion of the IRAS. [Para 17]

■

Hence, the Tribunal ought not to have further deliberated upon contents of the certificate which is already held to be applicable in the facts of the case in the absence of any other material on record to demonstrate that the veracity of the certificate issued by IRAS is doubtful and merely because the Tribunal is of the opinion that the language of the certificate is not conducive to the opinion of the Tribunal, the matter could not have been restored to the Assessing Officer in face of the observation made by this Court regarding the same certificate dated 09.01.2013 issued by the IRAS. [Para 18]

No. 3 of Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 and definition of 'Government Authority' given under 2(zf) of the said Notification, it is evident that if any 'pure services' are provided to a Governmental Authority by way of any activity in relation to any function entrusted to a Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution or a Panchayat under article 243G (from 13-10-2017) of the Constitution and that 'Governmental Authority' is an Authority or a Board set up by an Act of Parliament or a State legislature or established by the Government with 90 per cent or more participation by way of equity or control to carry out any function entrusted to a Municipality under article 243W of the Constitution, then the same is exempted vide Sl. No. 3 of the Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 6.1]

In the case at hand, CMWSSB is created vide The Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Act, 1978 with 100 per cent contribution by way of Government [i.e., by way of takeover of assets and liabilities from Chennai Municipal Corporation and Tamil Nadu Water Supply and Drainage Board] and controlled by the Government by way of appointing Directors of the CMWSSB to carry out the functions of supplying water for Domestic, Industrial and Commercial purposes as well as Sanitation Conservancy by way of disposal of Sewerage. TWAD is a Board constituted by an Act of Tamil Nadu State Legislature called Tamil Nadu Water Supply and Drainage Board Act, 1970 with 100 per cent contribution by way of Government and controlled by Government by way of appointing Directors of the TWAD entrusted with the development of Water Supply and Sewerage facilities in Municipalities and Panchayats in the State of Tamil Nadu, except Chennai Metropolitan Development. The Twelfth Schedule or article 243W of the Constitution list the functions of the Municipality at Sl. No. 5 as 'Water Supply for Domestic, Industrial and Commercial purposes' and at Sl. No. 6 as 'Public Health, Sanitation Conservancy and Solid Waste Management'. The Eleventh Schedule or article 243G of the Constitution list the functions of the Municipality at Sl. No. 5 as 'Water Supply for Domestic, Industrial and Commercial purposes' and at Sl. No. 6 as 'Public Health, Sanitation Conservancy and Solid Waste Management'. Thus it is clear that the Constitution list the functions of the Panchayat at Sl. No. 11 as 'Drinking Water' and at Sl. No. 23 as 'Health and Sanitation'. Thus it is clear that in respect of services received in relation to functions pertaining to Municipality, CMWSSB is a 'Governmental Authority' as defined under 2(zf) of the Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended. However, in respect of services received in relation to functions pertaining to Panchayat, TWAD is a 'Governmental Authority' only from 13-10-2017 as defined under 2(zf) of the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended. [Para 6.2]

The petitioner-firm is an SSI unit engaged in the business of manufacturing rice from paddy. The first appellate authority allowed the appeal filed by the asessee - petitioner. On appeal by the Department, the Tribunal decided the appeal in favour of the Department. When revision filed, this court granted one more opportunity to the petitioner for compounding the offence and to continue to enjoy the benefit of exemption. Accordingly petitioner sought to compound the offence and there is no grievance with regard to that part. With regard to the other issue regarding sustainability of levying tax under section 5A of the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963 a Division Bench of this court while passing verdict in a revision held that the issue therein was covered by virtue of the ruling rendered by the apex court in Peekay Re-rolling Mills (P) Ltd. The appellants manufactured certain goods falling under T.I. 68 and availed benefit of concessional assessment based on 'invoice price' under Notification 120/75-CE dt. 30.4.1975. A demand for differential duty was also raised. The Assistant Collector dropped the proceedings, but the Collector (Appeals) held that the price charged by the holding company was relevant for computing assessable value.

Exemption under Notification 28/79-C.E. for aerated waters which do not contain caffeine was denied to the petitioners, manufacturers of aerated water, on the ground that the benefit of the concessional rate of duty had not been passed on by the petitioners to the buyers/consumers. The Assistant Collector had informed the petitioner-Company that while the tariff rate for aerated waters had been raised to 60%, the effective rate for the goods was 30% ad valorem by virtue of the Notification. On perusal of the notification the Company came to the conclusion that the advice was incorrect due to an erroneous interpretation of the notification and, accordingly, submitted a revised classification list in which the effective rate was shown as 60% and exemption claimed in excess of 30% ad valorem. Challenging the finding of the authorities that the amount covered by the relief given by Notification 28/79 would go to the benefit of the manufacturers, the petitioners contended that the notification does not contain any specific provision that the exemption was not available to the manufacturers and should be passed on to the consumers. The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading 'PU Foam Products' and 'Matresses' (Coir/Foam/Spring) product from various units located across the India. The unit of assessee located at 'Kala Amb' (Himachal Pradesh) was eligible for various subsidies of Central Excise-duty and sales tax etc. and also deduction under section 80-IC in respect of profits derived from the unit.

The Assessing Officer during scrutiny proceedings observed that certain international and specified transactions were carried out by the assessee was within meaning of sections 92B and 92BA. It referred the matter to the TPO for determination of ALP of said transactions.

The TPO found the profit delcared by the section 80-IC eligible unit was exceptionally higher (30.71 per cent) as compared to other non-80-IC eligible unit and thus according to him there had been shifting of profit to 80-IC unit from non-80-IC units.

The assessee, in transfer pricing study, selected five comparables and computed their average operating margin at 2.90 per cent. The assessee further explained that the incentive provided by the Government to the unit and high-value product sold as the main reason for higher profit in case of 80-IC unit.

The TPO disputed the arm's length price of inter-unit (specified domestic) transactions with Kala Amb unit computed by the assessee and proposed a downward adjustment of Rs. 11.97 crores to the income of the assessee.

The adjustment had been computed as excess profit transferred in the ratio of the SDT expenses to the total expenses of the eligible unit.

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order included the adjustment proposed of Rs. 11.97 crores by the TPO.

Aggrieved, the assessee filed objections before the DRP. The DRP directed as under:

-

On the issue of manner of allocation of common expenses, while competing deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the eligible unit the assessee itself had allocated Rs. 9.14 crores to the eligible unit and the same amount had been taken by the TPO, hence no further directions were issued on the issue.

-

On the issue of non-allocation of finance cost, while computing deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the eligible unit, the Assessing Officer/TPO should allocate finance cost (excluding income-tax) in the ratio of sales/operative revenue of the Kala Amb unit and recompute SDT expenses considered for adjustment accordingly.

-

On the issue of impact of exemption of taxes on the profitability of Kala Amb unit, the Assessing Officer/TPO should compute the operating profit margin without considering the excise duty, sales tax and income-tax.

-

On the issue of invoices for transfer of other consumables/packing materials, the assessee had apparently transfered the materials to the 'Kala Amb' unit at a higher cost than the cost price of purchase from 3rd parties; therefore there was apparently no basis for enhancing the cost price of Kala Amb unit; however the DRP directed the Assessing Officer/TPO to examine the details submitted in this regard and give a specific finding in the final order.

Pursuant to the direction of the DRP, the Assessing Officer, computed operating profit of the eligible unit excluding excise duty and sales tax at Rs. 10.58 crores. While computing this operating profit excluding excise duty and sales-tax, the Assessing Officer allocated head office expenses of Rs. 9.14 crores. On the direction of the DRP to examine the details of price at which material was transferred to the eligible unit from other units of the assessee, the Assessing Officer/TPO perused few invoices produced by the assessee on test check basis but found the same not readable and incomplete. The TPO/Assessing Officer also observed that goods have been transferred to the eligible unit from non-eligible unit without adding any markup and thus resulted in shifting of the profit to the eligible unit and concluded that purchase made by the eligible unit from the non-eligible unit was not at arm's length and was below the prevailing market rate. In view of the conclusions drawn, the TPO /Assessing Officer computed the adjustment in final assessment order at Rs. 5.57 crore.

, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. [Para 9.9] Further, there is no express provision under the Act restricting the application of section 92C for determining the income at arm's length where such income is eligible for deduction under section 10A. On the contrary, there is a proviso to section 92C(4) which prohibits the deduction under section 10A on the income to the extent enhanced as an effect of a determination of ALP. [Para 9.10]

Thus, the proviso itself vividly reflects the intent of lawmakers that the provisions of chapter X shall prevail in all the cases of international transactions falling under the umbrella of section 92 including the income-qualified for exemption under section 10A. In other words, it can be said that the intention of the statute was very much lucid that section 92 should be invoked even when the assessee is entitled to deduction under section 10A. In the light of above perceivance, there is no need to refer to other means of interpretation if the words are clear and free from any ambiguity. However, if the words in the statute are vague and ambiguous, then external aid may be consulted for interpretation. This connotes that the statute should be read as a whole; therefore, the point which is not clear in one section may be explained in another section. [Para 9.11]

Accordingly, if the purpose or object of Chapter X and/or section 10A is being defeated, then it is up to the legislature, if they think so, to reconstruct the law as per the required object. [Para 9.12]

However, language used in section 92 is clear, unambiguous, and do not lead to any absurd meaning. Thus, there is no need to look into the intention or purpose of the statute or application of reasonable construction. Accordingly, it is meaningless to apply the principles of purposive or object-based rules of interpretation as contended by the assessee [Para 9.13]

Regarding the contentious of the assessee that budget speech & memorandum explaining the provisions, it is noted that it is also a settled legal position that headings or marginal notes do not govern a provision where the legislature has used plain and unambiguous language. It is when the language is equivocal only then, help can be taken from the circulars, marginal notes or the Finance Minister speech or memorandum explaining the provisions to interpret the provision of the Act. The Finance Minister speech and memorandum explaining the bill will not provide any aid to the assessee in the given facts & circumstances. [Para 9.15]

In the context of the CBDT Circulars bearing Nos. 12/2001 dated 23-08- 2001 and 14/2001 dated 9-11-2001, it is merely explaining the understanding of statutory provisions regarding the transfer pricing. Further, it is a well-settled principle that the departmental circulars are not binding on this court. These circulars cannot be used to usurp the power of a judicial body while exercising its jurisdiction, including interpreting the statutory provisions [Para 10]

Without prejudice to the above, if it is agreed to apply the purposive interpretation while invoking the provisions of chapter X in the given facts and circumstances, then the same interpretation should also be extended in the context of the provision of section 10A. It is because the provision of chapter X cannot be seen in isolation as the issue on hand has direct nexus with the provision of section 10A. Thus it becomes pertinent to refer to the purpose of introducing section 10A. [Para 10.1]

From the above, it is clear that the spirit behind introducing section 10A was to bring foreign exchange in India. Granting exemption from Tax under section 10A was incidental and not the main object. Furthermore, where amount fetched by the Indian AE as revenue and/or the amount paid to its counter-part, AE outside India, as expenditure is lower and higher respectively and does not correspond to an ALP, the same will adversely affect the inflow of foreign exchange in India. Perhaps this was the reason to insert the proviso in section 92C(4). Accordingly, even if the purposive interpretation is applied in respect to the provisions of chapter X along with provisions of section 10A, it could not be held that provision of chapter X should not be applied where the assessee is eligible for the benefit of section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the object of inserting section 10A in the statute will stand unaccomplished. [Para 10.2]

The assessee established a captive power plant (CPP) of 30MW capacity in the state of Andhra Pradesh that supplied power to its cement manufacturing unit (CMU) in the same state. The CPP was an eligible business as defined in section 80-IA(4) and, thus, assessee was entitled to the tax holiday specified in section 80-IA. The transfer of power from the CPP to the CMU forms a specified domestic transaction (SDT) as defined in section 92BA that came to be inserted by the Finance Act, 2012 from 1-4-2013.

During the year under consideration, CPP transferred 17.17 crore units of power to CMU and, for the purpose of computation of the aforementioned tax holiday, applied a rate of Rs. 6.29 per unit. The rate was based upon the computation of the landed cost of power purchased by the CMU from the Southern Power Distribution Company of AP Limited.

On reference, the TPO was of the opinion that differences specified in rule 10B(1)(a)(ii) have to be taken into account and that only the base cost of energy (Rs. 5.25 per unit) supplied by the Distribution company could be applied for the purpose of benchmarking and other components like ToD charges, Demand charges etc. do not apply. Accordingly, TPO, applying CUP, considered only the energy cost of Rs. 5.25 per unit in arriving at the Arms Length Price and did not take into consideration any of other components charged by the Distribution company. By doing so, the TPO was of the opinion that differences between the CPP and the Distribution company could be made comparable.

On reference, the DRP agreed with the view of the TPO.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

"The State Government has come with Circular dated 15th January, 1988 and undisputedly the tax has already been paid on the goods in transaction in question, therefore, it is necessary that the Assessing Officer is treated to have power to give waiver but for that he has to obey and observe the formalities and requirement of Circular dated 15th January, 1988 and therefore, view taken on 5th March, 1988 by the learned Tribunal is likely to be set aside. Therefore, the order dated 5th March, 1998 is set aside and the matter is relegated to the assessee to verify and obtain the required information and obtain certificate if necessary as required under Circular dated 15th January, 1988 to extend the benefit to the applicant/revisionist accordingly.'' (Para 11)

All these documents were placed before the Assessing Officer in response to queries raised by him with regard to sale of undertaking to subsidiary of the assessee. The assessee has filed the 'business transfer agreement' entered for sale of undertaking alongwith the 'valuation report' of the Govt. After calling for all these evidences and examining the entire facts brought on record, the Assessing Officer has examined the allowability of claim under section 80-IA and in fact has made part disallowance on such deduction. Hence, it cannot be held that the Assessing Officer has not conducted any enquiry or investigated the issue which he was required to do so before allowing the claim of deduction under section 80-IA or has allowed without examining the assessee's transaction with its subsidiary. One of the key allegations of the Commissioner is that the Assessing Officer should have made a reference to the TPO as per the CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003. First of all, it would be relevant to see, whether there was any such instruction issued by the CBDT to the Assessing Officer for making any reference to the TPO for specified domestic transaction. From the perusal of the said Instruction No. 3/2003, it is seen that guidelines for reference to the TPO has been made only in respect of determination of arm's length price in relation to the international transaction under section 92B. There is no whisper about specified domestic transaction for the reason that there was no concept of specified domestic transaction under the Act when said instruction was issued on 20-5-2003. The specified domestic transaction for the purpose of determination of ALP has been brought in the statute only by the Finance Act, 2012. Once there was no CBDT instruction or guidelines for reference to the issue involving specified domestic instruction to the TPO at the time of passing the assessment order, then where is the question of any non-compliance of CBDT Instruction by the Assessing Officer.

In the instant case the assessee had collected sales tax as a part of dealers’ price. At the year-end the sales tax portion, which formed the part of dealers’ price had been bifurcated and had been claimed as a capital subsidy. The State Government through the Notification No. 1179, dated 31-3-1995 had provided sales tax exemption with an objective to promote the development of certain industries which had been set-up or undertaken modernisation, diversification, backward integration by way of fixed capital investment of Rs. 50 crores or more. The exemption from sales tax or benefit of reduced rate of tax was available to those units which had started production or had carried out expansion or modernisation or backward integration, etc., between 1-12-1994 and 31-3-2000. Para 2 of the Notification specifies that the exemption or reduction in the rate of sales tax including the additional tax would not be more than 5 per cent of the sale of goods. In case where tax rate was more than 5 per cent including additional tax, the balance was to be paid by the unit. Para 7(2) of the Notification provides for the exemption of sales tax to the extent of exemption or reduction in tax. Item (2) of the Schedule includes Greater Noida Industrial Development Area wherein exemption from sales tax to the extent of 200 per cent of capital investment had been provided. None of the clauses of the notification authorised the assessee to collect the sales tax and retain the same with it. The exemption of sales tax was available from the date of first sale or the date within the period of six months from the date of production, whichever was earlier. The said notification also provided that the eligibility certificate to the assessee would be issued by the Joint/Additional Director of concerned development authority and the same would be produced before the concerned Assessing Officer. The Additional Director Industries, Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority, issued eligibility certificate to the assessee. As per this certificate fixed capital investment was of Rs. 51,57,95,446. The date of commencement of production was 9-3-1998 and the first sale was affected on 27-3-1998. The assessee applied for exemption from trade tax [sales tax]. The exemption from trade tax [sales tax] was provided from 27-3-1998 to 26-3-2013 for a period of 15 years or till the time the exemption of sales tax was availed of to the extent of 200 per cent of the fixed capital investment, i.e., Rs. 1,02,75,90,892, whichever was earlier. This certificate also provided the items, i.e., colour TVs, washing machines and air-conditioners on which exemption from sales tax was provided. Another certificate was issued on 27-9-2000 in respect of printed circuit voice for CTV number 8,12,000 and microwave oven 1,00,000. In this certificate, the sales tax exemption in the first three years had been provided to the extent of 100 per cent; for next three years at 75 per cent; for next two years at 50 per cent; and for next two years at 25 per cent. In all exemption from sales tax was provided for 10 years. [Para 9]

Neither the certificates issued by the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority nor the notification issued by the State Government authorised the assessee to collect sales tax from its customers. The assessee had been exempted from collecting the sales tax from customers on the sales made with effect from 27-3-1998. In fact, during the course of hearing, neither the notification had authorized the assessee to collect sales tax nor the assessee had collected the sales tax as such. The assessee had included the element of sales tax in the dealers’ price as a sale price of the product. From the annual audit report under the Companies Act as well as tax audit report under the Act, it was found that the auditor had taken a view that the short term capital gains arising on account of transfer of plant and machinery by assessee-company to its holding company was not to be considered as transfer within the meaning of section 45 inasmuch as the assessee’s case was covered by provision contained in section 47(v ). [Para 14] Now, the question arose as to whether view of the auditor could be considered to be a bona fide basis upon which the assessee had made a claim in the return of income that short term capital gain arising on transfer of plant and machinery to its holding company was not taxable. [Para 15]

On perusal of the provision of section 47(v ), it is clear that this section grants exemption in case of transfer of a capital asset as between holding company and wholly owned subsidiary, where the transferee is an Indian company. It provides that nothing contained in section 45 shall apply to any transfer of a capital asset by a subsidiary company to the holding company if the whole of the share capital of the subsidiary company is held by the holding company and the holding company, i.e., transferee is an Indian company. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the capital asset had been transferred by the assessee-company, being a subsidiary company, to its holding company. The share capital of the assessee-company to the extent of 99.66 per cent was held by the holding company to which the capital assets were transferred. The balance share capital to the extent of 0.36 per cent were held by the directors of holding company and their relatives. The auditor in the annual audit report had given an opinion that any loss or gain arising from the transaction of sale of fixed assets by the assessee company to its holding company would be covered by section 47(v) and as such any gain arising therefrom would not be chargeable to tax under section 45. The observation made in the annual audit report under Companies Act was at the stage at which the account were first audited under the Companies Act. The assessee had to file its return of income as per provisions contained in the Act. However, in the instant case, the tax consultant, who was also the tax auditor of the assessee-company, in its tax audit report under section 44AB, had also given an identical view that the transaction in question would be covered by section 47(v ) and, hence, short term capital gain arising on sale of plant and machinery would not be chargeable to tax under section 45. This view given by the tax consultant and the tax auditor in its report was on the basis that 99.64 per cent of the shares of assessee company were held by its holding company to which the assets were transferred and the remaining 0.36 per cent of share capital were held by directors of holding company and their relatives implying thereby that whole of the share capital of the assessee-company were being controlled or held by holding company. This opinion given by the tax auditor might not be acceptable in the light of the language used in section 47(v ) where one of the conditions provided is that whole of the share capital of the subsidiary company must be held by the holding company. In the instant case, 100 per cent share capital of the subsidiary company was not held by the holding company but the share capital was being by the holding company only to the extent of 99.64 per cent. There was not much difference between 100 per cent share capital and 99.64 per cent capital, which is held by the holding company particularly in view of the fact that the balance 0.36 per cent of share capital of assessee-company were held by the directors of holding company and their relatives. Therefore, the view taken by the tax consultant could be a plausible one taken to advance the benefit of transfer of assets by subsidiary company to holding company within the meaning of section 47(v ) read with section 45 after giving a liberal and wider meaning to section 47(v ). The assessee had acted upon the advise given by the auditor in both annual tax report prepared under Companies Act as well as tax audit prepared under Income-tax Act. It was not the case where an opinion was given only at the time of preparing the audit report under Companies Act but it was the case where the opinion was also given by the Tax consultant while preparing the return of income for the assessee. It was, thus, a case where the assessee had acted upon the advice given by the tax auditor. [Para 16]

Now, the question arose as to whether the deduction claimed by the assessee on the basis of advise of the tax consultant supported by tax audit report as well as annual audit report could said to be a false claim made by the assessee so as to attract penalty provisions contained in section 271(1)(c). [Para 17]

Provisions of section 8 of CST Act

The provisions of sub-sections (2A) and (5) of section 8 of the CST Act clearly enable the State Government to exempt the tax payable under the CST Act in public interest by issuing appropriate notification.
