Sequence of facts on record

It is not in dispute that the assessee had sold the goods in question which were manufactured by 'B' that was holding a valid exemption certificate under rule 28A. The assessee had claimed central sales tax exemption of such goods in terms of notification dated 4-9-1995 by urging that such exemption was in respect of sale of goods which were manufactured by any dealer in the State of Haryana who held a valid exemption certificate. The core controversy pertains to the interpretation of notification dated 4-9-1995 which has been issued by the competent authority in exercise of power under section 8(5) of the CST Act. [Para 13]

Notification dated 4-9-1995

The notification dated 4-9-1995 has been issued in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (5) to section 8 of the CST Act by the Governor of Haryana in public interest. As per the notification, no tax is payable under the aforesaid Act with effect from 1-4-1988 on sale of goods during the period of exemption that are manufactured in the State of Haryana by any dealer, who holds a valid exemption certificate under rule 28A. Proviso to the said notification stipulates that the dealers should have also not charged any tax under the CST Act on the sale of goods manufactured by him. [Para 14]

Sub-section (5) to section 8 begins with the non obstante clause and empowers the State Governments to issue a notification in the official gazette subject to the condition(s) as may be specified and under clause (a) direct that no tax shall be payable by any dealer having his place of business in the State in respect of sale in the course of inter-State trade or commerce, etc. and under clause (b) in respect of all sales of goods or classes of goods, etc. [Para 15]

Provisions of rule 28A of Haryana Rules

The rule 28A as per heading relates to class of industries, period and other conditions for exemption/deferment from payment of tax.

Sub-rule (1) of rule 28A makes it clear that industries are covered under this rule and the said industries would not be entitled to any deferment or exemption from payment of tax under any other provisions of these rules. The expression 'eligible industrial unit' is defined in clause (f) to sub-rule (2). Similarly 'eligibility certificate', 'exemption certificate', etc. are defined in clauses (j) and (k) to sub-rule (2). Clause (n) to sub-rule (2) defines the expression 'notional sales tax liability' and clause (ii) states that the amount of tax payable under the CST Act on sales of finished product of eligible industrial unit made in the course of inter-State trade or commerce shall be computed at the rate of tax applicable as if the sales were made against Form 'C'.

In other words, inter-State trade or commerce of finished products of eligible industrial units will be treated as notional sales tax liability. The reference in this clause is to the eligible industrial unit and sales of finished products made by the said units, which are sold in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. [Para 16]

The purport and impact of rule 28A is with reference to eligible industrial unit is not only clear from the definition clauses which define eligibility certificate, exemption certificate, etc. but also from sub-rule (4)(a) which stipulates that the benefit of tax exemption or deferment shall be given to an eligible industrial unit holding exemption or entitlement certificate for the period specified.

It cannot be held that avoidance of tax is a condition precedent for invoking the provisions of section 92C/92CA. There is no requirement of establishment of ‘tax evasion’ before initiation of proceedings for determination of ALP. [Para 17] SECTION 40A vs . CHAPTER X - The assessee contended that where any payment is made in respect of an expenditure which is excessive or unreasonable having regard to the fair market value of goods, services or facilities to the concern in which assessee has substantial interest, the disallowance is permissible under section 40A of the Act which overrides the other provisions of the Act and consequently, the provisions of section 92CA could not be invoked. Such contention of assessee was unsustainable. Section 40A has overriding effect over the provisions relating to the computation of income under the head ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’ . That means, it has overriding effect over the provisions contained in Chapter IVD, i.e. , sections 28 to 44DA only. Hence, the provisions of section 40A(2) would not and cannot override the provisions contained in Chapter X of the Act. Even otherwise, if there are different provisions over the same subject, then, in law, the specific provisions would prevail. So, even assuming that provisions of section 40A are attracted, these are the general provisions applicable to all transactions while the provisions of Chapter X are specific provisions relating to international transactions only. Therefore, the provisions of Chapter X which are more specific would apply to the instant case. [Para 19]

SECTION 10A VS. CHAPTER X - The assessee had also submitted that income of the assessee being exempt under section 10A, the over-pricing or under pricing of an international transaction would not affect the computation of income. This argument was without force in view the specific provisions contained in the first proviso to section 92C(4) which clearly state that no deduction under section 10A/10AA or section 10B or under Chapter VIA shall be allowed in respect of the amount of income by which the total income of the assessee is enhanced after computation of income under this section. [Para 20]

It is abundantly clear that the Legislature while introducing the enactment did comprehend a situation requiring investigation and addition on account of computation of ALP in the cases the assessee is entitled to benefit under section 10A/10AA or section 10B. In the light of specific provision, it is difficult to contend that ALPs cannot be determined under section 92C or 92CA where the assessee is entitled to the benefit of above sections. [Para 21]

In the light of above discussion, it was to be held that although Chapter X has title ‘Special provision relating to avoidance of tax’ and aim of various sections under Chapter X is to check avoidance of taxes, diversion of income and funds by non residents from India, it is not necessary that the Assessing Officer must demonstrate such avoidance and diversion of tax before invoking provisions of section 92C and 92CA. Consequently, it is to be held that before invoking relevant provisions there is no legal requirement under provisions contained in Chapter X that Assessing officer should prima facie demonstrate that there is tax avoidance. No importance was to be attached to the fact that the taxpayer is entitled to benefit under section 10A/10AA. [Para 22]

IV. LEGALITY OF CBDT INSTRUCTION NO.3 OF 2003, DATED 20-5-2003 As per the impugned I nstruction, the CBDT has directed all the officers of the department to refer the matter of determination of ALP to the TPO where the aggregate value of international transaction and transactions exceed Rs. 5 crores. As is clear from the circular, the idea of issuing instructions under reference is to avoid selection of small cases with international transaction less than Rs. 5 crores for scrutiny of transfer price and to avoid arbitrariness in the application of the provision. All cases where aggregate value of international transactions exceed Rs. 5 crores, are required to be referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer. The limit has now been increased to Rs. 15 crores. Having regard to the object stated in the Circular, no fault can be found nor any illegality seen in the instructions.

When the provisions of section 92CA(i) are read with Circular of the CBDT (Instruction No.3) dated 20-5-2003, it becomes ‘necessary’ for the Assessing Officer to refer the question of determination of transfer pricing of international transactions to the TPO. He has no discretion in the matter in the light of limit fixed by the CBDT. The Assessing Officer has only to look at the aggregate value of international transactions disclosed by the assessee in the audit report and then follows directions of the CBDT The Assessing Officer, therefore, is left with a very limited role under section 92CA(1). Likewise, while granting approval to the action of the Assessing Officer, the Commissioner has only to see whether aggregate value of international transaction is more than Rs. 5 crores or not. If it is more than Rs. 5 crores, he has to grant approval in the light of directions of the CBDT. These directions are mandatory and binding on the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner. The fact that directions are not binding on the assessee or the C ourts is immaterial. The relevant question to be answered is whether circulars are binding on the departmental authorities. The question has an obvious answer. [Para 44]

Therefore, there is no illegality in the directions issued by the CBDT.[Para 45]

V. ALP DETERMINED BY TPO - HOW MUCH BINDING ON ASSESSING OFFICER FOR MAKING ASSESSMENT

Section 92CA(6) would come into operation only in the cases where the Assessing Officer in the assessment order has adopted the order of the TPO. Now if subsequently, the TPO rectified his order in terms of section 92CA(5), the Assessing Officer is duty-bound to pass an order in conformity with order of the TPO. Otherwise it can lead to anomaly and, therefore, it is provided that where the TPO’s order is amended to rectify a mistake apparent from record, the Assessing Officer must also rectify assessment order in conformity with above order. The TPO’s order under sub-section (3) of section 92CA cannot be treated as final and binding on the Assessing Officer. It does not mean that the order of the TPO is of no value or consequence. The words ‘having regard to’ convey definite meaning and are strong enough to enjoin upon the Assessing Officer a duty to pass order and adopt transfer pricing as determined by the TPO, unless there are very good grounds to modify or alter the transfer pricing ordered by the TPO. Only after recording reasons, the Assessing Officer can take transfer pricing other than one determined by the TPO. There may be cases in which the assessee after ALP is determined by the TPO and before his order is made the basis of assessment, may get such authentic material to show that transfer pricing determined by the TPO is not correct or should not be blindly adopted without modifying it. However, where the Assessing Officer has adopted the orders of the TPO and computed assessments accordingly, there is no illegality in the procedure followed by the Assessing Officer. [Para 51]

There is nothing to suggest that the TPO’s report on transfer pricing is conclusive and debars the Assessing Officer from looking at any other material. The aforesaid conclusion is also in line with latest change made in section 92CA by the Legislature through the Finance Act, 2007. [Para 52]

■

The provisions of section 92CD(1) are unambiguous and even if a return has been filed prior to an assessee entering into an APA, he is entitled to furnish a modified return declaring his income in accordance with the terms of the APA. Subject to certain exceptions, the APA is binding both on the assessee and the revenue. [Para 19]

■ It is clear that the scheme of providing for an APA is to remove any uncertainty as to the determination of an income of an assessee engaged in international transactions with associated enterprises. The assessee is required to declare his income in accordance with the APA. Except in certain cases, where there is a change in law and facts or the agreement is occasioned by fraud or misrepresentation, the APA would be binding. Sub-sections (5), (6) and (7) of section 92CC provide for the same in unambiguous terms. [Para 20]

■

It is apparent from a plain reading of sub-section (4) of section 92C that the same is inapplicable. The said sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to compute the total income, having regard to the ALP determined by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (3) of section 92C. [Para 22]

■

Sub-section (3) of section 92C provides that the Assessing Officer can proceed to determine the ALP only in cases he is of the opinion on the basis of material that (a) the price charged or paid in international transaction, has not been determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 92C; or (b) that information and documentation relating to the international transaction has not been maintained as mandatorily required; or (c) that the information or data for computing the ALP is unreliable; or there is failure on the part of the assessee to furnish any information or document required to be furnished along with the notice. [Para 23]

■

It is apparent that in a case where the assessee voluntarily computes the ALP pursuant to an APA entered into with CBDT, none of the conditions as set out in sub-section (3) of section 92C are attracted. It follows that sub-section (4) of section 92C is not attracted. [Para 24]

■

More importantly, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C also clearly states that no deduction under section 10A or 10AA or 10B or under Chapter VI-A would be allowed in respect of the amount of income by which the total income of the assessee is enhanced after computation under the said section. Thus in a case where the assessee voluntarily declares his income based on the ALP determined on the basis of an APA, there would be no occasion for the Assessing Officer to enhance the income of the assessee. [Para 25]

■

Absent any enhancement of income, the proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is clearly inapplicable. [Para 26]

■

It is also necessary to bear in mind that in terms of section 10AA(1), the profits and gains of an enterprise, as referred to in clause (j) of section 2 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, from an eligible unit, which is derived from export of articles or things are exempt. [Para 27]

■

The ALP is imputed to transactions to determine the profits and gains that are derived by the assessee from any international transactions (or specified domestic transactions) in order to assess the real income of the assessee after eliminating any bias or element of transfer of profits. [Para 28]

■

Thus, indisputably, the income computed on the basis of ALP would provide a measure of the profits or income derived by the activities carried on by an assessee. The proviso to section 92C(4) essentially limits exemption under section 10AA in cases where the income computed is enhanced by the Assessing Officer under section 92C. [Para 29]

■

It is also relevant to refer to the CBDT Circular No.14/2006. [Para 30]

■

The said circular also amply clarifies that the first proviso to sub-section (4) of section 92C is applicable where the total income of the assessee as computed by the Assessing Officer is "higher than the income declared by the assessee". [Para 31]

■

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer has not enhanced the income declared by the assessee. The assessee had voluntarily factored in the ALP pursuant to the APA entered into with the CBDT, for computing the income as declared in its returns. [Para 32]

■

In view of the above, there is no infirmity in the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal in rejecting the revenue's contention that exemption under section 10AA of Chapter VI-A, is not available in respect of declared income of the assessee insofar as it relates to the TP adjustments made pursuant to the APA. [Para 34]

Asstt. CIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278 / [2023] 291 Taxman 11 / [2022] 449 ITR 1 (SC) clarifies that institutions such as the respondent, which claim GPU status, need to be scrutinised more closely and such activities are in the nature of service "in relation to" trade, commerce or business. [Para 7]

■ The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Asstt. CIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278 /[2023] 291 Taxman 11 /[2022] 449 ITR 1 (SC), under the Chapter 'Summation of Conclusion,' has held as below: "D. Trade promotion bodies Bodies involved in trade promotion (such as AEPC), or set up with the objects of purely advocating for, coordinating and assisting trading organisations, can be said to be involved in advancement of objects of general public utility. However, if such organisations provide additional services such as courses meant to skill personnel, providing private rental spaces in fairs or trade shows, consulting services, etc. then income or receipts from such activities, would be business or commercial in nature. In that event, the claim for tax exemption would have to be again subjected to the rigours of the proviso to Section 2(15) of the IT Act. H. Application of interpretation At the cost of repetition, it may be noted that the conclusions arrived at by way of this judgment, neither precludes any of the assessees (whether statutory, or non-statutory) advancing objects of general public utility, from claiming exemption, nor the Taxing Authorities from denying exemption, in the future, if the receipts of the relevant year exceed the quantitative limit. The assessing authorities must on a yearly basis, scrutinise the record to discern whether the nature of the assessee's activities amount to "trade, commerce or business" based on its receipts and income (i.e. whether the amounts charged are on cost-basis, or significantly higher). If it is found that they are in the nature of "trade, commerce or business", then it must be examined whether the quantified limit (as amended from time to time) in the proviso to Section 2(15), has been breached, thus disentitling them to exemption." [Para 8]

■

On cumulative reading of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, which now governs the field, Court is of the view that the case of the respondent has to be examined in the light of Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority (supra). [Para 9]

■

Hence, Directorate of Income Tax (Exemption), Chennai, is directed to re-examine the case of the respondent afresh and pass orders within a period of three months, following the dictum laid by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority (supra). [Para 10]

■

Accordingly, the Tax Case Appeal is disposed of. There shall be no order as to costs. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 92C,  read with section 92CA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustment - General) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether where in transfer pricing proceedings, Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to TP report filed by assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished, impugned addition made to assessee's ALP merely on basis of proposal made by TPO was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 54][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Where in transfer pricing proceedings, Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to TP report filed by assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished, impugned addition made to assessee's ALP merely on basis of proposal made by TPO was not sustainable  IT/ILT : Overseas taxes paid by assessee abroad were not eligible for relief under section 90

FACT: During relevant year, the Assessing Officer made certain addition on account of transfer pricing adjustments in relation to international transactions entered into by assessee with its AE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted said addition.

In appellate proceedings, invoking the provisions of rule 27 of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 the assessee sought to support the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) by raising a plea that under section 92C or 92CA, it was the statutory duty of the Assessing Officer to decide independently, whether the determination of arm's length price by the assessee should be accepted, or whether or not after applying the provisions of section 92CA, the transfer pricing adjustment should be made.

It was further submitted that in the present case, in compliance of the CBDT Instruction No. 3 of 2003, dated 20-5-2003 the Assessing Officer did not himself examine the issue of transfer pricing and with the approval of the Commissioner (Appeals), made a reference to the TPO under section 92CA(1). The Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply their minds to the transfer pricing report, or to any other material or information or document. The TPO made an adjustment which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order. On their part, the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) did not discharge necessary judicial functions conferred upon them under section 92C or 92CA.

HELD: The assessee's support to the impugned order on both counts is found to be correct. The Assessing Officer erred in not himself examining the issue of transfer pricing and with the approval of the Commissioner, made a reference to the TPO under section 92CA(1); that the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to the TP report filed by the assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished. The TPO made an adjustment which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order. Thereby, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) did not discharge necessary respective judicial functions conferred on them under sections 92C and 92CA.

Further, the assessee is also correct in contending that no TP adjustment can be made in a case like the present one, where the assessee enjoys benefit under section 10A or 80HHE, or where the tax rate in the country of the associated enterprises is higher than the rate of tax in India and where the establishment of tax avoidance or manipulation of prices or establishment of shifting of profits is not possible. [Para 54]

On the basis of the above reasons, accepting the pleas raised by the assessee to support the order of Commissioner (Appeals) order, without going into the merits of this ground, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 55]

purchase & order handling services and sales services under the CCA and hence, the DRP confirmed the action of the TPO in determining the arm's length price of the said services at NIL value. It is pertinent to note that the aforesaid actions of the DRP and the TPO go against the basic tenet of the Indian Transfer Pricing Laws and violate the provision of sub-section (3) of section 92CA read with sub-section (3) of section 92C. In the assessee's case under consideration, the TPO/Assessing Officer has not selected any method (out of six methods), therefore, the arm's length price (ALP) computed by the Assessing Officer/TPO is not in accordance with the provisions of section 92C (1), hence the TPO/Assessing Officer should delete the addition. [Para 32]

Now, addressing the issue relating to 'benefit test'. The revenue alleged that the assessee had failed to satisfy the 'benefit test' in respect of payments made by the assessee under the CCA (Agreement) for receiving purchase services, order handling services and sales services. The assessee has submitted before the TPO, the detailed nature of the aforesaid services and copies of documentary evidences of receipt of services on sample basis. The assessee submitted, a brief chart to prove the benefit test. This chart explains the nature of services, main functions, and documentary evidences for receipt of services along with paper book reference. This chart also explains the relevant para of the Cost Contribution Agreement (CCA). The assessee received the purchase & order handling services and sales services and documented them properly. The assessee also submitted the certificate issued by PWC Austria, about the costs allocated to AT&S India Pvt. Ltd. The copies of 78 chains of e-mail, job description sheets of 10 individual employees of the CCA team, evaluation reports of 6 global customers and flow chart of quotation processing services prove that assessee has received benefit from these services. The revenue has not disputed that these services have not been received by the assessee, he disputed only the 'benefit test', that assessee did not get the benefit out of these services. Assessee has proved that he had received the benefit from these services, by way of submitting a brief chart containing the services obtained. Therefore, the assessee has satisfied the 'benefit test', and for that rendering of intra group services by AE and payment made thereon were in the nature of third party, which would willing to pay. [Para 33]

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1), has not made any adverse comment under section 37 in respect of the services received under the CCA, for purchase services, order handling services and sales services. During the course of scrutiny assessment proceedings, the assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer the same evidences of receipt of purchase services, order handling services and sales services as those submitted to the TPO, as per the direction of the Assessing Officer. It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer, after examining the aforesaid details, did not make any adverse comment under section 37. As per the provision of sub-section (1) of section 37, the Assessing Officer is authorized to examine whether an expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) is incurred by an assessee wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business in the matter of computation of the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

In the assessee's case under consideration, the Assessing Officer has not disallowed the benefit of services received by the assessee under the Cost Contribution Agreement. The authority of the TPO would be to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price ('ALP') and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which the assessee benefits. That exercise of actual verification would be left to the Assessing Officer under section 37. The Assessing Officer could, therefore, determine under section 37 that the expenditure claimed was not for the benefit of the business, and thus, disallow that amount, this does not restrict or in any way bypass the functions of the TPO. The jurisdiction of the TPO is specific and limited i.e. to determine the arm's length price of an international transaction in terms of Chapter X read with rules 10A to 10E of the Income-tax Rules. Therefore, the assessee has derived benefits from these services as per CCA agreement and hence the arguments advanced by the revenue is not acceptable. [Para 34]

HEADNOTE: Section 65 (83) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered accountant’s services - Assessee was a practising chartered accountant - Revenue levied service tax on certification service provided by assessee holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 - Whether since certification follows transfer pricing audit, certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ - Held, yes - Whether, since verification of books of account precedes issue of certificate and such verification would fall within scope of ‘Accounting and auditing’, it could not be said that assessee was not rendering auditing service liable to tax and, therefore, impugned order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 3] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998

FACT: The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

HELD: The certification relating to computation of income from international transactions is in accordance with the provisions of section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 10E of Income-tax Rules. [Para 2]

The certification follows transfer pricing audit. Therefore, the certification in question would clearly fall under ‘Audit/certification services’ even as per the clarification, dated 7-10-1998, issued by the Ministry of Finance. The verification of the books of account precedes issue of a certificate and such verification will fall within the scope of ‘Accounting & auditing’ function. Therefore, it could not be said that what the assessee was rendering was not ‘auditing service’ liable to service tax. Accordingly, the impugned order was to be upheld and the appeal was to be rejected. [Para 3]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the activity of business process outsourcing (BPO) services in the field related to accounting & taxation such as book-keeping, VAT returns, payroll, management accounting, and audit. The assessee was providing these services to the firm, namely DC, which was an AE of the assessee. The assessee provided these services from the unit which was an STPI unit eligible for deduction/exemption under section 10A. The assessee benchmarked its transaction with AE by applying internal CUP method prescribed under section 92C and claimed that its transactions with the AE were at arm length price. However, the TPO opined that TNMM was the most appropriate method.

The assessee carried the matter to DRP and vehemently objected the rejection of CUP method and selection of TNM method as most appropriate method, comparable selected by the TPO and comparable rejected by the TPO as suggested by the assessee. The assessee also propositioned that it was enjoying the benefit of deduction under section 10A. Therefore, there was no reason to charge a lower price from the AE. Moreover, given the circumstances of the case, the effective tax rate in the UK would be higher than the effective tax rate in India, which as a result of section 10A was 0 per cent. As such, there was no motive and incentive in shifting the profits from India to the UK, where the rate of tax was comparatively higher. However, DRP rejected the contention of the assessee.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is cardinal rule of interpretation that where the language used by the legislature is clear and unambiguous then plain and natural meaning of those words should be applied to the language and resort to any rule of interpretation to unfold intentions is permissible where the language is ambiguous. [Para 9]

Now, the controversy in the instant case is disguised in the question as to whether the provisions of chapter X shall be invoked in a situation where the assessee is enjoying tax exemption under section 10A and/or where there is no motive to avoid tax. The purpose of enacting transfer pricing provisions was to put a stop to the avoidance of tax by shifting taxable income outside India. Similarly, extending the fundamental of intendment to section 10A it is comprehended that this particular section is purported to boost the business of those undertakings which are situated in free trade zones (FTZ) and engaged in export of article or things or computer software services etc. by exempting their income from levy of tax. Thus, here the question arises as to whether the transfer pricing provisions can be invoked concerning the international transaction carried out by the assessee with its AE where the former is enjoying exemption under section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the assessee might not have any motive to shift the income from India to a foreign country as the same has already been exempted under section 10A [Para 9.8]

In this connection, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable. Before going into the impact of the rescission of the exemption notification, one should first understand the statutory charge of service tax on the practising chartered accountants, as given in Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994,—

(a) Meaning of practising chartered accountant [Section 65(83)] : Practising chartered accountant means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

(b) Taxable service [Section 65(105 )(s)] : Taxable service means any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity, in any manner.

Position before withdrawal of exemption notification

2. Before rescission of the service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, i.e., upto February 28, 2006, all services, except those mentioned below, provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA were exempt from service tax—

(a)accounting and auditing; or

(b)cost accounting and cost auditing; or

(c)secretarial auditing; or

(d)verification of declarations in prescribed forms of compliances for obtaining a certificate of commencement of business or commencement of other business under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(e)signing of the annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(f)certification that requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, 1956 have been complied with as regards statutory guidelines for appointment of managerial personnel and payment of managerial remuneration to them without the approval of the Central Government under section 269 and Schedule XIII, of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(g)certification of documents to be filed by companies with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956; or

(h)certification in Form No. 1 that the whole of the amount remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a period of three years from the date of transfer to the special account under section 205(1)/(2) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been transferred to the General Revenue Account of the Central Government under the Companies Unpaid Dividend (Transfer to General Revenue Account of the Central Government) Rules, 1978; or

(i)certification of documents under the Exports and Imports Policy of the Government of India; or

(j)certification for exchange control purposes which a practising chartered accountant can issue as documentary evidence in support of certain applications under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973; or

(k)certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957.

Thus, in case any practising CA/CS/ICWA was rendering any service other than (a) to (k ) enumerated above, like legal or taxation consultancy service, etc., he wasn’t liable for service tax.

However, any service provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, which fell under the ambit of any other taxable service, was liable to service tax under the category of that other taxable service. For example, if a chartered accountant also provided manpower recruitment services to his clients, then he was liable to service tax on such services under the category of manpower recruitment service.

Reasons behind issuance of earlier exemption notification

3. The said exemption notification was issued on the principles of equity. The then Government had recognized the fact that the—

(i)practising CA/CS/ICWAs were providing services like legal consultancy, etc., which were equally being provided by other professionals like advocates and legal practitioners and, therefore,

(ii)levy of service tax on such services provided by practising CA/CS/ICWAs and non-levy of service tax on the same services provided by advocates and legal practitioners would be inequitable levy.

Having recognized the abovesaid facts the aforesaid exemption notification was issued to prevent the levy of service tax from being unjust and inequitable.

Position after withdrawal of exemption notification

4. After the withdrawal of the aforesaid exemption notification by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, i.e., with effect from March 1, 2006 all the services provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, in his professional capacity, are chargeable to service tax.

What are the matters not covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

As per ICAI's views, scope of audit u/s 92E does not cover matters as under: Form No. 3CEB

What are the matters required to be stated by the auditor in Form No. 3CEB?

Form No. 3CEB requires the auditor to state:

(a) that he has examined all accounts and records relating to international transactions entered into by the assessee during the relevant previous year. [Para 1 of Form No. 3CEB]

(b) that proper information and documents as are prescribed have been kept by the assessee in respect of international transactions entered into. [Para 2 of Form No. 3CEB]

(c) that the particulars required to be furnished under section 92E are given in the Annexure to the form and these particulars are true and correct. [Para 3 of Form No. 3CEB]

The words "true and correct" emphasize factual accuracy of the information given in the Annexure to Form No. 3CEB (Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing)

What are the matters required to be given in Annexure to Form No. 3CEB?

The Annexure to Form No. 3CEB are divided into 2 parts - Part A containing clauses 1 to 6 which are dealing with routine information about the assessee. Part B containing clauses 7 to 13 require list of associated enterprises and details about various international transactions.

According to the Guidance Note on Transfer pricing, the following points should be kept in mind :

♦ Obtain an authenticated statement of particulars to be given in Form No. 3CEB from the assessee.

♦ If any item is covered by more than one of the clauses in the Annexure, the auditor should make a suitable cross references to such items at appropriate places.

♦ If there is difference of opinion between the auditor and the assessee, both points of view should be stated with the relevant information. This will enable the tax authority to take a decision in the matter.

♦ If a particular clause in the Annexure is not applicable, the auditor should state 'N.A.' or 'Not Applicable' against the relevant item.

♦ Particulars should be examined and furnished in accordance with the law in force during the relevant previous year even though form of report may not have been amended to bring it in conformity with amended Income-tax Act.

♦ The Annexure should be signed by the auditor after completing his procedures on the information contained in it.

What are the points to be kept in mind by auditor regarding Para 1 of Form No. 3CEB?

Para 1 requires that auditor to affirm that he has examined the accounts and records of assessee relating to the international transactions entered into by the assessee during the previous year ending on 31st March. The auditor is required to examine only records relating to international transactions. The auditor should:

♦ Obtain from the assessee a complete list of both financial and non-financial accounts and records maintained. From this list, identify and call for the records required for his examination.

♦ Obtain a management representation as to the completeness of 'accounts and records'.

♦ If the auditor under section 92E is not the statutory auditor, he should:

1. Clearly state in his report that figures from general purpose audited financial statements have been used and relied upon.

2. Give in report a reconciliation between the figures given in his report and the figures shown in the general purpose financial statements.

3. State that he has relied upon the work done by the statutory auditors.

4. Keep in mind SA 600(Revised)Using the Work of Another Auditor.

♦ Use his professional skill and expertise and apply such tests as required in the circumstances.

♦ Apply appropriate sampling techniques if internal controls are strong.

♦ Keep in view the concept of 'materiality' is relevant in audit under section 92E.

♦ Conduct audit as per Standards on Auditing(SAs) as well as guidance notes issued by ICAI.

♦ Ensuring completeness of the list of international transactions is assessee's and not auditor's responsibility.

♦ Use his professional skill and expertise and apply such tests as required by circumstances to ensure whether the register/list of international transactions meets the requirements of law.

♦ Obtain a management representation from the assessee containing the following particulars regarding each associated enterprise with whom the assessee has entered into international transactions

(i) name

(ii) address

(iii) legal status

(iv) country of residence

(v) linkages among various associated enterprises

INTRODUCTION 1. The presence of multi-national enterprises in India and their ability to allocate profits in different jurisdictions by controlling prices in intra-group transactions made the issue of ‘transfer pricing’ a matter of serious concern, as it led to tax avoidance under the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’). INCOME-TAX ACT-AMENDMENT OF 2. The Act was, consequently, amended by the Finance Act, 2001. The earlier section 92 was substituted by sections 92 to 92F with effect from April 1, 2002. These provisions are in Chapter X, titled ‘Special provisions relating to avoidance of tax’. The sub-heading read ‘Computation of income from international transaction having regard to arm’s length price’. These provisions spelt out a detailed scheme for computing the Arm’s Length Price (ALP) of international transactions. The Finance Act, 2002, inserted with effect from June 1, 2002, section 92CA, titled ‘Reference to Transfer Pricing Officer’, thereby enabling the Assessing Officer, where he ‘considers it necessary or expedient so to do’, with the previous approval of the Commissioner, to refer to the TPO the computation of the ALP in relation to an international transaction entered into by an assessee in any previous year. |

The assessee had established two captive electricity and steam generation units for the generation of electricity and steam. The assessee had sought exemption under section 80-IA(4)(iv) in respect of Co-generation Unit 1, specifically for the supply of electricity and steam to its non-specified unit, the Paper Unit.

■

The assessee had adopted the Transaction Net Margin Method (TNMM) for determining the arm''s length price for the transfer of power from the specified Co-generation Unit-1 to the non-specified Paper Unit and the sale value of the power had been determined by the assessee at Rs. 41.21 crores, based on a rate of Rs. 6.73 per KWH for a total of 61.24 crores units of power.

■

The Assessing Officer adopted a rate of Rs. 3.875 per unit (KVAH), instead of the assessee’s applied rate of Rs. 6.73 per unit (KWH). The Assessing Officer derived this rate by averaging the adjusted rate of Rs. 4.74 per unit (after making adjustments from Rs. 4.74 per unit) from PSPCL and the rate of Rs. 3.01 per unit from the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX). Consequently, the Assessing Officer computed a difference in the sale price of power and made an addition of Rs. 17.48 crores.

■

On appeal, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer''s approach was inconsistent with the provisions of section 92C(1), read with rule 10B, and section 80-IA(8), which govern the determination of arm''s length price and transfer pricing adjustments.The rate of 76.73 per KWH adopted by the assessee for the transfer of power was lower than the comparable rate for generating electricity from biomass fuel, as available in the public domain and the rate adopted by the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) of Rs. 5.98 per unit of PSPCL(Power Corporation) for deriving average was not justified, as the assessee was categorized as a power-intensive unit, and not under the general category.TPO wrongly deducted distribution loss, transmission loss, and cross-subsidy from the rate, leading to an incorrect revised adjusted sale rate of Rs. 4.74 per KVAH per unit for power supplied by PSPCL and the TPO failed to apply the appropriate division factor of 0.92 to convert KVAH into KWH. The price at which surplus power was supplied by producers to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) is determined by state regulations and contracts and, therefore, cannot be considered the market value for the purposes of Section 80-IA(8).

FAQs on Transfer Pricing Audit

SRINIVASAN ANAND G.

CA

Who is primarily responsible to furnish information in Form No. 3CEB - Taxpayer or the auditor?

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill,2012 clarifies that "If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under section 92E then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction so as to make a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer." Thus, from the Explanatory Memorandum, it is clear that it is the primary responsibility of an asssessee to furnish correct and complete details of all international transactions/SDTs undertaken by him during the year.

Who can be appointed for conduct the audit envisaged under section 92E

Who is eligible to be the auditor u/s 92E?

According to section 92E, the report should be an 'accountant'. Section 92F(i) defines 'accountant' has having the same meaning as in Explanation below section 288(2). According to the above mentioned explanation, it covers a CA and Restricted State auditor.

According to ICAI's 'Guidance Note on Report on International Transactions under section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Transfer Pricing)' hereinafter referred to as "Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing" :

♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

♦ Ascertaining and reporting whether the assessee has maintained proper information and documentations prescribed in respect of international transactions entered into by him.

(vi)Certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets under wealth tax.

Following services provided by practising CA/CS/CWA were not taxable up to 28-2-2006, as these were not covered under any other head of taxable service - (a)Services regarding legal or taxation consultancy (b) Fees for appearing before taxation authorities (c) Fees for issuing non-statutory certificates (d) Accounts writing (and not ‘accounting’).

1.3 Withdrawal of exemption - The Notification No. 59/1998-ST dated 16-10-1998 was withdrawn w.e.f. 1-3-2006 and hence service tax was payable w.e.f. 1-3-2006 on all services (statutory as well as non-statutory) provided in the professional capacity. This created discrimination.

Many representations were made to Government by ICAI, ICWAI, ICSI and other bodies. Writ petitions were filed by many practising members in their personal capacity.

It was urged that there should be level playing field between practising CA/CS/CWA and other professionals.

Partial relief to professionals

2. Finally, partial relief has been granted to practising professionals. Services relating to representing clients before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law have been exempted vide Notification No. 25/2006-ST dated 13-7-2006. There is no exemption for such services provided during the period 1-3-2006 to 12-7-2006.

The term ‘statutory authority’ should cover the following -

(a)Income-tax Officers, Central Excise Officers and Sales-tax Officers when they are adjudicating an issue or hearing an appeal.

(b)Registrar of Companies, Regional Director in Ministry of Company Affairs, Registrar of [Cooperative Societies etc. only when they are adjudicating an issue.

(c)Other statutory authorities like Municipal Corporations etc. when some adjudication or appeal is there.

(d)Adjudication by SEBI Authorities under SEBI Act.

(e)Tribunals like ITAT, CESTAT, CLB, CAT, SAT etc.

2.1 No relief in case of other non-statutory services - Admittedly, Government has realised that there was discrimination and some relief has been given. However, the relief is partial.

There is no relief in case of other non-statutory services like tax consultation, preparation and filing of tax returns, accounts writing work and issuing non-statutory certificates.

There is also no relief in case of other services like appearing before various authorities for permissions, clearances, licenses etc. where there is no legal proceeding is pending.

All these services (except probably non-statutory certificates) can be issued even by professionals other than practising CA/CWA/CS. Hence, these services should also be exempt, to ensure level playing field.

2.2 Hope for complete and retrospective relief - It is hoped that full relief will be given and status quo ante shall be fully restored.

It is also hoped that relief will be granted at least for the period 1-4-2006 to 12-7-2006. It is true that an exemption notification cannot be issued with retros-pective effect but retrospective exemption can be given by Parliament which has plenary powers.

If retrospective amendments can be made to nullify effects of judgments of Supreme Court and High Courts, there is no reason why retrospective amendment cannot be made for granting relief to practising CA/CS/CWA who were and are facing discriminatory treatment.

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Nor is the tax auditor required to examine or report whether the assessee has maintained proper records as required by Rule 10D regarding international transactions. Nor is he required to examine whether the Arm's Length Price has been determined for international transactions in accordance with any of the recognised methods specified in Section 92F. That is the subject of the audit to be carried out under Section 92E, and the report is to be furnished in Form No. 3CEB.

The tax auditor must report in this clause only if a primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1). If no primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1), the tax auditor has no duty to report. The tax auditor is not even required to report if the primary TP adjustment has not been made as per the APA entered into by the assessee. If primary TP adjustment has been made according to the APA, then the reporting obligation under this Clause is triggered.

This clause also does not deal with Thin Cap adjustments under Section 94B. That is the subject matter of Clause 30B.

This Clause also does not deal with the issue of shares at a premium to non-resident investors by a closely held company that attracts Section 56(2)(vii). That is the subject matter of Clause 29A.

Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. Nevertheless, the tax auditor may find it useful to examine if any of the non-price terms and conditions of international transactions are not at arm's length from the angle of Clause 30C.

HEADNOTE: Section  92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing -  Computation of Arm’s length price (Adjustments - Deletion of) - Assessment year  2021-22 - Assessee-company was engaged in trading of spices, oil seeds, seeds, coffee, tea, dry fruits etc. - It had entered into international transaction with its Associated Enterprises (AEs) - TPO made certain adjustments to assessee's income - Assessee contended that solitary ground on basis of which TPO had discarded TP study of assessee was that segments filed by assessee were not audited - It was noted that TPO had discarded certificate of auditor in a summary manner - Whether even if, conclusion of TPO in arriving at PLI was taken into consideration, same was within tolerance limit of +/- 1 per cent - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no adjustment was called for in this case and adjustments made by TPO were to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of trading of spices, oil seeds, seeds, coffee, tea, dry fruits etc. It entered into international transaction with its associated enterprises (AEs) and third parties.

■

The Assessing Officer made reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) for computing the arm's length price (ALP) of the international transaction entered into by the assessee with its AE. The TPO made certain adjustments.

■

The assessee filed objections before the Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) and assailed the draft assessment order of the Assessing Officer. The DRP gave certain directions and then the TPO passed the fresh TP order.

■

It was pertinent to note here that in the fresh TP order, the adjustments were revised to the tune of Rs. 1.64 crores, after the directions of the DRP. Then, the Assessing Officer passed the final assessment order and framed the assessment.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

In this case, the solitary ground on the basis of which the TPO has discarded the TP study of the assessee is that the segments filed by the assessee were not audited. The TPO has discarded the certificate of the auditor in a summary manner. Further, even if the conclusion of the TPO in arriving the PLI is to be accepted, then also the same is within the +/-1 per cent tolerance limit. Therefore, no adjustment is called for in this case and the adjustments made by the TPO are hereby deleted. [Para 9]

■

Further, the assessee has rightly relied upon the order of the Co-ordinate Bench of the Madras Tribunal in the case of Honeywell Electrical Devices & Systems India Ltd., wherein, it has been held that filing of audited segments is not necessary, if the accounts are audited and the figures mentioned therein are not disturbed by the TPO. Respectfully, following the decision of the Co-ordinate Bench, the opinion of TPO with respect to filing of audited segments results is not correct. [Para 10]

■

In the result, the appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 11]

10. In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

IS IT NECESSARY THAT TAX AUDIT UNDER SECTION 92E SHALL BE A CA IN FULL-TIME PRACTICE?

11. Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

IN CASE OF COMPANIES, IS IT NECESSARY THAT AUDIT UNDER SECTION 92E BE CONDUCTED BY STATUTORY AUDITOR?

12. No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

WHETHER A CA OR FIRM OF CAs APPOINTED AS TAX CONSULTANTS CAN CONDUCT AUDIT UNDER SECTION 92E?

13.A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as tax auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

CAN A CA OR CA FIRM WHO IS INTERNAL AUDITOR OF ASSESSEE CAN ALSO BE AUDITOR U/S 92E?

14. No.Internal auditor cannot give audit report under section 92E.

IS THERE ANY LIMIT ON THE NUMBER OF AUDITS UNDER SECTION 92E WHICH A CA/CA FIRM CAN ACCEPT?

15. No. There is no limit on number of audits under section 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

IS THERE ANY MINIMUM FEE TO BE CHARGED BY CA FIRMS FOR TAX AUDITS?

16. No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

YOGENDRA BANGAR*

Withdrawal of Service Tax Exemption to Practising Chartered Accountants - An unjust move by Government!

Exemption granted to certain services provided by CAs, CSs and ICWAs, by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 stands withdrawn by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006. Is this withdrawal unjust and unjustifiable? Is it discriminatory? How damaging is it to the practice of CAs, etc.? The author here examines the issues from legal as well as moral angle. The abrupt move on the part of the Government is going to create a feeling of insecurity among the professional affected and cause harm to the healthy growth of their profession. Applying the logic of the Kerala High Court decision in Malappuram District Parallel College Association v. Union of India [2006] 150 Taxman 624, wherein levy of service tax on parallel colleges was held to be discriminatory, the author feels that the withdrawal of exemption to CAs/CSs/ICWAs may not pass the test of constitutionality.

Introduction

1. Chartered accountants, being professionally qualified and proficiently trained, are providing most valuable services to the people of this nation and abroad in the matters pertaining to accountancy, audit, management and technical consultancy and consultancy in the matters pertaining to various State as well Central laws. Their professional attitude and devotion are earning name and fame for the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and also for other fellow chartered accountants. Now, the chartered accountants are equally competing with the legal practitioners in the field of State and Central legislations as well as with the advocates and owing to varied experience and vast potential of the chartered accountants, the people are preferring to avail the services of the chartered accountants in place of other practitioners engaged in the similar fields. The facts aforesaid are widely accepted ones, which need no evidence.

Is it wrong for a person providing valuable services to the society and the Government to expect equitable treatment from the Government? If the answer to this question is ‘Yes’, then, what the Government has done by issuing Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants is just and all right. But if the readers answer this question as ‘No’, then, one should read the succeeding paras of this article to know how the move of the Government in issuance of Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants has turned out to be unjust and devastating for the practising chartered accountants.

The same is the case with the professionals engaged in practice in the field of company secretaryship and cost accountancy. The exemption from service tax provided to practicing company secretaries and practising cost accountants has also been withdrawn by the aforesaid notification.

The service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable.

This clarification seems to be heartening for these professionals so far. But this was not the end. By Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated October 16, 1998 [G.S.R. 624(E), dated October 16, 1998] has been withdrawn. Scope of services taxable

2. The question now for consideration is that, what is the scope of services taxable under these services and also whether the services provided by these professionals can be covered under any other category? According to section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, ‘taxable service’ in this context means any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a practising chartered accountant/practising cost accountant/practising company secretary in his professional capacity, in any manner. The words professional capacity are very confusing and may be very controversial. If these words were not there in this definition, then all the services provided by these practising professionals would have been taxable. But due to presence of these words there is going to be a dispute.

There can be two aspects of this situation :

u First, whatever can be provided only by these practising professionals can be called as provided in professional capacity and all other services are not covered under these services. For example, certain statutory audit can be done only by these professionals, so the same is covered under these services. But accounting work can be done even by the non-practising professionals, so the same is not covered under these services. This interpretation also seems to be in accordance with this definition, otherwise the words ‘professional capacity’ had not been used.

5.10 Proceedings before TPO for determination of Arm's Length Price in respect of specified domestic transactions [Section 92CA]

5.10-1 Pre-amended provisions

Section 92CA of the Act provides that the Assessing Officer, if he considers it necessary or expedient to do so, may, with the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner, refer the mat-ter of determination of Arm's Length Price (ALP) in respect of an international transaction or Specified Domestic Transaction (SDT) to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). Once a reference is made to the TPO, the TPO is competent to exercise all powers that are available to the Assessing Officer under Section 92C(3) for the determination of ALP and consequent adjustment.

Further, under Section 92E of the Act, there is a reporting requirement on the taxpayer to file an audit report in the prescribed form before the Assessing Officer (AO) containing details of all international transactions or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer during the year. This audit report is the primary document with the AO, which contains the details of international transactions and/or SDT undertaken by the taxpayer. If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under Section 92E, then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction/SDT so as to make a reference to the TPO.

Section 92CA provides that if, during the course of proceeding before him, an international transaction comes to the notice of the TPO, which has not been referred to him by the AO, the TPO can proceed to determine the ALP in its respect as well. It also provides for the computation of ALP by the TPO of those international transactions, details of which have not been furnished in the audit report referred to above. These provisions are in place in sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of the section 92CA. However, at present, the above-noted provisions of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA do not extend to SDTs.

5.10-2 Amendment by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 has amended sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of Section 92CA to enable the TPO to deal with SDTs which have not been referred to him by the AO and/or in whose respect audit report under section 92CE has not been filed.

These amendments will take effect from 01-04-2025 and will, accord-ingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2025-26 and subsequent assessment years.

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act provides that the Assessing Officer may refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction to a Transfer Pricing Officer. Such a reference can be made where:—

The Assessing Officer considers it is necessary or expedient to do so, and

(a)

Eliminating the interface between the Transfer Pricing Officer and the assessee or any other person to the extent technologically feasible;

(b)

Optimising utilisation of the resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation; and

Introducing a team-based determination of arm's length price (ALP) with dynamic jurisdiction.

FAQ 72. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

(e)

FAQ 74. How to calculate the interest on excess money that needs to be repatriated after a primary adjustment?

Rule 10CB provides the rate of interest at which interest has to be calculated on excess money or part thereof that is not repatriated within the time limit. Where the international transaction is denominated in Indian rupees, the rate of interest will be the one-year marginal cost of fund lending rate of the State Bank of India as of 1st April of the relevant previous year, plus 325 basis points (plus 3.25%). Where the international transaction is denominated in foreign currency, the rate of interest shall be the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) as of 30th September of the relevant previous year plus 300 basis points (plus 3%).

It is possible that the amount of imputed interest income on the excess money not repatriated to India may relate to more than one year. Having regard to Rule 10CB, the interest liability extends till the date of repatriation. Accordingly, for the relevant year under audit, such liability in respect of imputed interest may extend not only to the primary adjustment but may also relate to the primary adjustment made in the earlier years.

It is well-settled principle that instructions/circulars issued by the CBDT have a binding effect on the Assessing Officer. More specifically, the binding nature of the above-mentioned instruction issued by the CBDT has been confirmed by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in case of Sony India (P.) Ltd. v. CBDT [2007] 288 ITR 52. At para 37 of the said order, the Delhi High Court has concluded as below:

"For these reasons, we hold that the impugned Instruction No. 3, dated 20-5-2003 issued by the CBDT is consistent with the statutory objective underlying section 92CA(1) and acts as a guidance to the Assessing Officer in the exercise of discretion in referring an international transaction to the TPO for determination of its ALP. It is neither arbitrary nor unreasonable, and is not ultra vires the Act."

This view has also been taken by the ITAT, Bangalore Bench in the case of Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. (supra). At paras 44 and 45 of the order, the Tribunal has observed as below:

"44 . . . . Therefore, when provisions of section 92CA(1) are read with Circular of CBDT (Instruction No. 3), dated 20-5-2003, it becomes 'necessary' for the Assessing Officer to refer the question of determination of transfer pricing of international transactions to the TPO. He has no discretion in the matter in the light of limit fixed by the board. The Assessing Officer has only to look at the aggregate value of international transactions disclosed by the assessee in the audit report and then follow directions of CBDT. The Assessing Officer, therefore, is left with a very limited role under section 92CA(1). Likewise while granting approval to the action of the Assessing Officer the CIT has only to see whether aggregate value of international transaction is more than Rs. 5 crores or not. If it is more, he has also to grant approval in the light of directions of CBDT. These directions are mandatory and binding on the Assessing Officer and the CIT(A). The fact that directions are not binding on the assessee or courts is immaterial. The relevant question to be answered is whether circulars are binding on the departmental authorities. The question has an obvious answer.

The issue of legality and validity of above directions was raised before Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Sony India (P.) Ltd. (supra). Their Lordships have also upheld validity of directions of CBDT.

45. In the light of above discussions, we do not find any illegality in the directions issued by the Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)."

Since the circulars issued by the CBDT have a binding affect on the tax authorities, Circular No. 14/2001 issued by the CBDT would also have a binding effect on the Assessing Officer/TPO who is duty bound to demonstrate that the assessee has manipulated its prices to shift profits outside India, before any transfer pricing adjustment is made. It was found that information technology services availed by assessee also related to business carried on by assessee - Whether information technology services availed had to be aggregated with other transactions being intrinsically linked to other international transactions undertaken by assessee - Held, yes - Whether since various documents were filed by assessee which included certificate of AE evidencing not only availment of services but also basis of cost for such services and similar services were availed by other group entities from AE at same rates as charged to assessee, order of TPO/Assessing Officer was unjustified - FACT: The assessee had entered into international transactions of import of raw materials, trading goods and components, export of finished goods, income from services, information technology services availed and reimbursement of expenses with its associated enterprises. The first five transactions were benchmarked together by using TNMM. The case of assessee that all these transactions need to be aggregated as they were interdependent on each other while benchmarking international transactions to be at arm's length price.

However, the transaction of information technology services availed had been segregated by the TPO.

The assessee claimed that the said information technologies services had been availed by it from its AE, namely, Eaton China for Information Technology (IT) and related support services. The assessee also during the course of assessment proceedings filed certificate issued by Eaton China certifying the factum of provision of services by it to the assessee. Eaton China also confirmed that other Eaton group companies availing same services were also charged on the same basis as the assessee.

The TPO was of the view that the assessee had to prove that the services were rendered and the second aspect of intra-group service was the quantification of such services in terms of actual expenditure incurred and commensurate benefit derived therefrom. The TPO thus, held that where the assessee had failed to prove the receipt of services and benefits derived from services with supporting evidence, the arm's length price of transactions was treated as Nil and hence, adjustment was proposed to be made to the arm's length price.

HELD: In the first instance, TPO cannot sit in the judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises the role of TPO is to determine the arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by the assessee and whether the same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables.
