1. A Firm of chartered accountants has the gross billing for the year ending on 31-3-2006 as under:— Since the service provided by the firm with respect to audit was only 2.30 Lakh hence the firm is not collecting and paying service tax in the year 2006-07 on the assumption that it is eligible for the benefit of exemption available to the small service providers as per Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) up to the value of 4 Lakh of collection. Please advise properly.

The total taxable service rendered by this firm of Rs.4.30 Lakhs in the previous year ended on 31-3-2006 hence the firm is not eligible for the exemption scheme available to this firm.

For this purpose there is clear provision in the Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) in the form of conditions mentioned in clause 2 of the scheme. The exact wording of clause 2(viii) is as under:—

"(viii)The aggregate value of taxable services rendered by a provider of taxable service from one or more premises, does not exceed rupees four lakhs in the preceding financial year."

Here, to be eligible for exemption scheme available to small service providers, the aggregate value of taxable service should not be more than Rupees 4 Lakh in the preceding financial year and both the Audit services and taxation services were part of taxable service though the tax was exempt on the taxation services. Let us see the exact wordings of the Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 in this respect:—

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994(32 of 1994); and in suppression of the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) No. 57/98 Service tax, dated 7-10-1998, the Central Government, being satisfied that it is necessary in the Public interest so to do, hereby exempts the taxable service provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity to a client, other than the taxable service related to—

(i)Accounting and auditing; or

(ii)to (xi) Various services Like certification etc. mentioned,

from whole of the service tax leviable thereon.

Here that the service is taxable but this taxable service is exempt from paying the whole of tax. The point here is that the taxable service is exempt from paying the tax and in that case its structure of taxable service remained intact but the tax payable on it is exempt.

Hence the value of taxable service provided by the firm of Chartered Accountant is Rs. 4.30 Lakhs and as per provisions of clause 2(viii) of the exemption notification, the service provider having turnover of taxable service over Rs.4 Lakhs is not eligible for exemption scheme provided to the small service provider.

Though while claiming exemption under this notification "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" means excluding the taxable service on which no service tax is payable and this has been provided in Explanation (B) the said notification and the "the aggregate value not exceeding Rupees 4 Lakhs" is applicable for the claiming the exemption but to ascertain the status "Small service provider" and the eligibility of the assessee to claim the exemption which is based on "the aggregate value of taxable service rendered" of the previous year, no such explanation is issued and in absence of any clarification from the Government in this respect,the opinion mentioned above is given.

The revenue alleged that the assessee had failed to satisfy the 'benefit test' in respect of payments made by the assessee under the CCA (Agreement) for receiving purchase services, order handling services and sales services. The assessee has submitted before the TPO, the detailed nature of the aforesaid services and copies of documentary evidences of receipt of services on sample basis. The assessee submitted, a brief chart to prove the benefit test. This chart explains the nature of services, main functions, and documentary evidences for receipt of services along with paper book reference. This chart also explains the relevant para of the Cost Contribution Agreement (CCA). The assessee received the purchase & order handling services and sales services and documented them properly. The assessee also submitted the certificate issued by PWC Austria, about the costs allocated to AT&S India Pvt. Ltd. The copies of 78 chains of e-mail, job description sheets of 10 individual employees of the CCA team, evaluation reports of 6 global customers and flow chart of quotation processing services prove that assessee has received benefit from these services. The revenue has not disputed that these services have not been received by the assessee, he disputed only the 'benefit test', that assessee did not get the benefit out of these services. Assessee has proved that he had received the benefit from these services, by way of submitting a brief chart containing the services obtained. Therefore, the assessee has satisfied the 'benefit test', and for that rendering of intra group services by AE and payment made thereon were in the nature of third party, which would willing to pay. [Para 33]

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1), has not made any adverse comment under section 37 in respect of the services received under the CCA, for purchase services, order handling services and sales services. During the course of scrutiny assessment proceedings, the assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer the same evidences of receipt of purchase services, order handling services and sales services as those submitted to the TPO, as per the direction of the Assessing Officer. It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer, after examining the aforesaid details, did not make any adverse comment under section 37. As per the provision of sub-section (1) of section 37, the Assessing Officer is authorized to examine whether an expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) is incurred by an assessee wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business in the matter of computation of the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

In the assessee's case under consideration, the Assessing Officer has not disallowed the benefit of services received by the assessee under the Cost Contribution Agreement. The authority of the TPO would be to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price ('ALP') and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which the assessee benefits. That exercise of actual verification would be left to the Assessing Officer under section 37. The Assessing Officer could, therefore, determine under section 37 that the expenditure claimed was not for the benefit of the business, and thus, disallow that amount, this does not restrict or in any way bypass the functions of the TPO. The jurisdiction of the TPO is specific and limited i.e. to determine the arm's length price of an international transaction in terms of Chapter X read with rules 10A to 10E of the Income-tax Rules. Therefore, the assessee has derived benefits from these services as per CCA agreement and hence the arguments advanced by the revenue is not acceptable. [Para 34]

9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

9.1 Safe harbour rules [Section 92CB]

Section 92CB relates to power of CBDT to make safe harbour rules (SHR). For this purpose, safe harbour means the circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee.

Section 92CB(1) provides that the determination of arm's length price (ALP) under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to SHR.

Section 92CB(1) has been substituted with effect from assessment year 2020-21 to provide that apart from the determination of ALP, the determination of the income referred to in section 9(1)(i) shall also be subject to SHR.

Section 9(1)(i) covers various types of income e.g. income through or from any business connection in India, any property in India, etc. Further, it has various Explanations including

(a)

Explanation 2 ("agency business connection")

(b)

Explanation 2A ("SEP")

(c)

Explanation 3A (income from advertisement etc.)

It appears that the CBDT now has the power to make rules for computation of all the types of income referred to above.

Explanation to section 92CB defining safe harbour is, amended to provide that safe harbour would now also include circumstances in which income tax authorities shall accept the income under section 9(1)(i) declared by the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2020-21. In the following cases, it has been held that the safe harbour provisions in respect of transfer pricing were not applicable to assessment years prior to introduction of section 92CB/rules thereunder:

(a)

Rolls Royce India (P) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 69 taxmann.com 209 (Delhi - Trib.)

(b)

However, in Dy. CIT v. Minda Acoustic Ltd. [2019] 107 taxmann.com 475 (Delhi - Trib.), it was held that the Safe Harbour Rules can always be adopted as guidance in respect of the assessment years prior to their insertion.

9.2 Advance pricing agreement [Section 92CC]

Section 92CC relates to advance pricing agreement (APA).

Hitherto, section 92CC(1) provided that the CBDT, with the approval of the Central Government, may enter into an APA with any person, determining the ALP or specifying the manner in which ALP is to be determined, in relation to an international transaction to be entered into by that person.

The scope of section 92CC(1) has been widened with effect from 1-4-2020 to provide that the CBDT may also enter into an APA with any person determining income referred to in section 9(1)(i), or specifying the manner in which said income is to be determined, as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India by or on behalf of that person, being a non-resident.

The Finance Minister, in her speech stated as follows:

"In order to provide tax certainty to taxpayers in the matter of attribution of profit to permanent establishment (PE), it is proposed to widen the scope of Advanced Pricing Agreement (APA) and Safe Harbour Regime (SHR), by providing that determination of attribution of profit to PE shall also be in the scope of SHR and APA." (para 2.1 of Annex to Part B of Budget Speech)

The rationale for the amendment is explained in Explanatory Memorandum as follows:

"It has been represented that the attribution of profits to the PE of a non-resident under clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 9 of the Act in accordance with rule 10 of the Rules also results in avoidable disputes in a number of cases. In order to provide certainty, the attribution of income in case of a non-resident person to the PE is also required to be clearly covered under the provisions of the SHR and the APA.

In view of the above, it is proposed to amend section 92CB and section 92CC of the Act to cover determination of attribution to PE within the scope of SHR and APA."

FAQ 90. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

FAQ 91. Whether Treaty Shopping is ipso facto an IAA and reportable in Clause 30C?

Treaty shopping is not, per se, an IAA. Treaty Shopping is to be reported only if it is abusive, i.e. it satisfies the definition of IAA. In Her Majesty The Queen v. Alta Energy Luxembourg S.A.R.L [2022] 144 taxmann.com 23 (SCC), the Supreme Court of Canada held that GAAR could be invoked against treaty shopping only if it perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states. Treaty Shopping per se is not abusive tax avoidance [Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement in Indian GAAR] so as to attract GAAR. Treaty shopping is abusive tax avoidance and attracts GAAR, but only when treaty shopping perverts the treaty bargain between two contracting states.

TRANSFER PRICING IS SERIOUS BUSINESS 14. Adoption of a transfer price different from declared price may have serious consequences. No deduction under section 10A, 10AA, 10B or Chapter VI-A is admissible in respect of addition consequent to adoption of the arm’s length price. There is no immunity from penalty leviable against deemed concealment on the difference between reported and assessed income, unless justified by reasonable cause under section 273B. Failure to keep accounts and documents as required under section 92D will merit penalty under section 271AA. Failure to get audit certificate will attract penalty under section 271BA.

It has been held that the burden to prove that declared rate is the transfer price under the rules is placed on the assessee as decided by the Tribunal in Aztec Software Technology Services Ltd.’s case (supra). In fact, that is also the view taken in the countries, where transfer pricing rules are in vogue. To take an example, Australian rulings would not discredit findings of the tax authorities unless bad faith could be shown as decided in San Remo Macaroni Co. v. Commissioner of Taxation [1999] FCA 1468. Deficiency of information is a fault, which could not be attributed to revenue, so that burden of proving arm’s length price lay on the taxpayer. New Business Tax System (Thin Capitalisation and Other Measures) Bill, 2000 would seek to place even greater responsibility on foreign investors with significant interest in Australian ventures.

The seriousness of transfer pricing is highlighted by a recent Instruction indicating the effect of transfer pricing exercise undertaken by tax administration in India. The resort can now be made to Mutual Agreement Procedure under Indo-U.S. Double Tax Avoidance Agreement in respect of taxes, inter alia, imposed by application of Transfer Pricing Rule vide Instruction No. 10 of 2007, dated October 23, 2007. It provides for stay on demand subject to pendency of reference for availing MAP on confirmation from Foreign Tax and Tax Research Division of the CBDT and bank guarantee for the amount due and interest thereon.

The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted said addition.

In appellate proceedings, invoking the provisions of rule 27 of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 the assessee sought to support the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) by raising a plea that under section 92C or 92CA, it was the statutory duty of the Assessing Officer to decide independently, whether the determination of arm's length price by the assessee should be accepted, or whether or not after applying the provisions of section 92CA, the transfer pricing adjustment should be made.

It was further submitted that in the present case, in compliance of the CBDT Instruction No. 3 of 2003, dated 20-5-2003 the Assessing Officer did not himself examine the issue of transfer pricing and with the approval of the Commissioner (Appeals), made a reference to the TPO under section 92CA(1). The Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply their minds to the transfer pricing report, or to any other material or information or document. The TPO made an adjustment which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order. On their part, the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) did not discharge necessary judicial functions conferred upon them under section 92C or 92CA.

HELD: The assessee's support to the impugned order on both counts is found to be correct. The Assessing Officer erred in not himself examining the issue of transfer pricing and with the approval of the Commissioner, made a reference to the TPO under section 92CA(1); that the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) failed to apply their mind to the TP report filed by the assessee, or to any other material or information or document furnished. The TPO made an adjustment which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order. Thereby, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) did not discharge necessary respective judicial functions conferred on them under sections 92C and 92CA.

Further, the assessee is also correct in contending that no TP adjustment can be made in a case like the present one, where the assessee enjoys benefit under section 10A or 80HHE, or where the tax rate in the country of the associated enterprises is higher than the rate of tax in India and where the establishment of tax avoidance or manipulation of prices or establishment of shifting of profits is not possible. [Para 54]

On the basis of the above reasons, accepting the pleas raised by the assessee to support the order of Commissioner (Appeals) order, without going into the merits of this ground, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 55]

Provisions of section 92D(3) can be applied in the following circumstances :

(i)

in the course of the proceedings under the Act before the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals).

(ii)

Any documents or information prescribed under sub-section (1) may be required.

information is required to be furnished under sub-section (3) within 30 days (as extended by another 30 days) from the receipt of notice issued in this regard.

Thus, the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) may require (from any person) any information or document as may be prescribed. Word 'any' information or document cannot ordinarily mean 'all' the documents prescribed under rule 10D. The word 'required' is important as it rules out option with the assessee and makes it obligatory to furnish the requisite information.

It is clear from above that the power under section 92D(3) can be used in the course of the assessment proceedings, i.e., in proceedings for determination of ALP and only for requiring to furnish prescribed information or documents under rule 10D. It being a provision connected with procedure to help an assessment, must be purposefully construed. But, regulation does not provide any time or stage when power to issue notice is to be exercised. However, scheme of assessment do indicate the stage at which it is to be issued and the purpose which is required to be achieved through the issuance of such a notice. [Para 24.6]

Transfer Pricing (TP) continues to be one of the most significant international tax issues for multinational enterprises globally. India, recognising its importance in curbing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)introduced TP provisions in 2001. Since its inception, the Indian TP regime has evolved, keeping pace with both market dynamics and continued global tax developments.

As the Indian tax landscape continues to evolve, there are several critical areas that require attention in the upcoming Union Budget 2025. The following outlines key areas where we believe regulatory intervention and reform are necessary, along with our specific expectations for the forthcoming budget.

Compliance

Maintenance of TP Documentation: Since the introduction of TP provisions in 2001, the threshold for maintaining TP documentation for taxpayers has been set at INR 1 crore in aggregate value of international transactions. However, as businesses expand and related-party transactions increase, this threshold appears outdated. The expectation is to raise the threshold for mandatory TP documentation at INR 10 crores, in line with the growing scale of multinational enterprises in India.

Exemption of Non-Residents from TP Certification: Currently, non-resident taxpayers earning income from interest, dividends, royalties, or technical fees, do not need to file their income tax return in India, provided taxes have been appropriately deducted on said income by the taxpayer. However, these taxpayers are still required to mandatorily furnish a TP Certificate if such taxable income is earned from parties in India. Given that these non-resident taxpayers are exempted from furnishing their income tax return subject to meeting the above stated conditions, it is recommended that such taxpayers should also be exempted from furnishing the TP certificate, aligning with the broader tax compliance simplification.

Recalibration of the Arm's Length Range: Under the existing TP regulations, India uses an arm's length range between the 35th and 65th percentiles while determining arm's length pricing. However, this range diverges from internationally accepted standards.

To align India's regulations with global norms, the expectation is to revise the range to an interquartile range, spanning from 25th percentile to the 75th percentile, which better reflects the true variability in arm's length pricing.

Dispute Management and Resolution

Expedited Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) Process: The APA regime has been a powerful tool for Indian taxpayers looking to mitigate related-party transaction disputes and achieve certainty on their arm's length pricing. While the APA program has been successful as compared to traditional dispute resolution routesdelays in processing APA applications have resulted in a significant backlog. To enhance efficiency, we recommend streamlining the APA process by categorising applications based on their complexity. Complex cases could be allocated to more experienced teams, while simpler cases should be subject to shorter timelines for resolution. This bifurcation would enable faster conclusions, benefitting both the tax authorities and taxpayers.

Expansion and Re-evaluation of Safe Harbour Provisions: Plenty of small taxpayers have opted for the Safe Harbour regime in order to conclude their arm's length pricing in a streamlined manner. However, the applicable benchmarks are typically higher in this regime as compared to available alternatives. While the small taxpayers do get to enjoy this benefit of convenience, the threshold restrictions in the Safe Harbour regime makes it inaccessible to the taxpayers with comparatively higher value of transactions, forcing them into complex dispute resolution processes. To make this regime more accessible, the Government may re-evaluate the Safe Harbour provisions by (a) increasing the transaction thresholds to cover a larger number of companies, and (b) adjusting the rates to be closer to actual comparable benchmarks, thereby encouraging broader adoption and reducing litigation risks.

As referred in the paras above, under section 92, what has to be determined is 'the income arising from an international transaction', which needs to be computed in the hands of the assessee, having regard to arm's length price of international transaction undertaken by the assessee. In other words, the Assessing Officer before making reference to the TPO has to come to a finding that it is either necessary or expedient to make reference to the TPO for computation of ALP of international transactions undertaken by him. So, the first step in this regard is that the Assessing Officer should come to a finding that some income arises from the international transaction undertaken by the assessee, which needs to be benchmarked and its ALP needs to be determined. [Para 65]

The question which arises is how the Assessing Officer comes to know that there is an international transaction undertaken by the assessee. The first and foremost is the audit report submitted by the assessee in Form No.3CEB, which is self declaration made by the assessee that it has entered into international transactions with its AE/s. Once such declaration is made, then the Assessing Officer has to come to a finding that the income arising from such an international transaction needs to be computed to find out whether it is at ALP by applying any one of the prescribed methods under section 92C(1). This is the preliminary satisfaction of the Assessing Officer. [Para 66]

The Courts have held that this satisfaction needs to be recorded by the Assessing Officer before making reference to the TPO, who shall carry out detailed analysis of international transactions undertaken by the assessee applying the most appropriate method and determine ALP of international transactions. It may be pointed out that role played by the Assessing Officer while making reference to the TPO is at variance to the role of the TPO, who has to finally determine ALP of international transactions undertaken by the assessee. [Para 67]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company, a subsidiary of Singapore based company, was a distributor of a variety of car audio visuals, car entertainment accessories, etc. It had filed its return for relevant assessment year on 24-9-2009 declaring a loss of Rs. 59.51 crores.

■

The Assessing Officer referred the case of the assessee to the TPO for determining the arm's length price (ALP), who proposed adjustment of Rs. 5.62 crore vide order dated 30-1-2013 passed under section 92CA(3).

■

Consequentially, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment at reduced loss vide order dated 21-5-2013 passed under section 144C.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) restricted the transfer pricing adjustment to Rs 4.50 crores.

■

In the instant appeal the assessee raised additional ground that the TPO’s order was barred by limitation under section 92CA(3A), since it had to be passed at least 60 days prior to expiry of limitation for completing assessment under section 153, i.e., on or before 29-1-2013.

HELD: ■

A conjoint reading of the relevant provisions of sections 92CA(3A) and 153(1) shows that the TPO is required to pass order under section 92CA(3A) at any time before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation referred to in section 153 for making assessment order expires. The Division Bench of the Madras High Court in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215/444 ITR 636 (Madras) has upheld the decision of Single Judge holding that [Para 15]

■

The period of limitation for passing the assessment order in the instant case expires on 31-3-2013. The time limit for passing the order under section 92CA(3A) is sixty days prior to the date on which the limitation referred in section 153 expires. Thus, the limitation in the present case for passing the order under section 92CA(3A) expires on 29-1-2013. The TPO passed the order under section 92CA(3A) expires on 29-1-2013. A perusal of clause 43 of Circular No. 3/2008, dated 12-3-2008 shows that the word 'month' has been used therein instead of 'days' used in the Act. Undoubtedly, two months may not necessarily be equal to sixty days always as specified in the Act. 'Two months' as mentioned in Circular can be more or even less than sixty days. Therefore, expression issued to evaluate limitation period as specified in the Act has to be strictly followed. [Para 16]

PRESS RELEASE

LEVEL PLAYING FIELD FOR C.As IN SERVICE TAX AFFECTED - ICAI

FEBRUARY 28, 2006

1. The practising chartered accountants will be adversely affected due to the withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98-Service tax, dated 16th October, 1998. Is it deliberate or unintentional

8. The withdrawal of this notification is not unintentional and it is very clear from the initial Government reaction issued through a letter written by the Joint Secretary, TRU, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue to all Commissioners, Chief Commissioners immediately after release of the notification withdrawing the exemption. Let us see the relevant portion related to the notification under consideration in this article which we can term as first Departmental clarification in this respect :—

The following exemptions are withdrawn with effect from March 1, 2006 :—

2. Exemption for services, other than accounting, auditing, and statutory certification services, provided by a practising chartered accountant, company secretary or cost accountant in his professional capacity. Consequently all services provided by such persons in their professional capacity become taxable - As written by Joint Secretary, TRU, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, in D.O.F. No. 334/4/2006- TRU, dated 28-02-2006 to all Commissioners, Chief Commissioner and DG.

Service tax is a tax on services and not on a tax on the service provider or on the professionals providing the services. This fact was also pronounced by various Courts while deciding the constitutional validity of the service tax on various services.

The exemption notification was also issued on the same consideration because the field of providing this service is open for various other professionals and if getting same type of services from a particular professional, say chartered accountants, attracts service tax then this has two side effects. One is that the other professional will have the upper hand compared to the chartered accountants only because they need not to pay service tax. Secondly, it will snatch the level playing field from a professional. Hence, in this particular case this is a tax on a professional or on a particular profession and not on a particular service because the others providing the same service need not to pay the tax.

On both these grounds the withdrawal of this exemption notification is totally discriminatory, unwarranted and unjustified and as a remedial action the exemption notification should be restored in the same spirit in which it was initially provided.

During the year under consideration, CPP transferred 17.17 crore units of power to CMU and, for the purpose of computation of the aforementioned tax holiday, applied a rate of Rs. 6.29 per unit. The rate was based upon the computation of the landed cost of power purchased by the CMU from the Southern Power Distribution Company of AP Limited.

On reference, the TPO was of the opinion that differences specified in rule 10B(1)(a)(ii) have to be taken into account and that only the base cost of energy (Rs. 5.25 per unit) supplied by the Distribution company could be applied for the purpose of benchmarking and other components like ToD charges, Demand charges etc. do not apply. Accordingly, TPO, applying CUP, considered only the energy cost of Rs. 5.25 per unit in arriving at the Arms Length Price and did not take into consideration any of other components charged by the Distribution company. ENLARGED SCOPE OF SERVICE TAX ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS Please explain the new levy of service tax on Chartered Accountants. From which date this new service tax is introduced and how it will be applicable?

The service tax on Chartered Accountants was introduced in 1998 and at that time an exemption from payment of service tax was granted to Chartered Accountants, ICWAs and Company Secretaries on all the services rendered by them except for the following:—

(i)Accounting and auditing

(ii)Cost accounting and cost auditing

(iii)Secretarial auditing

(iv) to (xi) Various verification and certification services.

- Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

Due to this notification, all other services including the consulting services were exempt from service tax but now with effect from 1st March, 2005 the above exemption Notification has been withdrawn. Hence the services exempted under this exemption, due to this withdrawal have become taxable and the major effect of this withdrawal of exemption is that the tax consultancy service provided by Chartered Accountants have become taxable and this will include the Income-tax consultancy, Sales tax and VAT consultancy, service tax consultancy.

It should be noted that no new service has been introduced but due to withdrawal of an exemption notification the consultancy services of the Chartered Accountants have become taxable and it is from the date of withdrawal of this exemption notification i.e., 1st March, 2005.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with a company by name Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited, for the development of the software technology park and the transfer of 74% of the share of the petitioner to the said company, on the understanding that the transferee company had to fund the development of the park.

Thereafter, the petitioner made an application in November 2005 to the Chairman of the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee through the office of the Director of Software Technology Park of India, Chennai, for setting up an information technology park under the STP Scheme.

The petitioner also entered into two agreements with Pacifica Infrastructure Company Private Limited and another company by name E-lights Technopark Private Limited for the effective funding and implementation of the project.

On 17.10.2006, the Inter Ministerial Standing Committee granted in principle approval for the setting up of the infrastructure facility under the STP Scheme in 'Freedom IT Campus '. The Government of India, in turn, granted permission by a communication dated 22.10.2006 in terms of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2004-2009.

As per the letter of permission so granted, the petitioner was entitled to import capital goods worth Rs. 2500 lakhs, by availing the benefits of Notification No. 153/93 dated 13.8.1993. But, the goods and services were to be used for the purpose of export of software and IT services by the STP Units located within the infrastructure facility at the park. The permission for import of items was valid for a period of two years from the date of issue of the letter of permission.

Clause 30A(a) requires the tax auditor to give a "Yes/No answer" to the question of whether any primary adjustment to transfer price, as referred to in section 92CE(1), has been made during the previous year. Clause 30A(b)(iii) requires reporting whether the excess money available with the associated enterprise is required to be repatriated to India as per the provisions of section 92CE(2). If the adjustment relates to an assessment year before the assessment year 2017-18, or the primary adjustment is of less than ` 1 crore, the excess money is not required to be repatriated to India, and this question may be answered as "No". If the answer to the question in clause 30A(b)(i) is "yes", the tax auditor needs to report against clause 30A(b)(ii) the relevant clause of section 92CE(1) under which adjustment falls and the amount of adjustment also. Clause 30A(b)(iii) requires reporting whether the excess money available with the associated enterprise is required to be repatriated to India as per the provisions of section 92CE(2). If the adjustment relates to an assessment year prior to assessment year 2017-18, or the primary adjustment is of less than ` 1 crore, the excess money is not required to be repatriated to India, and this question may be answered as "No". In case the excess money has not been repatriated within the prescribed time, the imputed interest income, which would be the secondary adjustment, needs to be computed and reported in Clause 30A(b)(v).

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacture & sale of paper. It had set up a Captive Power Plant [CPP] to meet the power requirements of its manufacturing unit.

Assessee operated an eligible power generating undertaking profits of which were eligible for deduction under section 80-IA(8) and the power generated by the eligible unit was entirely consumed captively by the non-eligible unit and the assessee had ascertained the transfer value of power to non-eligible unit at Rs. 8.41 per unit. The said transaction being in the nature of specified domestic transaction had been benchmarked using internal CUP Method in the transfer pricing audit report filed in Form 3CEB.

After examining the Transfer Pricing Study Report and the details furnished by the assessee, the TPO show caused the assessee to explain as to why the power generated by the eligible unit and transferred to the non-eligible unit should not be benchmarked at the rate at which power generating stations sold electricity to exchange boards/distribution companies. According to TPO, the CPP was a power generating unit and the SEB from which the non-eligible unit purchased power, was a distribution unit and, therefore, the comparison of CPP with SEB was unwarranted, since they were functionally dissimilar.

TPO observed that the rate at which power was being purchased by the manufacturing unit from SEB cannot be taken as the open market value at which power could be sold by CPP in the market and, the benefit under section 80-IA can be claimed only with reference to the rate fixed by Tariff Regulatory Commission for sale of electricity by power generating companies. The TPO, therefore, rejected the benchmarking analysis performed by the assessee and substituted the transfer price of power determined by the assessee at Rs. 8.41 per unit with the tariff of Rs. 3.73 per unit, as notified by UPERC for sale of power by the power generation stations to its State distribution company, Accordingly, the arm's length sale value of the eligible unit was computed resulting in adjustment.

, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. [Para 9.9] Further, there is no express provision under the Act restricting the application of section 92C for determining the income at arm's length where such income is eligible for deduction under section 10A. On the contrary, there is a proviso to section 92C(4) which prohibits the deduction under section 10A on the income to the extent enhanced as an effect of a determination of ALP. [Para 9.10]

Thus, the proviso itself vividly reflects the intent of lawmakers that the provisions of chapter X shall prevail in all the cases of international transactions falling under the umbrella of section 92 including the income-qualified for exemption under section 10A. In other words, it can be said that the intention of the statute was very much lucid that section 92 should be invoked even when the assessee is entitled to deduction under section 10A. In the light of above perceivance, there is no need to refer to other means of interpretation if the words are clear and free from any ambiguity. However, if the words in the statute are vague and ambiguous, then external aid may be consulted for interpretation. This connotes that the statute should be read as a whole; therefore, the point which is not clear in one section may be explained in another section. [Para 9.11]

Accordingly, if the purpose or object of Chapter X and/or section 10A is being defeated, then it is up to the legislature, if they think so, to reconstruct the law as per the required object. [Para 9.12]

However, language used in section 92 is clear, unambiguous, and do not lead to any absurd meaning. Thus, there is no need to look into the intention or purpose of the statute or application of reasonable construction. Accordingly, it is meaningless to apply the principles of purposive or object-based rules of interpretation as contended by the assessee [Para 9.13]

Regarding the contentious of the assessee that budget speech & memorandum explaining the provisions, it is noted that it is also a settled legal position that headings or marginal notes do not govern a provision where the legislature has used plain and unambiguous language. It is when the language is equivocal only then, help can be taken from the circulars, marginal notes or the Finance Minister speech or memorandum explaining the provisions to interpret the provision of the Act. The Finance Minister speech and memorandum explaining the bill will not provide any aid to the assessee in the given facts & circumstances. [Para 9.15]

In the context of the CBDT Circulars bearing Nos. 12/2001 dated 23-08- 2001 and 14/2001 dated 9-11-2001, it is merely explaining the understanding of statutory provisions regarding the transfer pricing. Further, it is a well-settled principle that the departmental circulars are not binding on this court. These circulars cannot be used to usurp the power of a judicial body while exercising its jurisdiction, including interpreting the statutory provisions [Para 10]

Without prejudice to the above, if it is agreed to apply the purposive interpretation while invoking the provisions of chapter X in the given facts and circumstances, then the same interpretation should also be extended in the context of the provision of section 10A. It is because the provision of chapter X cannot be seen in isolation as the issue on hand has direct nexus with the provision of section 10A. Thus it becomes pertinent to refer to the purpose of introducing section 10A. [Para 10.1]

From the above, it is clear that the spirit behind introducing section 10A was to bring foreign exchange in India. Granting exemption from Tax under section 10A was incidental and not the main object. Furthermore, where amount fetched by the Indian AE as revenue and/or the amount paid to its counter-part, AE outside India, as expenditure is lower and higher respectively and does not correspond to an ALP, the same will adversely affect the inflow of foreign exchange in India. Perhaps this was the reason to insert the proviso in section 92C(4). Accordingly, even if the purposive interpretation is applied in respect to the provisions of chapter X along with provisions of section 10A, it could not be held that provision of chapter X should not be applied where the assessee is eligible for the benefit of section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the object of inserting section 10A in the statute will stand unaccomplished. [Para 10.2]

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading 'PU Foam Products' and 'Matresses' (Coir/Foam/Spring) product from various units located across the India. The unit of assessee located at 'Kala Amb' (Himachal Pradesh) was eligible for various subsidies of Central Excise-duty and sales tax etc. and also deduction under section 80-IC in respect of profits derived from the unit.

The Assessing Officer during scrutiny proceedings observed that certain international and specified transactions were carried out by the assessee was within meaning of sections 92B and 92BA. It referred the matter to the TPO for determination of ALP of said transactions.

The TPO found the profit delcared by the section 80-IC eligible unit was exceptionally higher (30.71 per cent) as compared to other non-80-IC eligible unit and thus according to him there had been shifting of profit to 80-IC unit from non-80-IC units.

The assessee, in transfer pricing study, selected five comparables and computed their average operating margin at 2.90 per cent. The assessee further explained that the incentive provided by the Government to the unit and high-value product sold as the main reason for higher profit in case of 80-IC unit.

The TPO disputed the arm's length price of inter-unit (specified domestic) transactions with Kala Amb unit computed by the assessee and proposed a downward adjustment of Rs. 11.97 crores to the income of the assessee.

The adjustment had been computed as excess profit transferred in the ratio of the SDT expenses to the total expenses of the eligible unit.

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order included the adjustment proposed of Rs. 11.97 crores by the TPO.

Aggrieved, the assessee filed objections before the DRP. The DRP directed as under:

-

On the issue of manner of allocation of common expenses, while competing deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the eligible unit the assessee itself had allocated Rs. 9.14 crores to the eligible unit and the same amount had been taken by the TPO, hence no further directions were issued on the issue.

-

On the issue of non-allocation of finance cost, while computing deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the eligible unit, the Assessing Officer/TPO should allocate finance cost (excluding income-tax) in the ratio of sales/operative revenue of the Kala Amb unit and recompute SDT expenses considered for adjustment accordingly.

-

On the issue of impact of exemption of taxes on the profitability of Kala Amb unit, the Assessing Officer/TPO should compute the operating profit margin without considering the excise duty, sales tax and income-tax.

-

On the issue of invoices for transfer of other consumables/packing materials, the assessee had apparently transfered the materials to the 'Kala Amb' unit at a higher cost than the cost price of purchase from 3rd parties; therefore there was apparently no basis for enhancing the cost price of Kala Amb unit; however the DRP directed the Assessing Officer/TPO to examine the details submitted in this regard and give a specific finding in the final order.

Pursuant to the direction of the DRP, the Assessing Officer, computed operating profit of the eligible unit excluding excise duty and sales tax at Rs. 10.58 crores. While computing this operating profit excluding excise duty and sales-tax, the Assessing Officer allocated head office expenses of Rs. 9.14 crores. On the direction of the DRP to examine the details of price at which material was transferred to the eligible unit from other units of the assessee, the Assessing Officer/TPO perused few invoices produced by the assessee on test check basis but found the same not readable and incomplete. The TPO/Assessing Officer also observed that goods have been transferred to the eligible unit from non-eligible unit without adding any markup and thus resulted in shifting of the profit to the eligible unit and concluded that purchase made by the eligible unit from the non-eligible unit was not at arm's length and was below the prevailing market rate. In view of the conclusions drawn, the TPO /Assessing Officer computed the adjustment in final assessment order at Rs. 5.57 crore.

The APA program has begun with a bang and has kept the fast pace and co-operative approach that was promised by the Indian government. As mentioned earlier, a challenge for the APA program will be the increasing workload, as more and more taxpayers opt for APA.

Commenting on the current assessment, appeal, and litigation process is redundant as these points have been mentioned many times in many forums. Keeping the points brief, the important factors to be considered for improving the audit process are the following: Incentives of the TPOs should be set to encourage fair dealing rather than maximizing adjustments at all costs;

Taxpayers should be picked for transfer pricing audits on the basis of risk assessment rather than simply meeting the Rs. 15 crore criterion. This is likely to reduce the burden on TPOs and will allow them to delve more deeply in more complicated situations;

The transfer pricing regulations should be modified to introduce the concept of interquartile range (which is an internationally accepted practice) to replace the current concept of using average for determining the arm's length price. Using average encourages the use of comparable company/transaction data that is on an extreme end; and

Training of the TPOs in the concepts of transfer pricing to enable them to appreciate business and economic facts while determining the arm's length price.

In view of the foregoing discussion it is possible to visualise a system where all the three – SH, APA and normal audit co-exist together and address different segments of the economy. A taxpayer should have the option to choose any of the three depending upon the volume, complexity and value of international transactions. A lot will depend on the implementation as best of regulations can be made redundant by unreasonable approach during implementation.

Relationship with customs laws 8. The concept of transfer pricing was already present in the Customs Act in the form of Customs Valuation Rules. Under these rules, unless an exception applies, the ‘Assessable Value’ is the invoice value (i.e., ‘Transaction Value’). For customs duty, either the transaction value is accepted as the assessable value or the case is referred to the Special Valuation Branch (SVB), which then determines the assessable value. The issue is whether the assessable value determined under the Customs Act would be accepted by the IT Department as an ‘Arm’s Length Price’? There is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect. The invoice value of imported goods shall be the transaction value, only if the Customs Officer has no reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of the value declared. However, the IT Department may contend that customs authorities merely ensure that the import price is at least equal to the assessable value and in particular, customs authorities may not investigate whether the goods are overpriced. However, it appears that the customs authorities’ acceptance of a transaction value could serve as documentation support for proving that it is an arm’s length prie. In the event, the IT Department arrives at an arm’s length price, which is different from the assessable value, can the customs authorities reopen their assessment and revalue the imports? As per the Customs Act, the authorities can reopen assessment within a period of 5 years provided there is concealment. Practically, the chances of reopening the case are remote because the objective of customs authorities and IT authorities are contrary.2

Relationship with FEMA

9. Under Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), an issue could arise in case of imports, wherein the IT Department determines an arm’s length price, which is lower than actual import price. In such a case, it will be interesting to see whether the RBI would take a stand that the Indian entity has overpaid and hence the excess amount paid by Indian entity should be brought back into India. As per section 8 of the FEMA, an Indian resident has to bring into India all foreign exchange amounts, which are due or accrued to him. The issue is whether an Indian resident has to bring into India, additional foreign exchange on account of an adjustment made by the IT authorities under TP regulations? Broadly, the literal interpretation of the word ‘due’ would mean the amount ‘due’ as per contractual agreement and not the amount assessed by IT authorities which is determined long after the transaction is completed. Currently, consultancy fees up to US $ 100,000 can be remitted abroad under automatic approval and for fees exceeding US $ 100,000, one has to apply to RBI, which may accept or reject the same. The issue is whether the RBI approval is sufficient confirmation that the transaction is at arm’s length? Though there is no mandatory provision under the IT Act to this effect, the RBI approval could serve as supporting document. Secondly, can the IT authorities determine an arm’s length price, which is specially rejected by the RBI? Example: Indian company makes an application for payment of consultancy fees exceeding US $ 100,000 to its foreign parent company, which is rejected by the RBI. Can IT authorities assess the foreign parent company for "arm’s length price" exceeding US $ 100,000 ?1

Conclusion

10. Hence, it is felt that though India has made a very good start in amending section 92 of the Act and making transfer pricing illegal and punishable with huge amount of fines, it is felt that a lot more can still be done. As already stated above, the said changes are still to come on lines with the international standards in this field. The analysis done in this paper was only an illustration of the flaws in the present law of transfer pricing in India and the possible changes that can be introduced in it. A lot more needs to done in areas like that of documentation where a large number of documents needs to be submitted, irrespective of the size of the enterprise. This would obviously result in a huge administrative and financial burden on the smaller enterprises. Similarly, it is felt that the penalties imposed in case of violations are excessive as compared to similar laws in other jurisdictions etc.

Keeping in mind the fact that tax legislations ought to be guided by certain canons such as that of neutrality, effectiveness, certainty, simplicity and flexibility, it is clear that the existing section 92 does not in anyway achieve this goal. The ambiguity that is present in the existing provisions becomes all the more worrisome given the economic context of India, which is a developing country and which clearly requires assistance of the FDIs brought in by the MNCs into the country for its economic development. The inflow of this FDI is bound to be affected unless the issue of vagueness in section 92 is immediately addressed to and suitable amendments be made thereto.

This clause will apply only to assessees who carry on international transactions and to whom transfer pricing provisions of Chapter X apply. Primary Transfer Pricing Adjustments are what are known in popular parlance as "transfer pricing adjustments" or TP Adjustments."Primary adjustment" to a transfer price means the determination of transfer price in accordance with the arm's length principle resulting in an increase in the total income or reduction in the loss, as the case may be, of the assessee.

The e-tax Guide-Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2016 edition) of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore defines "transfer pricing adjustment" or what is referred to as "primary transfer pricing adjustment" in section 92CE(1) as under:

"3.34 Transfer pricing adjustment

In the event the related parties do not transact with each other at arm's length prices, tax authorities may for tax purposes, substitute the price of the transaction with one that could have been charged if the parties were unrelated. The adjustment to arrive at that price is known as a transfer pricing adjustment."

A primary TP adjustment covers the following TP adjustments,—

(i)

a TP adjustment to transfer price made suo motu by the assessee in his return of income;

(ii)

a TP adjustment to the transfer price made by the Assessing Officer has been accepted by the assessee;

(iii)

a TP adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement (APA) entered into by the assessee under section 92CC;

(iv)

a TP adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules framed under section 92CB; or

(v)

a TP adjustment arising from the resolution of an assessment by way of the mutual agreement procedure (MAP under an agreement (DTAA) entered into under section 90 or section 90A to avoid double taxa-tion.

In the context of Section 92CE and Clause 30A, it is clear that the primary TP adjustments contemplated in Clause 30A are those made regarding international transactions. Domestic TP adjustments are not contemplated

From the perusal of the said Instruction No. 3/2003, it is seen that guidelines for reference to the TPO has been made only in respect of determination of arm's length price in relation to the international transaction under section 92B. There is no whisper about specified domestic transaction for the reason that there was no concept of specified domestic transaction under the Act when said instruction was issued on 20-5-2003. The specified domestic transaction for the purpose of determination of ALP has been brought in the statute only by the Finance Act, 2012. Hence, holding the assessment order erroneous for the reason that, the Assessing Officer should have made a reference to the TPO in accordance with CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003 is wholly misconceived and misinterpreted. Once there was no CBDT instruction or guidelines for reference to the issue involving specified domestic instruction to the TPO at the time of passing the assessment order, then where is the question of any non-compliance of CBDT Instruction by the Assessing Officer.

IV. LEGALITY OF CBDT INSTRUCTION NO.3 OF 2003, DATED 20-5-2003 As per the impugned I nstruction, the CBDT has directed all the officers of the department to refer the matter of determination of ALP to the TPO where the aggregate value of international transaction and transactions exceed Rs. 5 crores. As is clear from the circular, the idea of issuing instructions under reference is to avoid selection of small cases with international transaction less than Rs. 5 crores for scrutiny of transfer price and to avoid arbitrariness in the application of the provision. All cases where aggregate value of international transactions exceed Rs. 5 crores, are required to be referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer. The limit has now been increased to Rs. 15 crores. Having regard to the object stated in the Circular, no fault can be found nor any illegality seen in the instructions.

When the provisions of section 92CA(i) are read with Circular of the CBDT (Instruction No.3) dated 20-5-2003, it becomes ‘necessary’ for the Assessing Officer to refer the question of determination of transfer pricing of international transactions to the TPO. He has no discretion in the matter in the light of limit fixed by the CBDT. The Assessing Officer has only to look at the aggregate value of international transactions disclosed by the assessee in the audit report and then follows directions of the CBDT The Assessing Officer, therefore, is left with a very limited role under section 92CA(1). Likewise, while granting approval to the action of the Assessing Officer, the Commissioner has only to see whether aggregate value of international transaction is more than Rs. 5 crores or not. If it is more than Rs. 5 crores, he has to grant approval in the light of directions of the CBDT. These directions are mandatory and binding on the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner. The fact that directions are not binding on the assessee or the C ourts is immaterial. The relevant question to be answered is whether circulars are binding on the departmental authorities. The question has an obvious answer. [Para 44]

Therefore, there is no illegality in the directions issued by the CBDT.[Para 45]

V. ALP DETERMINED BY TPO - HOW MUCH BINDING ON ASSESSING OFFICER FOR MAKING ASSESSMENT

Section 92CA(6) would come into operation only in the cases where the Assessing Officer in the assessment order has adopted the order of the TPO. Now if subsequently, the TPO rectified his order in terms of section 92CA(5), the Assessing Officer is duty-bound to pass an order in conformity with order of the TPO. Otherwise it can lead to anomaly and, therefore, it is provided that where the TPO’s order is amended to rectify a mistake apparent from record, the Assessing Officer must also rectify assessment order in conformity with above order. The TPO’s order under sub-section (3) of section 92CA cannot be treated as final and binding on the Assessing Officer. It does not mean that the order of the TPO is of no value or consequence. The words ‘having regard to’ convey definite meaning and are strong enough to enjoin upon the Assessing Officer a duty to pass order and adopt transfer pricing as determined by the TPO, unless there are very good grounds to modify or alter the transfer pricing ordered by the TPO. Only after recording reasons, the Assessing Officer can take transfer pricing other than one determined by the TPO. There may be cases in which the assessee after ALP is determined by the TPO and before his order is made the basis of assessment, may get such authentic material to show that transfer pricing determined by the TPO is not correct or should not be blindly adopted without modifying it. However, where the Assessing Officer has adopted the orders of the TPO and computed assessments accordingly, there is no illegality in the procedure followed by the Assessing Officer. [Para 51]

There is nothing to suggest that the TPO’s report on transfer pricing is conclusive and debars the Assessing Officer from looking at any other material. The aforesaid conclusion is also in line with latest change made in section 92CA by the Legislature through the Finance Act, 2007. [Para 52]

However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13] In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

Even in such a situation, the statute does not permit the TPO to assume the jurisdiction to determine the arm's length price of a specified domestic transaction not reported to him. There may be number of cases where the assessee may bona fide hold a belief that certain transaction is not a specified domestic transaction and therefore, would not report the same under section 92E. Whether bona fide or not, not making a report by the assessee of a specified domestic transaction would not leave the revenue without remedy. As clarified by CBDT in the instructions dated 20-5-2013, it is always open for the TPO who notices such transaction during the course of the proceedings before him to call for a reference by the Assessing Officer. If the Assessing Officer does make a report, only then TPO can undertake further steps as envisaged under sub-section (2) and other sub-sections of section 92CA. As noted, the statute is sufficiently clear. The legislature while expanding the scope of the transfer pricing study by the TPO to a transaction not referred him or not reported by the Assessing Officer, under sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, has confined the applicability thereof only to international transactions. The TPO exercising such powers suo motu in relation to a specified domestic transaction would be transgressing his jurisdiction and in the process would render the requirement of sub-section (1) of section 92CA redundant. As noted, the reference that the Assessing Officer can make to the TPO would have the approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner.[Para 19]

The arm's length principle of transfer pricing is based on the premise that the amount charged by one related party to another for a product must be the same as if the parties were not related. An arm's length price in respect of a foreign transaction, therefore, is the price which that transaction would obtain in the open market. Determination of arm's length price, when dealing with proprietary goods and services or intangibles, can be a much more complicated matter, as compared to determining such price in case of products such as commodities. A controlled transaction normally would meet the arm's length standard, if the results of the transaction are consistent with the results that would have been obtained if an uncontrolled entity was engaged in the same transaction, under the same circumstances. It may not always be possible to come across identical transactions and, therefore, the TPO, in such cases, would need to refer to comparable transactions made under comparable circumstances. [Para 32]

FAQ 74. Mr. A, a sole proprietor, agreed to transfer his personal property to Mr. X and received some non-refundable advance against such a deal. The sale could not materialise as Mr. X could not pay the whole amount, and the advance money was forfeited by Mr. A. What are the disclosure requirements? Section 56(2)(ix) of the Income-tax Act provides for taxability of any sum received as an advance in the course of negotiations for the transfer of a capital asset, and such sum was forfeited due to non-transfer of such capital asset. A new Clause 29A to Form 3CD has been inserted to report any advance received from the buyer but forfeited due to the non-materialisation of a deal to the sale of the capital asset.

The auditor is not required to report any such forfeited amount in respect of a personal capital asset or stock-in-trade. Any advances received and forfeited towards the sale of stock-in-trade would be taxable under section 28(i), and would not be required to be reported since the amount would be credited to the profit & loss account.

The requirement of reporting arises only on forfeiture of advance. If an advance has been received and has been outstanding for a considerable time, there is no requirement to report such amount unless and until it is forfeited by an act of the assessee.

FAQ 75. Should any consideration for the issue of shares that exceed the fair market value of the shares received by a start-up be reported in clause 29?

Reporting obligation under Clause 29 is triggered if a closely held company issues unquoted shares at a premium. In such case, the excess of the premium over the fair market value of the shares shall be taxable as income from other sources in the hands of the company.

The DPIIT's recognised start-ups are exempted from the applicability of Section 56(2)(viib) subject to the satisfaction of various conditions prescribed under the notification issued by the DPIIT13. Therefore, Clause 29 shall apply only to closely held companies except DPIIT-recognised start-ups that satisfy the condition for exemption. If the private limited company in question is a DPIIT-recognised start-up eligible for exemption under section 56(2)(viib), the e-mail received from CBDT regarding eligibility for exemption must be verified by the tax auditor, and suitable remarks should be made regarding the applicability of the exemption and the non-applicability of Clause 29.

Section 56(2)(viib) and Notification issued by the DPIIT16 prescribe various conditions for a start-up to claim exemption from payment of tax under this provision. In case of failure to comply with these conditions, the consideration received from the issue of shares, as exceeding the fair market value of such shares, shall be deemed to be the income of the company chargeable to tax for the previous year in which such failure takes place. When the exemption is withdrawn, it shall be deemed that the company has underreported the income in consequence of the misreporting, and consequently, a penalty of an amount equal to 200% of tax payable on the underreported income shall be levied as per Section 270A14.

FAQ 76. How to report the Impermissible Avoidance Arrangement entered into by the assessee?

Clause 30C of Form 3CD requires the Tax Auditor to report "Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements" (IAA) entered into by the assessee during the previous year and to quantify the tax benefit arising in the aggregate in the previous year to all the parties to such arrangement.

The tax auditor should examine whether the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner or the Approving Panel has, in any earlier previous year, declared any arrangement as IAA. If any arrangement has been declared to be an IAA, the tax auditor should further examine whether any transaction pertaining to or in connection with such declared IAA has taken place during the previous year under the audit. If yes, the tax auditor is expected to report this fact in the audit report. The tax auditor should also report tax benefits in the previous year arising from such transactions to all the parties to the arrangement. If he is unable to ascertain the tax benefit arising in the previous year, in the aggregate, to all the parties to the arrangement, he should indicate the same in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

The auditor should examine if any reference has been made for declaring an arrangement as an impermissible avoidance arrangement in any earlier previous year. If such references have been made, the auditor should report the fact in Form 3CA or Form 3CB, as the case may be.

However, a plain reading of the section provides for the business or goods or services or transaction referred in the relevant sections and does not suggest the applicability of SDT provisions only in case of claim of tax holiday. Keeping in perspective the stringent penal provisions, taxpayers are recommended to maintain robust transfer pricing documentation and make appropriate disclosures in the Form irrespective of whether tax holiday is being claimed. Another interesting case could be when a transaction gets covered by two clauses of the Form. An example may be that of an expenditure incurred by the taxpayer, payment of which has been made to a person referred to under section 40A(2)(b) of the Act. The same expenditure may also get covered under the clause that provides to cover any business transacted between the assessee and other person as referred to in section 80-IA(10) (where the taxpayer is required to determine the arm's length price of the expenses and income of the eligible undertaking and demonstrate that the same has not resulted in more than ordinary profits). The question in such case is whether such item should be included under one clause or both the clauses. In the event, the same is included under both the clauses, it will automatically increase the aggregate value of transactions, which appears to be not intended by law. However, it may also be noted that justification of arm's length price under two clauses may require use of different methodology (depending on the facts of the case). Prima-facie, since double inclusion leading to increased value of transactions may not represent the facts correctly, the taxpayers may choose to disclose the same under one clause while justifying the same to meet with arm's length standard under both the clauses in the TP documentation.

Apart from the above, another important milestone is the online filing of the Form from AY 2013-14. The e-utility for uploading Form No. 3CEB is supported by a java application unlike the excel utility which is commonly used for filing of the income tax returns online by individuals as well as corporate taxpayers. Though this is a welcome step, however being a transition phase, there would be a lot of challenges both for the taxpayers as well as the Chartered Accountants (CAs) to overcome, for successful implementation of the same.

The online filing process is also complex. It requires the CA to register himself/ herself and his/her digital signature certificate (DSC) on the income tax website. Thereafter, the taxpayer is also required to register his/her CA who would be signing off his Form No. 3CEB. Post uploading of the Form by the CA, the taxpayer is required to approve the same with his/her DSC on the income tax website. Thus, once this two way process is completed, the Form would be considered as filed in all respects The date of filing the Form No. 3CEB would be the date on which the CA has uploaded the Form.

In view of the various practical issues (in disclosures and filing/uploading) in the Form, it is expected that the CBDT would clarify certain areas in the Form shortly. Though the amendments in the Form are to include various recent amendments, the CBDT has also tried to cover certain cases with a view to reduce controversy on account of exclusion/inclusion of certain items from the ambit of transfer pricing, which is a welcome step. The amendments would clearly achieve more disclosures in a structured way.

Doctrine of unjust enrichment is not applicable if certified by Chartered Accountant that duty not recovered and shown in balance sheet as loans and advances - Deepak International v. CCST (2014) 304 ELT 438 (CESTAT SMB) * India Steel International v. CC (2015) 318 ELT 646 (CESTAT).

In CCE v. Paradeep Phosphates (2009) 238 ELT 690 (CESTAT), selling price was below cost price excluding excise duty as certified by Cost Accountant and the amount was shown as 'receivable' in balance sheet. It was held that doctrine of unjust enrichment is not applicable - similar view in South India Paper Mills v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 651 (CESTAT SMB).

Certificate of CA is only a piece of evidence and in itself not sufficient to show that burden has not been passed to other person - CC v. BPL Ltd. (2010) 259 ELT 526 (Mad HC DB) * CC v. SNS Overseas (2012) 275 ELT 621 (CESTAT).

In Tarapur Coatings v. CC (2009) 234 ELT 466 (CESTAT SMB), Chartered Accountant prepared cost sheet as per CAS-4 and certified that burden of excess duty was absorbed by appellant and that there was no price rise during relevant period. Duty was shown as receivable. It was held that refund is admissible.

In Quality Offset Printers v. CC (2008) 230 ELT 671 (CESTAT SMB), CA issued a general certificate based on balance sheets of previous year, current year and subsequent year that the incidence of duty has not been passed on. It was held that refund is admissible.

In Memirex & Co. v. CCE 2004(174) ELT 216 (CESTAT), it was held that certificate from Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence.

In A K Enterprise v. CC 2006 (199) ELT 67 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that mere certificate from Chartered Accountant is not sufficient to rebut presumption that duty has been passed on to buyer - same view in CC v. BPL Ltd. (2010) 259 ELT 526 (Mad HC DB).

In India Agencies v. CC (2007) 212 ELT 507 (CESTAT), it was observed that Chartered Accountants are professional interested in their clients and issue such statements. In absence of conclusive evidence that duty has not been passed on, doctrine of unjust enrichment applies.

In Chambal Fertilisers v. CC 2006 (200) ELT 231 (CESTAT), it was held that though certificate of Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence of not passing duty burden, department can ask for records to check whether statement of Chartered Accountant is correct. Refund cannot be rejected simply on the ground that certificate of Chartered Accountant is not conclusive evidence. - followed in Flair Impex v. CC (2009) 238 ELT 794 (CESTAT SMB).

However, mere certificate of CA that service tax has not been recovered separately in invoice is not sufficient to establish that the burden of tax has not been passed on to the buyer - Multi Mantech International v. CST (2009) 18 STT 229 (CESTAT SMB).
