In the instant case the assessee had collected sales tax as a part of dealers’ price. At the year-end the sales tax portion, which formed the part of dealers’ price had been bifurcated and had been claimed as a capital subsidy. The State Government through the Notification No. 1179, dated 31-3-1995 had provided sales tax exemption with an objective to promote the development of certain industries which had been set-up or undertaken modernisation, diversification, backward integration by way of fixed capital investment of Rs. 50 crores or more. The exemption from sales tax or benefit of reduced rate of tax was available to those units which had started production or had carried out expansion or modernisation or backward integration, etc., between 1-12-1994 and 31-3-2000. Para 2 of the Notification specifies that the exemption or reduction in the rate of sales tax including the additional tax would not be more than 5 per cent of the sale of goods. In case where tax rate was more than 5 per cent including additional tax, the balance was to be paid by the unit. Para 7(2) of the Notification provides for the exemption of sales tax to the extent of exemption or reduction in tax. Item (2) of the Schedule includes Greater Noida Industrial Development Area wherein exemption from sales tax to the extent of 200 per cent of capital investment had been provided. None of the clauses of the notification authorised the assessee to collect the sales tax and retain the same with it. The exemption of sales tax was available from the date of first sale or the date within the period of six months from the date of production, whichever was earlier. The said notification also provided that the eligibility certificate to the assessee would be issued by the Joint/Additional Director of concerned development authority and the same would be produced before the concerned Assessing Officer. The Additional Director Industries, Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority, issued eligibility certificate to the assessee. As per this certificate fixed capital investment was of Rs. 51,57,95,446. The date of commencement of production was 9-3-1998 and the first sale was affected on 27-3-1998. The assessee applied for exemption from trade tax [sales tax]. The exemption from trade tax [sales tax] was provided from 27-3-1998 to 26-3-2013 for a period of 15 years or till the time the exemption of sales tax was availed of to the extent of 200 per cent of the fixed capital investment, i.e., Rs. 1,02,75,90,892, whichever was earlier. This certificate also provided the items, i.e., colour TVs, washing machines and air-conditioners on which exemption from sales tax was provided. Another certificate was issued on 27-9-2000 in respect of printed circuit voice for CTV number 8,12,000 and microwave oven 1,00,000. In this certificate, the sales tax exemption in the first three years had been provided to the extent of 100 per cent; for next three years at 75 per cent; for next two years at 50 per cent; and for next two years at 25 per cent. In all exemption from sales tax was provided for 10 years. [Para 9]

Neither the certificates issued by the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority nor the notification issued by the State Government authorised the assessee to collect sales tax from its customers. The assessee had been exempted from collecting the sales tax from customers on the sales made with effect from 27-3-1998. In fact, during the course of hearing, neither the notification had authorized the assessee to collect sales tax nor the assessee had collected the sales tax as such. The assessee had included the element of sales tax in the dealers’ price as a sale price of the product. In the States other than Uttar Pradesh, the sales tax so collected as a part of dealer’s price had been paid to the respective State Governments, whereas in the case of the assessee the assessee was not liable to pay sales tax, as exemption had been provided to the extent of 200 per cent of fixed capital investment, the sales tax element which was embedded in the sale price had been retained by the assessee as excess sales consideration. At the year-end the assessee had allocated the sales tax element from dealer’s price and had claimed the same as capital subsidy. Therefore, the collection of dealer’s price had been made in the ordinary course of trading activities. When the assessee was not permitted to collect the sales tax under the notification issued by the State Government the collection of sales tax as a part of dealer’s price was nothing but constituted a trading receipt. [Para 10]

Exemption under Notification 28/79-C.E. for aerated waters which do not contain caffeine was denied to the petitioners, manufacturers of aerated water, on the ground that the benefit of the concessional rate of duty had not been passed on by the petitioners to the buyers/consumers. The Assistant Collector had informed the petitioner-Company that while the tariff rate for aerated waters had been raised to 60%, the effective rate for the goods was 30% ad valorem by virtue of the Notification. On perusal of the notification the Company came to the conclusion that the advice was incorrect due to an erroneous interpretation of the notification and, accordingly, submitted a revised classification list in which the effective rate was shown as 60% and exemption claimed in excess of 30% ad valorem. Challenging the finding of the authorities that the amount covered by the relief given by Notification 28/79 would go to the benefit of the manufacturers, the petitioners contended that the notification does not contain any specific provision that the exemption was not available to the manufacturers and should be passed on to the consumers. The departmental authorities submitted that while determining the normal price of goods under Section 4, only the amount of duty actually paid by the petitioner should be deducted.

may, by notification,--

(a)

extend the period of taking over the management of the Board for such further term, not exceeding twelve months, as it may consider necessary; or

(b)

re-constitute the Board by making fresh appointment to all posts of the Board on such terms and conditions as the Central Government may consider necessary, and in such case, any person who stand removed from their offices under clause (a) of sub-section (2) shall be deemed disqualified for appointment." 3.18 So, it is clear from the above mentioned Section that in normal course of time, the Central Government does not have any control in the management of the Board, and it operates as an autonomous body. The applicant, in this case, referred a particular transaction when the Board of SMPK is managing and exercising the administrative and financial power, so the Central Government had no control over the management in that period and the Central Government only plays a supervisory role. It is also to be mentioned here that the Central Government is liable to place a full report to be laid before the Parliament for taking control of the management of the Board, as prescribed u/s 49 of the Act.

When the board of SMPK takes administrative and financial decisions, raises loans, pays salaries and other financial benefits to its employees and retired employees, decides the rate for assets and services available at the port, creates master plan for infrastructural projects, without any intervention from the Central Government, it should not considered that the Central Government has an ownership, by way of control, in SMPK. Hence, SMPK is controlled by the Board which is an autonomous body.

3.19 SMPK is audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Art 149 of the Constitution of India mentions

"The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States and of any other authority or body as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States as were conferred on or exercisable by the Auditor-General of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution in relation to the accounts of the Dominion of India and of the Provinces respectively." (emphasis added)

As the audit of SMPK is done by the CA&G, it does not prove that Central Government holds the ownership of SMPK.

3.20 It is a settled principle that the exemption notification should be interpreted strictly and the person who prays for exemption from tax is liable to prove that such exemption notification is applicable for him. So, in this case, the burden of proof lies on the appellant who fails to determine the percentage of ownership of the Central Government in SMPK. In this matter, I would like to rely on the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case of Commissioner of Customs (Import) v. Dilip Kumar & Company (Civil Appeal No. 3327 of 2007)/[2018] 95 taxmann.com 327/69 GST 239/361 ELT 577 (SC) where the apex court pronounced:

"To sum up, we answer the reference holding as under

(1) Exemption notification should be interpreted strictly; the burden of proving applicability would be on the assessee to show that his case comes within the parameters of the exemption clause or exemption notification.

(2) When there is ambiguity in exemption notification which is subject to strict interpretation, the benefit of such ambiguity cannot be claimed by the subject/assessee and it must be interpreted in favour of the revenue."

3.21 Therefore, in paucity of supporting evidences, the undersigned prayed before the authority that the exemption should not be allowed as it does not cover all conditions laid down in the notification mentioned above.

The assessee was engaged in the business of execution of construction contracts. It entered into a contract with one 'A' for construction of power project in the Special Economic Zone (SEZ).

It filed an application under section 80 for determination on the question as to whether any tax was payable by it on the sale of goods in the course of execution of works contract to 'A' in the SEZ.

The Determining Authority held that in view of provisions of section 5A, the assessee was not liable to pay tax on the sale of goods in the SEZ to 'A'. But there should be an endorsement of the Customs Authority to prove that the sale was made to the developer or co-developer of SEZ.

The assessee obtained endorsement of the Customs Authority on the purchase bills before the entry of the goods into SEZ for use in execution of the works contract. It raised running bills to 'A' on achievement of milestone as stipulated in the works contract.

In the return filed for the assessment year 2008-09, it claimed exemption under section 5A from payment of tax on the sale of goods to 'A' in the SEZ.

The Assessing Authority denied exemption under section 5A on sale of goods to 'A'.

The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on the ground that the running bills which were issued by the assessee to 'A' did not bear the endorsement of the Customs Authority. For this purpose, he placed reliance upon rule 42(2A).

The Tribunal held that while rule 42(2A) prescribed a procedure to the effect that if the tax invoice was endorsed by the Customs Authority, then the sale will be treated as a zero rated sale under section 5A, it was simply a procedural rule and did not lay down any condition precedent that only on fulfilment of such condition, the sale had to be treated as zero rated sale. It was directory in nature, non compliance of which would not deprive the assessee of the right to claim zero rated sale under section 5A. Section 21(1) of the Gujarat Special Economic Zone Act, 2004 granted exemption from payment of tax on sale or purchase of goods in the SEZ. Hence, tax was not leviable on the sales in question.

Since there is no regular assessment, checks will be by way of audit of accounts of dealers.

Internal audit - There will be audit wing in department and certain percentage of dealers will be taken up for audit every year on scientific basis. The audit wing will be independent of tax collection wing, to remove bias. There will be cross verification with Central Excise and Income Tax also. [para 2.13 of White Paper on State-Level VAT]

Audit by outside Agencies - VAT laws of some States provide for audit by outside agencies.

This is practically outsourcing of work of State tax department. Once the figures are checked by an independent auditor, work of tax authorities is considerably reduced and scrutiny of returns by departmental officers becomes easy.

In some States, audit can be done only by Chartered Accountants. In some eight States (Assam, Kerala, Orissa, Uttaranchal, Maharashtra etc.), audit can be done either by Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountants.

In AP, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Karnataka, audit can be done by CA, cost Auditor or Sales Tax Practitioner (STP).

In Karnataka, audit report is required if turnover exceeds Rs 25 lakhs.

In Delhi, the dealer is required to submit copy of audit report u/s 44AB of Income Tax Act (This report is required when turnover exceeds Rs 40 lakhs per annum) No separate audit is prescribed, unless special audit is ordered by department.

In Sales Tax Practitioners' Association of Maharashtra v. State of Maharashtra (2008) 170 Taxman 371 = 14 STT 348 = 14 VST 69 (Bom HC DB), it has been held that audit can be conducted only by Chartered Accountants and Cost Accountants. Audit cannot be conducted by Sales Tax Practitioners or Advocates - followed in Kar Salahakar Sangh v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2013) 60 VST 126 (MP HC DB), where rule providing certification only by Chartered Accountant was held valid.

The contention that the phrase "goods exempted by notification" occurring in Section 15 of TNVAT Act would not cover transaction under clause (b) of Section 30(1) of TNVAT Act, does not merit acceptance for the following reason. Section 15 of TNVAT seeks to define what is exempted sale in the absence of any definition in Section 2 of TNVAT as Section 2(20) only defines exempted goods. For the purpose of TNVAT, sale of goods specified in the fourth schedule and goods exempted by notification by the Government are exempted sale. Section 30 of TNVAT is in pari materia with Section 17 of TNGST Act dealing power to notify exemption or reduction of tax. Clauses (a) or (b) or (c) under Section 30(1) TNVAT circumscribes the power of government to notify exemption/reduction of tax in specified contingencies and would fall within the ambit of exempted sale as defined under Section 15 of TNVAT. Hence, no exception could be carved out as contended by the petitioner, as it would amount to re-writing the statute.

24. As far as the decision of the Chattisgarh High Court in the case of Steel Authority of India (supra), it arose out of a tax appeal under the provisions of the Central Excise Act, 1944, with regard to benefit provided by Rule 6(6)(i) of the Cenvat Credit Rules 2004 could be availed by the assessee on a date prior to substitution and whether substituted rule is retrospective or not. Under the substituted rules not only clearance to unit, but clearance to a developer was also exempted from operation of Rule 6(1) to 6(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules 2004. In the background of those facts, the Court proceeded to examine the SEZ Act and held that the said Rule was only clarificatory and the substituted Rules were to come into force from when the rules were enforced. The findings/observations made by the Hon'ble Court as regards the effect of the SEZ Act cannot be interpolated into the facts of the present case. Further, Section 2(m) of the CSEZ Act defining export cannot be read in isolation while claiming benefit of ITC under Section 18 of the TNVAT and essentially satisfy the conditions in clauses (i) to (iii) of Section 18(1) of TNVAT Act.

25. Similarly the decision of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh in the case of Parke-Davis Employees Union v. A.P., Industries Infrastructure Corpn. Ltd. 2009 (2) ALT 290, also deals with the SEZ Act and does not pertain to any decision with regard to the VAT Act.

Commissioner [2012] 52 VST 286 (Mad.), the petitioner therein established that the sale to 100% EOU was in the course of export supported by documents such as bill of ladding export invoice etc., and therefore, this Court held that Section 18 of the TNVAT Act, would apply and the dealer was entitled to refund of the input tax. In the cases on hand no such attempt has been made by any of the petitioners to produce any such document rather it is a admitted case that the nature of sale effected by them was neither exported as such or consumed or used in the manufacture of other goods that are exported as specified in Section 18(1) of the TNVAT Act.

[1964] 14 STC 742 (SC), pertain to a notification issued under Section 9 of the AP General Sales Act exempting from tax the sale or purchase of certain goods. The claim for exemption by the appellant was denied and the reasoning given by the department was disapproved by the Hon'ble Supreme Court. Interpreting the exemption notification and pointing out that if the intention can be gathered from the construction of the statute or the rule or by the necessary implication therefrom, the matter is different and in the said case, the position was contrary. The said decision cannot be applied to the facts of this case in the light of the clarity as found in the Section 18 of the TNVAT Act.

There was registration certificate dated 30-6-2000 with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991. The object of the exemption notification was neither to protect the owners of the trade mark nor the consumers from being misled. These were considerations which were relevant in disputes arising under the Trade Marks Act. The object of the exemption Notification No. 1/93-CE was to grant benefits to those industries, which did not have the advantage of a brand name. [Para 16] It is correct to say that the Registrar of Trade Marks can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect. Making the registration certificate applicable from retrospective date is based on principle of deemed equivalence to public user of such mark. This deeming fiction cannot be extended to Excise Law. It is confined to the provisions of the Trade Marks Act. In a given case like the instant one, where there was evidence with the department of the trade mark being owned by company ‘K’ and there was evidence of the appellants trading on the reputation of ‘K’ which was not rebutted by them, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect could not confer the benefit of exemption notification upon them. In the instant case, issuance of registration certificate with retrospective effect from 30-9-1991 would not tantamount to conferment of exemption benefit under the Excise Law, once it was found that the appellants had wrongly used the trade mark of company ‘K’. [Paras 17 & 18]

If the SSI unit wrongly affixes a trade mark of another person, be it registered or not, or if it uses the trade mark of an ineligible person, such default would not be eliminated by the principle of deemed equivalence embodied in section 28; as that principle is based on a deeming fiction, which fiction is confined only to the provisions of that Act. [Para 20]

Consequently, the appeals were to be dismissed.

PER COURT

"The Trade Marks Act has been enacted to amend and consolidate the law relating to trade marks, to provide for registration and better protection of trade marks and for prevention of the use of fraudulent marks. Under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act, registration gives to the registered proprietor of the trade mark the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods in respect of which the trade mark is registered and to obtain relief in respect of infringement of the trade mark in the manner provided by the Trade Marks Act. It is correct to say that the Registrar, Trade Marks, can issue registration certificate under section 28 of the Trade Marks Act with retrospective effect". [Para 17]

The assessee was running a proprietary concern. The assessee purchased shares of a company, UIL which were allotted to him on preferential basis. During the relevant assessment year, the assessee sold said shares and earned LTCG which was claimed as exemption under section 10(38).

■

The Assessing Officer observed that there was abnormal rise in prices of the share value of the said scrip which was not commensurate with the actual performance of the said company. The Assessing Officer also issued notice under section 133(6) to UIL, which was not complied with. He, thus, considered scrip as penny stock. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer denied the claim of exemption under section 10(38) and brought the same to tax as unexplained cash credit in the hands of the assessee. Since the said sum was treated as accommodation entry, corresponding commission expenditure was also added as unexplained cash credit under section 68 by the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made by the Assessing Officer on the ground that the Assessing Officer had merely relied on the report of the Investigation Wing and statement of various brokers and other persons as recorded by the Investigation Wing and had alleged that the share transactions were pre-arranged, sham, bogus and in the nature of accommodation entries.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal :

■

The assessee had claimed exemption under section 10(38) on LTCG arising out of trades carried out by him in the shares of company CCL. The Assessing Officer passed assessment order accepting claim of the assessee.

■

Subsequently, the Principal Commissioner noted that there was a very detailed report of the DGIT (Inv) based on the searches/survey conducted on a large number of hawala operators and entities controlled by them where they admitted to be providing entries through penny stock which also included name of CCL. He further noted that the Assessing Officer had evidence in hand in form of report from the investigation Wing, which alluded that the scrip of CCL was one of 84 scrips which was used by conniving operators and brokers to book unlawful LTCG and claim exemption under section 10(38). He thus invoked revisionary jurisdiction under section 263 on ground that the Assessing Officer had failed to take into account factual matrix and had not conducted any kind of independent verification or enquiries of his own and had merely allowed claim of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of blended packet tea at its two units located at Dharwad and outside Dharwad. Dharwad unit was exempt from payment of sales tax under Notification dated 19-6-1991.

The Assessing Authority inspected the business premises of the assessee and having noticed that the maximum retail price (MRP) mentioned on the tea packets sold from the Dharwad unit and outside Dharwad unit was similar opined that the assessee had added the tax component to the sale price of Dharwad tea though not under the nomenclature of tax or cess. Hence, the assessee had violated clause (e) of Explanation III to the Notification dated 19-6-1991 and was not entitled to the benefit of exemption. He, therefore, rejected the claim of exemption on the turnover of Dharwad tea based on notification dated 19-6-1991.

The First Appellate Authority upheld the view of the Assessing Authority.

The Tribunal held that though the assessee had considered the local tax element in the price fixed, but it could not be stated that it had collected the local taxes as such from the consumers in view of the fact that in the invoice against Karnataka Sales Tax and Central Sales Tax it was specifically left blank in respect of Dharwad tea. Mere mentioning of MRP on the Dharwad tea did not by itself a proof of any collection of tax in terms of sales tax laws. It accordingly allowed the appeal of the assessee.

The High Court affirmed the order passed by the Tribunal. It held that on the Dharwad tea there was a clear mention of exemption of tax in terms of the note at the end of the invoice itself. Therefore, the buyer was told in unmistakable terms that what was being paid as sale price and not as sales tax.

On appeal to Supreme Court:

The appellant - assessee is a manufacturer of toughened safety glass including wind screen, door screen, side screen and back screen. It applied for the grant of "recognition certificate" u/s 4B of the U.P. Trade Tax Act, but the certificate was granted only in relation to automobile safety toughened glass and not to other items. By Notification No.ST-II-7551×-91-76 dated 31st December 1976 issued under U.P. Trade Tax Act, 1948 purchase of raw materials and packing materials in relation to the items specified in the Notification was exempted from sales tax. Item No.2 of the Notification read, "Glass and glasswares, including optical glass in all forms". In the subsequent Notification No. ST-II 4519 /×-7 (19)/87 dated 29th August, 1987 the corresponding entry read as "Glass and glassware, including optical glass in all its forms, but excluding ornamented or cut glass "bangles". Since the assessee was granted recognition certificate only in relation to Automobile safety toughened glass and not to other items, the assessee preferred an appeal to the Asst. Commissioner, who directed to amend the recognition certificate including purchase of raw materials and packing materials in relation to all items manufactured by it. The Tribunal affirmed the decision of the First Appellate Authority. High Court, on the other hand, held that the appellant assessee was not entitled to exemption in relation to those articles. Technical Inspection service :

The work order requires AGPL to carry out jobs such as the following : Washing; Preparing Vehicle for display; PDI w/o. O/C/; PDI with O/C, PT as per Schedule, Waxing as per Schedule; Rewaxing; PDI & PT with O/C; Removing & Redoing PT Refurnishing etc.

On receiving this work order AGPL undertakes the jobs as indicated in the vehicle data sheet. The data sheets give details of defects and rectificatory action under various heads, namely leakages, electricals, mechanicals, body paint, body fitments.

The rectification job of these defects certainly seems to be activities conducted by any vehicle repair shop. If the argument of revenue is accepted, every motor garage will become a 'technical inspection and certification' agency. This would lead to a ridiculous situation. The meaning of technical inspection and certification conveys the purpose of certification along with inspection to meet specified standards.

The kind of certification covered under this definition refers to certification to ensure that characteristics of the goods meet specified standards. The standards may relate to functionality, utility, quality or safety. The definition of technical inspection cannot be read to mean that any checks on functionality, safety etc. would amount to technical inspection and certification. The word "technical inspection and certification" would appropriately refer to certain standards laid down in some statute or some Guidelines.

For example in the Motor Vehicles Act certain standards are required to be met. Other examples of technical inspection are the Food Safety Standards which require articles of food and drinks to meet certain standards of composition of ingredients etc. Similar is the case where pharmaceutical products are required to meet certain specified standards by law.

In the present case the job card or vehicle data sheets clearly indicate that AGPL are merely rectifying/replacing some damaged/defective parts etc. By no stretch of imagination can this activity be termed as technical inspection and certification. Hence, demand was set aside. [Para 7]

Storage and Warehousing :

AGPL has merely rented space out to TML. Although they arranged for security, the expenses on this account are met by TML. There is a clear finding of the Commissioner that handling, management and safekeeping of the vehicles is the responsibility of TML. Even the security is paid for by TML and so are the telephone expenses and diesel expenses.

None of the ingredients which are essential part of 'warehousing and storage service' are fulfilled so as to cover the activity of AGPL under this service. In fact this view is supported by Board Circular referred to above. Hence, demand was dropped. [Para 8]
